conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. After taking a week off work for a minor injury, the client returned to find several emails marked urgent and a meeting rescheduled without their input. I keep telling myself: "They must be frustrated with me for missing time. I probably let the team down and caused extra work for everyone." and I've been feeling guilty, anxious, embarrassed.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense you’d feel guilty and embarrassed after coming back to that. In CBT, we sometimes look at how the same situation can lead to very different feelings depending on the thoughts we attach to it, so I’m curious what you noticed yourself doing after those thoughts showed up?
I... kind of shut down and just started checking my email over and over. I didn’t really know what else to do.

That sounds like a really understandable way to react when your mind is trying to make sense of something stressful. What you’re describing can sometimes be a kind of personalization, which is a very common stress response rather than a flaw, so if someone else looked at the exact same situation, how might they interpret it differently?
…Maybe they’d think the team was just moving things along while I was out. That it wasn’t necessarily about me.

That seems like a really important alternative, and it makes sense that it could take some of the weight off. If you actually believed that interpretation instead, how do you think you would feel — maybe less guilty, less anxious, or something else?
…Probably less guilty. Maybe just a little calmer, I guess.

That shift sounds meaningful — even a little less guilt and a bit more calm could change the moment quite a bit. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?
…I guess I wouldn’t have checked my email so much. Maybe I would’ve just replied to what was actually urgent and left the rest for later.

That’s a really useful observation, and it shows how the same emails and meeting could lead to a very different experience depending on the thought attached to them. What does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?
…It seems like my thoughts change how bad it feels. If I think it’s about me, I get more anxious and act differently.

That’s a really clear insight, and it sounds like you’ve noticed the thought is what turns the situation into something heavier for you. In your own words, what’s the new perspective you’re starting to see about this situation?

I’m starting to see that the emails and meeting changes don’t automatically mean they’re upset with me. It could just be the team handling things while I was out, and I’m the one making it feel more serious by assuming it’s my fault. I think that’s a little relieving, honestly.

It sounds like there’s a little more room now between the changes at work and the story your mind was quickly attaching to them, and that space seems to be bringing some relief. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: If people at work or in my social circle find out I’m separated, they’ll think I’m a failure who couldn’t keep my life together. I keep imagining coworkers judging me in meetings, friends pulling away, and my reputation quietly collapsing because I couldn’t make my marriage work.

That sounds like a heavy mix of shame and anticipation, and it makes sense your mind is scanning for every possible sign of rejection. When worry gets loud, it can start treating what could happen as if it will happen, so what are some concrete, observable clues you’ve noticed that suggest this worst-case outcome is not actually unfolding?

I mean, I guess people haven’t exactly started avoiding me or anything, but that’s also kind of the point—they probably don’t know yet. At work everyone’s still being polite, which doesn’t really prove much, and honestly this feels a little like you’re asking me to find evidence that people aren’t judging me when the bigger issue is that they probably will once they find out.

You’re right to push back; “people are polite” isn’t proof they won’t judge you, and it makes sense that feels flimsy when the feared outcome is still possible. If those clues are real and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you think is the more realistic outcome instead, and what would that likely look like at work and with friends?

I mean, the more realistic outcome is probably that most people don’t say anything and just keep going with their lives, which is kind of nice but also not exactly comforting. Maybe a few people get awkward or curious, but I’m not sure that means they’re secretly judging me so much as just not knowing what to say.

That sounds pretty grounded: most people likely keep moving, and awkwardness doesn’t automatically equal judgment. If you imagine the worst did happen anyway, what would you actually do first, then next, step by step, and how do you think you’d be doing a month or two later?

I don’t know, that feels a bit like rehearsing a disaster movie for no reason, but fine—first I’d probably keep my head down and avoid oversharing, then figure out who actually needs to know and what I’d say. A month or two later, I’d probably still be annoyed and embarrassed, but I doubt I’d be completely destroyed by it, which is maybe not the comforting answer you want.

It sounds like you just mapped out a way through it, even if you don’t like the exercise, and that matters. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what is different about it?

Honestly, it feels a little less huge, but I’m not going to pretend that means the problem is solved. I still think the worry is partly reasonable, but now it’s more like “this could be embarrassing” instead of “my whole life is over,” which is annoying but at least less dramatic.

That’s a meaningful shift, even if it’s not a total fix, and it makes sense you’d still see some realism in the worry. Given what you worked through today, what would be the first question you could ask yourself the next time this starts to spiral, to slow it down before it turns into “my whole life is over”?

I guess the first question would be something like, “What do I actually know right now versus what am I predicting?” Not saying that magically stops the spiral, but it might keep me from treating every awkward possibility like a fact.

That sounds like a pretty useful filter, especially since you’re not pretending it erases the worry, just separates facts from forecasts. When you ask that question in the moment, what kinds of “know” versus “predict” items do you think would show up first for you?

I’d probably know things like: I’m separated, some people at work already treat me normally, and nobody has actually said anything awful to my face. The “predict” stuff is everything else—people assuming I’m unstable, friends backing away, or my career taking a hit because of it. I’m not thrilled to admit it, but just separating those two might keep me from spiraling quite as fast.

That’s a solid distinction, even if you’re not exactly delighted by it, and it sounds like you can already see how the spiral gets built from predictions piled on top of facts. When you look at those predictions one by one, which one seems to have the strongest evidence behind it, and which one seems to be carrying the most fear?

I guess the one with the strongest evidence is that some people might get a little awkward or curious, because that’s kind of normal and I’ve seen that happen with other people. The one carrying the most fear is definitely the career one — the idea that this somehow makes me look unreliable or less put together at work, even though I don’t really have proof of that. I don’t love admitting it, but the fear seems bigger than the evidence there.

That’s a pretty sharp observation, even if it’s uncomfortable to say out loud. When you notice the fear is bigger than the evidence around work, what does that suggest about what your mind is protecting you from, and what would it mean if that fear were treated as a hypothesis rather than a fact?

I guess it’s probably trying to protect me from feeling exposed or looking incompetent, which makes sense even if it’s overdoing it. If I treated the career fear as a hypothesis, I’d have to admit it’s something to test instead of just assuming it’s true, which is a little irritating because it means I can’t keep calling it a certainty. But maybe that would at least stop me from acting like I’ve already been judged.

That irritation makes sense, because letting it be a hypothesis means giving up the certainty that the worry has been using to keep you on alert. If you were to test that career fear, what would you notice that would count more as evidence for it, and what would you need to see to start questioning it?

I’d count it as evidence if people at work started acting noticeably different — fewer direct conversations, being left out of things, or if my performance feedback suddenly changed for no obvious reason. I’d start questioning it if I kept getting the same normal responses I get now, or if someone actually treated me the same after finding out, instead of me just assuming the worst. I’m still not thrilled about the whole idea, but I can see that “test it” is a lot more specific than just worrying in circles.

You’ve made that a lot more concrete, and it makes sense you’re still not thrilled—this is exactly the kind of thing that feels vulnerable to notice in real time. When you look at those work cues, which ones would actually be about people’s behavior versus your mind filling in the gap, and what would help you tell the difference?

I think the behavior cues would be things like someone actually avoiding me, excluding me, or changing how they talk to me in a way I can point to. The mind-filling-in-gap part is when I read a neutral pause or a short email and immediately decide it means they’ve heard something and are quietly judging me. What would help me tell the difference is probably forcing myself to look for repeat patterns instead of one-off moments, because right now I tend to treat a single awkward interaction like proof.

That’s a very clear distinction, and it sounds like you already know your mind tends to turn ambiguity into a verdict pretty fast. When you catch yourself doing that, what would a “repeat pattern” need to look like before you’d be willing to treat it as meaningful rather than just a one-off?

I guess it would need to be the same kind of thing happening with multiple people, more than once, over a real stretch of time — not just one weird email or a quiet meeting. Like if I kept noticing the same exclusion or shift in tone across different situations, then I’d start taking it seriously. Until then, I’m probably just giving too much weight to isolated moments because I’m already on edge. Saying that out loud, it does sound like my brain is trying to build a case before it actually has one.

That’s a pretty honest read of it, and it sounds like you can see the pattern more clearly now without pretending the fear is gone. If you were to put the shift into your own words, how would you describe the new perspective you’ve reached?

I’d say I’m still worried, but I’m less convinced that the worry is telling me the truth. It feels more like my brain is taking a real stressor and turning it into a full story about judgment and career damage without enough evidence. I can see now that there’s a difference between “this is uncomfortable and could be awkward” and “this is going to ruin everything,” and I’ve been blurring those together. That doesn’t make it easy, but it does make it feel a little more manageable.

It sounds like you’re noticing the worry as a stress response that can overreach, rather than as a reliable verdict about what’s ahead, and that distinction is giving you a little more room to breathe. What feels like the most important thing to carry forward from that shift the next time this starts to build?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I'm worried that my change in sleep is making me more irritable, and I might snap at my partner or family and hurt our relationship. Then there's I'm worried that if I keep sleeping badly, I won't have enough energy to keep up with family responsibilities and people will think I don't care. And I also keep thinking about: I'm worried that my sleep changes mean I’m becoming less present with my family, and that they’ll feel ignored or distant from me.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind keeps circling when those worries feel so important. Sometimes it can help to sort worries into ones that are productive, meaning there’s something actionable you can do, and ones that are unproductive, meaning they’re more hypothetical or outside your control; which of those three worries feels like the first one keeping you up?
…Probably the one about being irritable and snapping at my partner or family. That one feels the most immediate.

That sounds really immediate, and it makes sense that it would grab your attention first. When you look at that worry closely, is there a concrete action you could take with it, or does it feel more like a “what if” that’s harder to control?
…It feels more like a “what if.” I can try to step away when I’m tense, but I can’t really control whether I’ll feel irritable.

That makes sense — it sounds real, even if it’s not something you can fully control right now. Would setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to think about it help you park it for tonight, and what is the next worry on your mind?
…Maybe. I could try that. The next worry is probably about not having enough energy for family responsibilities.

That sounds like a heavy one to carry, especially when family responsibilities matter so much to you. When you look at that worry closely, does it feel like something you can take a concrete action on, or does it feel more outside your control?
…It feels partly outside my control. I can try to rest better, but I can’t fully control how much energy I’ll have.

That makes a lot of sense, and it sounds like there’s only so much you can influence there. If it helps, you could note this one for your worry time since it’s partly outside your control, and is there one more worry that’s been showing up?
…Yeah. The last one is about being less present with my family and them feeling ignored.

That sounds painful, especially when being present with your family matters to you. When you look at that worry, does it seem like something you can take a concrete action on, or does it feel more like a fear about what others might think or feel?
…It feels more like a fear about what they might feel. I can try to be more present, but I can’t control whether they’ll interpret me as distant. That part makes me feel a little guilty, honestly.
That guilt makes sense, given how much you care about them. As you look at all three worries now, how would you put into your own words what’s shifted about how you’re seeing them?

I think I’m seeing that all three worries are real to me, but not all of them are things I can directly fix tonight. The main shift is that they feel a little less like emergencies and more like worries I can set aside and come back to later, even though I still feel guilty about them. I guess that makes them feel slightly more manageable.

It sounds like you noticed a meaningful shift from having these worries feel urgent and all-consuming to seeing that some of them can wait without losing their importance, even if the guilt is still there. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. After moving into a smaller apartment following retirement, the client discovered that several boxes had been unpacked and placed in the wrong rooms by a family member, making it hard to find everyday items and reinforcing the feeling that others were deciding things for them. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It takes courage to look at this without just brushing it off, especially when it’s tied to feeling like other people are making choices for you. If you’re willing, we can map one episode together in four steps—trigger, warning signs, response, and outcomes—and before the anger fully hit, what were the early warning signs in your body or behavior, like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?
I guess there was some tension, but I’m not sure this four-step thing is really necessary. It was mostly just that sudden hot feeling and wanting to fix it myself before anyone else “helped” again.

That makes sense, and I can hear why a structured model might feel unnecessary when the main thing was that sudden hot surge and the urge to take control back. Those warning signs are often the best window for change because they show up right before the explosion, when a pause is still possible—on a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?

I don’t know, maybe a 7, though I’m not convinced numbers really tell you much here. I ended up snapping at them and started moving the boxes around myself because I wanted it done right, which probably made me look more annoyed than I meant to.

Thanks for being that honest, especially about the part that didn’t feel great to admit. When you look at it afterward, what happened externally with the other person, and then what happened inside you right away and over the next few hours or days?

Externally, they backed off and kind of got quiet, which I suppose is exactly what I’d expect, and I just kept reorganizing the boxes myself because I didn’t want to argue. Honestly, the whole thing left me irritated and a bit embarrassed afterward, but I’m not sure sitting around analyzing it is going to change the fact that I hate people messing with my space.

It makes sense that you’d be irritated and embarrassed when your space felt crossed, and I hear the skepticism about whether analyzing it helps. Looking at that cycle—someone changed your space, you felt the hot surge and urge to take over, you snapped and reorganized, and then they backed off while you felt irritated and embarrassed—what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment, before the response, that might change the outcome?

I’m not sure there’s some magic trick in that moment, but I suppose I could stop for a minute instead of immediately charging in. Maybe say, “I need a few minutes before I deal with this,” and then actually walk away so I don’t end up snapping and making it worse.

That sounds like a pretty grounded idea, especially coming from someone who’s not buying into “magic tricks” and still found a possible pause. How realistic does that feel in the heat of the moment, and what would need to be in place to make it actually possible for you?

Realistic? Maybe if I catch it early, but once I’m already at that boiling point I’m not sure I’ll remember to do some neat little pause. I’d probably need the other person to actually back off the first time instead of hovering, and maybe for me to have a place to go that isn’t right there in the middle of the mess.

That sounds pretty practical, and it makes sense that “boiling point” is already too late for a clean reset. When you picture the moment just before that point, what would be the earliest sign that tells you you’re still in time to step away, and what would you notice about the difference if the other person actually backed off?

Probably the first sign is that tight, restless feeling in my chest and jaw before I start moving faster and talking sharper. If they backed off right away, I think I’d feel less cornered and maybe not have to prove anything by fixing it all myself. I’m not saying that solves everything, but it would probably keep it from turning into a full argument.

That’s a useful read on it, and I hear you’re not claiming it fixes everything, just that it might stop the argument from escalating. When you notice that chest-and-jaw tightness and the urge to prove yourself, what do you think that urge is protecting for you in that moment?

I suppose it’s protecting the feeling that I still have some say over my own life, which sounds a bit dramatic when I say it out loud. After retiring and moving, there’s already been so much that’s decided for me, so when someone starts shifting my things around, I react like I have to take the wheel back immediately. I’m not thrilled to admit that, but I can see that might be part of it.

That doesn’t sound dramatic to me so much as it sounds connected to a real loss of control, and I appreciate how honestly you’re naming it. When you react to take the wheel back, what do you notice you’re afraid might happen if you don’t act immediately?

I guess I’m afraid it’ll turn into me losing even more say, like once I let it slide, people will just keep deciding things for me. And maybe I’m also afraid I’ll end up feeling useless, which I don’t particularly want to admit. It’s not a very proud feeling, but that’s probably part of why I react so fast.

That doesn’t sound unproud to me so much as honest about what gets touched when your space is changed and your say feels at risk. When that fear of losing say or feeling useless shows up, what does snapping or taking over do for you in the short term, and what does it cost you afterward?

In the short term, it makes me feel like I’ve reclaimed a bit of control, at least long enough to stop that helpless feeling. But afterward it costs me the peace of the room, and usually the other person gets wary or distant, which I don’t exactly enjoy even if I pretend I don’t care. I suppose it also leaves me feeling a bit foolish once I’ve cooled off.

That’s a pretty clear tradeoff: a quick hit of control, then distance and that foolish feeling afterward. When you put those two sides next to each other, what does it suggest to you about what the snapping is really solving, and what it’s actually leaving untouched?

It suggests snapping is only solving the immediate urge to feel in charge again, not the bigger problem underneath it. It gives me a momentary sense of control, but it leaves the real issue untouched, which is that I’m feeling unsettled and maybe more dependent on other people than I want to be. If anything, it may be making that worse by pushing people away and making me feel even less steady afterward. I don’t love admitting that, but I can see that’s probably what’s happening.

That’s a pretty important shift, and I appreciate you sticking with it even though it wasn’t comfortable to say out loud. If you were to put this new understanding into your own words, what would you say has changed for you about what’s really happening when you snap?

I think what’s changed is that I can see I’m not just angry about the boxes themselves. I’m reacting to the feeling that my space and choices are slipping out of my hands, and snapping is my way of grabbing that back fast. The problem is, it only gives me a brief sense of control and then leaves me more unsettled, so it’s not really solving what I think it is.

That’s a really important insight—you’re noticing that the reaction makes sense in the moment, but it also leaves you clearer that the real issue is that sense of losing your footing and wanting it back quickly. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of frustration lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really uncomfortable, and it makes sense you’d want something more concrete than just “deal with it.” If we map it together for a moment, what would you call the feeling as specifically as you can right now, and how strong is it from 0 to 100?
I don’t know, “frustrated” seems as specific as it needs to be. If you want a number, maybe around 60, but honestly I’m not sure these scales do much for me.
That skepticism makes sense, and I appreciate you being direct about it. Since “frustrated” and 60 are enough for now, what was one specific moment or thought that seemed to set it off most clearly?

Probably when I realized the family get-togethers don’t really feel the same anymore. People are all doing their own thing, and it feels like I’m supposed to pretend that doesn’t bother me. I’m not sure there was one big moment—it’s more like a slow build-up, which is why I’m not convinced picking apart a single thought is all that useful.

That slow build-up makes a lot of sense, and it sounds especially frustrating to feel like you’re expected to just act fine. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a flash?

Honestly, I don’t know that there was some neat little automatic thought—it was more like, “Well, this is just what it is now,” and that’s disappointing. Maybe also, “Why does everything have to change?” But I’m not sure dissecting the exact wording is going to fix anything.

That sounds like a pretty honest read of it, and I can see why the wording itself doesn’t feel like the main issue if the bigger thing is that sense of disappointment. When “this is just what it is now” showed up, what did you do right away, and was there anything you started avoiding after that?

I mostly just sat there and got annoyed, honestly—I didn’t do anything very dramatic. If anything, I’ve been avoiding calling attention to it at the get-togethers, because I don’t see the point in making a big deal out of something that’s apparently “just the way it is now.”

That makes sense—you stayed quiet and kept it contained rather than making a scene, which sounds like a way of protecting yourself in the moment. What tends to happen right away when you avoid bringing it up, and what seems to build over time after that?

Right away, nothing much happens except I’m annoyed and the conversation keeps going, which is probably the point. Over time I guess it just makes me feel more left out and irritated, but I’m not sure talking about it would improve anything—it might just make it awkward.

That sounds like a pretty familiar tradeoff: less awkward in the moment, but more left out afterward. If you imagine the awkwardness you’re trying to avoid, what do you think feels most at stake for you in that moment?

I guess what feels at stake is looking needy or like I’m complaining when everybody else seems fine with it. I don’t really want to be the one making the whole thing uncomfortable just because I’m bothered by it. But I can admit there’s also something in there about not wanting to feel pushed aside and then just swallowing it.

That’s a really clear and honest way to put it, and it makes sense that you’d want to avoid both seeming needy and feeling pushed aside. When you notice yourself “swallowing it,” what does that seem to say about what you believe would happen if you did say something?

I suppose it says I’d probably end up sounding petty or over-sensitive, which is not a look I’m interested in. And maybe, if I’m being honest, I think nothing would really change anyway—people would nod, and then it would still be the same. That’s part of why I keep it to myself, even though I can see that doesn’t exactly make me feel better.

That’s a pretty tough spot to be in—trying to avoid sounding petty while also expecting it won’t change anything anyway. When you keep it to yourself, what does that seem to protect you from most: the awkwardness, the disappointment, or something else?

Probably the disappointment more than anything. If I say something and it doesn’t change, then I’ve just confirmed what I already suspect, and that feels worse than staying quiet. I know that’s not exactly a great strategy, but at least it keeps me from having to watch it fall flat in real time.

That makes a lot of sense—you’re not just avoiding a conversation, you’re avoiding the feeling of having your expectation confirmed in a way that lands hard. If staying quiet protects you from that “it fell flat” moment, what does it cost you over time?

I guess over time it costs me feeling more disconnected than I already do. conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. During a meeting, the boss criticized the client's recent work and said it needed major revisions. I keep telling myself: "I always mess up at work, and this means I'm not good enough for this job." and I've been feeling anxious, ashamed, discouraged.

That sounds really painful, especially when it landed in front of other people and left you feeling ashamed and discouraged. In CBT, the situation itself can stay the same, but the meaning we give it can change what we feel and do next; what did you find yourself doing after those thoughts and feelings showed up?
I... kind of shut down and didn’t say much after that. I just kept replaying it in my head and avoided talking to anyone about it.

That makes a lot of sense—when something stings that much, shutting down and replaying it can feel almost automatic. The thought “I always mess up” sounds like it may be stretching this one moment into a bigger conclusion, which is a very common pattern rather than a flaw; if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what’s another way they might interpret it?
…Maybe they’d say it was just feedback on one project. That it doesn’t mean I’m bad at my job.

That sounds like a much more balanced way to look at it, and I can hear how it softens the meaning a bit. If you actually believed it was just feedback on one project and not a verdict on you, how do you think you would feel—maybe less ashamed, less anxious, or something else?
…Probably less ashamed. Maybe still anxious, but not as hopeless.

That’s an important shift—less ashamed and not as hopeless sounds like it would have given you a little more room to breathe, even if the anxiety was still there. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?
…I think I would’ve spoken up a little more. Maybe asked a question instead of just shutting down.

That’s a really useful observation, especially because the meeting itself didn’t change, but your response to it did. What does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?
…It seems like my thoughts change how bad it feels. If I think it means I’m failing, I react a lot worse.

That’s a really clear insight, and it sounds like you’ve been able to see the difference between the event itself and the meaning your mind attached to it. In your own words, what new perspective are you taking from this about the boss’s criticism?

I’m starting to see that the criticism was about the work, not a statement about my whole ability. It still hurts, but it doesn’t automatically mean I’m failing or that I don’t belong there. I think I can use it as feedback instead of proof that I’m not good enough.

It sounds like you were able to separate the sting of the criticism from the bigger story you had been carrying about yourself, and that shift seems to have opened up a little more room for you to see it differently. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of anxiety lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds pretty uncomfortable, and it makes sense you’d want something more concrete than just “anxiety.” If we map it out together, what would you call the main feeling right now as specifically as you can, and how intense is it from 0 to 100?

I mean, “anxiety” is still the easiest word for it, even if that sounds vague. If I had to be more specific, it’s probably more like dread and pressure, maybe a 70 out of 100—but honestly I’m not sure how much naming it changes anything.

That makes sense—“anxiety” is a workable label, and dread and pressure at a 70 sounds like a lot to carry, so I get why you’d wonder whether naming it helps. When you think of one specific moment when it spiked, what was happening right then, or what thought showed up first?

Honestly, I’m not sure there was some dramatic moment—it’s more like it’s been sitting in the background all day. If I had to pick one, it probably spikes when I think about the mortgage and whether I’m just one bad month away from things getting ugly, which is not exactly a fun thought to sit with.

Yeah, that sounds less like a single event and more like a background alarm that flares when the mortgage comes into view, and I can see why that wouldn’t feel fun to sit with. In that exact moment, what went through your mind right then—what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a quick flash?

I don’t know that there was one neat thought—it’s more like a bunch of annoying “what ifs” hitting at once. Probably something like, “If I miss a payment, everything starts sliding,” which I know sounds dramatic, but that’s where my head goes.

That doesn’t sound dramatic to me; it sounds like your mind is trying to forecast a worst-case slide when the mortgage feels threatened. When that thought hit, what did you do right away, and what did you start avoiding afterward?

I mostly just sat there and spiraled for a bit, then I started checking my bank stuff and the mortgage balance again, which probably didn’t help. After that I avoided opening any emails or letters that looked even remotely financial, because I figured if it was bad news I’d rather not know immediately.

That makes a lot of sense: checking and then avoiding are both pretty understandable ways of trying to get a little control or relief when the mortgage stuff feels threatening. What did those choices do for you right away, and what seems to happen with the anxiety over time after you check or avoid?

Right away, checking gives me a tiny bit of relief because at least I feel like I’m doing something, but it’s short-lived and usually just gives me more numbers to worry about. Avoiding helps for the moment too, because I don’t have to deal with it, but then the anxiety kind of lingers and comes back stronger later, so I’m not sure this is some big insight.

That’s fair—you’re noticing the pattern, but it still feels more like a nuisance than a breakthrough. If checking gives brief relief and then more worry, and avoiding gives brief relief and then the anxiety comes back stronger, what does that suggest to you about what your mind is learning from those moves?

I guess it suggests my mind is learning that the mortgage is something I should keep treating like an emergency, even when I’m not actually in one. Which is frustrating, because the checking and avoiding both seem to feed the whole thing instead of settle it. I’m not saying that means I know what to do differently yet, but I can see the loop a little more clearly.

That’s a pretty important observation, and I can hear how frustrating it is to see the loop without yet having a clear exit from it. If your mind is treating the mortgage like an emergency, what do you notice it’s predicting would happen if you didn’t check or avoid, even for a short time?

I guess it predicts that I’d miss something important and then things would snowball before I could do anything about it. Like if I don’t check, I’m being irresponsible, and then I’ll get blindsided by some notice or payment issue. I know that sounds a little extreme, but that’s the kind of thing my head jumps to.

That doesn’t sound extreme so much as like your mind is trying to prevent a costly surprise, which makes sense given the mortgage pressure. When you call not checking “irresponsible,” what standard are you using for responsible here, and how realistic is it that checking every time would actually prevent a snowball?

I guess my standard is basically “a responsible adult stays on top of bills and doesn’t let anything slip,” which sounds reasonable until it turns into me checking every little thing like it’s a crisis. And no, checking every time probably doesn’t actually prevent the snowball—it mostly just makes me feel temporarily less helpless, then more worked up. So I can see there’s probably a difference between staying informed and acting like I have to monitor it constantly.

That’s a really clear distinction, and it sounds like you’ve already shifted from “I have to monitor constantly” to “there may be a difference between staying informed and feeding the alarm.” If you had to put this new perspective into your own words, what’s the main thing you’re seeing now?

I’m seeing that my anxiety isn’t just about the mortgage itself, but about how I keep responding to it like it’s already an emergency. Checking gives me a little control in the moment, but it also trains me to stay on high alert, and avoiding just lets the fear build up in the background. So the main thing I’m noticing is that I may need to stay informed without constantly feeding the panic, even if that feels a little uncomfortable at first.

You’re noticing something important about the difference between being appropriately informed and getting pulled into the emergency mode your mind keeps trying to create, and that kind of clarity can open up some room to respond rather than just react. As you leave today, what feels like the most useful question to carry forward the next time that urge to check or avoid shows up?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. At lunch in the office cafeteria, she noticed a coworker glance at her plate after she chose a smaller meal than usual and then turn back to their own conversation. I keep telling myself: "They noticed I’m eating differently and probably think something is wrong with me. Everyone at work can tell I’ve been messing up my eating, and now they’re judging me." and I've been feeling embarrassed, anxious, self-conscious, irritated.

That sounds really uncomfortable, especially when a small moment at lunch turns into a whole story about being judged. In CBT terms, the cafeteria moment itself is one thing, but the meaning your mind attached to it can shift what you felt and what you did next—what did you notice yourself doing after those thoughts hit?

I mean, I just sat there feeling awkward and tried to eat fast so no one would keep looking at me. I don’t really know if this “meaning my mind attached to it” thing matters that much — they did look, and it felt pretty obvious, so I’m not sure I’m overthinking it.

It makes sense that it felt pretty obvious in the moment, and I get why you’d be skeptical of the “meaning” piece if the look itself seemed real. If someone else saw the exact same glance at your plate, what are a couple of other ways they might explain it besides “they’re judging me”?

I guess they could’ve just been looking around or noticed my food by accident, but honestly that feels a little like stretching. Maybe they were just curious for a second and then moved on, which doesn’t exactly make me feel better.

Yeah, I can see why that doesn’t feel comforting yet, even if it’s a more ordinary explanation. If you actually believed they were just curious for a second and then moved on, what emotion would you notice most strongly—embarrassment, relief, irritation, anxiety, or something else?

Honestly, probably still embarrassment first, maybe with a little irritation because I hate that I’m even thinking about this. I’m not sure it changes much whether they were curious or judging me — it still feels like I got put on the spot, and that’s the part I can’t shake.

That makes sense — even if the story changed a bit, the feeling of being put on the spot can still hit hard, and I hear how frustrating it is to keep circling it. With embarrassment and irritation instead of the original thought that you were being judged, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

I don’t know, maybe I would’ve still eaten fast and tried not to look up, because either way I felt awkward. I’m not convinced the behavior would’ve changed that much just because the label changed from “judging me” to “put on the spot” — it still would’ve made me want to disappear.

That pushback makes sense; if the feeling was intense, it can seem like the thought didn’t matter much at all. And yet the cafeteria scene stayed the same while the meaning you gave it shifted, and then your feelings and behavior followed — what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I guess it tells me thoughts and feelings are connected, but that still feels kind of obvious and not especially useful when the reaction is already happening. I’m not totally convinced this explains much beyond “I felt bad and then acted awkward,” which I already knew. Maybe it means the thought matters more than I want to admit, but I’m still not sold on how much that changes anything.

That skepticism makes sense, especially when it feels like you’re just naming what already happened rather than getting anywhere new. If the thought “they’re judging me” is even partly what ramps up the reaction, what do you notice it pushes you to do in the moment that a more neutral thought might not?

I guess it makes me want to shut down and get out of there faster, like avoid eye contact and just power through the meal. If I were less sure they were judging me, maybe I wouldn’t feel as urgent about escaping or replaying it afterward. I’m not saying that fixes it, but I can see it might be part of why I react so strongly.

That’s a pretty important link you just noticed, even if it doesn’t feel like a fix yet. If the urge to escape and replay it afterward gets stronger when the thought is “they’re judging me,” what does that suggest about what you might actually be reacting to in the cafeteria moment?

Maybe I’m reacting less to the glance itself and more to what I think it means about me—like being seen as “messing up” or being noticeable in a bad way. I don’t love saying that out loud, but it does seem like the reaction gets bigger when I assume there’s some judgment attached. So maybe the real trigger is the fear of what other people are making it mean, not just the fact that they looked.

That feels like a pretty honest step, especially given how much you don’t like where it points. If the bigger trigger is the fear of what it means about you, what does that fear seem to be saying you’d lose or risk in that moment?

I guess it would be saying I’d lose looking normal, or at least looking like I have it together. If people think I’m messing up my eating, then I’m worried they’ll see me as kind of unstable or like there’s something wrong with me. That feels embarrassing to admit, but I think that’s the risk I’m reacting to.

That sounds really tender to say out loud, and it makes sense that embarrassment would show up when the risk feels like being seen as not having it together. When your mind says “they’ll think something is wrong with me,” what does that say you believe other people would need to see in you for you to still feel okay?

I guess it says I need people to see me as normal, competent, and not visibly struggling. If they can’t tell anything is off, then I feel like I’m safe somehow — which sounds a little dramatic, but that’s honestly how it feels. I’m still not thrilled about admitting that, though.

That doesn’t sound dramatic to me; it sounds like you’ve found something pretty central to how the alarm gets triggered. If “safe” depends on looking normal and not visibly struggling, what do you notice happens inside you the moment you think someone might see past that?

I tense up immediately, like my whole body goes on alert. It’s not just embarrassment, it’s this rush of panic that I’m being exposed and don’t have control over how I’m coming across. Then I start scanning for signs that people noticed, which probably makes me feel even worse. I guess that’s the moment it stops being about lunch and starts feeling like a threat.

That makes a lot of sense, and it’s pretty striking how fast the shift goes from lunch to threat once the “exposed” feeling kicks in. When your mind labels it as exposure and loss of control, what do you notice you start treating as the danger—your coworkers’ reactions, or the possibility that they’ll confirm something you already fear about yourself?

Probably the second one, if I’m being honest. The coworkers’ reactions matter, but what really scares me is what it would confirm about me — like that I’ve lost control and other people can see it. I think that’s why it feels so intense; it’s not just “they noticed,” it’s “now it’s obvious something is wrong.” I don’t like admitting that, but it does seem more accurate than just saying I’m worried about their reactions.

That sounds like a really important shift, even if it’s uncomfortable to say out loud. If you were to summarize what’s changed in your view of the cafeteria moment, how would you put it in your own words?

I think I was treating the glance like proof that people were noticing I’m not okay, when it might have just been a glance. What actually set me off wasn’t the lunch itself so much as the feeling that I was being exposed and that it confirmed something is off with me. I can see now that I was reacting to the meaning I gave it, not just what happened. I’m still embarrassed by it, but it feels a little more clear than it did before.

It sounds like you were able to separate the moment itself from the story your mind attached to it, and that brought a little more clarity even though the embarrassment is still there. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: If I keep saying no to after-work drinks and weekend plans, people at work will stop including me and I’ll end up isolated. Then I’ll get distracted, miss something important, and lose my job or get passed over, which would wreck my finances and make me feel completely unsafe.

That sounds really scary, and I can hear how quickly your mind is moving from “could happen” to “will happen.” What are some concrete, observable clues you’ve noticed so far that suggest this worst-case outcome is not actually unfolding?

I mean, I guess no one has actually said I’m being excluded, if that’s what you mean. But that doesn’t really prove much—people don’t exactly announce when they’re starting to leave you out, so I’m not convinced that’s a great test.

That makes sense; silence from people isn’t the same as proof, and it’s reasonable to be skeptical of that as a test. If those clues are real and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you think is the more realistic outcome instead?

Honestly, the more realistic outcome is probably just that things get a little awkward and I get left out of some casual stuff, not that I instantly get fired or anything dramatic. But I also don’t think it’s as harmless as you’re making it sound—if I’m not around, people do notice, and that can still affect how I’m seen.

That sounds pretty grounded: awkwardness and missing some casual stuff is a very different picture from instantly losing your job, and I hear you that being seen as less present still feels meaningful. If you walked me through the worst-case version step by step, what do you imagine you’d actually do first, then after that, and at some point would you expect yourself to be okay again?

I guess first I’d probably notice people stopping asking me to things, then I’d start worrying more at work and overthinking every interaction, and after that I’d probably pull back even more because I’d feel awkward. Maybe I’d be okay again eventually, but that assumes it doesn’t spiral, and I’m not really convinced it would just sort itself out that easily.

You’ve just mapped out a path where the worst case has steps, not an instant collapse, which is important even if it still feels pretty threatening. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what feels different about it?

It feels a little less like an immediate disaster and more like a slow slide, which is maybe useful, but I’m not ready to call that reassuring. I still think the basic problem is real—if I keep opting out, people probably will notice and that can matter.

That’s a fair place to be—you’re not dismissing the risk, just noticing it looks more like a gradual pattern than a catastrophe, which is a real shift. Given what you worked through today, when that worry shows up next time, what’s the first question you could ask yourself to interrupt the spiral?

I mean, I guess the first question would be whether I’m actually seeing evidence that people are pulling away, or if I’m just filling in the blanks. I’m not totally sold on the idea that one question is going to stop the spiral, but it might at least slow me down long enough to check whether I’m jumping ahead.

That sounds like a pretty practical way to slow things down, even if you’re not buying the idea that it magically fixes anything. If you did ask yourself that question in the moment, what signs would count as real evidence versus just your mind filling in the blanks?

Real evidence would be something like people explicitly not inviting me anymore, or me repeatedly hearing about plans after the fact from the same few people. Filling in the blanks would be me assuming they’re annoyed or replacing me just because I wasn’t at one drinks thing or I felt awkward in a conversation. I’m still not thrilled about the whole idea, but I can see there’s a difference between actual patterns and me basically mind-reading.

That’s a pretty sharp distinction, and I hear that you’re still not thrilled but are seeing the gap between evidence and mind-reading a bit more clearly. When you catch yourself filling in the blanks, what would you want to check against first so you can tell whether it’s a pattern or just one awkward moment?

I’d probably check whether it’s happening across multiple situations or just one awkward moment I’m fixating on. Like, are people generally including me, or am I taking one skipped invite and turning it into a whole story? I still think my brain will jump to the worst version pretty fast, but I can see the value in checking for a pattern before I decide it means something big.

That sounds like a pretty useful filter, especially since you’re already noticing how fast your mind turns one skipped invite into a bigger story. When your brain jumps to the worst version, what do you imagine it’s trying to protect you from?

Probably from being caught off guard, I guess. If I assume the worst first, then I’m not as blindsided if people are actually pulling away or if something at work shifts. It’s not a great strategy, but I can see it’s trying to keep me from feeling stupid or unprepared.

That makes a lot of sense—your mind is trying to protect you from surprise and the feeling of being unprepared or foolish. When it jumps to the worst case, what does that strategy cost you in the moment, and what do you notice it gives you back?

It costs me a lot of mental energy, mostly—I get tense, distracted, and I end up replaying everything instead of just being present. But I guess it does give me a weird sense of control, like if I’ve already imagined the worst, it can’t hit me as hard. I’m not saying it’s a good trade, just that I can see why my brain keeps doing it.

That’s a really clear read on the trade-off: a lot of tension and replaying in exchange for a sense of control, even if it’s not a great one. If that control is the payoff, what does your mind seem to be telling you would happen if you didn’t run the worst-case scenario first?

I think it’s telling me that if I don’t run through the worst case ahead of time, I’ll be naive and caught off guard when something bad happens. Like I’ll miss the warning signs, and then I’ll have no time to react or protect myself. That’s probably why it feels so hard to let go of—it’s not really about expecting disaster, it’s about being afraid of being unprepared if things do start shifting.

That makes a lot of sense; it sounds less like you’re dramatizing things and more like you’re trying not to be caught flat-footed. If being “prepared” is the goal, what would being prepared actually look like in a way that’s different from mentally rehearsing the worst case?

I think being prepared would look more like paying attention to what’s actually happening and having a plan if there are real signs of distance, instead of just running disaster scenarios in my head. Like, if I notice a pattern, I could decide how I want to respond rather than assuming I already know the outcome. The more I say it out loud, the more I realize my version of “preparing” is mostly just exhausting myself in advance. I’m not totally comfortable with that, but it does seem different from being genuinely ready.

That’s a really honest shift, and I hear you still feel uneasy about it while also noticing the difference between real preparedness and wearing yourself out in advance. How would you put this new perspective into your own words?

I think I’ve been treating anxiety like it’s the same thing as being prepared, when really it’s more like I’m trying to control uncertainty by exhausting myself with worst-case scenarios. I still think there’s a real possibility that pulling back socially could affect how people see me, but that’s not the same as proving some disaster is already happening. A more useful approach would probably be paying attention to actual patterns and then deciding what to do, instead of assuming the outcome ahead of time. That doesn’t make me feel relaxed, but it does seem more accurate.

It makes sense that you’re not calling it “fine” or suddenly relaxed, and at the same time you’re seeing a clearer difference between being genuinely prepared and getting pulled into certainty-seeking through worst-case thinking. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. During a family dinner, his spouse mentioned making a long-term retirement plan and asked him to review the budget, which made him feel pressured and afraid that he would not be able to provide enough for the family. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It takes a lot of courage to look at this so honestly, especially when there’s shame mixed in with it. We can map it together in four steps—trigger, warning signs, response, and outcomes—and start with the moment before the anger fully hit: what were the early warning signs in your body or behavior, like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

Yeah, I can see it more clearly when I slow it down. Right before I snapped, I felt this tightness in my chest and shoulders, and my jaw was clenched without me even realizing it. My mind started racing ahead to worst-case scenarios, like not being able to retire properly or letting my family down, and I got really quiet and irritable. I also noticed I started cutting people off a little in the conversation, like I was trying to protect myself before anyone could say something else that would make me feel more exposed.

You’re noticing the exact moment where things start to shift, and that’s often the most useful place to work because there’s still a little space before the reaction takes over. On a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?

At its peak, I’d say the anger was probably around an 8 out of 10, maybe even a little higher for a moment. I raised my voice, got sharp in the way I answered, and basically shut the conversation down by saying I didn’t want to talk about retirement right then. I didn’t yell or say anything cruel, but I could feel myself becoming cold and defensive, like I was trying to create distance because I felt overwhelmed and embarrassed. Afterward, I felt guilty and frustrated with myself, because I knew I wasn’t really reacting to the budget itself as much as to the fear underneath it.

Thank you for being so honest and precise about it; that kind of reflection gives us a lot to work with. When you look at the aftermath, what happened externally in the room with your spouse, and then what happened inside you afterward, both right away and over the next hours or days?

Right after it happened, the room got really tense and quiet, and I could tell my spouse was hurt and frustrated, even though she tried to stay calm. I think I made her feel like I was shutting her out, which isn’t what I wanted, but I can see how it came across that way. Inside, I felt embarrassed almost immediately, and then guilty on top of that because I knew I’d turned something practical into an emotional blow-up. Over the next few hours, I kept replaying it in my head and feeling this mix of shame and fear, like maybe my reaction was proof that I’m not handling the pressure as well as I should.

You’re seeing the whole cycle very clearly now: the retirement trigger, the chest and shoulder tension, the racing worst-case thoughts, then the sharp response and the guilt afterward. Looking at those warning signs you described, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment before the response that might change the outcome?

I think one thing I could do is name what’s happening instead of pushing through it silently, like saying, “I’m getting overwhelmed and I need a minute before I can talk about this well.” If I caught the tightness in my chest and jaw earlier, I could also take a short pause, breathe, and maybe step away for a few minutes instead of letting the fear turn into defensiveness. I realize that would feel vulnerable, but it seems better than pretending I’m fine until I snap. It might also help my spouse understand that I’m not rejecting the conversation, I’m just trying not to react from panic.

It sounds like you’ve moved from seeing this as “I just lose my temper” to recognizing a specific chain where fear and overwhelm show up first, and that’s a meaningful shift. What would you say has changed in how you understand your reaction now?

I think what’s changed is that I don’t see this as random anger anymore. It feels more like my temper is the last step in a chain that starts with fear, pressure, and this deep worry that I’m failing my family somehow. That makes me feel a little sad, honestly, because it means there’s something more vulnerable underneath the anger that I haven’t been paying enough attention to. At the same time, it gives me some hope, because if I can catch the fear earlier, maybe I don’t have to end up reacting in the same way.

There’s a lot of insight in noticing that the anger isn’t the whole story, and that underneath it there’s something more tender that has been asking for attention. As you sit with that, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of anxiety lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense you’d feel unsure what to do with it, especially if it’s been building up. Would you be willing to help me map it out together by naming the emotion as specifically as you can right now, and then rating how intense it feels from 0 to 100?

I mean, I guess it’s anxiety, but that feels kind of obvious and a little too neat. If I had to put a number on it, probably like an 80 out of 100 most days, maybe higher when I’m at work and thinking about the pregnancy stuff.

Yeah, that makes sense — “anxiety” can feel a bit too tidy when what you’re actually living with is much messier, and an 80 most days sounds really intense. Can you think of one specific moment at work when it spiked, and what was happening or going through your mind right then?

I guess one specific moment was when I was in a meeting and realized I was basically just trying to look normal while thinking about whether I’m going to be able to keep up with everything once the pregnancy gets more complicated. It’s not like there was some dramatic trigger; it just kind of hits me all at once, which is annoying because it makes it sound more manageable than it feels.

That sounds frustrating — it’s not a neat, dramatic trigger, it’s more like a sudden wave while you’re trying to hold it together in the middle of work. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment, and what was the automatic thought — the thing you told yourself right then, even if it was just a flash?

I mean, I’m not sure it was some clean little thought like therapy wants it to be. It was more like, “I can’t keep doing this if I’m already this overwhelmed,” and then immediately, “great, now I’m going to mess everything up.”

That doesn’t sound neat at all; it sounds like a pretty fast spiral, and I can see why the “automatic thought” language would feel annoying when it’s really that messy in the moment. What did you do right after that hit you, and was there anything you started avoiding afterward?

I mostly just sat there and tried to look like I was paying attention, which I probably was not doing very well. Afterward I avoided asking any questions or bringing up the pregnancy stuff again because I didn’t want to seem like I was falling apart at work, which feels kind of ridiculous to say out loud.

That doesn’t sound ridiculous; it sounds like you were trying to get through the meeting and protect yourself from looking overwhelmed, which is understandable. What happened right away after you held back, and what has that choice seemed to cost you over time?

Right away, mostly I just felt relieved that I didn’t say anything stupid, so I guess it “worked” in the short term. Over time, though, it’s made me more tense because now I’m constantly acting like everything is fine, and that’s getting exhausting, even if I’m not totally convinced talking about it changes much.

That makes a lot of sense — if keeping quiet gave you immediate relief, it’s understandable that part of you would question whether talking helps, even while the constant pretending is clearly draining. When you notice that exhaustion building, what does it seem to be costing you most: your energy, your focus, or something else?

Mostly my energy, I think. I get through the day, but by the time I’m done I feel kind of wrung out, like I’ve spent all my effort just trying not to look panicked. And yeah, my focus too — I’m reading the same thing three times sometimes, which is not great, but I can admit that’s probably part of what’s making this feel so out of control.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense that the effort of looking okay would leave you feeling wrung out and less able to focus. When you’re reading the same thing three times, what do you notice you’re telling yourself about what that means, and how does that affect the anxiety?

Usually I tell myself it means I’m not handling this well enough, like I should be able to keep up and I’m failing at that. Then the anxiety just jumps up more because it turns into proof that I’m already losing control, which is probably not helping, obviously. I can see how that spiral makes it worse, even if I’m still annoyed that it does.

That sounds like a really tight loop: one slip at work turns into “I’m failing,” and then the anxiety starts treating that as evidence. When you say “failing,” what standard are you comparing yourself to in that moment, and where do you think that standard came from?

I guess the standard is this version of me who’s supposed to keep everything together without making it anyone else’s problem. And honestly, that probably came from work and from me just being used to acting like I can handle things on my own, which feels a little embarrassing to admit. I’m starting to notice that the bar might be unrealistically high, even if I’m not exactly ready to be all “and now I’ll be gentle with myself” about it.

That doesn’t sound embarrassing to me; it sounds like you’ve been carrying a rule that’s been useful for a long time, even if it’s starting to feel punishing now. When you imagine that “keep everything together and don’t make it anyone else’s problem” rule, what do you notice it asks you to give up or hide?

It asks me to give up basically any sign that I’m struggling, which is annoying because that’s a lot of the reality right now. I end up hiding how scared I am, and probably how much I need someone to just say, “yeah, this is hard,” without making it a whole thing. I’m not thrilled to admit that, but I can see that the rule is costing me more than I thought.

That’s a really important shift, and I can hear how reluctantly you got there, which makes it feel more real rather than forced. If you put it in your own words, what would you say has changed in how you see that rule and what it’s been doing to you?

I think I’m starting to see that the “handle everything alone” rule isn’t actually keeping me safe; it’s just making me more isolated and more exhausted. I used to think pushing through meant I was coping, but it might just mean I’m getting better at hiding how bad it feels. That’s a little uncomfortable to admit, because I still don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but I can see that pretending I’m fine is part of what’s feeding the anxiety.

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. The client noticed that over the past few weeks they have been skipping breakfast, eating lunch later than usual, and choosing more convenience foods during busy workdays. In the CBT model, the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the thoughts we attach to it, so I’m curious—what did you find yourself actually doing after those thoughts and feelings showed up?

After those thoughts hit, I mostly just got more in my head about it instead of actually changing anything. I’d skip breakfast, then tell myself I had already messed up, so I might as well just grab whatever was easiest when I got hungry. Sometimes I’d get so busy or stressed that I’d ignore hunger until I was really drained, and then I’d end up overeating or choosing something quick and not very satisfying. Afterwards I usually felt even worse, like I was proving to myself that I really don’t have good control right now.

That sounds like a really frustrating loop, and it makes sense that it would leave you feeling worse afterward. I’m noticing a lot of “should” language in how you’re making sense of it, which is a very common pattern rather than a character flaw—if someone else looked at the exact same situation, how else might they interpret what was happening?

I think someone else might see it as me being overloaded, not as me failing. They might say I’ve been under a lot of work pressure, and when that happens my routines get disrupted because I’m trying to keep up, not because I don’t care. It’s hard to say that about myself, though, because my first instinct is still to read it as weakness or lack of discipline. But if I’m being honest, I can also see that I’ve been stressed and running on empty, and that probably affects my choices more than I want to admit.

That alternative interpretation sounds more compassionate and also more realistic given the pressure you’ve been under. If you were to really believe that you were overloaded rather than weak or undisciplined, what feeling would come up most strongly for you?

I think the strongest feeling would be relief, honestly, because it would take some of the shame out of it. I’d probably also feel sad, though, because it would mean admitting I’ve been carrying more than I’ve been acknowledging. There’s also a bit of anxiety in that, because if I’m overloaded, then I have to face that my usual way of pushing through isn’t really working right now. But overall, I think I’d feel more understanding toward myself instead of constantly feeling like I’m failing.

That’s a really important shift—you’re noticing that relief and self-understanding could change the whole emotional tone from shame and self-criticism. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

If I’d felt relief and more understanding instead of shame, I think I would have paused and been less likely to spiral into “I’ve already messed up.” I might have actually eaten something earlier, even if it wasn’t perfect, instead of waiting until I was completely drained. I also think I would have been kinder to myself about being busy and maybe planned a simpler option rather than treating it like a failure. It feels like that mindset would have made it easier to take a small, practical step instead of getting stuck in self-criticism.

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re seeing how the thought changes the feeling, and the feeling changes what you do. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you?

What’s changed is that I’m starting to see this less as a personal failure and more as a stress response. Instead of assuming I’m lazy or undisciplined, I can see that I’ve been overloaded and that my habits are getting disrupted because I’m under pressure. That doesn’t make it ideal, but it does make it feel more understandable and less shameful. I think it also means I have a little more room to respond with small, practical choices instead of immediately judging myself.

That skepticism makes sense, and I’m glad you said it plainly because the role did change, so we’re not pretending that part away. I mean, sure, someone else could say it’s just company reorganization and not some personal verdict. But that feels a bit like spinning it when I’m the one who still has to deal with the uncertainty and the hit to my income and standing.

That doesn’t sound like spinning to me; it sounds like you’re noticing the real uncertainty and the practical hit, which is a fair concern. If you actually believed, even a little, that this was company reorganization rather than a verdict on your value, what feeling do you think would show up first?

Probably relief, I guess — or at least less of that tight, panicky feeling. But I’m not sure I fully buy that, because even if it’s “just” reorganization, it still has real consequences, so I don’t want to talk myself into feeling better than I should.

That’s a fair concern, and I’m not suggesting you should feel fine about real consequences. Still, it’s useful that you can already see a difference between panic and relief; with that lighter feeling in the room, how might what you did in that meeting have been different?

Maybe I would’ve listened more instead of just mentally bracing for the worst, I guess. But I’m not convinced that would’ve changed much in the moment — it’s not like I could’ve negotiated the whole thing away just by thinking differently.

You’re right that thinking differently wouldn’t have rewritten the meeting or the company decision, and that’s an important limitation to name. At the same time, you already noticed that the thought shift could have changed whether you were bracing or listening, so what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I guess it tells me thoughts do affect how I experience things, but that doesn’t exactly feel like a breakthrough — it’s kind of obvious. I’m still wary of making that sound like the main issue, because the actual situation is still a problem and I don’t want to minimize that.

You’re right, it’s not a breakthrough to notice that thoughts affect experience, and it makes sense that you’d be wary of minimizing a real problem. Given that the situation is still a problem, what seems most important to figure out right now: what the change actually means, or how much of the distress is coming from the meaning your mind is attaching to it?

Probably both, but if I’m being honest, I think I need to sort out what the change actually means first. If I don’t know whether this is a temporary business move or the start of something worse, my mind is going to keep filling in the blanks with the worst-case version. I can see there’s also a layer of meaning-making on top of it, though, and that might be part of why it’s hitting so hard.

That makes a lot of sense — if the facts feel unclear, your mind will try to complete the picture, and it’s understandable that it reaches for the worst-case version. Looking at the actual evidence you have so far, what points suggest this is a temporary business move, and what points suggest it might be something bigger?

Well, the temporary side is that they framed it as a readjustment, not a layoff, and they said responsibilities were being reassigned across the team. That said, the bigger-worry side is that they were vague about what my role will look like long term, and vague usually doesn’t feel great in a business setting. So I can see why my brain is jumping ahead, even if I still don’t like how quickly it does that.

It makes sense that vague language would set off the alarm system, especially when there’s a mortgage and a family in the background. When your mind jumps ahead from “vague” to the worst-case version, what is it predicting will happen next?

It’s predicting that this is the first step toward me being pushed aside, then maybe losing income or status, and eventually not being able to provide the way I should. That sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but that’s basically where my head goes. I can see that I’m filling in a lot of gaps with a pretty ugly story.

That’s a really clear read on the story your mind has been building, and it takes some honesty to say it that plainly. Given everything you’ve just noticed about the facts, the gaps, and the meaning your mind adds, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached in your own words?

I think the new perspective is that the role change is real and still worth being concerned about, but it doesn’t automatically mean I’m being judged as less valuable or that everything is falling apart. My mind has been treating uncertainty like evidence of the worst-case outcome, and I can see that I’m filling in a lot of blanks with fear. That doesn’t make the situation good, but it does mean my reaction may be bigger than the facts I actually have right now. I’m still uneasy, but I can at least see that there’s a difference between “this is uncomfortable and unclear” and “this is definitely a sign I’m in trouble.”

It makes sense that this still feels uneasy, and I appreciate how clearly you noticed the difference between what’s genuinely uncertain and what fear was adding on top of it. The next time that gap shows up, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?
