conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. After retirement, I learned that my former workplace had changed my scheduled hours and responsibilities without asking me, and I felt blindsided when I was told I needed to come in earlier and stay later for a project I had not agreed to. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It takes a lot of courage to look at this so honestly, especially when you’re already feeling regret about it. If we map one recent moment together, we can start with the trigger, then the warning signs, the response, and the outcomes; before the anger fully hit, what were the early warning signs in your body or behavior — things like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

I remember my jaw tightening first, and my shoulders went up without me noticing. My chest felt hot, and there was this buzzing feeling in my head like I was getting flooded all at once. I also started talking faster and more sharply, which is usually a sign I’m already past the point of being calm. Looking back, I think I felt cornered and disrespected before I even fully understood what I was reacting to.

That sounds like a very clear early warning pattern, and it also sounds like the moment where there’s still a small window before things spill over. On a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?

When it peaked, I’d say it was about an 8 or maybe even a 9. I raised my voice and started interrupting, which is not how I want to be, but in that moment I felt like I had to defend myself because it seemed so unfair. I remember saying something sharp about how they couldn’t just change things on me and expect me to be fine with it. Afterward I felt embarrassed and drained, like I’d let the situation take me over instead of handling it the way I would have wanted.

Thank you for being so honest about that; it takes real courage to describe both the anger and the regret so clearly. When you look at what happened next, what did you notice externally in the room with the other person, and what happened inside you afterward, both right away and over the hours or days that followed?

In the room, I could see the other person pull back a little, and that made me feel even more exposed, like I had crossed a line I couldn’t take back. Right away I felt a mix of embarrassment and anger at myself, because part of me still felt justified, but another part knew I had escalated things. Over the next few hours I kept replaying it in my head, and by the evening I felt exhausted and sad, almost ashamed that something about retirement and these changes could still get under my skin so deeply. It also left me feeling unsettled, because I realized how much this touched on being ignored and not having any control.

It makes a lot of sense that being pulled back from would intensify the exposure and shame, especially when the whole situation already touched that feeling of being ignored and having no control. Looking at those warning signs you described, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment — before the response — that might change the outcome?

I think the biggest thing I could do differently is notice the body signs earlier and give myself permission to pause before I keep talking. If I felt my jaw clench and my chest heat up, I could say something like, “I need a minute to think,” and step away instead of pushing through the anger. That feels hard for me because part of me worries that pausing means backing down, but I can see now that it would actually be a way of protecting myself and the conversation. I also think reminding myself that I’m reacting to feeling disrespected, not necessarily to every word being said, might help me slow it down before it turns into a blowup.

You’re noticing something important here: the pause isn’t the same as giving up, and the anger seems tied to feeling disrespected and cornered rather than to every detail in the moment. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has shifted for you?

I think what’s shifted is that I can see my anger isn’t just about the schedule change itself — it’s really about what it means to me, like being overlooked, controlled, or not respected. I also realize that if I pause, I’m not surrendering; I’m giving myself a chance to respond with more choice instead of just reacting out of hurt. That’s hard for me because I’ve always equated staying in the moment and pushing back with being strong, but now I can see there’s strength in slowing down too. I feel a little relieved saying that, because it means I’m not just “an angry person” — I’m someone with a very specific trigger that I can learn to handle differently.

It sounds like you’ve found a really meaningful distinction between the schedule change itself and the deeper hurt it touches, and there’s something important in how you’re beginning to see pausing as a form of strength rather than giving up. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. During sexual activity with his partner, he had difficulty maintaining an erection and the encounter did not go as planned. In CBT terms, the situation itself doesn’t usually decide the outcome on its own; the meaning you gave it seems to have driven a lot of the feelings and reaction. Honestly, I mostly just shut down and avoided my partner for the rest of the night, which probably made it worse. But I’m not sure I buy the whole “meaning drove the reaction” thing — it felt pretty straightforward to me: I couldn’t perform, so of course I felt awful.

It makes sense that it felt straightforward to you, and I hear the pushback on the CBT piece. I’m wondering if the “I’m a failure as a man and husband” part is a kind of labeling, which is a really common mind move rather than a character flaw; if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what’s another way they might interpret it?

I get that you’re trying to reframe it, but honestly it still feels like a pretty big deal, not just “labeling.” Someone else might say it was just a bad night or stress, sure, but that’s easier to say when it’s not happening to you.

If you actually took the “just a bad night or stress” interpretation seriously, what emotion do you think would show up most strongly for you?

I guess maybe relief, but I’m not sure I’d feel much of that in the moment because part of me would still be thinking, “Okay, but what if this keeps happening?” It’s hard not to go straight to embarrassment and worry, because one bad night doesn’t exactly erase the fear that there’s something wrong with me.

That makes a lot of sense—relief and embarrassment aren’t the same emotional place, and the fear of “what if this keeps happening” can pull you right back into worry. If relief had been the stronger feeling in that moment instead, how might your behavior have been different?

Maybe I would’ve just stayed present instead of mentally spiraling and pulling away. But I’m not sure that’s a realistic “if” — relief feels like a fantasy when you’re lying there thinking your body just failed you.

It makes sense that “relief” feels far-fetched when the thought hitting you is “my body failed,” and I hear how real that spiral felt. In that moment, the situation stayed the same, but the thought clearly changed the feeling and what you did next—what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I mean, I get the point that thoughts affect feelings, but that still doesn’t mean the thought was wrong or just “causing” everything. To me it mostly says the situation was upsetting enough that my mind went straight to the worst conclusion. I’m not sold that changing the thought alone would actually fix much.

You’re making a pretty reasonable distinction there, and I’m not hearing you say the thought is automatically false so much as that it felt like the most believable conclusion in that moment. If your mind went straight to the worst case, what do you notice that worst-case thought did to your body or behavior right after it showed up?

Yeah, my body basically went into panic mode — I got tense, my chest felt tight, and I just wanted to disappear. So I can see that the thought didn’t just stay in my head; it kind of took over the whole moment.

That sounds like a really intense surge in your body, and it makes sense that shutting down felt like the safest move in that moment. If the thought “I’m a failure” had pulled your body into panic and distance like that, what do you notice it might have been trying to protect you from?

Maybe it was trying to protect me from feeling even more embarrassed, or from having to look at my partner and see disappointment. If I shut down first, at least I don’t have to sit there and feel rejected in real time. I’m still not saying it’s a great strategy, but I can see it might have been trying to keep me from feeling worse.

That’s a really clear observation, and it makes sense that shutting down could feel like a way to dodge the sting of embarrassment and possible rejection. If that strategy is trying to protect you in the short term, what do you notice it ends up costing you afterward?

It costs me pretty much the thing I care about most, which is feeling close to my partner afterward. I end up creating more distance, and then I feel guilty on top of embarrassed, so it kind of snowballs. I can see that it protects me from the immediate moment, but afterward it doesn’t really leave me in a better place.

That’s a pretty important tradeoff to notice, and it sounds frustrating that the short-term protection ends up costing you closeness and piling on guilt. If you look at that snowball effect, what seems to be the first small point where things start to turn away from the closeness you want?

I think it starts the second I notice the erection issue and immediately assume my partner is disappointed. That’s when I go from being in the moment to scanning for signs I’ve messed everything up. After that, I get quiet and pull back, and then the distance kind of builds on its own.

In the moment, I’m mostly using my own fear as evidence — like, “this must mean I’ve let her down” — and then I start reading into little things like silence or a change in her expression. It makes the story a lot harsher than it probably needs to be. About my partner, I start assuming she’s disappointed or less attracted to me, even when I don’t actually know that. I’m starting to see that I didn’t just react to what happened — I reacted to the story I built around it almost immediately. conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. At the start of the school year, the client volunteered to help organize a community tutoring program and received several comments from parents and staff thanking them for stepping in and saying the program would be more successful with their support. I keep telling myself: "They’re just being polite. Anyone could do this, so it doesn’t really mean I’m doing anything valuable." and I've been feeling dismissive, discouraged, and mildly anxious.

That sounds really discouraging, especially when the comments seem positive but your mind quickly discounts them. In CBT, we often look at how the same situation can lead to very different feelings depending on the interpretation we give it, so I’m curious: when those thoughts came up, what did you actually do in response?

I mostly just smiled, thanked them, and then tried to move on, but inside I felt myself pulling back a bit. I found myself second-guessing whether I should keep volunteering so much, because if it’s not really valuable, then maybe I’m just taking up space. Later I replayed the comments over and over, almost like I was trying to prove to myself that they didn’t mean anything. I also noticed I felt less motivated for the next planning step, which was frustrating because part of me genuinely does want to help.

That sounds like a very familiar kind of mental tug-of-war: part of you wants to take in the positive, and another part quickly dismisses it, which can happen when someone is under stress and not because of any flaw in you. If another person looked at the exact same comments from the parents and staff, what else might they conclude about what those remarks meant?

I think another person might conclude that the comments were genuine and that people were noticing something specific about the way I was helping. They might think the parents and staff were relieved to have someone dependable step in, and that my support actually made things easier for them. Saying “anyone could do this” feels like my automatic way of shrinking it, but if I were looking at it more fairly, I’d probably see that not everyone does step forward or follow through. It’s a little uncomfortable to admit, but part of me may be afraid that if I accept the praise, I’ll somehow feel pressured to keep proving myself.

That’s a really thoughtful and honest shift, and it makes sense that part of you would want to protect yourself from the pressure that praise can bring. If you actually believed that interpretation instead, how do you think you would feel—what emotion comes up most strongly?

If I באמת believed that the comments were genuine and that I was actually making a difference, I think I’d feel a mix of relief and warmth first. There would probably also be a little pride, which is uncomfortable for me to admit, because I’m not used to letting myself sit with that. At the same time, I think I’d feel some anxiety too, because then it would seem more real that people are counting on me. So the strongest emotion might be a combination of appreciation and pressure, almost like I’d be relieved to matter but nervous about what that means going forward.

That’s a really clear distinction—you’re noticing that the same comments could lead to relief and warmth, but also pressure, which is very different from feeling dismissed and discouraged. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

If I’d felt more relief and warmth in that moment, I think I would have been more present instead of mentally backing away. I might have been able to smile and actually let the compliments land, rather than immediately trying to disprove them in my head. I also think I would have felt more willing to keep engaging with the planning, because I wouldn’t have been assuming that my involvement was unnecessary or somehow intrusive. Even with the pressure still there, I suspect I would have responded with a bit more confidence and steadiness instead of second-guessing myself so much.

That sounds like a meaningful shift—you’re noticing that the comments may say something real about your impact, even if part of you still feels the pressure that comes with that. In your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve arrived at?

I think my new perspective is that the comments probably weren’t just politeness—they were a genuine sign that people noticed my effort and found it helpful. I can accept that I’m making a difference, even if that brings some anxiety along with the relief and pride. conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. While reviewing monthly bills after retirement, the client noticed the mortgage payment was still tight and got frustrated when the bank website showed the next payment due sooner than expected. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It takes some courage to look at this honestly, especially when you’re already not proud of it. We can map it out together in four parts—what set it off, the early warning signs, how you responded, and what happened after—and before the anger fully hit, what were the first signs in your body or behavior, like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

I guess my shoulders got tight, but I’m not sure this is some big body-signs project. It was more like seeing that payment and thinking, “Great, even retirement can’t slow this down,” and then I was already annoyed.

That makes sense, and I get why the “body signs” idea can sound a bit overdone when what really hit you was the thought about retirement and the payment. The tight shoulders are actually useful because they show up in that window before the explosion, when there’s still a pause possible; on a scale from 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?

Probably a 6 or 7, not some dramatic 10. I just muttered at the screen, slammed the laptop shut, and had to walk away before I said something worse—though I’m not convinced grading my anger really fixes the bill.

Thanks for being that honest about it; the fact that you walked away before saying something worse matters. What happened externally in the room after you shut the laptop, and what was it like inside you right afterward and then over the next few hours or days?

I paced around the kitchen for a bit, then just made coffee and avoided looking at the bills again. Honestly, I felt irritated and embarrassed afterward, and then later it settled into this tired, resigned feeling like, “Well, this is retirement now, I guess.”

You’re laying out the whole chain pretty clearly: the bill and payment timing hit first, your shoulders tightened, then the muttering and shutting the laptop followed, and after that came the irritation, embarrassment, and that resigned tiredness. Looking at those warning signs you described, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment before the response that might change the outcome?

I mean, maybe I could step away for a minute and not stare at the screen like it personally offended me, but I’m not sure that magically changes a mortgage. I guess if I catch the tight shoulders sooner, I could pause before I start muttering and do something boring like make tea or take a walk.

That sounds pretty grounded, and I get the skepticism that stepping away doesn’t change the mortgage itself. How realistic does that feel in the heat of the moment, and what would need to be in place to make it actually possible for you?

Realistic? Maybe if I remember to do it, which is the whole problem, isn’t it. I’m not against stepping away, but if I’m already wound up about the mortgage, I’m not sure I’m going to suddenly become a zen master because I made tea.

That makes sense—you’re not asking for magic, just something that’s actually doable when you’re already wound up. What do you notice about the moment you’re most likely to remember a pause, and what might make that reminder more automatic than trying to be a “zen master”?

Probably right when I see the amount due or the due date on the screen—that’s the moment it starts to go sideways. If I had some stupidly simple cue, like getting up as soon as my shoulders tighten or saying “pause” out loud, maybe I’d catch it before I start stewing. I’m not promising it’ll work every time, but that seems more realistic than expecting myself to suddenly be calm about a mortgage.

That sounds like a pretty practical read on it, and I respect that you’re not dressing it up as some miracle fix. When you picture the shoulders tightening and the “pause” cue, what do you think you’d be giving yourself in that moment that you don’t get when you keep staring at the screen?

I guess I’d be giving myself a little space before I make it worse. Staring at the screen just seems to feed the whole “this is never going to get easier” spiral, whereas a pause might at least stop me from turning annoyance into a full-on mood for the rest of the day. I’m not saying it solves the mortgage, but it might keep me from acting like the mortgage is trying to start a fight.

That sounds like a pretty useful distinction: the pause wouldn’t fix the mortgage, but it might interrupt the spiral before it takes over the whole day. When you say “this is never going to get easier,” what do you notice that thought does to your mood and your behavior in that moment?

It makes me feel boxed in, like I’m already behind and there’s no point trying to sort it calmly. Then I get more irritable and start acting like the whole thing is a burden I have to wrestle with right then, instead of just a bill to deal with. I can see how that thought ramps things up faster than the mortgage itself does.
That’s a pretty important shift, and you put it in your own words well. If you were to sum up what you’ve noticed about that thought and how it affects you, how would you say it now?

I’d say the real problem isn’t just the mortgage payment, it’s the thought that it means retirement is already failing me. Once I tell myself that, I get boxed in and start reacting like I’m trapped instead of just dealing with a bill. That thought seems to turn a manageable frustration into something bigger and more personal. Catching it earlier might actually help me not blow it out of proportion.

You noticed how quickly the meaning you attach to the mortgage can turn a practical pressure into something that feels personal and confining, and it sounds like catching that earlier opens up a bit more room to respond rather than get swept up in it. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

When I’m spun up, just telling myself it’ll be okay doesn’t seem to do much, but having a specific next step gives me something to hold onto. I’m still not thrilled about needing that, but it does sound more accurate than pretending I should just “relax.”

Probably the smallest version is just stopping and writing down the one thing that’s actually in front of me, instead of letting my mind run ahead five steps. If I can do that, then maybe I can pick the next single action rather than trying to solve the whole mess at once. I’m not saying it’s a cure, but it does seem more realistic than just hoping I’ll magically calm down.

That sounds like a practical, grounded way of working with this rather than pretending the worry will vanish, and I can hear you being honest about the limits of it. I think it would probably slow the moment down enough that I’m dealing with an actual task instead of the whole imagined collapse. That doesn’t make the pressure go away, but it might keep me from getting pulled under by it as fast. I can see that if I’ve got something concrete in front of me, I’m less likely to sit there spiraling about everything that could go wrong. It still feels fragile, but maybe not as hopeless as it did at the start.

That feels like a real shift, even if it’s still fragile — it’s moved from “everything collapses” to “I can slow it down by getting concrete.” If you had to put the new perspective into your own words in one or two sentences, what would you say it is?

I’m still worried, but I don’t think it’s accurate to say one mistake means everything falls apart. What seems more true is that I get overwhelmed, and when I do, I need to stop and narrow it down to the next concrete step instead of letting my mind run the whole disaster scenario. That doesn’t make the pressure go away, but it gives me a better chance of handling it without freezing.

That sounds like a really important shift in how you’re making sense of the pressure—less about everything collapsing, and more about noticing when your mind starts racing ahead and then coming back to what’s directly in front of you. conversations.content: If I keep saying the wrong thing during this reconciliation, I’ll permanently damage my relationship and my spouse will never trust me again. I’m afraid one bad conversation could make everything feel broken beyond repair, and then we’ll just drift further apart until there’s no real way back.

That sounds really frightening, and it makes sense that your mind would want to protect you by scanning for danger. When we worry, our mind can treat what could happen as if it will happen, even though those are very different—what concrete, observable clues have you noticed that suggest this worst-case outcome may not actually come true?

A concrete clue is that my spouse is still willing to talk and hasn’t shut me out completely, even when the conversations get uncomfortable. They’ve also said they want to see whether we can rebuild things, which feels important because it suggests this isn’t already decided. When I look at the actual evidence, it seems more like we’re in a fragile place than a hopeless one. I think my fear is making every awkward moment feel like proof that we’re failing, when really it may just mean we’re both hurt and trying to figure it out.

That feels like a very grounded read of the situation, and those clues do sound like real evidence rather than wishful thinking. If those clues are accurate and the worst-case outcome doesn’t happen, what do you imagine is the realistic, most likely outcome instead?

I think the most likely outcome is that reconciliation will be slow, awkward, and uneven, but not impossible. We’ll probably have some conversations that go well and others that leave us feeling misunderstood or tired, and that won’t mean everything is ruined. I can imagine trust rebuilding in small pieces if we stay consistent and keep showing up honestly, even when it’s uncomfortable. It still feels vulnerable, but more like a process with setbacks than a single make-or-break moment.

That sounds like a very balanced and realistic way of seeing it, and I hear how it still feels vulnerable even with that perspective. If you let yourself imagine the worst actually happening, what would you do first, then next, and how do you think you might find your footing over time?

If the worst happened, I think the first thing I’d do is try not to react impulsively or force another conversation before I’d had a chance to calm down. Next, I’d probably reach out for support from someone I trust and try to sort through what actually happened versus what I’m telling myself about it. Over time, I think I’d find my footing by focusing on the parts of my life I can still stabilize—my routines, work, and the relationships that are steady—so it wouldn’t feel like my whole world was collapsing at once. Even imagining that outcome, I notice I’d still want to respond thoughtfully rather than give up immediately, which tells me I’m more resilient than I sometimes assume.

That’s a really important realization, and it sounds like you just showed yourself there would still be a path through even the worst case. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what feels different about it?

It feels less overwhelming now than it did at the start, though it’s still there in the background. When I first described it, the worry felt like an emergency, like one mistake would instantly destroy everything. Now it feels more like a serious concern I need to handle carefully, but not something that automatically means disaster. What feels different is that I can see there are still options, and that makes the fear feel more manageable and less absolute.

That shift sounds meaningful, especially moving from “emergency” to “serious but manageable,” and it makes sense that having options would soften the fear. How would you summarize, in your own words, the new perspective you’ve reached about this situation?

I think my new perspective is that this reconciliation is important and fragile, but it’s not as all-or-nothing as my fear was making it seem. A difficult conversation or an awkward moment doesn’t automatically mean the relationship is broken beyond repair—it may just mean we’re both hurting and still figuring things out. I can see that I have some ability to respond thoughtfully, slow things down, and make repairs rather than assuming the worst. That makes the situation feel more painful than easy, but also more workable and less hopeless.

It sounds like you’re noticing how much room there is between “this is failing” and “this is easy,” and that in that space you can respond with more steadiness and choice than your fear was allowing. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I'm scared of sleeping alone in the dark. So I just staying up late, asking to sleep with a parent, leaving a light on all night, avoiding going to bed alone.

That sounds really hard, and a lot of kids feel scared of sleeping alone in the dark, so you’re definitely not the only one. It makes sense that avoiding it helps for a little while, but it can also keep you from finding out what might actually be okay or even kind of nice at bedtime. When you think about facing that fear, what scary “what if” thoughts pop up—the things you imagine going wrong?

I mean, the scary thing is just that it feels wrong and unsafe, like something bad could happen and I’d be alone. But also, why do I have to think of “what if” thoughts if I already know I don’t like it?

That makes a lot of sense—if it feels wrong and unsafe, of course your brain is going to act like something bad could happen, and I get why you’d wonder why we’d bother with “what if” thoughts at all. A little secret is that “what if” thoughts don’t have to be all bad; we can also look at what could go right. What are some good “what if” thoughts—things that could go well if you faced the fear?
I guess maybe nothing bad happens and I just feel dumb for worrying. But “what if it goes right” sounds kind of fake when it still feels scary, so I don’t know why that would help.

That makes sense, and I’m glad you said it plainly—when something feels scary, “what if it goes right” can sound fake, even if it’s possible, because our brains usually shout the scary version first. If both kinds of “what if” could be true, which good one would you want to try to remember next time the scary feeling shows up?

I don’t know, maybe “nothing bad happens” or “I can handle one night,” but that still feels like wishful thinking. And honestly, if I’m already scared, I’m probably not going to remember some nice thought in the dark.

That’s a fair pushback, and it makes sense that a “nice thought” can feel slippery when you’re already scared in the dark. When you think about the moment the fear starts, what usually happens first in your body or in your mind that makes it hardest to remember anything helpful?

Usually my heart starts pounding and I keep listening for noises, which makes everything feel worse. And honestly, once I start thinking “something’s wrong,” I’m not going to be like, “oh cool, helpful thought time,” because that sounds unrealistic.

Yeah, that sounds really intense, and it makes sense you’d push back on anything that sounds too “nice” when your body is already acting like danger is here. When your heart is pounding and you’re scanning for noises, what do you notice happens to the scary feeling when you keep checking for signs something’s wrong?

It gets worse, obviously. The more I listen for stuff, the more normal noises sound creepy, so it feels like I’m proving I should stay awake. I know you’re probably going to say “stop checking,” but that’s easier to say than do.

That makes a lot of sense, and I’m glad you called out that “easier to say than do,” because your brain is treating checking like proof that danger is real. When you listen for more and more noises, what does that do to your confidence that you can tell the difference between a real problem and a normal house noise?

I guess it makes me trust myself less, because then everything starts sounding like a problem. Like, if I keep checking, I’m kind of training myself to think normal stuff is scary. I don’t love admitting that, but it does seem to make it worse.

That’s a really sharp observation, and I can hear it wasn’t easy to admit. If checking is teaching your brain that normal noises are dangerous, what do you notice that says your brain might be learning the wrong lesson here?

Maybe the fact that I only feel better for like two seconds after checking, and then I need to check again, means it’s not actually fixing anything. And yeah, it does seem like my brain is learning “stay alert or else,” which is probably not super helpful. I still don’t really like that, but I can see why you’re saying it.

That’s a really important catch, and it makes sense that you still don’t like it because noticing a pattern doesn’t magically make it feel easier. If your brain is learning “stay alert or else,” what do you think it would start learning instead if the checking happened a little less?

Maybe it would learn that not every little sound means something bad, I guess. Or that I can actually stay in bed without having to keep proving I’m safe every two seconds. I’m not saying I like that idea, but… maybe my brain would get less jumpy if I didn’t keep feeding it.

That’s a really thoughtful shift, especially since you’re not pretending it suddenly feels good. What would you say your new idea is, in your own words, about what checking does and what might happen if your brain got less of that “proof”?

I think checking makes me feel better for a second, but then it teaches my brain that the dark is still a big danger, so I keep needing to check again. If I checked less, my brain might slowly get used to the noises and stop acting like every little thing is an emergency. I’m not saying I’d be fine right away, but maybe I’d be less jumpy over time. That’s kind of annoying, because it means the checking is part of the problem, not just the solution.

You just noticed something important: the thing that gives you a quick bit of relief can also keep your brain on high alert, which is a pretty frustrating realization. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of frustration lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really uncomfortable, and it makes sense that you’d want some way to make sense of it. If we slow it down together, what would you name the feeling as specifically as you can right now, and how strong is it from 0 to 100?

I think the main feeling is frustration, but there’s also hurt underneath it and maybe some resentment. If I had to put a number on it, it’s probably around an 80 right now. It feels especially strong when I think about my in-laws and how I keep trying to be respectful, but I still end up feeling judged or not fully accepted. I’m realizing part of the frustration is that I don’t know how to say all of that without sounding disrespectful myself.

That sounds really painful, especially when you’re trying so hard to be respectful and still end up feeling judged or unseen. When you think back to the most recent moment that brought that 80-level frustration up, what was the specific situation or thought that triggered it?

The most recent moment was at a family dinner when my mother-in-law made a comment about how I handle things in the house, like she was just being “helpful,” but it landed like criticism. I remember thinking, “No matter what I do, it’s never quite right,” and that hit me harder than I expected. I stayed polite in the moment, but inside I felt myself getting really tense and kind of small. Afterward I kept replaying it and feeling angry that I can’t seem to speak up without worrying I’ll be seen as difficult.

That makes a lot of sense, especially with how quickly it shifted from “helpful” to feeling like criticism and left you tense and small. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, the thing you told yourself right then, even if it was just a flash?

In that moment, the automatic thought was probably, “I’m being judged again, and I just have to take it.” There was also a flash of, “If I say anything, I’ll make it worse and they’ll think I’m rude or defensive.” I remember feeling like I had to stay very careful and agreeable, even though inside I wanted to say, “That hurt.” It left me feeling trapped between protecting myself and keeping the peace.

That sounds like a really tight bind to be in, wanting to protect yourself while also trying to keep the peace. What did you do in response to that feeling right away, and what did you start avoiding afterward?

Right away, I just went quiet and kept smiling, almost like I was trying to hold myself together in a way nobody would notice. I changed the subject and stayed extra polite, but inside I could feel myself shutting down a bit. Afterward, I started avoiding thinking about the dinner too much because it made me angry, and I also started avoiding the idea of bringing it up with my husband or anyone in the family. I think I was avoiding the possibility of conflict, but also avoiding admitting how hurt I actually felt.

That makes a lot of sense — going quiet, staying polite, and then avoiding it afterward sounds like a way of trying to protect yourself in the moment, even though it also kept the hurt tucked away. What were the consequences of that for you right away, and over time, and now that you can see the full chain — trigger, thought, emotion, behavior, consequence — is there any link in that chain where a small shift might interrupt the whole pattern?

Right away, the consequence was that I felt even more alone with it, like I had swallowed everything and was carrying it by myself. Over time, I think it builds into resentment because nothing gets resolved, and then I start feeling anxious before family events, almost like I’m bracing for the next comment. Looking at the whole chain, I think the small shift could be catching the automatic thought earlier—before I go completely quiet—and reminding myself that feeling hurt doesn’t automatically mean I’m being rude. Maybe if I can name what I’m feeling, even just to myself or my husband, it would keep it from turning into this bigger shutdown pattern.

That’s a really clear shift—you’re noticing how the silence protects you in the moment but also leaves you carrying it alone afterward. What would you say, in your own words, is the new perspective you’re starting to reach about this pattern?

I think I’m starting to see that my silence isn’t really solving anything—it’s just helping me get through the moment while making the hurt build up later. A new perspective for me is that being affected by something doesn’t mean I’m overreacting or being disrespectful; it just means something mattered to me. I’m also realizing that I’ve been treating my comfort and my voice like they have to come second all the time, and that’s part of why I end up feeling resentful. Maybe the goal doesn’t have to be confronting everything immediately, but just being more honest with myself and the people I trust about what I’m feeling before it turns into shutdown.

It sounds like you’re noticing that staying quiet has been costing you in a different way, and that your feelings can matter without meaning you’re being too much or disrespectful. As you leave today, what feels like the most important part of that shift to hold onto?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. The client was on vacation and checked work emails several times during the trip. I keep telling myself: "I should be able to fully relax on vacation and not think about work at all. If I’m still checking emails, I’m failing at taking care of myself and I’m not handling my responsibilities well enough." and I've been feeling anxious, guilty, frustrated, tense.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense that those thoughts would leave you feeling anxious and guilty. In CBT, we often look at how the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the meaning we give it, since the situation itself is often more neutral than the interpretation. When those thoughts and feelings showed up on vacation, what did you actually do next?

I started checking my email more, almost like I was trying to prove to myself that I was still on top of things. Then I’d feel worse because I wasn’t really present with the people I was with, so I’d get tense and irritated and kind of shut down. I also kept mentally going over work problems instead of enjoying the trip, like I was stuck in this loop I couldn’t get out of. After that, I’d tell myself I should just be grateful to be on vacation, which honestly made me feel even more guilty for not relaxing “correctly.”

That sounds like a really exhausting loop, and it makes sense that the “should” thoughts would add another layer of pressure on top of the vacation itself. When we hear words like “I should” or “I’m failing,” that often points to a very common pattern in CBT rather than a character flaw. If someone else looked at the exact same situation, what is another way they might interpret it?

I think someone else might see it as I was trying to balance being on vacation with still feeling responsible, not as me failing. They might say checking email a few times means I’m conscientious, but it doesn’t automatically mean I’m bad at resting or that I ruined the trip. They could also see that I was under a lot of pressure internally, so my anxiety was probably making it harder to be present rather than proving something wrong about me. Honestly, I can kind of see that more compassionate view, even though part of me still feels like I should have done better.

That more compassionate view feels thoughtful and grounded, and it makes sense that part of you can see it even while the “should” voice is still loud. If you actually believed that interpretation instead, how do you think you would feel—what emotion comes up most strongly?

I think I’d feel a lot more relief, honestly, like my chest would unclench a little. I’d probably still feel some disappointment that I wasn’t fully able to switch off, but it wouldn’t feel so loaded with shame or failure. The strongest emotion might be compassion toward myself, because I can see I was trying to manage two competing pressures at once. I think I’d also feel calmer and less defensive, like I wouldn’t need to keep proving that I was “doing vacation right.”

That’s a really meaningful shift—you can already notice how much lighter and less defensive it feels when shame loosens its grip. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

I think I would have checked my email once, set a boundary with myself, and then actually put the phone away instead of spiraling back to it every few minutes. I probably would have been more present with the people I was with, and less tense or irritable, because I wouldn’t have been spending so much energy judging myself. I also think I might have let myself enjoy parts of the trip without feeling like I had to earn that relaxation or prove I deserved it. Overall, I think I would have been calmer and more flexible, instead of stuck in that anxious loop.

That sounds like a really clear shift, and it’s important that you can already see the difference between the anxious loop and the more flexible response. In your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about what checking email on vacation meant?

I think the new perspective is that checking email on vacation wasn’t proof that I was failing or incapable of resting—it was more a sign that I was anxious and trying to manage responsibility while also being away. It shows I was under pressure and maybe not fully able to switch off, but that doesn’t make me a bad employee or mean I ruined the trip. I can see that the harsh “I should be able to relax perfectly” thought was what made it feel so painful, not just the email itself. A more balanced view is that I was doing my best in a stressful moment, and I can learn from it without shaming myself.

I really hear the shift in how you’re making sense of that moment now—less as a verdict on who you are, and more as a stressful response to pressure that pulled up a very harsh standard. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

That’s a really clear shift—you’re seeing how the pressure to “do it right” may be shaping the whole experience more than the vacation itself. If you had to put the new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed?

I still don’t love the idea that my own expectations are driving so much of this, but it does seem more accurate than blaming the trip itself. I’d say it’s a possibility, not a certainty. It’s possible there are old patterns in both of us that retirement is bringing out, but I’m not ready to say that’s the main explanation. That feels like a thoughtful, grounded shift—you’re not pretending things are fine, and you’re also not locking onto the most catastrophic explanation. I’m not saying that would solve everything, but it seems possible we’ve been escalating over misunderstandings that happen fast and get out of hand. That’s a hard thing to admit, because it means I’m not just reacting to her—I’m also reacting to my own assumptions.

Usually it’s a feeling in my chest or jaw before I’ve even fully processed what she said. I can tell I’ve already decided it was criticism because I start preparing my defense instead of actually listening. Looking at it that way, I guess the problem isn’t just what she says—it’s how quickly I turn it into an attack in my head.

That’s a hard thing to sit with, because it means I may have been treating her like the opponent when she might have been wanting reassurance.

That’s a really substantial shift, and I can hear how hard-won it is to see both your own defensiveness and her possible loneliness at the same time. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you’re understanding these arguments?

I think I’m starting to see that these arguments aren’t just proof that we’ve stopped caring about each other. A lot of what’s happening is that I’m feeling exposed and defensive, and she may be feeling just as overwhelmed and unheard, so we both come in ready to protect ourselves. That doesn’t make the fights okay, but it does make them seem less like the relationship is doomed and more like we’ve gotten stuck in a pattern that’s feeding on itself. I’m not happy about that realization, but it does feel more accurate than the story I started with.

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of fear lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

Right now I’d say it’s around an 85 out of 100. Even saying it out loud makes it feel more real, but also a little easier to look at.

After that, I avoided being alone with my thoughts, which is hard because that’s usually when I reflect best, but in this case it just felt dangerous. I can see now that I was trying to protect myself from panic, even though it also kept the fear alive.

Right away, the consequence is that I feel a little less flooded, but only for a moment, and then the fear comes back stronger because I haven’t actually dealt with it. If there’s a point where I could interrupt it, I think it might be right when I notice the spiral starting and before I completely shut down or distract myself. Even a small pause to name what’s happening, instead of immediately running from it, might help me feel a little more in control.

That’s a really meaningful shift—you’ve noticed how the short-term relief of avoidance can end up feeding the fear, and you’re also seeing a possible pause point before the spiral takes over. In your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about what’s happening and what might help?

I’m seeing more clearly that the fear isn’t just coming from the legal situation itself, but from the way my mind jumps into worst-case scenarios and then tries to protect me by avoiding them. That avoidance gives me brief relief, but it also makes the fear feel bigger and more real over time. The new perspective is that I may not be able to control everything happening, but I can notice the spiral earlier and pause instead of immediately shutting down. Even naming what I’m feeling might help me stay a little more grounded and less trapped by it.

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. The client received an outstanding personal achievement at work and had to share it with colleagues and family while continuing normal responsibilities. I keep telling myself: "If I feel anxious and unsettled about this achievement, it must mean I am not truly proud of it or that it is not as good as others think." and I've been feeling anxiety, guilt, self-doubt, and disappointment.

In the CBT model, the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m curious: when those thoughts showed up, what did you actually do next?

I think I tried to act normal and keep functioning, but internally I was spiraling. I kept replaying conversations in my head, wondering if I sounded arrogant or if I had somehow exaggerated what happened, and I ended up feeling like I needed to downplay the achievement. I also avoided really celebrating it with other people because doing that made me feel exposed, almost like I was waiting for someone to point out that I didn’t deserve it. At the same time, I became more critical of myself and pushed harder at work, as if I needed to prove the achievement was real.

That sounds exhausting, and it also makes sense that you’d try to protect yourself by downplaying it and working even harder when you felt exposed. I’m hearing a possible “because I feel anxious, this must mean something is wrong with the achievement or with me” kind of conclusion, which is a very common emotional-reasoning pattern rather than a character flaw; if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what is another way they might interpret it?

Someone else might say that the anxiety doesn’t mean the achievement is fake or undeserved, but that it’s actually a sign of how much I care about doing well and how visible this feels. They might see the discomfort as a reaction to being recognized, not proof that I’m arrogant or unworthy. Honestly, I can also imagine someone saying that it makes sense to feel overwhelmed when something big happens and people start expecting you to carry it confidently right away. That perspective feels a little kinder, even though part of me still struggles to believe it.

That kinder perspective seems to give you a little more room to breathe, even if it doesn’t fully land yet, and it makes sense that part of you would still be skeptical. If you actually believed that interpretation instead, how do you think you would feel—what emotion comes up most strongly?

I think the strongest emotion would be relief, honestly, because it would take some of the pressure off having to prove that I deserve the achievement every second. I’d probably also feel a little sadness or grief, because I realize how much of this has been me robbing myself of being able to enjoy something that mattered to me. And underneath that, I think there would be some pride that feels safer and more real, like I could let myself acknowledge that I worked hard and it meant something without immediately questioning it.

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re noticing that relief, sadness, and a safer kind of pride would create a very different inner experience than anxiety and self-doubt. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

If I’d felt more relief and that safer kind of pride, I think I would have been able to let people celebrate with me instead of immediately trying to shrink it down. I probably would have been more present in conversations, less focused on scanning for signs that I sounded arrogant or fake. I also think I wouldn’t have pushed myself so hard afterward just to “prove” it, because I might have trusted that the achievement already stood on its own. It feels almost sad to realize how different that could have been, because I think I would have actually allowed myself to enjoy it a little.

That sadness makes a lot of sense, because it sounds like you’re seeing how much the old meaning kept you from settling into the achievement itself. As you look at it now, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached in your own words?

I think the new perspective is that my anxiety doesn’t mean the achievement was fake or that I’m secretly undeserving—it means the moment felt important and vulnerable. I can see now that I was treating discomfort as evidence against myself, when it may actually just be a normal reaction to being seen and recognized. It also feels more compassionate to say that I was overwhelmed, not ungrateful or arrogant. I’m starting to believe I can let the achievement be real without having to constantly prove it all over again.

What you noticed there feels like a real shift—from reading your discomfort as a verdict on you to recognizing it as part of what it can feel like when something meaningful is finally visible. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from that new way of understanding yourself?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of frustration lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really uncomfortable, and it makes sense that you’d want something more concrete than just “feeling bad.” If we map it out together, what would you call the main emotion most specifically right now, and how intense is it from 0 to 100?
I mean, I guess “frustrated” is still the main thing, but I’m not sure putting a number on it actually helps much. It’s probably around a 70, maybe higher when I’m trying to get anything done.

That makes sense—if the number feels a bit artificial, the 70 still tells us this is hitting pretty hard, especially when you’re trying to get things done. What was one specific moment recently when it spiked like that, and what was happening right then?

Honestly, it was this morning when I was trying to answer emails and keep getting interrupted by family stuff, so I just felt myself getting more and more irritated. I get that you want a specific example, but I’m not totally sure one moment is the whole issue—it feels more like everything is piling on lately.

That sounds really frustrating, and I can see why it feels like more than one moment if it’s been piling up on you. When that interruption happened this morning, what went through your mind right then — what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a quick flash?

Honestly, my first thought was basically, “Seriously? I can’t even get through a few emails without someone needing something.” But I don’t know if that’s some deep automatic thought or just me being annoyed and trying to stay focused.

That sounds like a pretty immediate, understandable reaction rather than something “wrong” with you, and it gives us a useful starting point. When that hit, what did you do right away, and was there anything you started avoiding after that?

I just kept pushing through the emails, but I was definitely getting more curt and distracted. I don’t know if I’d call it “avoiding” anything — I mean, I still did the work, I just started putting off dealing with the family stuff because I was too irritated to handle it calmly.

That makes sense—you weren’t shutting down completely, but the irritation was still changing how you showed up and making the family piece harder to deal with. What were the consequences of that right away, and then later on, and now that you can see the whole chain, is there any link where a small shift might interrupt the pattern?

Right away, the main consequence was I got less productive and probably snapped a little more than I meant to, which just made everything feel worse. Later, I was still annoyed and then guilty about being annoyed, so that didn’t help either — but I’m not really convinced there’s some neat “small shift” that fixes it, because the interruptions are still going to be there.

That’s a fair pushback—if the interruptions stay, a “fix” can sound overly neat or unrealistic. When you say the interruptions are still going to be there, what seems to change most when you’re already irritated: the situation itself, or how you end up responding to it?

Probably how I respond to it, if I’m being honest. The interruptions are real, but when I’m already irritated I get sharper and less patient, and then everything escalates faster than it probably needs to. I still don’t think that means I can magically stay calm, but I can see that my reaction is part of what makes it spiral.

That’s a pretty clear read on the pattern, and it also makes sense that “stay calm” sounds unrealistic when you’re already loaded up. When you notice yourself getting sharper, what do you think that reaction is trying to protect or accomplish for you in that moment?

Probably to protect my focus, I guess — like, if I come across as sharp enough, maybe people will back off and I can actually finish something. And maybe it’s also trying to protect me from feeling like I’m already behind before the day even starts. I’m not saying it’s a great strategy, but that’s what it seems like it’s doing.

That sounds like a pretty practical function for the sharpness, even if it backfires later. If that reaction is trying to protect focus and keep you from feeling behind, what does it seem to assume would happen if you didn’t come across that way?

I guess it assumes people would keep interrupting me and I’d just let it happen, and then I’d never get anything done. Maybe it also assumes I’d look weak or like I’m not on top of things if I’m too accommodating. I’m not totally sure that’s fair, but that’s probably the logic underneath it.

That’s a really thoughtful read on it, and it makes sense that “being too accommodating” could feel risky if it gets linked with losing control or looking less competent. When you look at that assumption closely, what evidence do you have that people would actually see you as weak, and what evidence do you have that they might simply see you as unavailable in that moment?

I mean, I don’t have a ton of hard evidence that people think I’m weak — that’s probably more of a fear than a fact. Most of the time they’d probably just think I’m busy or unavailable, but in the moment it feels like if I don’t push back, I’ll get steamrolled. So I can see there’s a difference there, even if it doesn’t totally change how it feels.

That makes a lot of sense—the feeling of being steamrolled can be strong even when the evidence for “they’ll think I’m weak” isn’t really there. When that fear shows up in the moment, what do you notice it pushing you to do first: protect your time, protect your image, or something else?

I think it pushes me to protect my time first, but the image part is probably mixed in more than I want to admit. In the moment it feels like if I don’t come off firm right away, I’ll lose the whole day to other people’s needs, and that makes me overcorrect. So I end up sounding sharper than I intend, which is really more about trying to keep control than about the actual interruption.

That’s a pretty important shift—you’re seeing that the sharpness isn’t just about the interruption itself, but about trying to protect time and control before the day gets away from you. In your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about what’s happening in those moments?

I think I’m starting to see that the irritation isn’t just me being “bad at handling interruptions,” it’s more that I feel threatened by losing control of my time, so I go into protect mode fast. The sharpness is my way of trying to keep the day from slipping away, but it probably ends up making things harder instead of helping. So the problem isn’t just the interruptions — it’s the way I react to them because I’m already feeling behind and on edge.

It sounds like you just noticed a much deeper layer underneath the irritation: the reaction isn’t a character flaw, but a fast protective response when your sense of control and time starts to feel squeezed. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: If I can’t keep up with these new responsibilities, I might miss something important and that could hurt my performance review or bonus. Then there's I’m worried this role change will mean extra unpaid hours and I won’t have enough time or energy to manage my finances properly. And I also keep thinking about: If I make a mistake in this new role, I could lose my job and end up in a financial mess.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind keeps circling when those worries feel tied to your job and finances. Some worries are productive because there’s something you could actually do about them, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical or outside your control, and we handle them differently—what’s the first worry that’s keeping you up?

I don’t know, they all feel connected, so I’m not sure why it matters which one is “first.” If I had to pick, it’s probably the performance review one—because that’s the one that feels most immediate and not just me spiraling for no reason.

It makes sense that it feels connected, and I get why you’d question the point of sorting them out when they all hit at once. If we stay with the performance review worry for a moment, is there a concrete action you can take about it right now, or does it mostly sit in the realm of “what if” and things you can’t fully control?

Honestly, that feels a bit like a false choice—there’s some concrete stuff I can do, but a lot of it is still out of my hands. I can try to be organized and ask clarifying questions, but I can’t exactly control how my manager judges this transition.

That’s a fair pushback—there is some control here, and some of it is still up to your manager, so it’s not an all-or-nothing situation. What’s one small, concrete step you could take about the performance review worry, and exactly when would you do it?

I guess I could ask my manager for a clearer sense of what “doing well” looks like in this transition, but I’m not sure that’ll actually reduce the stress much. Maybe I’d send that message tomorrow morning, since waiting around and guessing is probably making it worse.

That sounds like a practical step, even if you’re not expecting it to magically fix the stress, and it makes sense that guessing is part of what’s keeping it alive. If we shift to the second worry about extra unpaid hours and your finances, would you say there’s a concrete action you can take there, or is it mostly outside your control?

Probably some concrete action, but not as much as you’re implying. I can track my hours more carefully and maybe set a limit for myself, but I can’t control whether the workload actually stays reasonable or whether my boss expects me to just absorb it.

You’re right that there’s a mix here, and I’m hearing that some of it is actionable while the workload itself still isn’t fully in your hands. If you were to focus on the concrete part for this worry, what would tracking your hours or setting a limit look like in practice, and is there one more worry you want to look at?

I mean, tracking hours sounds nice in theory, but if the workload is already bloated, I’m not sure a spreadsheet changes much except making me more aware of how bad it is. I could start noting my start/stop times this week and see if there’s a point where I’m consistently going over, but I’m not thrilled about turning my life into a timesheet. And yeah, the third worry is the job-loss one, which is probably the most catastrophic-sounding, if that matters.

That makes sense—tracking can feel like just documenting a problem instead of solving it, and I hear the reluctance there. With the job-loss worry, when you look at it closely, does it seem more like something you can act on right now, or more like a catastrophic “what if” your mind is running with?

It’s probably more of a catastrophic “what if,” yeah. I can do the basics—be careful, stay on top of things—but I can’t really control the whole chain of events my brain is jumping to. Saying that out loud does make it sound a little less solid than it feels at 2 a.m., though I’m not exactly relaxed about it.

That makes a lot of sense, and it’s pretty telling that it feels less solid once you say it out loud, even if the anxiety is still there at 2 a.m. Since this one is the catastrophic “what if,” and you’ve already got a way of handling the first two worries, what would be the best container for this third one so it doesn’t keep running the night on its own?

I guess the “container” would be not letting it hijack bedtime—maybe I could write it down earlier in the evening and tell myself I’ll deal with it during a set worry time tomorrow, instead of lying there arguing with my brain. I’m not saying that will magically stop it, but it does seem slightly less pointless than just wrestling with it at 2 a.m. And honestly, having some place to put it might be better than pretending I can think my way out of it in the dark.

That sounds like a pretty grounded shift—you’re not pretending it’ll vanish, just noticing that arguing with it in the dark hasn’t been helping much. If you were to try writing it down earlier in the evening, what would you want that note to do for you at bedtime, and what might get in the way of actually using it?

I’d want the note to basically tell my brain, “This is parked for now, you’re not solving it at midnight.” Ideally it would keep me from spiraling into the same loop and make bedtime feel less like an interrogation. What might get in the way is me deciding the note is stupid, or just ignoring it because I’m convinced I need to keep mentally rehearsing everything “just in case.”

That makes a lot of sense, especially with the part about mentally rehearsing “just in case,” because it sounds like your brain is treating worry like a job. When you notice yourself calling the note stupid or needing to keep rehearsing, what do you think that urge is trying to protect you from?

Probably from feeling unprepared and stupid if something goes wrong. If I keep rehearsing, I can tell myself I’m being responsible instead of caught off guard. I guess it’s also trying to protect me from the feeling that I’m not in control, which is annoying because it doesn’t actually give me much control.

That’s a really clear read on it, and it sounds frustrating to notice that the rehearsing is trying to protect you while also keeping you stuck. When you compare “feeling responsible” with “actually having control,” what do you notice about the difference between the two?

I think “feeling responsible” is more like an emotional signal — it makes me feel like I’m doing something, even if I’m really just spinning. Actual control is narrower and less comforting, but also more real: it’s things like asking for clarity, tracking hours, or writing the worry down instead of letting it run the night. The annoying part is that my brain seems to prefer the feeling of control over the actual kind, because the feeling is easier to cling to. Saying that out loud, I can see why I end up exhausted without really being more prepared.

That’s a really sharp distinction, and it sounds like you’ve noticed the trap without me needing to spell it out. If you had to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has shifted for you?

I think what’s shifted is that I can see I’ve been treating worry like it’s the same thing as being prepared, when really it’s mostly just keeping me activated and tired. The thoughts about performance, money, and losing the job still feel serious, but they don’t all need the same response—some need actual action, and the catastrophic ones need to be contained instead of endlessly rehearsed. I’m also noticing that my brain prefers the *feeling* of control, even when it’s not giving me anything useful. That doesn’t make the anxiety go away, but it does make it feel a little less like some all-powerful truth and more like a pattern I can interrupt.

It sounds like you’ve started to separate the real demands from the mental loop that has been trying to pass itself off as readiness, and that gives you a little more room to choose how you respond. As you leave here, what feels like the most important thing to carry forward from that distinction?

conversations.content: If I tell my coworkers I need to cut back on lunches and after-work plans because my finances changed, they’ll think I’m cheap or failing. I’m worried they’ll laugh at me, stop inviting me, and I’ll end up looking awkward and humiliated in front of the whole office.

Probably they’d just notice I’m skipping some things and maybe ask once, then move on. I guess the more realistic outcome is awkwardness for me, not some full office humiliation—but I still don’t love that, and I’m not convinced it’ll feel as minor in the moment as it sounds.

I guess it’s a little less huge than it sounded at the start, but I’m not ready to call it “better” just because I can survive it. It still feels embarrassing and annoying, and honestly I’m not sure this changes much beyond me admitting the panic story was probably bigger than the actual outcome.

Next time this worry shows up, what’s the first question you could ask yourself to interrupt the spiral based on what you worked through today?

I guess the first question would be, “What actual evidence do I have that this will turn into a disaster, instead of just being awkward?” I’m a little skeptical that asking myself a question will magically stop the spiral, but it might at least slow me down enough to not immediately assume the worst.

That skepticism makes sense, and it’s useful that you’re not expecting a magic fix—just a possible speed bump before the spiral takes over. If that question slows you down even a little, what would you want to notice next about the thought so you can tell whether it’s still a disaster story or just an awkward-but-manageable situation?

I’d want to notice whether I’m jumping straight to mind-reading, like assuming I know they’re judging me without any real sign of it. Also whether I’m treating “someone might notice” as the same thing as “everyone will think badly of me,” because those aren’t really the same. I’m still not thrilled by any of it, but that would at least help me check whether I’m reacting to facts or just the worst-case version in my head.

That’s a really sharp distinction, and it sounds like you’re already catching how the mind can inflate a small social signal into a whole-room verdict. When you notice “mind-reading” starting up, what evidence would count as a real sign of judgment versus just your anxiety filling in the blanks?

A real sign would be something concrete, like someone actually making a comment, teasing me, or noticeably excluding me afterward. Just a look or me feeling awkward wouldn’t really count, even though I’d probably want it to. I’m not saying I won’t still assume the worst sometimes, but I can see the difference a little more clearly now.

That’s a clear distinction, and it sounds like you’re separating actual evidence from the anxious urge to read into everything. If you noticed only a look or your own awkward feeling, what would be a more balanced way to interpret that in the moment?

I guess a more balanced interpretation would be that people are probably just busy, or I’m feeling self-conscious, rather than assuming they’re all judging me. A look doesn’t automatically mean anything bad, even if my brain wants to make it mean something. I’m still not going to pretend I’d feel calm about it, but I can see how jumping to “they think I’m pathetic” is probably doing more work than the actual evidence.

That sounds like a real shift, even if it hasn’t made the feeling disappear, and it makes sense that you’d still not feel calm about it. If you put it in your own words, what’s the new perspective you’ve reached about what a look or an awkward moment actually means?

I think the new perspective is that a look or awkward moment usually means very little on its own, not that people are secretly deciding I’m embarrassing or pathetic. My anxiety has been treating normal ambiguity like proof of judgment, and that’s probably the part I need to question. It still might feel uncomfortable, but discomfort isn’t the same as disaster. I’m starting to see that I can be self-conscious without that meaning anything terrible is actually happening.

It sounds like you’re noticing a real shift from treating uncertainty as evidence against you to seeing it as uncertainty, which gives you a little more room to question the story anxiety tries to write. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from that distinction between discomfort and danger?

I mean, I can stay with it, but I’m not sure “examining it carefully” changes much. It feels pretty obvious to me: if I can’t work, the bills don’t stop, and I’m the one who’s supposed to keep things together. Maybe I’m not saying it’s guaranteed, but it doesn’t seem like a crazy worry either.

I guess I can see I’m jumping ahead a bit, but that doesn’t make the worry feel any less real.

Beyond that, it’s mostly the bills still coming in and me not being able to do what I normally do, so it feels like the problem is already starting—not just some far-off possibility.

Maybe, but “exaggeration” makes it sound like I’m making a mountain out of nothing, and that’s not really fair. The problem is real; I’m just saying my brain is running ahead to the worst-case version of it. I can admit it may be bigger in my head than it is on paper, but I’m not convinced that means it’s exaggerated in a way that actually helps.

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. Received a call from the former workplace confirming the dismissal details and final paperwork, which brought up feeling dismissed and disrespected after retirement plans were already changing. Probably an 8, maybe higher in the moment, though I don’t really know what good the number does. I snapped at the person on the phone and then spent the rest of the day replaying it, which is exactly the part that annoys me—like I should be able to just let it go, but I couldn’t.

Externally, I probably sounded sharper than I meant to and cut the call short, which was not helpful, but I wasn’t about to sit there and be polite about it. Internally, I felt angry and embarrassed right away, then it turned into this stupid loop of replaying what they said and what I should’ve said back, which I suppose is useful somehow if the goal is to keep myself irritated.

Honestly, I’m not sure there *was* some magical “interrupt the chain” moment—I was already annoyed, and once the call started I doubt a deep breath would’ve fixed much. Maybe I could’ve told them I’d call back later instead of answering in that state, but that’s easier to say after the fact than in the moment.

What gets in the way is mostly habit and pride, I suppose—I see the call and I feel like I should deal with it immediately, even when I know I’m already irritated. What would have to be true is that I gave myself permission to let it ring or call back later without treating that like some kind of defeat. I’m not saying I’m eager to do that, but I can see how it might keep me from making things worse.

Probably something like, “This doesn’t have to be handled this second,” and “I’m too irritated to be useful right now.” I don’t love admitting that, but if I told myself pausing was just postponing a bad reaction rather than backing down, that might actually be believable. Still feels a bit contrived, though.

I suppose it would give me a split second to not react on pure irritation, which is probably the whole point. I’m not saying I’d suddenly become calm and wise about it, but I might choose not to answer right then and make myself worse. I think it’s easier if I’ve already decided in advance that I’m allowed to delay, instead of trying to invent permission in the middle of being annoyed. I’m not thrilled about that being true, but it does seem more accurate than pretending I’ll just be unfazed.

I guess I’d say I don’t have to prove anything by answering the phone the second it rings, especially if I’m already irritated. I still don’t like that I got so worked up, but I can see that giving myself permission to wait might actually be the more sensible choice.

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. During a meeting, the boss pointed out several mistakes in the client’s project update and asked for revisions by the end of the day. I keep telling myself: "I’m incompetent and my boss probably thinks I’m a failure." and I've been feeling embarrassed, anxious, discouraged.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense you’d feel embarrassed and anxious after being called out like that. In CBT, the idea is that the same meeting can land very differently depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m curious: when you had the thought “I’m incompetent,” what did you actually do next?

Honestly, I just sat there feeling like I'd been punched in the gut, then I went back to my desk and kept checking the update over and over. I guess I avoided talking to anyone for a while because I didn't want to look more stupid, but I’m not sure what that has to do with anything except that the whole thing was humiliating.

That sounds humiliating, and it makes sense you’d pull back and keep checking when it felt that intense.
