conversations.content: I’m afraid that because I’m getting divorced, people will see me as a failure. At work, friends, and family will quietly judge me and think I couldn’t keep my life together, and that reputation will stick to me. I worry that once people see me that way, they’ll respect me less and I’ll always feel exposed.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense that your mind would jump to the worst-case meaning of the divorce. When you look closely, what concrete, observable clues do you have that suggest this feared outcome is not actually a certainty, but only one possible outcome?

When I look at it more closely, I do have some evidence that it’s not a certainty. A few close friends have already been supportive and haven’t reacted like I’m broken or less capable, and at work no one has treated me differently so far. I also know people in my life who’ve gone through divorces and were still respected, which makes me realize I may be projecting my fear onto everyone else. It’s still hard to trust that, but the fact that I haven’t actually seen people rejecting me is a clue that this is more of a fear than a proven outcome.

It makes sense that it’s still hard to trust, and what you noticed are real clues, not wishful thinking. If those clues are accurate and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you think is the most realistic outcome instead?

I think the most realistic outcome is probably that most people will just take it as what it is: a painful life event, not a verdict on my character. A few people may feel awkward or not know what to say, but that doesn’t mean they’ll lose respect for me. I imagine the people who care about me will mostly be concerned and supportive, and everyone else will probably stay focused on their own lives. Even if it feels exposing, it may end up being more ordinary and less defining than I’m afraid it will be.

That sounds like a very grounded and compassionate reading of the situation, and it shows you’re already seeing this as more ordinary and less defining than the fear suggests. If you imagine, just for a moment, that the worst did happen and some people did judge you, what would you actually do step by step, and as you walk through that, what tells you whether you would eventually be okay?

If some people did judge me, I think I’d first try to remind myself not to react impulsively or explain myself to everyone. I’d probably lean on the few people I trust most, keep showing up at work, and focus on doing the parts of my life I can still control well, instead of trying to manage everyone’s opinion. What tells me I’d eventually be okay is that I’ve handled painful, humiliating-feeling things before and still found my footing, even when it took time. I think I’d still feel hurt, but I wouldn’t be destroyed by it.

You just showed a real path through even the worst case, which sounds important. As you notice that, how does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what feels different about it?

It feels less all-consuming now than when I first described it. The worry is still there, but it feels more like a possibility I can face rather than a certainty that will define me. What’s different is that I can see I’m not completely powerless if other people do judge me — I’d still have ways to steady myself and keep going. I also feel a little more grounded because I’m noticing the fear is about imagined future shame, not something that’s actually happening right now.

That feels like a meaningful shift, and you’ve done the work of seeing the fear more clearly rather than just from inside it. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you about the divorce and what it means?

I think what’s changed is that I’m seeing the divorce less as proof that I’ve failed and more as a painful transition that’s happening in my life. It still hurts, and I’m still embarrassed by parts of it, but it doesn’t automatically mean I’m irresponsible or less worthy of respect. I’m starting to believe that other people’s reactions may be more nuanced than the harsh story I’ve been telling myself. That makes the whole thing feel more survivable, even if it’s still really hard.

There’s a real shift in how you’re holding this now—from a story that defines you to something painful that you’re moving through, while still recognizing the hurt and embarrassment that come with it. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I keep thinking that if my financial situation keeps changing like this, I’m going to lose everything my family depends on, and I won’t be able to protect them. I don’t know how I’m supposed to stay calm when one bad stretch could put us in real trouble.

That’s a heavy thought to say out loud, and it makes sense that it feels hard to stay calm when your mind goes straight to your family’s safety. Let’s slow it down and look at it carefully together, not to brush past the fear, but to see what exactly this thought is claiming and whether it holds up when you examine it closely—can you stay with that with me for a moment?

I guess, but I’m not sure “examining the thought” is going to change the actual numbers in my bank account. It feels a little too tidy when the problem is real, not just in my head. Still, I can tell you what the thought is if that’s where you want to start.

You’re right to push back on that; the bank account is real, and it makes sense that anything that sounds too neat would feel off to you. If we look at the thought itself, is someone else’s opinion overly influencing your own, and what would you notice if you weighed both sides of that carefully?

I’m not sure whose opinion you think is driving this—this is mostly my own math and my own worst-case scenarios. I can weigh both sides, but honestly the “both sides” thing feels a bit abstract when the numbers can change next month and I’m the one who has to deal with it.

You’re saying this isn’t some borrowed worry—it’s your own reading of the numbers, and the part that feels abstract is being asked to step back when next month could look different again. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what's true, and what specific examples from the actual numbers make it feel more or less accurate?

Maybe, but I’m not convinced “exaggeration” is the right frame when the risk is losing ground I can’t easily get back. The actual numbers that make it feel real are that our income has been inconsistent, expenses don’t really pause, and even a small dip can wipe out the cushion faster than I’m comfortable with. On the other hand, I do know I’m jumping straight to catastrophe sometimes, which probably makes it feel even worse than the raw numbers do.

That’s a very grounded distinction: the inconsistency and shrinking cushion are real, and you’re also noticing the jump from risk to catastrophe. Given that, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

I mean, it’s a possibility, but I wouldn’t call it likely in the sense that it’s definitely around the corner. It feels more like a real risk that keeps getting bigger in my head because I can’t control the income swings, which is exactly what makes it hard to dismiss.

That makes sense—you’re not inventing the risk, you’re reacting to something genuinely unstable, and it’s hard to “just calm down” when control is limited. If someone else looking at the same income swings and bills had a different interpretation, what might they focus on that you’re not focusing on right now?

Maybe they’d focus on the fact that we haven’t actually fallen apart yet, which is true, but it also feels like a pretty thin comfort when the margin is so small. They might also point out that I’m looking at the worst month and acting like it’s the whole future, which I know I do, but that doesn’t exactly make the risk disappear.

You’re naming two things at once: the real thinness of the margin, and the way your mind can turn one bad month into the whole future, so it makes sense that “we haven’t fallen apart yet” doesn’t feel like much comfort. Is my thought overly critical?

Maybe “overly critical” isn’t the first phrase I’d use, but yeah, it can get harsh. I do think I’m treating every dip like proof that I’m failing my family, and that’s probably more punishing than accurate. I’m still not relaxed about the numbers, though—I just can see there’s a difference between a real problem and me beating myself up about it.

You’ve done a careful job separating the real financial strain from the harsher story your mind adds on top of it, and that distinction seems important here. If you were to rewrite the original thought so it stays honest about the risk without turning it into proof that you’re failing your family, what would a fairer version sound like?

Maybe something like: “Our finances are unstable right now, and that does create real risk, so I need to take it seriously.” But “serious risk” is different from “I’m definitely going to fail my family,” which is the part that seems too far. I’m still worried, just maybe not as convinced that the worst-case version is the only honest one.

That’s a pretty important shift—you’re keeping the risk real without turning it into a verdict on your character or your family. When you say the worst-case version is “too far,” what seems to be the key difference between a serious risk you can respond to and a conclusion that you’re definitely failing them?

I think the difference is that a serious risk means there are things I can still do about it, even if I don’t like any of them, while “definitely failing them” sounds like the outcome is already decided. The first one feels like a problem to manage; the second feels like a verdict on me, and that’s where I start spiraling. I’m not saying I’m suddenly fine, but I can see those aren’t the same thing.

That’s a clear distinction, and it sounds like you’ve moved from “this means I’m doomed” to “this is a real problem, but not a final verdict on me.” If you were to put the shift into your own words, what has changed in how you’re seeing this situation now?

I guess I’m seeing that I’ve been mixing up “we’re under real financial strain” with “I’m failing my family,” and those aren’t the same thing. The strain is still there, and it still needs attention, but it doesn’t automatically mean the worst outcome is certain. I’m not comfortable yet, but I can see I’ve been treating uncertainty like a verdict. That’s probably the main shift—I’m a little less stuck in panic and a little more in problem-solving, even if it’s reluctant.

It sounds like you’ve been able to separate the reality of the strain from the story your mind was attaching to it, and that gives you a little more room to think clearly even while this is still hard. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I'm worried that my grief is making me less focused at work, and I might start making mistakes on important tasks. Then there's I'm worried that if I miss a deadline or seem less energetic, my manager will think I'm not reliable anymore. And I also keep thinking about: I'm worried that if I can't keep up at the same pace, my career will stall and I won't be able to provide as well for my family.

That sounds really heavy, especially with the grief sitting alongside the pressure to keep everything steady for work and your family. Sometimes it can help to sort worries into ones that are productive—meaning there’s something concrete to do about them—and ones that are unproductive, where they’re more hypothetical or outside your control, because they each need to be handled differently; what is the first worry that is keeping you up?

The first one that keeps me up is the fear that my grief is making me less focused at work and I’ll start making mistakes. It feels the most immediate, because I can already notice my attention drifting and then I start worrying that I’m slipping. Once that thought starts, it’s hard to shut off, because I imagine one mistake leading to another. I think that’s the worry that’s closest to me right now, almost like it’s happening in real time.

That makes a lot of sense—when you can actually feel your attention drifting, it can seem like the whole thing is unfolding in real time. As you look at that worry, is there a concrete action you could take with it, or does it feel more hypothetical and outside your control?

I think there is a concrete part I can act on, even if I can’t control the grief itself. I could probably put more structure around my day, like breaking tasks into smaller pieces, double-checking the important ones, and maybe taking short pauses when I notice my mind wandering. At the same time, some of it does feel outside my control, because I can’t just will myself to be fully sharp all the time right now. So it’s a mix for me: I can manage the conditions a bit, but I can’t fully stop the grief from affecting me.

That sounds like a thoughtful, realistic way of seeing it—there’s something you can influence, and something you can’t fully control right now. What would be one small, concrete next step you could take, and exactly when today or tomorrow would you do it?

One small step I could take is to make a short list of my top three work tasks for tomorrow and break the first one into smaller pieces, so I’m not trying to hold everything in my head at once. I could do that tonight after dinner, maybe for 10 minutes before I try to wind down. I think that would help me feel a little more organized and less like I’m just bracing for mistakes. It doesn’t solve the grief, but it feels like a practical way to give myself a better chance of staying focused.

That sounds like a very grounded step, and it makes sense that having something concrete could ease some of that “bracing” feeling. Looking at the second worry about your manager’s view of you, does that feel like something you can take action on directly, or does it feel more outside your control?

I think it’s partly something I can act on, but it also feels a lot more outside my control than the first one. I can be proactive about communicating, staying on top of priorities, and maybe giving a little context if I need flexibility, but I can’t control how my manager interprets me on a given day. What makes it harder is that I tend to read into small things, like if I’m quieter than usual or not as quick in a meeting, I start assuming they’re judging me. So I’d say there are some concrete steps I can take, but a big part of the anxiety is about uncertainty and mind-reading, which I can’t really solve directly.

That’s a really clear shift—you’re noticing both the part you can influence and the part that gets amplified by uncertainty and mind-reading. In your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about this worry?

I think my new perspective is that I do have some control over how I show up, even if I can’t control every feeling or every reaction from my manager. I can communicate clearly, stay organized, and ask for what I need if it becomes necessary, instead of just silently assuming the worst. At the same time, I’m realizing that a lot of my anxiety comes from filling in blanks with negative assumptions, especially when I’m already feeling vulnerable from the grief. So instead of treating every small shift as proof that I’m failing, I want to be more careful about separating what I actually know from what I’m imagining.

It sounds like you’re leaving today with a steadier sense of what is actually within your reach, and a little more room to notice when grief and anxiety are turning unknowns into conclusions. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I keep imagining that getting dismissed from work will permanently damage my relationship with my wife. I picture her losing respect for me, seeing me as unreliable, and never really trusting me again, even if I find another job.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense your mind would jump to the worst-case when work feels tied to family stability. When you notice your mind treating “could happen” like “will happen,” what concrete, observable clues do you have that this outcome with your wife is not actually the most likely one?

Honestly, I don’t know if that’s the right question, because right now it feels pretty likely to me. But if I’m being fair, my wife hasn’t actually acted like she’s lost respect for me—she’s been supportive and practical, not judging me.

It makes sense that the feeling still says “likely,” and I’m hearing you’re also noticing real evidence from her behavior, not just wishful thinking. If those clues are accurate and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you think is the most realistic outcome with your wife instead?

I mean, maybe the realistic outcome is that she’s supportive at first and we get through it, but I still think there’d be some damage underneath that doesn’t just disappear. Even if she doesn’t say it out loud, I’d worry she’d be less confident in me for a while.

That’s a pretty fair distinction: supportive on the surface, with a worry about something underneath that might linger. If that worst case did happen and she seemed less confident for a while, what would you actually do step by step, and how do you imagine you’d know whether you were eventually okay?

I’m not sure mapping out a whole “step by step” plan really changes much, but fine—I'd probably try to stay calm, keep looking for work, and not make it into some dramatic marriage crisis. I’d know I was okay if we were still functioning as a team, she wasn’t pulling away, and we could talk about it without it turning into me feeling like a complete failure.

You’re noticing that even in the worst-case picture, there’s still a way through it, and that matters. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what is different about it?

It’s a little less absolute than it was, I guess, but I wouldn’t say it’s suddenly gone or anything. Mostly it feels more like a threat I can describe more clearly now, which is annoying, because that’s not the same as it feeling less real.

That makes sense—having a clearer picture of the threat doesn’t make it disappear, and it’s frustrating when “more specific” doesn’t feel the same as “less real.” Given what you worked through today, when this worry shows up again, what’s the first question you could ask yourself to interrupt the spiral?

I guess the first question would be, “What actual evidence do I have right now that my wife is losing respect for me?” But I’m not totally convinced that asking myself questions will stop my brain from running anyway.

That skepticism makes sense—your mind has probably had a lot of practice running the same loop, so it’s reasonable not to trust a question to magically shut it down. When you ask, “What actual evidence do I have right now?”, what would count as evidence either way, and what does it suggest about how much of this is happening in the present versus in your head?

I guess evidence either way would be what she actually says and does, not just what I’m guessing from her tone or my own anxiety. So if she’s still talking with me normally, making plans, and not avoiding me, that points one way; if she starts acting distant or contemptuous, that would be different. Right now, a lot of this seems to be more in my head than in the present, even though it still feels very real.

That’s a pretty important distinction, and I’m glad you’re separating actual behavior from the story anxiety builds around it. If this is mostly in your head right now, what do you make of the fact that it can still feel so convincing?

I mean, I guess that’s what anxiety does—it makes something feel true just because it feels intense. That doesn’t mean I’m completely making it up, but it does mean my brain is probably treating a fear like it’s a fact. I don’t love admitting that, but it does seem to fit what’s happening.

That’s an honest and pretty sharp observation, even if it’s an uncomfortable one to sit with. If your brain is treating fear like fact in this situation, what seems to be the actual cost of believing it so strongly right now?

I guess the cost is that I’m already acting like the relationship is damaged before anything has actually happened, so I’m tense and guarded around her for no good reason. It probably makes me more withdrawn and less useful, which is kind of the opposite of what I want. I don’t fully like saying that, but yeah, believing it this strongly is probably making me harder to be around.

That’s a pretty significant insight, even if it’s uncomfortable to say out loud. If being guarded is costing you the connection you want, what seems to happen in the moments right before you pull back from her?

Usually it starts with me noticing some small thing and reading too much into it, like a tone or a pause, and then I start assuming she’s thinking the worst. After that I get self-conscious, like I need to protect myself before she can judge me, so I go quiet or get a little distant. I don’t like that it happens that fast, but that’s probably the pattern.

That makes a lot of sense, and it also sounds like the jump from a small cue to a full story happens very fast for you. When you notice that first tone or pause, what are you telling yourself it means about you in that split second?

In that moment I’m usually telling myself it means I’m already letting her down somehow, like I’m failing at being the reliable one. It’s not even a fully formed thought most of the time—more like, “There it is, she’s disappointed,” and then I start acting as if that’s confirmed. When I’m honest, the reaction is probably more about my own fear of being seen as weak or useless than about anything she’s actually said.

That’s a really clear link: a small cue, then “I’m disappointing her,” then the fear of being seen as weak or useless takes over. If that fear is driving the reaction more than her actual behavior, what does that suggest about what you’re really reacting to in those moments?

I guess it suggests I’m reacting to my own shame more than to her. The dismissal is hitting some older fear that if I’m not providing or steady, I’m not much use, and then I assume she must see me that way too. So the real trigger may not be her tone at all—it’s what I think it says about me. That’s a hard thing to admit, but it does seem closer to the truth.

That’s a hard insight to land on, and it sounds like you’re seeing the difference between her actual reactions and the meaning your shame attaches to them. If you had to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has shifted for you today?

I think what’s shifted is that I’m seeing this less as “my wife is definitely losing respect for me” and more as “I’m scared of what dismissal says about me, and I’m projecting that onto her.” I still worry about the marriage stuff, but I can admit now that a lot of the certainty was coming from shame and anxiety rather than actual evidence. That doesn’t make it feel good, but it does make it seem more workable than before. I guess I’m realizing the problem isn’t just what happened at work—it’s the story I started telling myself about what it meant.

It sounds like you were able to separate the event from the story your mind built around it, and notice how much of the certainty was being fueled by shame and anxiety rather than solid evidence. As you leave today, what feels like the most useful question to carry with you the next time that old story starts to take over?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. After retiring, the client spends the morning alone at home and sees a photo of their spouse on the table. I keep telling myself: "I should be handling this better by now. I should be stronger, and I should be able to get through the day without falling apart." and I've been feeling sad, guilty, ashamed, overwhelmed.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense that the photo would bring a lot up for you. In CBT, the same moment can lead to very different feelings depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m wondering what you noticed yourself doing next after those thoughts and feelings showed up?
I just sat there for a while. Then I put the photo away and tried to keep busy, but I didn’t really feel better.

That sounds like you were trying hard to get through a very heavy moment, and it makes sense that keeping busy didn’t really touch it. I’m noticing the “I should” part in what you said, and that can be such a common way the mind talks when we’re hurting—if someone else looked at that same moment with the photo, what else might they say it meant?
…Maybe they’d say I’m grieving. That it’s just hard right now.

That sounds like a kinder and more accurate way to understand what’s happening, especially after such a loss. If you באמת believed, “I’m grieving, and this is just hard right now,” what feeling do you think would come up most strongly—sadness, relief, guilt, or something else?
…Mostly sadness. Maybe a little relief, too.

That makes a lot of sense—sadness, with a little relief, feels very different from shame and overwhelm. If that had been the feeling in that moment instead, how might what you did next have been different?
…I’m not sure. Maybe I would’ve just sat with it a little longer instead of trying to push it away.

That’s a really important observation, and it makes sense that you’d notice the urge to push it away. If the photo and the morning stayed the same, but the thought changed from “I should be stronger” to “I’m grieving,” what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I don’t know that I “avoided” anything dramatic — I mostly just sat there staring at my inbox and procrastinated opening the first email because it felt pointless. Then I ended up doing a bunch of low-stakes stuff like organizing tabs and pretending that counted as starting, which I guess is my way of dodging the actual work.

That sounds like a pretty recognizable pattern: the inbox hits, the “pointless” feeling shows up, and then the energy goes into safer tasks like tabs instead of the thing that feels loaded. What were the consequences of that right away, and then later in the day or over time?

Right away, the consequence was mostly just more guilt and more time lost, which is not exactly a groundbreaking insight. Later it snowballs into me feeling even more behind, then I’m irritated with myself for being “unproductive,” so the whole thing kind of feeds itself. It’s annoying because yes, I can see the pattern, but seeing it doesn’t magically make me stop doing it.

You’re right, noticing a pattern isn’t the same as changing it, and it makes sense that would feel irritating. When you say it “feeds itself,” what do you notice is the first link in that chain — the guilt, the self-criticism, or something else?

I think it starts with the self-criticism, honestly. The guilt shows up pretty fast too, but it’s usually after I’ve already told myself I’m being lazy or wasting time, so the criticism seems to kick the whole thing off. I hate that because part of me knows that kind of talk just makes me freeze more, but I still do it anyway.

That’s a really clear link, and it makes sense you’d hate it when the part of you that “knows better” still gets pulled into it. When that self-critical voice shows up and says “lazy” or “wasting time,” what does it seem to be trying to get you to do, or protect you from?

I guess it’s trying to scare me into doing something instead of drifting, like if I’m hard enough on myself I’ll finally get moving. But it mostly just seems to protect me from the more uncomfortable feeling that I’m not actually in control of how behind I feel. I don’t love admitting that, but maybe it’s less about laziness and more about trying to force myself out of panic.

That’s a pretty sharp observation, and I can hear how uncomfortable it is to say it out loud. If the self-criticism is trying to shove you out of panic, what does it seem to believe would happen if it didn’t use that pressure?

I think it believes I’d just completely drift and do nothing, like I’d sit there avoiding everything until the day was ruined. It probably thinks the pressure is the only thing keeping me from becoming totally useless, which is dramatic, but that’s the vibe. I don’t fully buy that anymore, though — it does seem like the pressure helps me start, but it also makes starting feel awful.

That sounds like a real shift, even if it’s not a neat one: the pressure may get you moving, but it also makes the whole starting process feel awful. If you put that new perspective into your own words, what do you think has changed in how you see the self-criticism now?

I guess I’m starting to see that the self-criticism isn’t just “motivation,” even though I’ve treated it like that for a long time. It does sometimes jolt me into action, but it also seems to make everything feel more threatening than it actually is, which is probably why I stall so hard in the first place. So instead of thinking of it as helpful toughness, maybe it’s more like a panic response that I’ve confused with discipline. That’s a little uncomfortable to admit, but it feels more accurate than the way I used to explain it.

That feels like a really honest shift—moving from treating that harsh inner voice as proof of strength to noticing how it can also turn up the threat level and make getting started feel much harder. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. During a tense conversation about retirement plans and household responsibilities, my spouse dismissed my concerns and said I was being unreasonable, which made me feel ignored and disrespected. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It takes courage to look closely at this, especially when it’s tied to feeling ignored and disrespected. If we map it together with an anger diary, we can look at the trigger, the early warning signs, your response, and what happened afterward; before the anger fully hit, what were the first signs in your body or behavior—things like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

Before I fully blew up, I could feel my jaw tighten and my shoulders get really stiff. My chest felt hot, and I noticed I was starting to talk faster and interrupt more, which is usually a bad sign for me. I also had this strong urge to prove my point, like if I didn’t defend myself right away, I’d just be brushed aside again. Looking back, I think I was already feeling hurt and cornered before the anger took over.

You’re noticing the warning signs very clearly, and that’s often the best window for change because it’s the moment before the explosion when a pause is still possible. On a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?

At its peak, I’d say the anger was around an 8 or 9 out of 10. I raised my voice, interrupted a lot, and started saying things in a sharper way than I intended, almost like I was trying to force myself to be heard. I also got up and walked away before the conversation could get even worse, but I was still stewing and replaying everything in my head. What I actually did wasn’t as bad as it could have been, but it definitely wasn’t calm or constructive.

Thank you for being so honest about that; it sounds like you were able to step away before it escalated further, even though it still felt really intense. What happened externally in the room with your spouse, and then what happened inside you afterward—right away and over the next few hours or days?

Externally, my spouse went quiet and looked hurt, and that made the whole room feel tense and distant. I think they saw my leaving as me shutting down, while I experienced it as trying not to say something worse. Right afterward, I felt shaky and embarrassed, and then the anger turned into a mix of guilt and sadness because I knew I had made the conversation harder. Over the next few hours and into the next day, I kept replaying it in my head, feeling both defensive and ashamed, like I wanted to justify myself but also knew I hadn’t handled it the way I wanted to.

It makes sense that you’re caught between wanting to protect yourself and feeling the pain of how it landed for both of you. Looking at that exact moment when your jaw tightened, your chest got hot, and you started interrupting, what is one thing you could do differently then that might change the outcome?

One thing I could do differently is pause and say out loud that I’m getting overwhelmed before I start pushing harder to be heard. Even something simple like, “I’m feeling myself getting worked up, and I need a minute so I don’t say this badly,” might help me avoid escalating. I think if I could step back early enough, I’d have a better chance of coming back calmer instead of reacting from that hurt and fear of being dismissed. It’s hard for me because part of me feels like pausing means losing the argument, but I can see now that it might actually help me stay in the conversation more constructively.

You’ve done a thoughtful job of noticing both the fear underneath the anger and the way pausing could serve the conversation rather than defeat it. As you take a step back and look at this shift, how would you put into your own words what has changed in the way you understand these moments now?

What’s changed for me is that I can see these blowups aren’t really just about anger—they’re also about feeling dismissed, hurt, and scared of not mattering. Before, I think I saw my reaction as something that just happened to me, but now I can see the early signs and the choice point before it gets out of control. I’m also starting to understand that pausing isn’t surrendering; it’s a way of protecting the conversation and my relationship. That feels hard, but it also gives me a little more hope that I can handle these moments differently.

It sounds like you’re seeing your reactions with much more clarity now—not just as anger, but as a signal that something deeper is getting touched, and that awareness is opening up space where there used to be only automatic momentum. What feels most important to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. It is the first week of the school year, and the client sees parents and children at the store buying school supplies. I keep telling myself: "I feel uneasy seeing all this, so this must mean I’m not handling retirement well and I’m falling behind everyone else." and I've been feeling anxious, discouraged, irritated.

That sounds really unsettling, and it makes sense that seeing all of that would stir up a lot at once. In the CBT model, the store scene itself is the same for everyone, but the meaning we attach to it can change the feelings and reactions quite a bit—when that thought showed up, what did you actually do next?

Honestly, I just kept moving through the store and tried not to look at the families, because it felt annoying and embarrassing at the same time. I’m not sure what “what did you do next” is supposed to prove—seeing a bunch of school stuff still seems like a pretty normal thing to react to. But I guess I did leave faster than I needed to and spent the rest of the day replaying it in my head.

It makes sense that you’d push back a bit; seeing school supplies and families is a pretty normal thing to react to, and the embarrassment/anxiety doesn’t say anything bad about you. I’m wondering whether the thought “I feel uneasy, so I’m falling behind” might be using your feeling as the evidence, and if someone else saw the exact same scene, what’s another way they might interpret it?

I mean, sure, someone else might just think, “It’s back-to-school season, of course the store is full of families.” But that doesn’t automatically make my reaction go away, and I’m not convinced it means anything deep either—I was just irritated and wanted out of there.

That’s fair; a different interpretation doesn’t erase the reaction, and irritation can just be irritation. If you actually believed, “It’s back-to-school season, of course the store is full of families,” how do you think you’d feel—would it be more like relief, neutrality, or something else?

Probably more neutral than anything else, I guess. But I’m not sure I “believe” that in the moment—I can say it sounds reasonable, yet the feeling still shows up anyway, which is part of why I’m not sold on this whole reframe idea.

That makes sense; it’s one thing to say a thought is reasonable and another to feel it in the moment, so I can see why you’d be skeptical. If the feeling had been more neutral instead of uneasy or embarrassed, how might your behavior have been different right then?

Maybe I would’ve just finished my shopping without hurrying out like I was doing something wrong. But I don’t know how useful it is to imagine a “more neutral” version of me when the real issue is that I did feel irritated and weird about it.

That’s a fair point, and I hear that the irritation and weirdness felt very real in the moment. If the store, the families, and the school supplies stayed exactly the same but the only thing that shifted was the thought you had about it, what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

It tells me thoughts can nudge the experience, sure, but that doesn’t mean they’re the main event or that changing them is some magic fix. I still think the situation itself was enough to make me annoyed. Maybe the thought made it worse, but I’m not ready to act like that’s the whole explanation.

That sounds pretty reasonable—you’re not buying a “magic fix,” and you’re also noticing the situation itself had an effect. If the situation was enough to make you annoyed, what do you make of the part where the same scene seemed to turn into “I’m falling behind everyone else” rather than just “this is back-to-school season”?

I suppose that part is probably me adding a whole extra layer to it. Seeing the kids and parents may have just hit a nerve about retirement and time passing, and my mind jumped to comparison before I even realized it. I still don’t love admitting that, but I can see it wasn’t only the store scene itself.

That’s a pretty important observation, even if it doesn’t feel great to admit it, and it sounds like you’re noticing the “extra layer” more clearly now. When your mind jumped to comparison, what do you think it was comparing your retirement to?

Probably to the version of life I used to have, when there was a school-year rhythm and I knew what my days were supposed to look like. And maybe to other people my age who still seem busy or needed in some obvious way, which is annoying to admit. I’m not saying that’s a fair comparison, just that I think that’s what my brain was doing.

That sounds like your mind was comparing the known rhythm you used to have with a retirement rhythm that still feels less defined, and I can see why that would feel annoying to notice. When you compare yourself to people who seem busy or needed, what does that comparison seem to be saying about you?

It seems to say that I’m somehow less useful now, or at least less in step with everyone else. Which I know is a pretty harsh way to look at it, but that’s the message that seems to be underneath it. I’m not saying it’s true—I’m just admitting that’s probably what my brain was telling me.

That’s a very clear read on the message underneath it, and it makes sense that it feels harsh to say out loud. When your brain tells you “less useful” or “less in step,” what do you notice happens to your mood or your urge to pull away in that moment?

It mostly makes me feel deflated, and then irritated on top of that, which is a bad combination. I get the urge to leave the situation or just stop looking at whatever is reminding me of it, because I don’t want to sit there and stew in the comparison. I can see how that kind of thought would make me pull back, even if I still think the whole thing starts with the situation itself.

That makes a lot of sense; when the thought turns into deflation and irritation, wanting to get away from it sounds pretty understandable. If you stayed in that moment a little longer instead of pulling back, what do you think you might have noticed about whether the situation itself was doing all the work or whether the comparison thought was adding something extra?

I think I might have noticed that the initial jolt was from seeing the school stuff, but the heavier feeling came from what I started saying to myself afterward. If I’d stayed with it, I probably would’ve seen that the store scene was annoying for a minute, while the “I’m falling behind” part is what kept it alive and made me want to leave. That’s a little uncomfortable to admit, because it means I was doing more to myself than I wanted to acknowledge.

That’s a pretty honest shift, and I can hear how uncomfortable it is to notice your own mind had a bigger role than you wanted to give it. If you put it in your own words, what’s the new perspective you’ve reached about that store moment?

I guess the new perspective is that the store and the school supplies did trigger something real, but they weren’t the whole story. What really dragged me down was the meaning I attached to it—this idea that feeling uneasy meant I was somehow behind or less useful now. I don’t fully like admitting that, but it does seem more accurate than blaming the whole thing on the scene itself.

It makes sense that you’re noticing the difference between what set things off and the story your mind built around it, especially when that story touches on being useful and keeping pace after retirement. What do you want to carry forward from noticing that distinction today?

conversations.content: If the foreclosure goes through, I’m afraid my spouse will see me as the reason we lost our home and never fully trust me again. I keep imagining that this will permanently damage our relationship, and that every conversation from then on will carry resentment, distance, and blame.

That sounds incredibly painful, and it makes sense your mind is trying to protect you by running ahead to the worst case. When we worry, though, it can treat what could happen as if it will happen, and those are very different—what concrete, observable clues have you noticed that suggest this worst-case relationship outcome may not actually come true?

One concrete clue is that my spouse has been upset, but not cruel—there’s still a lot of concern and teamwork in how we talk about it. They’ve asked practical questions about what we can do next rather than shutting me out or blaming me outright. I also notice that even in tense moments, we still check in with each other and try to stay on the same side. So I think part of my fear is filling in the blanks with a permanent breakup of trust, when the actual evidence so far is more complicated and maybe less hopeless than I’ve been telling myself.

Those are real observations, not wishful thinking, and it sounds like you’re noticing actual evidence of continued connection even under stress. If those clues are right and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you think is the realistic, most likely outcome instead?

I think the most likely outcome is that this will be a very hard period for both of us, and there will probably be moments of fear, frustration, and maybe even some grief or tension. But I don’t think it automatically means we’ll lose trust completely or stop caring about each other. More realistically, I can see us getting through it by being honest, making decisions together, and maybe even becoming more careful and supportive with each other. That doesn’t make it easy, but it feels a lot more possible than the permanent damage story my mind keeps telling me.

That sounds like a very grounded and balanced view, and it makes sense that the “permanent damage” story feels less convincing when you look at the actual evidence. If you were to imagine the worst truly happened, what would you do first, then next, and as you picture those steps, what tells you about whether you might eventually be okay?

If the worst happened, I think the first thing I’d do is try not to panic and make it worse by spiraling alone—I’d probably sit down with my spouse and be honest about what I’m feeling instead of pretending I’m fine. Next, I’d focus on the practical side: figuring out where we would stay, what resources we could use, and who we could lean on for help, even though that would be hard to face. When I picture those steps, it tells me I’m not helpless, and that even in a bad situation I would still have some ability to respond, problem-solve, and stay connected. That doesn’t make the loss less painful, but it does make me think I might eventually be okay, even if it takes time.

You just showed there’s a path through even the worst case, and that seems important given how overwhelming this felt at the start. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what feels different about it?

It feels a little less like a giant, all-consuming threat now and more like something painful that I could actually face step by step if I had to. At the beginning, the worry felt tangled up with shame and this sense that one bad outcome would mean everything was ruined, but now I can see there are still choices, support, and a way to respond. I’m still scared, and I don’t want to minimize what foreclosure could mean, but I feel less trapped inside the fear. What feels different is that I’m not just imagining disaster anymore—I’m also seeing my own ability to cope and stay connected.

It sounds like you’ve moved from feeling trapped in a disaster story to seeing that there are still options, support, and your own ability to cope, even though the fear is still real. If you were to put that shift into your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached?

I’d say my new perspective is that foreclosure would be a serious loss and a painful challenge, but it wouldn’t automatically destroy my marriage or my ability to keep going. I’m starting to see that my mind was treating the worst-case scenario like a certainty, when in reality there are still signs of connection, practical steps we can take, and support I can lean on. I still feel scared, but I don’t feel as powerless as I did before. What feels most important now is remembering that I can face this one step at a time instead of assuming it means everything is already ruined.

It sounds like you’re leaving with a steadier sense that this may be a painful chapter, not a verdict on your marriage or your future, and that shift in how you’re relating to the fear matters. As you hold onto that more grounded perspective, what feels like the most important takeaway to carry into the next time the worry starts to spike?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. At work, the client made a small mistake in an email and later received a brief correction from her manager. The error happened during a week when she had been struggling to focus after her close friend died. I keep telling myself: "I keep messing things up since my friend died. I’m clearly not handling anything well, and this is probably how I’ll be at work from now on." and I've been feeling sad, embarrassed, anxious, discouraged.

That sounds really painful, and I can see why your mind went straight to “this means something bad about me.” In CBT, the idea is that the situation itself is one piece, but the meaning you give it can change how you feel and what you do next, so what did you end up doing after those thoughts and feelings showed up?

Honestly, I mostly just stared at my inbox and reread the email a bunch of times, which probably wasn’t helpful. I get the “meaning” part, but this wasn’t just me being dramatic out of nowhere — I was already barely keeping it together after my friend died, so it felt like proof I’m slipping at work.

That makes sense, and I’m glad you pushed back on the “just dramatic” part, because this really does sound tied to how hard the grief has already been. I’m wondering if the mind might be taking one rough work moment and turning it into a bigger conclusion than the evidence actually supports—if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what else might they say it means?

Maybe they’d say I was tired and distracted because I’m grieving, which… sure, is true, but that still doesn’t make it feel great when I’m the one who has to deal with the mistake. I’m not convinced “it’s just one email” really explains much if I’m the one noticing I’m off more than usual.

That makes sense, and I hear why “it’s just one email” feels too thin when you’re the one living inside the mistake and noticing you’re off more than usual. If you actually believed the interpretation that you’re tired and grieving rather than “slipping at work,” what emotion would you expect to feel most strongly?

I guess maybe sadness or frustration, but I’m not totally buying that it changes much. Even if grief is part of it, I still made the mistake and still have to worry about how I’m coming across at work.

That’s a fair point, and I can hear that the mistake still matters to you even if grief is part of the picture. If the feeling in that moment had been sadness or frustration instead of “I’m failing at work,” how might your behavior have been different?

I mean, maybe I would’ve just corrected the email and moved on instead of spiraling, but I’m not sure that’s some huge breakthrough. It still feels a little too neat to say the emotion changes everything when the actual problem was that I was distracted and made a mistake.

That skepticism makes sense, and you’re right that the mistake itself didn’t disappear just because the emotion changed. If the email, the correction, and the distraction stayed the same but the spiral changed depending on the thought you were having, what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I guess it suggests my thoughts are affecting the spiral, but that still feels a bit obvious and not especially helpful when the trigger is real. It’s not like I can just think my way out of being grief-stricken and distracted, so I’m not sure what I’m supposed to do with that besides notice it’s happening.

You’re making a really fair distinction there—the trigger is real, and noticing that doesn’t magically make grief or distraction go away. If the best you can do right now is notice the spiral, what might you start to catch about the exact moment it turns from “I made a mistake” into “this means I’m failing”?

I think it happens pretty fast, honestly. Like I see the mistake, and then my brain immediately jumps to “this is what I’ve become since she died,” instead of just staying with the actual email. I can see there’s a moment where the thought gets bigger than the event, even if I still think the event matters.

That’s a really important observation, and it makes sense that the event still matters while the meaning your mind adds seems to swell fast. When your brain jumps to “this is what I’ve become since she died,” what does it seem to be predicting about you at work?

I guess it’s predicting that I’m going to keep screwing up and people will notice I’m not as sharp as I used to be. Maybe that I’m going to look unreliable or like I can’t really handle my job right now. I don’t love admitting that, but yeah, that’s probably what my brain is doing.

That’s a pretty clear read on what your mind is forecasting, and it makes sense that admitting it doesn’t feel great. If that prediction were true, what would it seem to say about you as a worker right now?

It would probably seem like I’m not dependable right now, which is… a pretty uncomfortable thing to say out loud. I guess it would make me feel like I’m not meeting the basic standard I usually hold myself to at work. And even saying that, part of me knows that’s a harsh conclusion from one bad week, but I can see why my brain goes there.

That’s an honest and pretty important distinction—you can see both the harshness of the conclusion and why your mind reaches for it. If this were just one bad week in the middle of grief rather than a sign of your basic standard at work, what would that suggest about how dependable you actually are?

It would suggest I’m probably still dependable overall, just not at my best right now. I don’t really like saying that because it feels like I’m making excuses, but I can see it’s different from “I’m suddenly bad at my job.” Maybe it means I’m having a rough patch, not that I’ve completely fallen apart.

That’s a meaningful shift, even if it still feels uncomfortable to name it that way. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words as simply as possible, how would you summarize what’s changed for you?

I think I’m starting to see that I turned one mistake into a story about my whole ability to function since my friend died. The mistake is real, and the grief is real, but that doesn’t automatically mean I’m failing at my job or becoming unreliable overall. It’s more like I’m having a rough patch and my brain is treating it like proof of something bigger. I’m still not happy about it, but that feels more accurate than the all-or-nothing version.

That feels like a really important shift—from treating one painful moment as a verdict on you, to noticing it as a rough patch happening in the context of real grief. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that after retiring, I’m already losing my professional edge and people will think I’m no longer capable or relevant. Then there's I’m worried I should have made different career choices earlier, and now I’m stuck replaying all the ways I could have done better. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried about how to explain my work history and retirement to friends or family at the holiday gathering without feeling judged.

That sounds exhausting, and given how much is piling up, it makes sense your mind is staying on alert. I’m wondering whether it helps to separate worries that point to something you could actually act on from worries that are more hypothetical or out of your control—what’s the first worry that is keeping you up?

I’m not sure splitting them up is going to magically help, but fine — the one that hits first at night is the retirement thing. It feels like if I’m not useful anymore, then the rest of it is just proof, and that’s what keeps looping in my head.

It makes sense that you’d be wary of a neat little exercise if the worry feels that real and sticky. When that thought shows up at night, does it point to something you can take a concrete action on, or does it seem more hypothetical and outside your control?

Honestly, it feels like mostly outside my control at 2 a.m., which is exactly why I’m annoyed by it. I can’t exactly go prove my usefulness in the middle of the night, and asking myself whether it’s “actionable” sounds a bit like rearranging deck chairs. But I suppose the only concrete thing I can do is stop feeding the loop and maybe write down what specifically I’m afraid people will conclude.

That makes sense—at 2 a.m. it’s not about solving anything, it’s about the loop feeling in charge, and I can hear why the “actionable” question sounded irritating. If you were to try one small step tonight, what exactly would you write down, and when tonight would you do it?

I guess I’d write: “I’m afraid people will think retirement means I’ve become irrelevant or less competent,” and maybe list the worst-case reactions I’m imagining. But I’m not convinced scribbling it down does much beyond letting me stare at it more—still, I could do it before I get into bed if that’s supposed to help me stop circling it.

That skepticism makes sense, especially if it feels like the page could just become another place for the worry to spin. As you look at that second worry, does it seem more like something you can take a concrete action on, or more like something outside your control?
Mostly outside my control, frankly. I can’t redo my career, and I’m not interested in pretending I can. At best I can decide whether to keep replaying it, but that’s easier said than done.

That sounds pretty clear, and I can hear you’re not interested in pretending the past can be rewritten. If the replaying is the part that’s in your control at all, what seems most realistic for tonight: setting a brief time to let it run on purpose, or choosing one concrete next step about how you want to handle it?

I’m not thrilled about either option, but I suppose a brief time to let it run on purpose sounds less annoying than trying to force some grand “next step” tonight. That said, I’m still not convinced this isn’t just a dressed-up way of making me sit with the same thoughts on purpose. Maybe if it’s limited and I actually stop when the timer ends, I’d be willing to try that.

It makes sense to be cautious if this starts sounding like a trick to make you suffer on purpose, and I hear that you’re willing to test it only if it stays limited. Looking at the third worry about explaining your work history and retirement to family or friends at the holiday gathering, does that seem more like something you could act on in some way, or more like a worry that just loops without much control?

That one feels a bit more actionable, I guess, because I can at least decide what I say and how much I say it. But I’m still worried I’ll freeze up or sound defensive if someone asks the wrong question, so it’s not exactly under control. Maybe I could think through one short answer ahead of time, though I’m not promising it’ll make me enjoy the holiday any more.

That makes sense—having a short answer ready could reduce the chance of freezing, even if it doesn’t make the holiday itself enjoyable. Since this one feels more actionable, what do you want that one short answer to sound like, and how could you keep it brief enough to feel usable?

Maybe something like, “I’m doing well and enjoying retirement, even if it’s a big adjustment. I’m keeping busy with a few things I care about, and I’m figuring out the next chapter.” That feels brief enough not to invite a whole interrogation, though I can already hear myself wanting to overexplain if I get nervous.

That sounds like a solid, concise answer, and it makes sense that nervousness could push you toward overexplaining even when you know brevity would feel safer. When you imagine yourself starting to ramble, what do you think you’d be trying to protect yourself from, and what would staying brief be protecting you from?

I suppose if I start rambling, I’m trying to protect myself from looking embarrassed, defensive, or like I’m failing some sort of test I didn’t agree to take. I think I’m filling in the blanks with my own fear, because the retirement shift feels so personal and exposed. That’s uncomfortable to admit, but it does sound more like my assumption than a fact.
That’s a meaningful shift, even if it’s uncomfortable to see it that clearly. In your own words, what’s the new perspective you’re noticing about what’s actually happening here?

I think I’ve been treating my fear as if it’s evidence, when really it’s more like a story my mind is generating because retirement feels uncertain and exposed. The holiday gathering is bringing that up, but it doesn’t actually prove I’ve become irrelevant or less capable. What seems more true is that I’m worried about how I’ll be seen, and that worry is making everything feel more judgmental than it necessarily is.

It sounds like you just made an important distinction between what your mind is telling you and what the situation actually proves, especially with how retirement and the holiday are stirring up that sense of being on display. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed about that difference?

...My jaw got tight, and I could feel my shoulders tense up. I started getting quiet, then I said something sharp.

conversations.content: If I’m messing up my eating habits now, I’m probably losing control in other parts of my life too, and I’m going to feel worse and less productive at work. I hate that I can’t seem to keep something this basic together.

That’s a pretty brutal thought to carry around, and I appreciate you saying it out loud. Could we slow it down together and look at it carefully—not to brush off how bad it feels, but to see whether it actually holds up when we examine it a bit?

I guess we can, but I’m not convinced this is some deep pattern instead of me just being bad at routine lately. It feels a little too easy to turn one messy habit into a whole psychological theory, but sure—what exactly are we testing?
That skepticism makes sense, and I’m not trying to force a big theory onto it. If we test the thought itself, is my thought based more on habit or a past experience than what’s true now?

Maybe, but I’m not sure that’s the right split. It could just be based on the fact that I’ve been inconsistent lately, not some old trauma or mental habit—sometimes a sloppy pattern is just a sloppy pattern.
That’s fair, and I hear you pushing back on making this more complicated than it may be. If we stay with the actual evidence instead of the label, could my thought be an exaggeration of what’s true?

Maybe, but “exaggeration” sounds like you’re already assuming the thought is wrong. If I’ve been eating badly for a couple weeks and my work is slipping a bit, that’s not me making up a catastrophe—it’s just not ideal. I can see that it doesn’t automatically mean everything is falling apart, but I’m not ready to call it exaggerated either.

That feels like a careful correction, and it makes sense not to jump to “wrong” when there’s some evidence of a real dip. Given what you’ve noticed so far, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

Probably more of a possibility than a likely scenario. I mean, I’m not pretending it’s nothing, but “I’m losing control in other parts of my life” feels like a leap from “my routine is off and I’m stressed.” It’s annoying, not proof that everything else is unraveling.

That sounds like a pretty grounded read of it, and I hear you separating “annoying” from “everything is unraveling,” which is a useful distinction. When that thought about losing control shows up, whose voice does it sound most like, and how much is it actually yours versus influenced by someone else’s opinion?

Honestly, that question feels a bit like a detour—I’m not sure it matters whose voice it is if the thought is still in my head. But if I had to answer, it sounds a lot like my own overreactive voice, with maybe some background noise from work culture and people who act like being perfectly disciplined is the baseline.

That makes sense; if the thought is yours, the source may matter less than whether it’s actually accurate, and I hear how the work-culture pressure adds fuel to it. What is the evidence for this thought, and what is the evidence against it?

For it: I’ve definitely been eating worse lately, and I’ve been a bit more scattered and less on top of things at work, so it’s not like the thought came out of nowhere. Against it: I’m still functioning, I’m not missing deadlines, and one rough stretch doesn’t automatically mean I’m losing control of my life. So, yeah, there’s evidence for “I’m off my game,” but not much for “everything is unraveling.”

That sounds like a pretty fairer picture, and I appreciate that you’re not sugarcoating it or pretending the rough stretch isn’t real. If the original thought is “I’m losing control in other parts of my life,” how might you rewrite it so it includes the evidence for being off your game without jumping all the way to everything unraveling?

Maybe something like: “My routine has been off lately, and that’s making me feel less sharp and more stressed, but it doesn’t mean I’m losing control of everything.” Or “I’m in a rough patch with eating and focus, but I’m still functioning and can probably steady things before they get worse.” That feels more accurate, even if I don’t love admitting I’m in a rough patch.

That feels like a more accurate way to say it, even if it stings a bit to name the rough patch directly. What do you notice changes in you when you use that version of the thought instead of the original one?

It’s a little less panicky, I guess. The original version makes it sound like I’m on the edge of a collapse, and this one is more like “okay, I’m off balance, but it’s not a disaster yet.” I don’t love that it still points to a problem, but it does feel more workable and less insulting.

That makes a lot of sense—less panicky and less insulting is a meaningful shift, even if it still isn’t exactly pleasant. When you hear “off balance, but not a disaster,” what does that seem to say about your capacity to steady things from here?

I mean, it suggests I’m not as stuck as the original thought makes me sound. If this is more of a rough patch than a total derailment, then I probably do have some room to adjust things instead of just spiraling about it. I’m still annoyed that it’s gotten this messy, but I can see that I’m not helpless here.

That’s a real shift, especially from “I’m helpless” to “I have some room to adjust things,” even if it’s still annoying. If you put the new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed about how you’re seeing this?

I think I’m seeing it less as a sign that I’m failing at life and more as a warning that I’m under more strain than I’ve been admitting. The eating stuff still matters, but it doesn’t automatically mean I’m spiraling or incapable of getting back on track. It’s more like I’ve drifted off course a bit, and that’s frustrating, but not the same thing as being out of control. I guess the shift is that I can admit there’s a problem without turning it into a verdict on me.

It sounds like you’re able to hold the problem in view without turning it into a judgment about your worth, and that’s a meaningful change in how you’re making sense of what’s been happening. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. After moving into a new residence, the client noticed that several boxes were still unpacked and the neighbors had not yet introduced themselves. I keep telling myself: "I’m never going to settle in here, and because no one has reached out yet, it means I won’t belong here or make any friends." and I've been feeling Anxious, lonely, discouraged, and overwhelmed.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense that unpacked boxes and quiet neighbors could stir up anxiety, loneliness, and discouragement. In the cognitive model, the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m curious: when those thoughts showed up, what did you find yourself actually doing?

I found myself avoiding the boxes and just sitting there feeling stuck, like I didn’t know where to start. I also kept checking the window and listening for signs that neighbors were around, but then I’d talk myself out of going out or introducing myself because I assumed they probably weren’t interested. Mostly, I withdrew and spent a lot of time ruminating, which made the whole place feel even more unfamiliar and lonely. The more I stayed in that loop, the more overwhelmed I felt, almost like I was proving to myself that I didn’t belong here.

That sounds like a really painful loop, and it makes sense that the uncertainty would pull you toward withdrawal and rumination. One thing I’m noticing is that the thought may be jumping to a conclusion from very little evidence, which is a very common mind pattern rather than a flaw; if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what is another way they might interpret it?

I think someone else might say that none of this necessarily means I won’t belong here. They might see the unpacked boxes as just a sign that I’m still in the middle of settling in, not evidence that I’m failing at it. And the neighbors not reaching out yet could simply mean they’re busy, shy, or waiting for the right moment, not that they don’t want to know me. Hearing it that way makes the situation feel a little less hopeless, though I can still feel how quickly my mind turns silence into rejection.

That’s a really thoughtful reframe, and it makes sense that it feels a bit less hopeless when you separate “not yet” from “never.” If you actually believed that interpretation instead, how do you think you would feel—what specific emotion comes up?

If I really believed that interpretation, I think I’d feel more hopeful and a little calmer, maybe even a bit curious instead of so defeated. I can imagine the anxiety easing some, because I wouldn’t be treating every quiet moment as proof that I’m unwanted. I’d probably still feel some loneliness, but it would feel more like temporary uncertainty than a final verdict about my place here. That shift alone makes me feel a little lighter, like there might actually be room for things to change.

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re noticing how the same situation could feel lighter, calmer, and less final when it’s seen as uncertainty rather than rejection. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

If I’d been feeling calmer and more hopeful instead of rejected, I think I would have started with one small box rather than avoiding everything. I might also have been more willing to step outside or at least make a simple introduction, like saying hello if I saw a neighbor, instead of assuming they didn’t want contact. I think I would have spent less time staring out the window and ruminating, and more time doing something that helped me settle into the space. Even that small change would probably have made the place feel a little less intimidating and a little more like somewhere I could grow into.

That sounds like a real shift, and it makes sense that even a small change in perspective could open up different choices and feelings. In your own words, how would you summarize the new way you’re seeing this situation now?

I’m starting to see that this situation doesn’t automatically mean I’m failing to settle in or that I don’t belong here. The unpacked boxes and the quiet neighbors are more about a transition still in progress, not a sign that things are hopeless. I can also see that my mind has been turning “not yet” into “never,” and that’s been feeding my anxiety and loneliness. If I can treat this as uncertainty instead of rejection, I think I have a better chance of taking small steps that actually help me feel at home.

It sounds like you’ve been able to notice a very important difference between a situation that is still unfolding and the harsher story your mind was telling about it, and there’s a lot of steadiness in that shift. The next time this feeling shows up, what might you want to remind yourself is the question worth asking first?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: What if my coworkers notice I seem distracted and think I’m handling my marriage badly? Then there's What if my friends judge me for trying to reconcile and think I’m making a stupid choice? And I also keep thinking about: If I’m around people and they ask how things are going, I’ll sound awkward and they’ll think I’m weak.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind feels stuck when it keeps looping over how other people might see you. Sometimes it can help to sort worries into two kinds: productive ones, where there’s something concrete to do, and unproductive ones, where it’s more hypothetical or outside your control; which of those three worries is the first one keeping you up?

I mean, I get the idea, but splitting them into “productive” and “unproductive” feels a little too neat when they all kind of blend together at 2 a.m. If I had to pick one, it’s probably the coworker thing first, because that feels the most immediate and annoying.

Yeah, that makes sense—at 2 a.m. those categories can feel pretty artificial. With the coworker worry, is there a concrete action you can actually take about it, or is it more about what you fear they might think, which would put it outside your control?

I guess there’s a concrete action in the sense that I can keep doing my job and not overshare, but that feels kind of obvious. The bigger issue is I can’t really stop them from noticing I’m off or deciding what that means, which is the part that keeps me spinning.

That sounds really frustrating, because the part you can’t control is exactly the part your mind keeps grabbing onto. Would it be worth setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to worry about the coworker piece on purpose, so you can try to park it for tonight, and what’s the next worry on your mind?

I mean, maybe, but “schedule a worry” sounds a little odd to me—like I can just turn it off tonight because I made an appointment with it tomorrow. If that’s the goal, I’m not super convinced it’ll work, but the next worry is the friends one, because that feels more personal and embarrassing.

Yeah, I get why that sounds a bit contrived, and it makes sense you’d be skeptical if it feels like a trick rather than something real. With the friends worry, is there any concrete action you can take about it, or is it mostly about what they might think, which would put it outside your control?

I mean, I can choose how much I tell them and maybe decide not to get into the details, so technically yes, there’s something I can do. But honestly, the hard part is still that I can’t control whether they quietly think I’m making a dumb choice, and that’s what I’m stuck on.

That makes a lot of sense—being able to set boundaries about what you share is concrete, but the part that hooks you is still the possibility of being judged, which you can’t actually control. Given that, would it fit more as something to save for a planned worry time than something to solve tonight, and is there one more worry on your mind?

Maybe, but I’m still not sold that “planned worry time” does much besides move the same thoughts to a different hour. I guess the last one is the awkward conversations thing—if people ask how things are going, I worry I’ll sound weird or weak and then I’ll keep replaying it afterward.

That skepticism makes sense; if it feels like the same worry in a different wrapper, of course you’d question it. With the awkward-conversations worry, when you picture it, is there anything you could actually do in the moment, or is it mostly about the story your mind tells afterward about how you came across?

I guess in the moment I could keep it brief and just say I’m dealing with some personal stuff, which is probably the only realistic thing I can do. The bigger problem is definitely the story afterward, where I’m replaying everything and deciding I sounded pathetic or awkward. So yeah, it feels less like I’m failing in the moment and more like my brain won’t let it go after.

That’s a really clear distinction—you can handle the moment with something brief, but the replay afterward is where your mind keeps dragging you back in. Since this one seems to have a concrete in-the-moment response, what do you notice about how that changes the third worry compared with when it was just swirling around with the other two?

I guess it makes it feel a little less huge, like there’s at least a script for the actual conversation instead of me just being doomed to freeze. But I’m still not convinced that helps with the part after, because that’s where I usually beat myself up. So maybe it changes it from “I have no idea what to do” to “I can do something, and my brain will probably still be annoying about it.”

That sounds pretty honest: having a script helps the moment, but your real battle is with the post-conversation beating-yourself-up, which is the part that feels harder to shake. When your brain starts replaying it afterward, what does it usually claim the replay is supposed to accomplish, and how well does that actually work for you?

I think it acts like it’s trying to protect me from being caught off guard again, or like if I analyze it enough I’ll somehow do better next time. But honestly, it usually just makes me feel worse and more stuck, not more prepared. So I can see that it’s not really helping, even if that’s what it tells me it’s doing.

That’s a pretty important shift—you’re noticing the replay is trying to look helpful, but it actually leaves you more trapped rather than better prepared. If you were to put that new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you about the way you see these worries?

I guess I’m starting to see that these worries aren’t all equally urgent just because they feel loud. A lot of what’s keeping me stuck is the replay afterward, and that part isn’t actually solving anything—it’s just making me feel more ashamed and tense. So maybe the real problem isn’t that I’m failing at handling people, but that my mind keeps treating other people’s possible opinions like they’re facts I need to fix. That doesn’t make it go away, but it does make it feel a little less like I’m powerless.

That feels like an important shift—there’s a little more space now between the feeling of urgency and what’s actually true, and it sounds like you noticed how much the after-the-fact replay has been adding to the weight rather than helping. …I usually just keep to myself and replay it over and over. I start feeling like I should be doing more, but then I don’t really know what to do.

Sometimes in grief, people discount the kind things others say as “just polite,” even when there may be something real in them, so if someone else looked at the very same situation, how might they interpret those comments and that message?
…They’d probably think people were just trying to be nice, but maybe also that I did help some. I don’t know, it’s hard for me to believe it for myself.

…Maybe I would have just said thank you and not kept replaying it so much. I probably would’ve been a little more open instead of shutting down.

In CBT, we often look at how the same situation can land very differently depending on the meaning we give it, because the event itself is one part and the thoughts we have about it can shape what we feel and do next. I nodded along a few times, but I didn’t really speak up because I was afraid I’d either sound rude or make the whole evening worse. They might see that I was hurt and overwhelmed, and that I was choosing restraint because I didn’t want to damage relationships in the moment. At the same time, I can see how my withdrawing might have looked like I didn’t care or didn’t have my own opinion, which bothers me because that’s not true.
