conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: If I keep missing deadlines and sounding distracted, my manager is going to think I can't handle this job anymore. Then there's Everyone on my team can probably tell I'm falling apart, and this divorce is going to make me look unreliable or weak. And I also keep thinking about: If I don't get my focus back soon, I'll miss a promotion or lose momentum in my career.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind is grabbing onto those career fears when you’re already under this much strain. Some worries are productive because they point to something actionable, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical, uncontrollable, or about things that may never happen, and they need different handling. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

I don’t know, splitting them into “productive” and “unproductive” feels a little neat when my brain is just screaming at me all night. If I had to pick one, it’s probably the first one — missing deadlines and sounding distracted — because that one seems the most real and immediate, not just some abstract fear.

That makes sense — when your mind is going full speed at night, a neat label can feel pretty disconnected from what it’s actually like. With the missing-deadlines worry, what part of it is something you could take a concrete action on, and what part is more hypothetical or outside your control?

I mean, I can maybe control whether I set better reminders, but I can’t exactly control the fact that my concentration is shot right now. The hypothetical part is all the stuff my brain jumps to — like my manager deciding I’m incompetent or this turning into some career disaster — but that doesn’t make it feel less real at 2 a.m.

You’re being pretty clear that there’s a real piece you can act on and a bigger piece that’s your mind filling in the worst-case story, and I get that it still feels very real at 2 a.m. What’s one small reminder-related step you could set up, and exactly when would you do it?

I guess I could set a couple of calendar alerts for my top deadlines tonight, but honestly that feels like a band-aid, not some breakthrough. If you want an exact time: after this, probably in the next 20 minutes, before I overthink it and do nothing.

That sounds like a practical move, even if it doesn’t feel transformative, and I can hear the frustration with wanting something bigger than a band-aid. With the second worry—your team seeing you as unreliable or weak—what part, if any, could you actually take action on, and what part is outside your control?

I mean, I can control whether I show up prepared and don’t completely disappear on people, sure. But I can’t control what they’re assuming about me or whether they decide “divorce = unreliable,” which is kind of the part that actually gets under my skin. So yes, there are action items, but a lot of this is just me trying to manage other people’s opinions, which feels pretty impossible.

That makes a lot of sense, and it’s frustrating when the part that hurts most is exactly the part you can’t control. Given that split, what seems like one concrete step you could take around showing up prepared, and if the opinion piece keeps looping, would setting a specific worry time later make any sense for that?

I mean, I can probably over-prepare for tomorrow’s meetings and make sure I have my notes in front of me, but that still doesn’t stop me from feeling like everyone can tell something’s off. And the “worry time” thing sounds a little artificial, but I guess if you want a specific slot, maybe I could try 7:30 tomorrow evening instead of letting it take over all night.

It makes sense that “worry time” can sound artificial when the feeling is already so intense, and you’re also being realistic about what you can and can’t control. Looking at the third worry — missing a promotion or losing momentum — what part of that is something you can actually influence right now, and what part is more of your mind projecting a future outcome?

I can influence whether I keep showing up, staying organized, and not totally checking out, so I guess there’s still some control there. The promotion part is mostly my brain fast-forwarding to a future I can’t verify yet, even though it feels pretty convincing when I’m exhausted. I don’t love admitting it, but maybe that one is more projection than fact right now.

That’s a pretty sharp distinction, especially given how convincing it feels when you’re exhausted. If the promotion fear is more projection than fact, what would you want to do with it tonight — give it a concrete action, put it into your worry slot tomorrow, or notice it and let it pass for now?

I think tonight it’s probably not worth trying to solve the promotion thing at 2 a.m., because that just turns into mental spiraling. I can maybe put it in the worry slot tomorrow and, for tonight, just notice it without chasing it every time it pops up. I’m not saying I love that plan, but it does seem a little less pointless than wrestling with it in bed.

That sounds like a pretty grounded read on what happens when you try to solve it at 2 a.m., even if you’re not exactly enthusiastic about the alternative. When you notice the promotion thought pop up tonight, what would “not chasing it” actually look like for you in that moment?

I guess it would mean catching myself before I start building a whole disaster movie around it and just naming it as “there’s that promotion thought again.” Then instead of following it, I’d try to get back to whatever I’m doing — or if I’m in bed, just not turn it into a full debate with myself. I’m not claiming I can do that perfectly, but it seems more realistic than pretending I can argue myself out of it at 2 a.m.

That sounds pretty practical, and I hear the skepticism about not being able to “argue” your way out of a 2 a.m. spiral. When you label it and stop the debate, what do you notice happens to the intensity of the thought, even a little?

It usually drops a notch, I guess — not gone, just less like it’s hijacking everything. The thought still shows up, but if I don’t keep feeding it, it’s a little less loud after a minute or two. I’m still not thrilled about how much effort this takes, but I can admit that arguing with it tends to make it worse.

That’s a useful observation, even if it’s annoying that the payoff is only “a notch” and not total relief. When you notice that arguing makes it worse and not feeding it makes it quieter, what does that suggest about what the thought is really asking from you in those moments?

I guess it suggests the thought isn’t actually asking me to solve anything right then, even though it feels like it is. It’s more like my brain is demanding certainty or reassurance, and the minute I try to give it that, it just keeps moving the goalposts. So maybe what it’s really asking for is attention, not an answer — and giving it less of that might be the only thing that helps, even if I hate how passive that sounds.

That’s a really clear insight, and I hear the frustration with how “passive” it can feel when what you actually want is relief. If you had to put the shift into your own words, what’s the new perspective you’ve reached about these thoughts and how to handle them?

I think the new perspective is that these thoughts feel urgent, but that doesn’t mean they’re all true or that they all need solving right now. A lot of this is my brain trying to force certainty about my job, my divorce, and how other people see me, and that’s just not something I can get at 2 a.m. So the better move is probably to separate what I can actually do — like reminders, prep, and a worry slot — from the part that’s just fear looking for attention. It’s not a great feeling, but I can see that feeding the spiral is making it worse, not better.

You caught something important there: the intensity of a thought can make it feel pressing without making it more trustworthy, and it sounds like you were able to separate the part that needs your attention from the part that’s just trying to pull you into the spiral. The next time that 2 a.m. certainty-seeking shows up, what is the first question you might ask yourself?

conversations.content: I’m scared this financial change means I’m not as secure as I thought I was, and I keep worrying that one bad month could throw everything off. I can’t stop thinking about how I’m going to keep up and what I’ll have to give up.

It makes sense that this feels scary, and I really appreciate how openly you’re naming it. Let’s slow this down together, not to brush past the fear, but to look at it carefully and see how much this thought is actually holding up when we examine it closely—would you be willing to stay with it for a moment?

Yes, I can stay with it. When I really look at it, the fear feels bigger than just the money itself—it’s like the money has come to represent whether I’m safe or in control at all. I know logically that one bad month probably wouldn’t ruin everything, but emotionally it still feels like the ground could shift under me. I’m willing to examine it, even though I can already tell there’s a lot of anxiety wrapped up in this for me.

That’s a really important realization, and it makes sense that the fear would feel bigger when it’s tied to safety and control rather than just numbers. Is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

When I look at it honestly, it feels more like a possibility than a likely scenario, even though my body reacts like it’s imminent. I can see that I’m jumping straight to the worst-case version, as if one difficult month automatically means everything starts collapsing, and that isn’t actually what the facts show. I do have some cushion and some ability to adjust, but the uncertainty still makes me feel vulnerable. I think the fear is more about not wanting to lose control than about a realistic prediction of disaster.

That’s a very clear and thoughtful observation—you’re noticing both the mismatch between the fear and the facts, and how strongly your body is still reacting. Is my thought based more on habit or a past experience than what’s true now, and can you think of a specific moment that might be shaping that reaction?

Yes, I think it’s probably more habit and past experience than what’s true right now. A specific moment that comes to mind is when I saw my parents get really stressed about money growing up, and even when things weren’t completely falling apart, it felt like the mood in the house could change fast if bills were tight. I think I learned to treat financial uncertainty like an emergency, even if the actual situation is more manageable than it feels. So now when my own finances feel less predictable, my body reacts as if I’m back in that same vulnerable place.

That’s a really meaningful connection, and it makes sense that your body would respond so strongly if it learned early on to treat money stress like an emergency. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what’s true?

Yes, I think it is an exaggeration of what’s true. My mind turns a real concern into a much bigger story, like “this is the beginning of everything unraveling,” when the actual situation is more contained and workable. I can see that I’m magnifying the uncertainty and treating discomfort like danger, which makes the whole thing feel much more catastrophic than it is. Even saying that out loud, I notice part of me still wants to believe the worst, but another part of me knows that’s not the full truth.

That’s a really important shift, and I hear both the part that still fears the worst and the part that’s starting to see the fuller picture. When you step back from this conversation, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached in your own words?

I think my new perspective is that the financial change is real and worth paying attention to, but it’s not the same as immediate danger or inevitable collapse. I’m seeing more clearly that my fear is being amplified by old patterns and by how strongly I connect money with safety and control. The facts suggest I have more cushion and flexibility than my anxiety wants to admit, even though uncertainty still feels uncomfortable. So instead of treating this like a disaster, I can start seeing it as a manageable challenge that brings up a deeper fear I’m still learning how to work with.

It sounds like you’re seeing the situation with a lot more accuracy now—letting the reality of the change stay real without letting the fear automatically turn it into catastrophe. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: What if something is wrong with me and I’m never going to have a normal, satisfying sex life? I keep worrying that this means there’s something broken in me, and that it will hurt my relationship if I can’t figure it out.

That sounds really heavy to carry, and I appreciate how openly you’re naming it. Let’s slow this down together, not to brush it aside, but to look carefully at whether this thought fully holds up when we examine it closely; as you stay with it, what feels like the strongest evidence to you that something is “broken”?

The strongest evidence, in my mind, is that I seem to have a hard time relaxing and actually enjoying sex the way I think I’m supposed to. I get in my head so much that it feels like my body and my mind aren’t cooperating, and that makes me worry something is fundamentally off. I also notice that I compare myself to what I assume other people experience, and that comparison makes me feel even more abnormal. It’s hard not to read all of that as proof that I’m broken, even though I know that might be a very harsh interpretation.

That makes a lot of sense, and I can hear how quickly those moments of tension and comparison get translated into a harsh story about yourself. If we hold that thought up gently and look at both sides, is my thought overly critical?

Yes, I think it probably is overly critical. When I’m in that mindset, I turn one difficulty into this huge conclusion about my whole body and future, and that doesn’t feel very fair. I can also see that I’m judging myself against an ideal that may not even be realistic, and that makes the thought even harsher. At the same time, it’s hard not to believe it when the anxiety feels so immediate and real.

That sounds like you can see both the fairness issue and how convincing the anxiety feels in the moment, which is a really important distinction. When that “I’m broken” thought shows up, is it based more on habit or a past experience than on what’s true right now, and can you think of a specific moment that would help us test that?

I think it’s probably based more on habit and past experiences than on what’s true right now. Once I’ve had a few moments where I felt anxious or disconnected, my mind seems to grab onto that and turn it into a bigger story that I just repeat automatically. A specific moment would be when I started feeling tense during sex and immediately assumed I was failing, even though nothing “bad” had actually happened. Looking back, that feels less like proof that I’m broken and more like a learned reaction that gets triggered when I feel pressure.

That’s a really important insight—you’re noticing how quickly a moment of tension gets turned into a bigger, automatic story, and that takes a lot of honesty to see. Given what you’ve just noticed about habit, past experiences, and pressure, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

I think it’s more of a possibility than a likely scenario, even though it can feel very likely when I’m in the middle of it. The thought that I’m “broken” is really the mind jumping to the worst conclusion from a few anxious moments, not a clear sign that something is fundamentally wrong. I can see that pressure and self-monitoring make everything feel more difficult, which makes the fear stronger, but that still doesn’t prove the fear is true. It’s uncomfortable to admit that, because part of me still wants certainty, but it does help me step back from treating the thought like a fact.

That’s a thoughtful shift, and I hear how uncomfortable but also relieving it is to loosen your grip on the thought without pretending the uncertainty is gone. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed?

I think what’s changed is that I’m starting to see this as a pattern of anxiety and pressure, not as proof that I’m broken. I still feel scared sometimes, but I’m less convinced that one difficult experience means something is fundamentally wrong with me or my future. It also helps me to realize that my mind has been treating uncertainty like danger, which makes everything feel much more serious than it may actually be. I’m not fully settled yet, but I do feel a little more able to step back and question the story instead of automatically believing it.

It sounds like you’re beginning to relate to these moments with a little more distance and curiosity, especially as you notice how quickly pressure and uncertainty can get turned into a much harsher story about yourself. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of frustration lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really uncomfortable, and it makes sense that you’d want something more concrete than just “feeling bad.” If we slow it down and map it step by step, what word fits the emotion most closely right now, and how strong is it from 0 to 100 at this moment?

I don’t know, “frustrated” seems close enough, though I’m not sure why we need to pin it down like it’s a lab sample. It’s probably around a 70, maybe 75, but honestly what seems more relevant is that everything feels off since this change in living situation.

That makes sense, and I can hear why the “lab sample” approach would feel annoying when the bigger issue is that everything feels off. If we focus on one concrete moment from the last day or two, what specific situation or thought seemed to set that frustration off?

Honestly, I’m not sure there was one neat trigger—it’s more like a steady drip of being out of place. Maybe yesterday when I couldn’t find anything in the new apartment, I just felt irritated and thought, “This is ridiculous, I can’t even relax in my own home.”

That steady drip of feeling out of place makes a lot of sense, and the “can’t even relax in my own home” moment sounds like it really hit a nerve. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a flash?

I mean, it wasn’t some profound insight—more like, “Great, now everything’s a hassle.” Maybe also, “Why did I have to deal with this at my age?” I’m not convinced digging for a single “automatic thought” changes much, but that’s probably the general flavor of it.

That sounds pretty understandable, and I’m not hearing anything dramatic there—just a very human “this is a hassle” reaction to a lot of change. When that feeling hit, what did you do right away, and what did you start avoiding afterward?

I mostly just stood there annoyed, then started shuffling things around and muttering to myself like that was going to fix it. Afterward I avoided unpacking the rest of the boxes because, frankly, I didn’t feel like getting more irritated. I’m not sure why this is supposed to be so revealing, but there you go.

That does give us a pretty clear chain, and I can hear the skepticism in “not sure why this is supposed to be so revealing.” Right away, when you shuffled things around and then avoided the boxes, what happened to the frustration in the moment, and what seemed to happen to it over the next few hours or days?

In the moment, it probably took the edge off a little because I was doing something, but not in any meaningful way. Later it just sat there and got worse because the boxes were still there and the place still felt wrong. So no, it didn’t exactly solve anything, if that’s where this is going.

That sounds frustrating in exactly the way you’ve been describing, and it makes sense you’d be wary if it seems like we’re just circling back to “it didn’t help.” When the boxes stayed there and the place still felt wrong, what did that seem to say to you about the situation or about how manageable this change is?

It mostly said to me that this whole thing is bigger than I want to admit, and that I’m not just being fussy about it. It made me think maybe I’m still not settled enough to handle this smoothly, which is irritating in itself. I guess, reluctantly, it also says avoiding it doesn’t make it go away — it just hangs around and keeps bothering me.

That’s a pretty clear and honest read on it, and I can hear both the irritation and the reluctant recognition in what you said. If avoiding it keeps it hanging around, what do you notice it costs you to keep treating the boxes and the new place as something to put off?

It costs me time, obviously, but more than that it keeps me in this low-grade irritated state all day, which is tiring. I also end up feeling a bit stuck and less in control, like I’m letting the place win somehow, which is not a great feeling. I’m not thrilled to admit it, but putting it off seems to make the whole thing loom larger than it probably is.

That sounds like a pretty honest read, and I can hear how irritating it is to notice the pattern while also not liking what it says about feeling stuck. When you say the place “wins” and the whole thing looms larger, what does that seem to suggest about what you need most in those moments?

I suppose it suggests I need some sense that I’m not at the mercy of the whole mess, even if I don’t like admitting that. Maybe I need a way to make the place feel a little more mine instead of just glaring at me from every corner. I’m still not convinced this is all as deep as you seem to think, but… yes, having some control would probably help.

That makes a lot of sense, and I’m not trying to make it more mysterious than it is if it feels pretty straightforward to you. If “more control” and “making it feel a little more mine” are the key pieces, what would be the smallest sign that the place was starting to feel that way?

I guess the smallest sign would be if I could walk in and not immediately feel that knot in my stomach. Maybe if one room had a few things set up the way I like—my books, a chair, something familiar—it would feel less like I’m temporarily camping in someone else’s space. I’m not saying that would solve everything, but it would at least be a start.

That sounds like a very concrete and sensible “start,” and I can hear that you’re not claiming it would fix everything, just shift the feeling a bit. If you imagine that one room set up your way, what do you notice it would change first in the way you think or feel when you come home?

I think the first thing it would change is that I’d feel less braced for irritation the second I walk in. Instead of thinking, “Here we go again,” I might actually feel a little calmer, maybe even relieved that there’s one corner of the place that feels familiar. I’m still not thrilled that it matters this much, but I can see that having even one room set up the way I want would probably make the whole place feel less hostile.
That’s a pretty meaningful shift, even if you’re not exactly celebrating it. If you put it in your own words, what new understanding have you reached about how the space affects your frustration?

I’m starting to see that the frustration isn’t just about boxes or clutter—it’s about the place not feeling like mine yet, which keeps me on edge from the moment I walk in. When the space feels unfamiliar, I seem to brace myself without even meaning to, and that makes everything feel more irritating than it probably needs to be. So the frustration is tied to not having any real foothold in the new setup, not just to being annoyed in general. I still don’t love admitting it, but making one part of the place feel familiar might actually take some pressure off.

It sounds like you just noticed how much of the edge comes from that unsettled “not-yet-mine” feeling, and there’s something important in seeing that the irritation has been carrying a larger meaning than clutter alone. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I’m so overwhelmed by this mortgage payment—I keep thinking that if I fall behind even once, everything will spiral and I’ll never catch up. I should be handling this better, but instead I feel like I’m one mistake away from losing control.

That sounds really heavy, and I appreciate how clearly you’re putting it into words. Let’s slow this down together, not to dismiss how intense it feels, but to look closely at whether that thought holds up when we examine it carefully; would you be willing to stay with it for a moment?

Yes, I can stay with it. When I really look at it, the fear feels bigger than the facts in front of me, but it still feels very real in my body. I think part of what scares me is that I’m treating one late payment like it would mean total failure, even though I know logically that’s probably not true. I’m willing to examine it, because I don’t want this fear to keep running the show.

That makes a lot of sense, and it’s important that you can notice the fear feels bigger than the facts even while your body still reacts strongly. When you look at that thought about a late payment meaning total failure, is my thought based more on habit or a past experience than what's true now?

Yes, I think it’s mostly coming from habit and fear, not from what’s actually happening right now. I’ve always linked money problems with shame and panic, so my mind jumps straight to the worst-case scenario before I’ve even checked the facts. There isn’t really evidence that one late payment would mean total failure, but emotionally it feels like proof that I’m not safe. I can see that this reaction is probably tied to old patterns more than the present situation, even though it still feels very convincing in the moment.

That’s a really thoughtful observation, and it sounds like you’re noticing both the old shame pattern and how convincing it can feel in the moment. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what’s true, and what specific facts from your actual situation make that feel a little more or less accurate?

Yes, I think it probably is an exaggeration of what’s true. The facts are that I have been able to make my payments so far, I do have a steady job, and this is a stressful situation but not an immediate collapse. What makes it feel less accurate is that I’m not actually in free fall right now—I’m just scared of the possibility of being stretched thin. What makes it feel more accurate, emotionally, is that I’ve been carrying a lot of tension around money for a long time, so my mind treats the risk like it’s already happening.

That’s a very clear distinction, and it sounds like you’re really separating what’s happening now from what your mind fears could happen. When you look at it that way, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

I think it’s more of a possibility than a likely scenario. I can see that my mind is treating it like an impending disaster, but realistically I’ve managed so far and there are probably steps I could take before it ever got that far. It’s hard to admit that because the fear feels so loud, but when I’m honest, the outcome I’m imagining is not the most probable one. What feels most true right now is that I’m anxious and vulnerable, not that I’m actually on the edge of losing everything.
That’s a really grounded shift, especially given how loud the fear has been. If you put it into your own words, what’s the new perspective you’ve arrived at about this mortgage worry?

My new perspective is that this mortgage worry is serious, but it’s not the same as total failure or inevitable collapse. I can see that my mind has been turning a real stressor into a worst-case story because money has always been tied to shame and fear for me. Right now, the facts are that I’m still managing, and the situation is stressful but not an emergency catastrophe. I still feel scared, but I’m starting to believe that I can respond to this instead of assuming I’m powerless.

It sounds like you were able to separate the real weight of this situation from the much harsher story your mind has been attaching to it, and there’s something important in noticing that you can feel scared without making it mean you’re helpless. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried my boss thinks I’m incompetent because I pushed back in that meeting. Then there's I keep thinking my coworkers noticed I sounded tense, and now they probably see me as difficult. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried people in the office are talking about me after that disagreement with my boss.

That sounds exhausting, and I can see why your mind keeps looping on it at night. Sometimes it helps to sort worries into ones that are productive—meaning there’s something concrete you could actually do—and ones that are unproductive, meaning they’re hypothetical or outside your control; of the three you named, which is the first worry that’s keeping you up?
I mean, maybe, but that sounds a little too neat to me. The one keeping me up first is probably the boss thing, because if I messed that up, the rest kind of follows anyway.

That makes sense, and I hear your hesitation about making it too tidy when it feels tangled in real life. If we stay with the boss worry for a moment, is there something concrete you can actually take action on there, or is it more of a hypothetical about what he thinks and what might follow?

I guess there might be something concrete, but not much right this second. I could maybe clarify with him tomorrow if needed, but mostly this is me guessing what he thinks, which feels pretty hypothetical and annoying.

That sounds frustrating, and it makes sense that guessing what he thinks would feel pretty hypothetical and annoying. Would setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to think about it help you park it for now, and what’s the next worry on your mind?

Maybe, but “parking it” sounds a little optimistic when my brain doesn’t exactly respect appointments. I can try the 10 minutes tomorrow, but right now the next worry is the coworkers thing — I keep picturing them noticing I was tense and deciding I’m difficult.

That makes sense, and I hear the skepticism—when your mind is already revved up, “parking it” can sound unrealistic. With the coworkers worry, is there anything concrete you could actually do about it, or is it mostly outside your control and based on what you think they noticed?
Mostly outside my control, which is kind of the problem. I can maybe act normal tomorrow, but I can’t exactly make them un-notice whatever they think they saw, if they even noticed anything at all.

That sounds really frustrating, especially when the worry is about other people’s impressions and you can’t control what they noticed or decided. Given that, would it make sense to set aside that one for your worry time tomorrow and, for now, is there one more worry still pulling at you?

I guess I can “set it aside,” though it still feels a bit like pretending I can schedule my brain. Yeah, the last one is the office talking-about-me thing, which is probably the most annoying because there’s no way to know if it’s real or just me spiraling.

That sounds annoying and I get why it feels hard to trust a “schedule” when your mind is still churning. If you look at the office talking-about-me worry, is there anything concrete you can do with it, or does it seem more like a hypothetical story your mind is building when you don’t actually have evidence?

Yeah, when I’m being honest, it’s mostly a story my brain is building. I don’t actually have evidence that people are talking about me, but it feels believable enough in the moment that I keep going there. I can see how that’s not very concrete, even if it still feels very real.

That’s a really clear distinction, and it makes sense that something can feel very real even when the evidence is thin. Since this one sounds like a story your mind is building rather than something concrete, would it fit to put it into the same worry-time container for tomorrow, and then what do you notice about how all three worries feel now that each one has a place?

I mean, I can try putting them in the same bucket for tomorrow, even if I still think my brain will probably ignore the plan at 2 a.m. It does feel a little less like three separate emergencies when I say them out loud like that. Still not exactly calm, but maybe slightly less tangled than before.

That makes sense, and I hear both the skepticism and the small shift—less tangled is still something, even if calm isn’t there yet. If your brain does go back to this at 2 a.m., what seems to be the very first thing it would be trying to get you to do?

Probably to replay the meeting again and try to figure out exactly what I said wrong. Then it would want me to start mentally drafting fixes or explanations for tomorrow, like if I can just think hard enough I’ll prevent whatever bad impression I’m imagining. I can see that’s the pattern, even if it doesn’t actually help much.

That’s a sharp read on the pattern, and it sounds exhausting to get pulled into replaying and fixing mode even when you can see it doesn’t really help. When you notice that urge to mentally draft explanations, what does it seem to be trying to protect you from?

Probably from looking incompetent, I guess. If I can preemptively explain myself, then maybe I won’t get blindsided by some bad reaction tomorrow. I’m not saying it’s a great strategy, but it does seem like that’s what it’s trying to do.

That makes a lot of sense, and I hear that the strategy is trying to protect you from being caught off guard, even if it’s not working very well. When you imagine preemptively explaining yourself, does it seem more likely to actually prevent a bad reaction, or more likely to keep you stuck in the fear of one?

Honestly, probably the second one. I can tell myself I’m preventing a bad reaction, but in practice I think I just end up rehearsing the fear over and over, which keeps it alive. It might make me feel temporarily prepared, but it doesn’t really seem to change what happens tomorrow. If anything, it probably keeps me more locked into the whole thing than I need to be.

That’s a pretty important observation, and I can hear how clearly you’re seeing the difference between feeling prepared and actually being stuck in the loop. If rehearsing keeps the fear alive without changing tomorrow, what do you make of the part of you that still insists on doing it?

I think that part of me is basically trying to create a sense of control where there really isn’t much. It’s not that it’s irrational in some total way — it just seems like an old habit that thinks endless rehearsal equals safety. But when I’m honest, it probably cares more about relieving the immediate anxiety than about actually helping me handle tomorrow any better.

That’s a very clear way of putting it, and it sounds like you’re seeing both the logic and the cost of that habit. If it’s mostly about getting immediate relief rather than helping tomorrow, what do you think keeps that part of you so convinced it still deserves the job?

I think because it has worked just enough in the past to feel worth keeping around, even if only in the short term. When I’m anxious, the relief from “doing something” is immediate, so my brain probably treats that as proof it’s useful. I guess it’s also hard for that part of me to accept that not doing the mental rehearsal might be better, because then I’d have to sit with uncertainty instead of trying to outthink it.

That’s a really honest read of it, and it makes sense that immediate relief can make a habit feel “useful” even when the longer-term cost is obvious. When you picture that part of you choosing certainty through rehearsal versus sitting with uncertainty, what does it seem to believe would happen if it stopped rehearsing?

I think it believes I’d just be left totally exposed, like I’d be walking into tomorrow without armor. It probably imagines the uncertainty would get so uncomfortable that I’d fall apart or make the situation worse by not being “prepared enough.” When I say it out loud, that sounds a little dramatic, but that’s probably the level my brain is operating on. And maybe the bigger fear is not even the boss reaction itself, but feeling helpless while waiting for it.

That doesn’t sound dramatic to me; it sounds like you’ve put words to a pretty raw fear underneath the rehearsal. When that helplessness shows up, what does it seem to be asking you to believe about your ability to handle tomorrow if you don’t keep thinking it through?

I think it’s asking me to believe I won’t handle tomorrow very well unless I’ve already figured everything out in advance. Like if I stop thinking about it, I’ll be caught off guard and won’t know what to say or how to act. That’s probably not completely true, but I can see why my brain goes there — it treats uncertainty like evidence that I’m not prepared enough. And maybe that’s the part I’m actually scared of: not the meeting itself, but the possibility that I’ll feel exposed and not in control.

That sounds like you’ve really landed on the core fear, and it makes sense that “not in control” would feel bigger than the meeting itself. If your brain treats uncertainty as proof you’re unprepared, what evidence does it usually ignore about how you’ve handled situations before without having everything figured out?

I guess it ignores that I’ve actually gotten through a lot of uncomfortable work situations without having a perfect script. Usually I don’t feel prepared in the moment, but I still manage to say something reasonable and keep going. It’s like my brain only remembers the times I felt shaky, not the times I was shaky and still handled it fine. So maybe the real evidence is that uncertainty doesn’t automatically mean I’m incapable, even though it feels that way when I’m stressed.
That’s a meaningful shift, and you’ve put it really clearly. If you were to sum up, in your own words, what’s changed in how you’re seeing this situation now, what would you say?

I think I’m seeing that I’ve been treating a lot of this like it’s concrete evidence when it’s really mostly my mind filling in gaps. The boss thing still matters, but the bigger issue seems to be that I equate uncertainty with danger and then try to solve that by rehearsing, which just keeps me anxious. I’m also noticing that I’ve handled uncomfortable work situations before without having everything nailed down ahead of time. So it feels a little less like “I’m in trouble” and more like “I’m stressed and my brain is overworking to protect me.”

It sounds like you’ve moved from reading the situation as proof that something is wrong to noticing how much of the pressure comes from your mind trying to make uncertainty feel safer, and that shift seems to be opening up a different way of understanding your stress. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried my injury is making me too dependent on my partner, and they’ll start feeling overwhelmed or resentful. Then there's I keep thinking my family will see me as weak or disappointing because I can’t keep up with everyone right now. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried my recovery will cancel family plans and I’ll let everyone down at the next gathering.

That sounds exhausting, especially when your mind keeps circling those worries at night. Some worries are productive in that they point to something actionable, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical, uncontrollable, or about things that may never happen, and we can handle those differently; what is the first worry that is keeping you up?

The first one is probably the one about my partner. It feels the most immediate, because they’re the one helping me day to day, and I keep worrying I’m becoming too much. Even when they seem patient, my mind jumps to what if they’re just being nice and actually feel trapped or drained. That’s the thought that keeps looping the most when I’m trying to fall asleep.

That sounds really painful, especially when the thought keeps replaying even after your partner seems patient. As you look at it closely, is this worry something you can take a concrete action on right now, or is it more hypothetical and outside your control?

I think it’s kind of both, but mostly hypothetical and outside my control right now. I can do some concrete things, like ask them how they’re doing and make sure I’m not assuming everything, but I can’t control whether they secretly feel overwhelmed or resentful. The part that really gets me is that I keep treating my fear like a fact, even though I don’t actually have evidence that they’re unhappy. So I guess the actionable piece is checking in honestly, but the bigger worry itself is more about uncertainty than something I can solve tonight.

That’s a really clear distinction, and it makes sense that the uncertainty itself is what’s keeping the loop going. What’s one small, concrete check-in you could do with your partner, and exactly when would you do it?

I think I could do a simple check-in tomorrow evening after dinner, when things are calmer and not rushed. I could say something like, “I know you’ve been helping me a lot, and I want to check in about how you’re doing with all of this—do you feel okay, or is there anything I can do to make it easier?” That feels concrete without making it into a huge emotional conversation in the moment. I think just asking directly might help me separate what’s actually happening from what my anxiety is inventing.

That sounds thoughtful and grounded, and it makes sense that a direct check-in could help you test the fear against reality. Looking at the second worry about your family seeing you as weak or disappointing, would you say there’s a concrete action you can take there right now, or is that one more outside your control?

I think that one is mostly outside my control too, at least in the sense that I can’t force them to see me differently if they already have some idea in their heads. I can be honest with them about what’s going on and not hide it, but I can’t control whether they interpret my injury as weakness or whether they compare me to how I usually am. What makes it hard is that it feels so tied to my identity, like I’m disappointing them just by not being able to show up the way I normally would. So I guess there is some action I can take, but the core fear is really about how they’ll judge me, which I can’t fully manage.

That sounds like an important shift, especially in noticing the difference between what you can do and what you can’t control. How would you summarize, in your own words, the new perspective you’re starting to have about this family worry?

I think the new perspective is that I can choose to be honest and present with my family, but I can’t control the story they tell themselves about my injury or whether they see it as weakness. I’m realizing that a lot of the distress comes from me assuming disappointment before it’s actually been shown to me. So instead of treating that fear like a fact, I’m trying to see it as uncertainty that I’m projecting onto them. That doesn’t make the worry disappear, but it does make it feel a little less absolute and a little more manageable.

It sounds like you’ve moved from treating that fear as something fixed and proven to noticing it as a story your mind is filling in around uncertainty, and that shift is giving you a little more room to breathe. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

…Maybe I could just leave the kitchen for a minute and not say anything right away. Or, I don’t know, take a breath before I talk.

…Not very realistic in the moment, honestly. I’d probably need a reminder or some kind of cue to actually remember to step away.

conversations.content: I keep thinking that if my marriage is ending, then I must have failed at the one thing I was supposed to get right, and everyone is going to see me as broken. I’m scared I’m going to be alone forever and never feel stable again.

That took a lot of courage to say out loud, and it makes sense that this feels heavy and frightening. I’d like to slow it down with you and look at that thought carefully—not to dismiss how intense it feels, but to see how well it actually holds up when we examine it together; would you be willing to stay with it for a moment?
I guess, but I’m not convinced this is going to change anything. It just feels like one more way of telling myself a nicer story while my life is still falling apart.

That skepticism makes a lot of sense when things feel this raw, and I’m not trying to paper over how painful it is. If we set aside the “nicer story” idea for a moment and look at the thought itself, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

I mean, it’s a possibility, obviously, but it doesn’t feel like a small one when I’m in it. My brain keeps treating it like a fact, not just a possibility, so I don’t really know how much that distinction helps.

That makes sense—when a thought has that much emotional weight, it can feel like a fact even if part of you knows it’s not. Is someone else's opinion overly influencing my own, and if so, whose voice shows up most strongly in those moments?

Maybe, but I’m not sure this is some dramatic “whose voice” thing. It mostly sounds like my own voice, honestly, just with all the judgment turned up, and maybe some leftover stuff from my parents about not messing up your life.

That sounds less like some dramatic outside voice and more like an old judgment pattern that’s gotten very loud, which is an important distinction. When that thought shows up, does it feel like it’s based more on habit or a past experience than on what’s true right now?

Probably habit, I guess. But that doesn’t make it feel any less true in the moment, which is kind of the problem—I know I’m overreacting and still can’t just turn it off. So yeah, maybe it’s old stuff, but it’s still running the show right now.

That sounds really frustrating, especially when you can see the pattern and it still feels in control. When the thought says “I’ve failed” or “I’ll be alone forever,” what facts are you actually using in that moment, and what part is coming more from the feeling itself?

Honestly, the “facts” are that my marriage is ending and I don’t have any guarantee this won’t happen again, so it’s not like I’m inventing the whole thing. The rest of it—the “I’ve failed at life” and “I’ll be alone forever” part—is probably the panic talking, but it’s hard to separate that when it feels so immediate.

That’s a very fair distinction—you’re not inventing the breakup, and it makes sense that the panic grabs onto the bigger conclusions. What is the evidence for this thought, and what is the evidence against it?

The evidence for it is that my marriage really is ending, and that feels like pretty major proof that I messed something up. But against it, I’m still functioning, I do have people in my life, and one relationship falling apart doesn’t actually prove I’m broken or doomed to be alone forever. I don’t love saying that out loud, but I can at least see that the thought is bigger than the facts.

That’s a really solid, grounded read of it, even if it doesn’t feel good to say out loud. If we’re not going for forced positivity, how would you rewrite the original thought so it’s more accurate and balanced, based on everything you’ve just noticed?

Maybe something like: “My marriage is ending, and that hurts a lot, but it doesn’t mean I’m a failure as a person. I’m scared about the future, and I don’t know what it will look like yet, but I’m not actually doomed to be alone forever.” That feels more accurate, even if I still don’t exactly believe it all the way yet.

That sounds like a much more accurate version, and it makes sense that believing it fully is still a work in progress. When you say you don’t believe it all the way yet, what seems to be holding onto the old version most strongly?

Probably the fear, honestly. When I’m alone with my thoughts, it’s like my brain goes straight back to worst-case scenarios because that feels safer than hoping for something better and being disappointed. And I think there’s still this part of me that equates being divorced with being fundamentally “less than,” even though I can see how unfair that is.

That makes a lot of sense—worst-case thinking can feel protective when disappointment feels unbearable, even though it keeps you stuck. When your mind says being divorced means being “less than,” what does it seem to be predicting would happen if you didn’t buy into that belief?

I think it’s predicting that if I let myself believe I’m not less than, I’ll get complacent or delusional and then get blindsided again. Like, if I stop criticizing myself first, other people will see the mess before I do and reject me for it. So the belief is almost like a weird shield, even though it’s also making everything worse.

That’s a really sharp observation, and it makes sense that a harsh belief can start to feel like protection when the alternative feels risky. When that “shield” shows up, what does it seem to be protecting you from in the short term, and what does it cost you over time?

In the short term, I think it protects me from feeling completely blindsided or stupid, like if I beat myself up first then it won’t hurt as much if someone else judges me. It also gives me this false sense of control, like I’m staying on top of the damage instead of just sitting in it. But over time it costs me a lot of peace, because I end up living inside this constant self-attack and it makes it harder to believe I could ever recover or be seen differently.

That’s a really clear tradeoff you just named, and it sounds like you can see both why the self-attack shows up and why it keeps hurting you. If you had to put the shift into your own words, what would you say you now understand about this belief and what it’s been doing for you?

I think I’m starting to see that the “I’m a failure” story isn’t really truth so much as armor—it shows up fast because it thinks it’s protecting me from humiliation and rejection. But the cost is that it keeps me trapped in fear and makes this divorce feel like proof that I’m fundamentally flawed, when that’s not actually what it means. So the belief is trying to help me by lowering the risk of being surprised, but it’s also making me treat myself like an enemy.

That’s a really important shift—you’re noticing how that harsh story has been operating less like a verdict and more like a shield, even while it’s been keeping you stuck in fear and turning pain into self-attack. What might you want to carry forward from the way you just made sense of it?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. During a team meeting, the client was told their responsibilities would shift immediately to include managing a high-priority project, with little notice and no discussion about workload or support. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It takes courage to look at this so honestly, especially when you’re not proud of how it came out. If we map it together as a short anger diary—trigger, warning signs, response, and outcomes—what were the first signs in your body or behavior before the anger fully hit, like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

The first signs were really physical before I even fully realized I was getting angry. My jaw got tight, my shoulders went up, and I could feel my heart beating faster as the meeting kept going. Mentally, I started getting stuck on the idea that they were just dumping this on me without asking, and I could feel myself wanting to interrupt. I also noticed I got very quiet for a minute, which is usually a sign for me that I’m trying to hold it in before it comes out badly.

That’s really useful to notice, because those physical shifts and the quiet moment sound like the earliest window where things could still change before it tipped over. On a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?

At its peak, I’d say it was around an 8 out of 10, maybe even a little higher for a moment because I felt really cornered and embarrassed. I didn’t explode right away, but I did interrupt the meeting more sharply than I meant to and said something like, “This is a lot to drop on me all at once,” with a pretty tense tone. After that I went quiet again, but I could feel my face getting hot and I was barely listening because I was still replaying how unfair it felt. Once the meeting ended, I left pretty abruptly and stayed upset for the rest of the day.

Thank you for being so honest about how intense that was and how it played out in the moment. When you look at the outcome in two parts, what happened externally in the room and with the other person, and then what happened inside you afterward, both right away and over the next hours or days?

Externally, I think it made the room feel tense pretty fast. The meeting kind of stalled after I spoke up, and I could tell the other person got more guarded, like they were trying to move past it without really addressing what I said. Inside, I felt embarrassed almost immediately, and then angry again at myself for not handling it better. Over the next few hours, I kept replaying the moment and feeling stuck between thinking I had a valid point and worrying that I came across as difficult or unprofessional.

You’re seeing the whole cycle very clearly now: the trigger in the meeting, the early physical warning signs, the sharper response, and then the tension and self-criticism afterward. Looking at those warning signs you described, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment—before the response—that might change the outcome?

I think the biggest thing I could do is pause before I speak, even if it’s just for a few seconds, and take a slow breath instead of trying to push through the feeling. If I noticed my jaw tightening and shoulders rising, I could remind myself that I’m getting activated and that I don’t have to answer immediately. I could also say something neutral like, “I want to think about this for a moment,” or ask to continue the conversation after the meeting so I don’t react from that cornered feeling. Honestly, that would probably help me feel less trapped and give me a chance to respond more clearly instead of from pure frustration.

That sounds like a meaningful shift, especially from feeling cornered to seeing that you may have a small pause point before things escalate. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you about this situation?

What’s changed for me is that I’m seeing this less as “I just lose control” and more as something that builds up in a pretty predictable way. I can notice the physical signs earlier now, and that gives me a small chance to slow things down before I say something sharp. I also realize the anger wasn’t just about the project itself—it was about feeling blindsided and not having any say, which helps it make more sense to me. That doesn’t excuse how I reacted, but it does make me feel a little more hopeful that I can handle it differently next time.

It sounds like you’re leaving with a clearer sense that this isn’t just something happening to you out of nowhere, but something you can begin to recognize earlier and understand more fully. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of uneasiness lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds pretty uncomfortable, and it makes sense to want some way to pin it down instead of just sitting with a vague “uneasy” feeling. If we map it together for a moment, what would you call the emotion as specifically as you can right now, and how strong is it from 0 to 100?

I don’t know that putting a neat label on it is going to change much, but if I had to guess, it feels more like worry mixed with a bit of irritation. Maybe a 60 out of 100 most of the time, though it comes and goes.

That makes sense, especially if the feeling isn’t tied to one simple label and it comes and goes at a fairly solid 60. When you think back to one specific moment it showed up most clearly, what was happening right then or what went through your mind?

Honestly, I’m not sure there was some big dramatic moment—it’s more of a general annoyance that keeps hanging around. If I had to pick one, it’s when people keep acting like this new family addition is some major life event I’m supposed to be thrilled about, and I’m just not there yet.

That sounds frustrating, especially when it feels like other people are putting a big emotional expectation on you that doesn’t match what’s actually true for you. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a quick flash?

Probably something like, “Here we go again, everyone expecting me to act delighted.” It’s not that I’m ضد the new family member or anything, I just get irritated when people assume I should feel a certain way on their schedule.

That sounds like a pretty clear automatic thought, and it makes sense that the irritation would spike when you feel pushed into a role you didn’t choose. What did you do in response to that feeling right away, and was there anything you started avoiding afterward?

Mostly I just kept my mouth shut and made the polite noises people expect, which I suppose counts as “dealing with it.” Afterward I avoided sticking around for the extra chatter about how wonderful everything is, because honestly I didn’t feel like pretending any harder than I already was.

That makes sense—you were trying to get through it without adding more friction, and the avoidance sounds like it was a way to stop the pretending from feeling any worse. What were the consequences of that right away, and then over time, and now that you can see the whole chain—trigger, thought, emotion, behavior, consequence—is there any link where a small shift might interrupt the pattern?

Right away the consequence was mostly that I got to leave without saying something I’d regret, so that part worked fine. Over time, though, I suppose it keeps me a little more on edge because I’m still carrying the irritation around instead of just having a normal conversation like everyone else thinks I should. If there’s a “small shift,” I’m not convinced it needs to be some therapy trick—I’d rather just have people stop pressuring me, but I guess I could maybe stay a little longer before bailing if that’s what you mean.

That makes a lot of sense—you found a way to avoid saying something regretful, but it also leaves you carrying the irritation afterward, and I hear the skepticism about “therapy tricks.” If you stayed a little longer next time, what do you imagine you’d need to say to yourself or notice in the moment so it felt more like your choice and less like just enduring it?

I suppose I’d need to remind myself that I’m not obligated to perform enthusiasm on command. If I could notice that I’m getting wound up before I hit the point of wanting to leave, maybe I could just take a breath and stay civil without feeling like I’m being trapped there. I’m not saying that fixes anything, but it might make it feel a little less like I’m just putting up with everyone.

That sounds pretty grounded, and I hear you not wanting to oversell it as some big fix. When you notice yourself getting wound up, what would be the earliest sign that tells you you’re at that point rather than already past it?

Probably the first sign is that I start tightening up and getting shorter in my answers, even if I’m still trying to be polite. I also notice I start mentally planning my exit instead of actually listening, which is usually a clue I’m getting past the point of being useful. I guess that’s the stage where I should probably slow down before I get fully annoyed.

That’s a useful bit of self-observation, and it sounds like you can catch the shift pretty early, before it turns into full annoyance. When you notice the tightening and the exit-planning, what do you think is happening in your mind about the situation or about the people around you?

I think part of it is that I start assuming the conversation is going to stay on that same track—lots of cheerful talk I’m supposed to match, whether I feel it or not. And then I probably start thinking people are more interested in getting the “right” reaction out of me than actually talking to me. I don’t love admitting that, but that seems to be where my head goes.

That sounds like a pretty painful place to be mentally, and it makes sense you wouldn’t love admitting it if it leaves you feeling cornered. When that thought shows up that people want the “right” reaction rather than really talking to you, what feeling does it create in you first—before the irritation takes over?

I think the first thing under the irritation is probably feeling shut out, like I’m already being sorted into a reaction before I’ve even had a chance to say anything. Maybe a little hurt, if I’m being honest, though I’d rather call it annoyance because that sounds less dramatic. It’s not exactly a pleasant thing to notice, but I can see why the irritation shows up so fast.

That’s a pretty important shift, and it sounds like you’re seeing that the irritation may be covering something more vulnerable underneath, which is not nothing. If you were to put that new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you understand what’s happening?

I suppose what’s changed is I can see this isn’t just me being annoyed for no reason. A lot of the irritation seems to come from feeling like people have already decided how I’m supposed to react, and that leaves me feeling a bit shut out. I still don’t like making a big emotional thing out of it, but I can admit there’s some hurt under the annoyance. That probably explains why it’s been sticking around instead of just passing.

It sounds like you’ve landed on something more precise than “just annoyance,” and there’s a lot of clarity in noticing how being boxed into a reaction can leave a person feeling shut out in the first place. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I keep worrying that no matter what I do, my in-laws are going to judge me and see me as not good enough, and I hate feeling like I’m constantly being tested. It makes me anxious that this tension will keep growing and start affecting my relationship and my work too.

That sounds really heavy, and I appreciate how clearly you’re putting it into words. Let’s slow this down together, not to dismiss how anxious this feels, but to look carefully at the thought and see how much it really holds up when we examine it closely, and I’d like to stay with it with you — what feels most true in that worry right now?

What feels most true is that I’m scared they’ve already decided who I am, and that anything I do now is just going to be filtered through that. I keep replaying conversations and looking for signs that I’ve said the wrong thing or come across as awkward, so it starts to feel like I’m under a microscope. I know part of this is probably my anxiety filling in gaps, but emotionally it still feels very real, like I have to prove I belong. And underneath that, I think I’m afraid of being rejected not just by them, but of my partner seeing me differently too.

That makes a lot of sense, especially the way the anxiety turns ordinary moments into something that feels scrutinized, and I can hear how painful it is to carry the fear of being rejected by both them and your partner. How might others interpret the same situation differently?

I think someone else might see it as my in-laws being a little distant or opinionated, but not necessarily as a judgment of my worth as a person or as a partner. They might interpret awkward moments as normal family tension or just people getting used to each other, instead of proof that I’m failing some test. I can also imagine my partner seeing it as me being overly hard on myself, rather than thinking less of me. It’s hard to fully believe that in the moment, but I can see that my mind may be making the situation feel much more personal and absolute than it actually is.

That’s a really thoughtful shift, and it sounds like you can already see how your mind may be turning distance and awkwardness into something far more personal and absolute. When you ask yourself, “Is my thought overly critical?”, what specific examples come up that make it feel that way?

A few examples come up right away. If they don’t respond quickly to a text or seem a little reserved in conversation, I tend to jump to “they don’t like me” instead of just seeing it as them being busy or naturally less warm. I also notice that after family gatherings, I replay every little thing I said and focus almost entirely on what might have sounded awkward, while ignoring any neutral or positive moments. When I’m honest, the thought does feel overly critical because it assumes the worst about me before there’s really solid evidence.

That’s a really clear and important insight, and it sounds like you’re noticing how quickly your mind moves from uncertainty to the worst-case meaning. Given what you’ve just described, is your thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

I think it’s more of a possibility than a likely scenario, even though it can feel very likely when I’m anxious. There isn’t really solid evidence that they’ve decided I’m not good enough; a lot of what I’m reacting to is ambiguity, and I tend to fill that in with the worst interpretation. When I step back, it seems more likely that they’re just reserved or that we’re still figuring each other out, rather than this being a fixed judgment of me. I can see that my anxiety makes the possibility feel much bigger than it probably is.

That feels like a meaningful shift, and I’m glad you can see the difference between what anxiety suggests and what the evidence actually supports. If you were to sum up this new perspective in your own words, what would you say it is?

I’d say the new perspective is that my in-laws’ behavior is not the same thing as a verdict on my worth, even if my anxiety keeps trying to make it feel that way. A lot of what I’ve been taking personally may actually just be normal distance, awkwardness, or people getting used to each other. I still feel hurt and uneasy, but I can see more clearly that I’m filling in gaps with the worst-case story. It feels a little more grounding to remind myself that this is a possibility I’m afraid of, not a fact.

It sounds like you were able to separate the feelings that come up from the story your anxiety wants to tell, and that created a little more room to see the situation with less self-blame. The next time this feeling shows up, what might you want to remind yourself to ask first?

Externally? She got quiet, looked hurt, and then the whole room felt tense, which I guess was not exactly a surprise. And she’d probably need to know I’m not using it to avoid the issue, just to stop myself from saying something worse. After a week of trying to wake up earlier and limit phone use, the client missed the new wake-up time on two mornings and spent extra time scrolling on the phone during lunch. The only thing that stands out is the fact that I failed twice, so this whole habit change is probably not going to work for me." and I've been feeling frustrated, discouraged, embarrassed.

That sounds frustrating and pretty embarrassing, especially when you were trying to make a real change. I’m wondering whether the missed wake-up and the scrolling were the whole story, or whether the thought “I already messed up” may have shaped how you felt and what you did next—what did you actually do in response to those thoughts and feelings?

Honestly, I’m not sure that distinction matters that much—missing the goal is still missing the goal. But I guess after I had that thought, I kind of gave up for the rest of the day, told myself I’d already blown it, and then I was less careful about the phone stuff too.

That makes sense—if it feels like you missed the goal, it’s easy to see why the rest of the day started to feel like a write-off. I’m noticing the mind may have zoomed in on the two misses and filtered out the parts where you were still trying, so if someone else looked at the exact same week, what might they say it showed instead?

Maybe they’d say I was being too hard on myself, but that sounds a little too neat. Sure, I did try for five days, but the two misses still feel like the real data point to me, not just “my mind zooming in.”

That pushback makes sense; “too neat” can sound like it’s glossing over the part that hurt. If you took the interpretation that you were being too hard on yourself and that the five days of trying mattered too, what emotion do you think would show up most strongly?

I’m not convinced that interpretation changes much, but if I go with it, I guess I’d feel mostly disappointed, maybe a little relieved that it wasn’t a total failure. Honestly, the stronger feeling is still frustration, because even if five days “count,” the two misses are the ones that keep jumping out at me.

That makes sense—there’s a real difference between “this is frustrating and disappointing” and “this means I failed,” even if the frustration still feels loud. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

I’m not sure it would have changed much in the moment, to be honest. Maybe I would’ve been less likely to blow off the rest of the day, or at least not used it as a reason to scroll more, but I’m not convinced disappointment is some magic fix. It still would’ve felt annoying and probably made me want to just stop trying for a bit.

That’s a pretty fair pushback—disappointment isn’t magic, and it still would’ve felt annoying and made you want to back off a bit. If the situation stayed the same but the thought changed from “I blew it” to “I’m disappointed,” what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I guess it tells me the thought changes the intensity a bit, but not the actual facts of what happened. I’m still not sure that means much beyond “reframing” it in a nicer way, because the annoying part is that I still missed the goal. But yeah, maybe the thought is part of why it felt like the whole day was ruined instead of just a bad morning.

That sounds like you’re separating the facts from the meaning pretty clearly, even if the meaning still feels annoying rather than helpful. If the thought made it feel like the whole day was ruined instead of just a bad morning, what did that belief push you to do—or stop doing—next?

It pushed me to stop trying to be intentional for the rest of the day. I basically told myself, “Well, this is already ruined,” so I was more likely to keep scrolling, skip being careful at lunch, and not really bother correcting course until the next day. I can see that the thought didn’t just describe the day — it kind of gave me permission to check out.

That’s a really sharp observation, and it sounds frustrating to notice how quickly “ruined” turned into permission to disengage. If that thought gave you permission to check out, what does that suggest about how much control the thought had over the rest of the day?

I guess it suggests the thought had more control than I want to admit. Not total control, because I still chose what I did, but it definitely nudged me into the “might as well” mindset pretty fast. That’s annoying to realize, because it means the problem wasn’t just the missed goal — it was also the story I told myself about what it meant.

That’s a pretty important distinction to notice, even if it’s annoying to see how much the story shaped the rest of the day. When you think about that “might as well” mindset, what does it seem to be protecting you from, if anything?

I hadn’t really thought of it as protecting me, but I guess it’s protecting me from feeling like I’m failing on purpose. If I tell myself “might as well,” then I don’t have to sit with the discomfort of trying hard and still messing up. That said, it’s a pretty lousy kind of protection, because it just turns one bad morning into a worse day.

That sounds really insightful, and I can hear why it feels like lousy protection when it ends up stretching one bad morning into the whole day. If “might as well” is helping you avoid the feeling of trying and still messing up, what does that say about what feels harder to tolerate: the mistake itself, or the meaning you attach to it?

I think it’s probably the meaning more than the mistake itself. The mistake is annoying, but the part that really gets to me is what it seems to say about me—like I’m not actually the kind of person who follows through. I’m not saying that’s rational, but that’s definitely where it stings.

That makes a lot of sense—the mistake is one thing, but the sting seems to come from what it appears to say about your character. When that “I’m not the kind of person who follows through” thought shows up, what evidence do you notice your mind using to back it up, and what evidence gets pushed aside?

It latches onto the two missed mornings and the lunch scrolling, and then kind of turns those into proof that this is who I am. What gets pushed aside is that I did stick with it for five days, and I was trying to change a habit that’s been automatic for a long time. So the evidence isn’t really “I never follow through,” it’s more like “I slipped and then let the slip mean too much,” which is a different thing, even if it doesn’t feel great to admit.

That’s a pretty clear shift, even if it doesn’t feel good to say out loud: you’re noticing the difference between a slip and a whole identity verdict. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you?

I think what’s changed is I’m starting to see that the two misses were real, but I was treating them like they proved something way bigger than they actually did. It wasn’t just “I failed,” it was “I failed, so I should stop trying,” and that second part is what really messed up the rest of the day. I’m still frustrated, but I can at least see that the habit problem and the self-judgment got tangled together.

It sounds like you were able to separate the facts of what happened from the much harsher meaning you had been attaching to them, and that distinction seems to have opened up a little more room for you than there was before. The next time that kind of moment shows up, what might you want to ask yourself first?
