conversations.content: If I get dismissed from work, people at the office will think I’m incompetent and talk about me behind my back. I keep imagining that when I run into coworkers or former clients, they’ll look at me with pity or embarrassment, and I’ll feel humiliated every time I leave the house.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense that your mind is trying to protect you by running through the worst-case image. When we worry, it can start treating what could happen as if it will happen, so what are some concrete, observable clues you have that suggest this worst-case scenario may not actually come true?

One clue is that I actually don’t know what my coworkers are thinking, and a few of them have been kind to me lately even though things at work are tense. I also realize that when people have left jobs before, most of the time everyone moved on pretty quickly, and it wasn’t as dramatic as it feels in my head. My manager has given me some feedback, but it hasn’t been outright dismissal, so I’m kind of jumping ahead to the worst outcome. I think part of me is filling in all the blanks with humiliation because that feels easier than sitting with the uncertainty.

That’s a very grounded observation, and it sounds like you’re noticing real evidence rather than trying to force yourself into reassurance. If those clues are right and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you think would probably happen instead, and what feels like the most realistic outcome?

I think the most realistic outcome is probably that if I do lose the job, people will be awkward for a little while and then mostly get back to their own lives. A few coworkers might be sympathetic or curious, but not nearly as focused on me as I imagine when I’m spiraling. I’d probably feel embarrassed and sad for a while, but not constantly humiliated the way I picture in my head. I guess the bigger truth is that it would be hard, but not the permanent social disaster I keep assuming it will be.

That sounds like a really balanced and honest view of what’s most likely, and I can hear how much relief and realism is starting to come in. Even if we stayed with the worst-case scenario for a moment, what would you imagine yourself doing step by step after that happened, and how do you think you might be doing a little further down the line?

If I got dismissed, I think the first step would be just getting through the immediate shock and probably telling one or two trusted people so I’m not carrying it alone. Then I’d need to handle practical things like updating my resume, looking at openings, and probably figuring out unemployment or finances, which feels overwhelming but doable in pieces. I imagine I’d feel really raw at first, but a few weeks or months later I’d probably be more focused on rebuilding than on the humiliation itself. Even in the worst case, I don’t think I’d stay stuck there forever.

You’ve just laid out a real path through even the worst case, and that seems to soften the idea that dismissal would be the end of everything. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what feels different about it?

The worry feels less like an absolute certainty now and more like something scary that might happen, but that I could actually handle if it did. Earlier it felt like dismissal would automatically mean humiliation, social judgment, and this huge collapse of my life, but now I can see there are steps I’d take and that people would probably move on more than I was imagining. It still scares me, and I can feel the sadness underneath it, but it feels less overwhelming and less final. I think what’s different is that I’m noticing the gap between the story my anxiety tells me and the more realistic outcome.

That’s a really clear shift, and it makes sense that the sadness can still be there even as the fear feels less absolute. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you?

I think what’s changed is that I’m seeing dismissal as a painful possibility, not a guaranteed catastrophe. I’m realizing I’ve been assuming other people would judge me much more harshly and for much longer than they probably would. It still hurts to think about, but now I can also see that I’d have ways to cope and recover instead of just being trapped in humiliation. That makes the fear feel more manageable, even if the sadness is still real.

That sounds like a meaningful shift in how you’re holding this—there’s still real pain there, and at the same time, a bit more room to see yourself as able to face it rather than be consumed by it. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried my coworkers will think I’m less competent now that I’m pregnant and start leaving me out of important work conversations. Then there's I keep thinking people at work will judge me if I need to sit down more, eat more often, or leave on time because of pregnancy. And I also keep thinking about: I’m afraid my friends will think I’m boring or high-maintenance if I say no to late dinners or plans that are too exhausting while I’m pregnant.

That sounds exhausting, especially when the same fears keep circling at night. Sometimes worries are productive because there’s something concrete you can actually do about them, and sometimes they’re unproductive because they’re hypothetical or outside your control; which of those three feels like the first worry that’s keeping you up?

I mean, I guess the work thing is first, but I’m not convinced separating them is that helpful because they all kind of run together at night anyway. It just feels like if I’m not constantly on top of everything, people will notice I’m pregnant and assume I’m less capable.

It makes sense that separating them feels a bit artificial when they all blur together at night, and I hear how high the pressure feels to stay “on top of everything” so no one notices a change. If we look just at the work worry for a moment, is there a concrete action you could take with it, or does it seem more like a hypothetical judgment from other people that’s outside your control?

I mean, maybe there are some concrete things, like keeping people updated and trying not to miss anything, but that doesn’t really stop the part I’m worried about. The bigger issue feels hypothetical, yeah, but it’s still hard to shrug off because I can’t exactly prove people won’t start treating me differently.

That makes sense — when the worry is about other people’s judgments, there’s no clean proof either way, so it can feel stuck in your head. Would you be willing to set aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to think about the work worry on purpose, and if so, what time would you choose?

I guess I could, but honestly it feels a little like scheduling time to worry, which sounds kind of backwards. If I had to pick, maybe 7:30 tomorrow evening, though I’m not really convinced that’ll make my brain stop doing this at 2 a.m.

It does sound backwards, and I get why you’d be skeptical if your brain is being stubborn at 2 a.m. With the work worry specifically, when you look at it closely, does it feel like something you can take concrete action on, or more like other people’s reactions are outside your control?

Honestly, mostly outside my control, which is kind of the annoying part. I can do the practical stuff — keep people updated, stay organized, whatever — but I can’t stop coworkers from deciding I’m less capable just because I’m pregnant. So yeah, there are some actions, but the thing actually keeping me up is the part I can’t control.

That makes a lot of sense — you can do the practical pieces, but the part that’s really grabbing you is the uncertainty about how other people will react, and that’s frustrating. That sounds exhausting, especially when your mind keeps circling at night trying to make sense of all three worries. Sometimes it can help to sort worries into ones that are productive—about something you can actually do something about—and ones that are unproductive, meaning hypothetical or uncontrollable, and they get handled differently; what is the first worry that is keeping you up?

The first one that keeps grabbing me is the worry that when I go to the school event, people will think I’m out of place because I’m retired and not really part of that world anymore. It feels embarrassing in a way, like I’m trying to step back into a room where I no longer belong. I know that may be more about my own fear than what anyone is actually thinking, but at night it gets very loud and convincing.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense that it feels louder at night when there’s less to anchor it. When you look at this worry closely, does it seem like something you could take a concrete action on, or does it feel more hypothetical and outside your control?

It feels mostly hypothetical and outside my control, which is part of what makes it so frustrating. I can choose to go to the event and be polite, but I can’t control whether anyone sees me as out of place or what story they make up about me. When I really sit with it, I think the bigger issue is that I’m afraid of being judged and feeling invisible in a place that used to feel familiar to me. So I suppose the concrete part is just deciding how I want to show up, even if I can’t control how it’s received.

That’s a very clear distinction, and it sounds like you’re seeing both the limits of control and the part that is still yours to choose. What is one small, concrete next step you’d be willing to take, and exactly when will you do it?

I think one small next step I’m willing to take is to decide ahead of time that I’ll go to the event for a set amount of time, rather than leaving it vague and letting my anxiety take over. I can choose to do that tomorrow afternoon, when things are calmer, and write down a simple plan for how I want to show up—just be polite, say hello, and then leave when I’ve stayed long enough. That feels concrete to me because it gives me something I can control without asking me to solve everyone else’s opinions. Even saying it out loud makes me feel a little less helpless.

That sounds like a thoughtful, grounded plan, and it makes sense that having something specific would ease some of the helplessness. Looking at the second worry—about saying hello and being seen as awkward or nosy—does that feel like something you can take a concrete action on, or does it feel more hypothetical and outside your control?

It feels mostly hypothetical and outside my control, though there is a small concrete piece in it. I can choose to say hello in a simple, respectful way, but I can’t control whether someone interprets that as friendly or awkward or nosy. What seems to be at the center of it is my fear of being misread, especially now that I’m retired and don’t have the same role to lean on. So I think the action is limited, but the bigger task is accepting that I can be kind and still not manage everyone’s reaction.
That’s a very thoughtful shift, and it sounds like you’re separating what you can control from what you can’t in a pretty clear way. How would you summarize this new perspective in your own words?

I think my new perspective is that I can choose my behavior, but I can’t control how other people interpret it. I can be simple, polite, and respectful when I say hello, and that has to be enough even if someone still thinks I’m awkward or nosy. What’s really happening is that I’m afraid of being misread now that I’m retired and no longer have the same identity to stand on. So the goal is not to get everyone to see me correctly, but to show up in a way that feels true to me and let go of the rest.

That feels like a meaningful settling into what is yours to shape and what isn’t, with a real shift toward trusting your own way of showing up even when you can’t steer the story others make of it. As you leave today, what feels like the most important part of that perspective to carry forward?

conversations.content: I’m worried that changing schools will throw everything off and I’ll never really settle in. What if I fall behind, make no friends, and end up feeling completely alone?

That sounds really heavy, and I appreciate how clearly you’re putting the fear into words. Let’s slow this down together—not to dismiss how real it feels, but to see whether this thought holds up when we look at it carefully; would you be willing to stay with it for a moment?

Yeah, I’m willing to stay with it. I think part of why it feels so intense is that school has always been one of the main places where I’ve measured whether I’m doing okay, so the idea of losing my footing there feels bigger than just a simple transition. When I think about it carefully, I can see I’m jumping straight to the worst-case scenario, but emotionally it still feels very convincing. I guess I’m also afraid that if I don’t adjust quickly, it means something is wrong with me rather than just that change is hard.

That makes a lot of sense, especially if school has been a place where you’ve measured your sense of being okay; of course a change there could feel like it says something bigger about you. Given that emotional pull, when you look at the thought from both sides, is my thought overly critical?

Yes, I think it probably is overly critical, even though it doesn’t feel that way in the moment. It’s like I’m taking a normal adjustment struggle and turning it into a judgment about my worth or ability, which is pretty harsh. On the other hand, I don’t think the fear is completely irrational either, because I do care a lot about doing well and fitting in, so the stakes feel high to me. But when I step back, the thought seems more like a scared inner voice than an accurate prediction.

That’s a really thoughtful distinction, and it sounds like you’re noticing both the harshness of the thought and the real importance school has for you. Am I basing this thought on feelings rather than facts, and what specific examples do you have that point one way or the other?

Yes, I think I’m basing a lot of it on feelings rather than facts, especially the fear and uncertainty that come with not knowing what the new school will be like. The facts I do have are more balanced: I’ve adjusted to changes before, and even if it took time, I eventually found my footing more than once. What makes the fear feel so convincing is that I’m imagining how bad it would feel if things went wrong, not necessarily what is most likely to happen. So when I look at it honestly, the evidence doesn’t really support the idea that I’ll fail or be completely alone—it mostly supports the idea that I’m anxious about a big change.

You’ve done a really careful job separating what you feel from what the facts actually show, and that kind of honesty matters a lot here. What is the evidence for this thought, and what is the evidence against it?

The evidence for the thought is mostly that this is a real change, and I do sometimes take a while to feel comfortable in new environments, so there is a genuine adjustment period I’m worried about. I also know I can get in my own head when I’m anxious, which can make me seem less open at first. But the evidence against it is stronger: I’ve handled transitions before, I usually do eventually connect with people, and struggling at the beginning doesn’t mean I’ll fail overall. So I think the thought has some emotional truth in it, but not much factual support for the worst-case outcome I’m imagining.

You’ve moved from seeing this as a prediction of failure to something more like a fear about adjustment, and that’s an important shift. If you were to put your new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed?

I think what’s changed is that I’m starting to see this as a difficult transition instead of proof that I’m going to fail. I still feel anxious about it, but I’m not quite believing the worst-case story as much, because I can see there’s evidence that I’ve adapted before. It feels less like “something is wrong with me” and more like “this is a hard change that I’ll need time to settle into.” That shift makes it feel a little less overwhelming and a little more manageable.

It sounds like you’re beginning to relate to this as a hard transition you’re moving through, rather than letting the worst-case story define what it means about you, and that seems to be making the experience feel more workable. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: If I try to reconcile with my spouse and it does not go well, people will see me as a failure. At my age, after retirement, I worry that family and friends will think I could not keep my marriage together and that I have somehow wasted my life.

That sounds like a heavy fear, and it makes sense that at this stage of life it could feel especially personal. When the mind worries, it can start treating what could happen as though it will happen, so I’m curious what concrete, observable clues you notice that suggest this worst-case outcome may not actually come true?

One concrete clue is that my family has generally been more compassionate than I give them credit for. Even when things have been difficult between my spouse and me, they haven’t openly judged me or treated me like I’ve failed. I also know that a relationship not working out would not automatically mean I wasted my life, because I’ve done a lot of good things as a parent, friend, and person. I think the fear is strong, but when I step back, I can see there’s more evidence that people would care about me than condemn me.

That sounds like real evidence you’re weighing, not wishful thinking, and it seems you’re already noticing that your fear is stronger than the actual pattern you’ve seen from your family and from your life overall. If those clues are accurate and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you think is the realistic, most likely outcome instead?

I think the most likely outcome is that people would be concerned for me, but not condemning. They might see the situation as painful and complicated rather than as proof that I failed at my life. Even if my marriage remains uncertain, I suspect I would still be respected for trying to handle it honestly and carefully. When I think about it that way, it feels less like an ending and more like a difficult chapter I would have to move through.

That feels like a much more balanced and grounded way of seeing it, and I hear the shift from “ending” to “difficult chapter.” If you were to imagine the worst really did happen, what would you actually do first, then next, and as you keep moving through it, what would tell you that you were eventually okay?

If the worst did happen, I think my first step would be to let myself grieve instead of trying to pretend I was fine. Then I would probably reach out to one or two trusted people, because I know I would not want to isolate myself with my thoughts. After that, I’d focus on practical things like my living situation, finances, and how to keep some steady routines in place. I think I would know I was eventually okay when I could think about the marriage with sadness but without constant panic, and when I felt I still had a sense of purpose and connection in my life.

You’ve just laid out a clear path through even the worst case, which suggests this fear isn’t a dead end but something you could move through with support, grief, and practical steps. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what feels different about it?

The worry feels less absolute now than it did at the start. Before, it felt like if reconciliation failed, it would mean something terrible and final about me, but now I can see there would still be steps I could take and people I could lean on. What feels different is that I’m not as trapped in the idea of being judged or ruined by it; I can more clearly see that I would probably be sad, but still intact. It feels like the fear has gone from being this huge, undefined threat to something painful but manageable.

That’s a meaningful shift, and it sounds like you’ve moved from seeing this as a verdict on your life to seeing it as something painful you could still face and recover from. In your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about reconciliation and what it would mean if it didn’t go the way you hope?

I think my new perspective is that reconciliation is important, but it is not the measure of my worth or the sum of my life. If it doesn’t go the way I hope, it would be painful and disappointing, but it would not mean I failed as a person or wasted my years. I would still have my relationships, my values, and the ways I’ve shown up for people over time. What I’m taking from this is that I can face uncertainty without assuming it will destroy me.

That sounds like a meaningful shift toward holding both the importance of reconciliation and a steadier sense of yourself, even if the outcome stays uncertain. As you leave with that in mind, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: If the school change means extra fees, new supplies, or transportation costs, I might not be able to keep up with the budget and could fall behind on the mortgage. Then there's I keep thinking I’ll miss some important enrollment deadline or paperwork requirement and my child won’t be properly registered. And I also keep thinking about: This change could force me to rearrange work hours, childcare, and pickups in a way that will completely disrupt the family routine.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind is grabbing onto all the practical pressure points at once. Some worries are productive because they point to something actionable, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical or not really in your control, and the way we work with each is different. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

I don’t know that splitting them into “productive” and “unproductive” really helps right now—it all feels pretty real when I’m trying to sleep. The first thing that keeps hitting me is the money piece, because if the school change means extra costs, that can snowball fast.

That makes sense; when you’re lying there at night, it’s hard to feel like any of it is “just a thought” if it could affect the mortgage. With the money piece, what part of it is something you can take a concrete action on right now, and what part is still hypothetical or outside your control?

Honestly, I’m not sure how much of this is “outside my control” if the bills still show up either way. I guess the concrete part would be checking what the actual costs are and whether there’s any assistance or fee waivers, but that still doesn’t make the worry go away if the numbers are bad.

It makes sense that the worry doesn’t vanish just because you can name a possible next step, especially when the numbers could still be bad. What’s one small concrete action you’d be willing to take to check the actual costs or assistance options, and exactly when tomorrow would you do it?

I mean, I can check the school’s fee list and maybe see if there’s any waiver info, but I’m not convinced that’s going to change much if they’re expensive. I could do it tomorrow evening after work, probably around 7, assuming I’m not already exhausted from the day.

You’re right to be skeptical that checking will magically fix anything, and it’s clear you’re trying to be realistic about the numbers. Looking at the second worry, how much of the enrollment deadline or paperwork piece is something you can take action on, and how much of it is outside your control?

I mean, the deadline itself is not exactly in my control, is it? What I can control is making sure I’ve got the right forms, documents, and dates, but if the school has some hidden requirement or changes something last minute, that’s the part that makes me uneasy.

You’re making a fair point—the deadline can’t be controlled, and the uncertainty about hidden requirements is what keeps it feeling risky. What’s one concrete way you could check the forms, documents, and dates tomorrow, and once you’ve got that covered, is there one more worry?

I guess I could go on the school website tomorrow and maybe call the office if the website is vague, but I’m not thrilled about spending my evening chasing paperwork that should’ve been clear in the first place. And yeah, the other worry is the schedule—if this means changing work hours and pickups, that’s going to throw the whole family routine off.

That sounds frustrating, especially when it feels like you’re being forced to spend energy on something that should already be straightforward. With the schedule piece, what parts are actually possible to plan or check, and what parts are still just your mind jumping ahead to the worst-case version?

I can check what the actual school hours and pickup windows are, and I can probably see whether my work schedule has any flexibility before I assume it’s a total disaster. The worst-case version is me picturing everything collapsing at once—work, childcare, evenings, all of it—but I guess I don’t actually know that yet. I still don’t love this, but yeah, maybe part of it is my brain racing ahead before I’ve even got the facts.

That’s a solid read on it, and I hear you not loving the process even while noticing the racing ahead. Since the schedule worry now has a concrete check, and the money and paperwork worries also have a next step or a place to revisit them, what do you notice about how they feel compared to when they were all swirling together?

I mean, they still feel stressful, but maybe not quite as all-consuming when I break them out like that. It’s a little less like this giant cloud and more like three separate problems I can at least look at one by one. I’m still not exactly calm about any of it, but I can see how my head was making it feel worse by lumping everything together.

That sounds like an important shift—you’re not pretending it’s fine, but you’re noticing the difference between one huge cloud and three specific problems. What do you make of the fact that the lumping-together itself seems to be part of what’s driving the intensity?

I guess it means I’ve been treating the whole thing like one giant emergency, when it’s really a few separate issues I can at least deal with in pieces. I’m not saying that makes it easy, but it does seem like the panic gets worse when I let it all stack up in my head. I still think the situation is legitimately stressful—I’m not just overreacting for no reason—but maybe the way I’m thinking about it is turning the volume up more than it needs to be.

That sounds like a pretty grounded shift, and I hear you being careful not to minimize how stressful this really is. If you were to put it in your own words, what’s changed in how you’re seeing this now?

I think I’m seeing that the stress is real, but my mind has been bundling a few unknowns together and treating them like they’re already disaster. Breaking it down doesn’t make the problems go away, but it does make them feel more specific and less overwhelming. I’m also noticing that part of what’s keeping me up is not just the school change itself, but the way I’m mentally running worst-case scenarios before I’ve even checked the facts. So I’m a little less stuck in “everything is falling apart” and more able to see, okay, these are separate things I can actually look at one at a time.

It makes sense that noticing the difference between the reality in front of you and the mind’s worst-case story could shift this from one huge blur into something more workable, even if it’s still stressful. As you leave today, what feels like the most useful question to carry with you the next time your mind starts bundling everything together?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. At work, a coworker made a casual comment about 'moving on' and 'getting back to normal' shortly after the death of her close friend. I don't know why it keeps happening.

...My jaw got tight. And I think I got really quiet right before I snapped.

...Probably an 8. I snapped at her and told her to stop saying things like that.

...She got quiet and looked hurt. I felt bad right away, and then later I just felt exhausted and embarrassed.

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. While dealing with the stress of imprisonment, the client was told that a routine request for a phone call and updated legal information would be delayed again, which felt like being ignored and trapped without control. I don't know why it keeps happening.

…My jaw got tight, and I felt my chest get hot. I was already clenching my hands before I said anything.

That sounds like a very clear early warning signal, and those moments before the explosion are often the best window for change because a pause is still possible. On a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?
…Probably an 8. I raised my voice and kept pushing for an answer, but I didn’t do anything physical.

…Maybe I could stop talking for a minute and unclench my hands. I don’t know, just step back before I say something worse.

conversations.content: I'm scared of dogs and other animals. So I just walking near dogs, going to parks where dogs might be, and being close to animals.

That makes a lot of sense, and lots of kids feel scared around dogs or other animals, so you’re not alone. Avoiding them can feel safer for a little while, but it can also mean missing out on things that might be fun or important to you. When you think about facing this fear, what scary “what if” thoughts pop into your mind about what might go wrong?

I think, “What if the dog runs at me and bites me?” And I also worry, “What if it jumps on me and I fall down?” Sometimes I think if there’s a big animal, it might chase me or make loud noises and scare me even more. Even if a dog seems nice, my brain still says it could suddenly do something bad.

Those “what if” thoughts sound really real, so it makes sense that your body feels scared when your brain keeps sending danger messages. Sometimes our brains focus only on what could go wrong, but “what if” thoughts can also go the other way too—what are some good “what if” thoughts, like things that could go well if you faced the fear?

Maybe a good “what if” is, what if the dog stays calm and just walks by and doesn’t bother me? What if I look at an animal from far away and realize it isn’t as scary as I thought? I also think, what if I stay brave for a little bit and then feel proud of myself afterward? And what if being near an animal helps my brain learn that not every dog or animal is dangerous?

Those are really thoughtful good “what ifs,” and it makes sense that your brain still jumps to the scary ones first because it’s trying to keep you safe. If both the scary and the good “what ifs” are possible, which good “what if” would you want to remember next time the scared feeling shows up?

I think I would want to remember, “What if the dog stays calm and just walks by?” because that feels the most believable to me. I also want to remember, “What if I stay brave for a little bit and feel proud afterward,” because I like the idea of being proud of myself. Even if I’m still scared, those thoughts might help me not run away right away. It would remind me that my brain is trying to protect me, but the situation might actually be okay.

That sounds really wise, and it’s impressive that you can notice both the scared part and the brave part of your brain at the same time. When you picture the dog staying calm and you feeling proud afterward, what do you notice happens to your fear level, even just a little?

When I picture the dog staying calm, my fear level goes down a little, but it doesn’t disappear. It feels like my scared part is still there, just not as loud for a moment. I also feel a tiny bit more curious, like maybe I could handle it if I took it slow. And thinking about feeling proud afterward makes the fear seem a little less powerful, because then I’m not only thinking about danger.

If that relief had been the feeling in that moment instead of “I ruined everything,” how do you imagine your behavior might have been different?

I guess I might have just asked him directly what was going on instead of going quiet and spiraling, but that feels a little too neat to be realistic. In the moment, I’m not sure I’d actually do that because I’d still be afraid of getting a half-answer or making things worse.

That sounds pretty realistic to me, especially with how much you’re trying to protect yourself from more hurt. I mean, it wasn’t some dramatic thought, which is why I’m not sure this is that helpful. It was more like, “Great, now the day is already ruined,” and then I just felt annoyed at everything.

That “the day is already ruined” thought makes a lot of sense as a quick, automatic reaction, even if it didn’t feel dramatic. What did you do right after that feeling hit, and was there anything you started avoiding because of it?

I mostly just got up, made coffee, and tried to push through the morning like normal, so I’m not sure there was some big reaction. I guess I avoided dealing with a couple emails right away because I was already annoyed and didn’t want to make it worse, but that feels pretty ordinary, not some deep insight.

That doesn’t sound trivial at all; getting up, pushing through, and putting off the emails sounds like a pretty understandable way to cope when you’re already irritated. What happened right away after you avoided them, and what seems to happen over time when that pattern repeats—does any link in that chain look like it might be the place where a small shift could interrupt the whole thing?

Right away, nothing dramatic happened — I just felt a little guilty and then more behind on the day, which is not exactly surprising. Over time, I guess it probably makes the frustration stick around longer, but I’m not convinced there’s some neat “link” to fix here; it mostly feels like I’m just tired and annoyed because my sleep’s been off.

That sounds pretty reasonable to me—if sleep is off, it makes sense that everything would feel more irritating, and I hear the skepticism about there being some neat fix. When the tired-and-annoyed feeling shows up, what do you notice it changes first: your patience, your thoughts about the day, or how you handle the next task?

Probably my patience first, if I’m being honest. I get shorter with people and everything starts feeling more annoying than it normally would, and then my thoughts about the day follow that—like, “this is going to be a long one.” I guess after that I’m less likely to tackle things head-on and more likely to just do the bare minimum until I feel less irritated.

That makes a lot of sense, and it sounds like the sleep disruption is showing up first as a shorter fuse, then as a bleaker read on the day, and then as pulling back a bit. When you notice that “this is going to be a long one” thought, what do you think it leads you to expect from the rest of the day?

Probably that the day is going to keep feeling harder than it should, and that I’m going to have to force myself through it instead of it just feeling normal. I guess I start expecting more little annoyances and less patience from myself, which makes me less willing to deal with things in the first place. It’s annoying to admit, but that probably does make the whole day feel heavier than it needs to.

That sounds like a pretty heavy loop to be carrying, and it makes sense that it feels annoying to notice it that clearly. When you expect the day to be harder and your patience to be lower, what do you notice happens to the way you interpret normal setbacks—does it change how big they seem?

Yeah, I think it does. Things that would normally be minor start to feel like a bigger deal, mostly because I’m already bracing for them to be annoying. It’s not like I’m catastrophizing every little thing, but I definitely have less room for it when I’m tired and already irritated.

That’s a pretty clear observation, and it sounds like you’ve noticed the shift is less about “overreacting” and more about having less capacity when you’re tired and braced for irritation. If you put that new perspective into your own words, how would you summarize what’s been going on?

I think what’s been happening is that my sleep being off has made me more worn down, so I have less patience than usual and everything starts feeling more irritating. Then I get into this mindset where I’m expecting the day to be difficult, which makes normal stuff feel heavier than it should. It’s not really that I’m making a huge deal out of nothing — I just don’t have as much room to handle small annoyances right now. So the frustration kind of feeds itself once I’m already tired.

It sounds like you noticed a really important pattern in how being more tired changes your capacity, and how that can make ordinary things feel much heavier without it meaning you’re “overreacting.” Given that, what’s the first thing you’d want to remind yourself of the next time you notice that worn-down, more reactive feeling starting to build?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that my injury is making me look unreliable, and my manager is going to think I can’t handle my role anymore. Then there's I keep thinking that if I miss even one deadline because of this, my career is basically stalled and I’ll never catch up. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried I’m falling behind my peers because I can’t work at my usual pace right now, and that the slowdown will hurt my chances for promotion.

That sounds exhausting, especially when your mind keeps looping on career consequences at night. Some worries are productive because they point to something actionable, and others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical or not really under your control, and we can sort them differently—what is the first worry that is keeping you up?

I guess the first one is that my manager is going to think I’m unreliable because of the injury, but honestly I’m not sure splitting them into “productive” and “unproductive” is that helpful when they all feel pretty real at 2 a.m. The one that hits hardest is probably the promotion stuff, because it feels like one bad stretch could have long-term consequences even if that’s not rational.

That makes sense; at 2 a.m. the labels can feel pretty abstract, and it sounds like the promotion worry carries the most weight for you. When you look at that one closely, is there a concrete action you can take with it, or does it feel more like a hypothetical outcome that’s outside your control right now?

Honestly, it feels like both, which is annoying. I can try to stay visible and keep doing solid work, but I can’t control how much weight people put on this injury or whether they decide I’m “behind.” So yeah, there are a few things I can do, but the bigger outcome still feels pretty outside my control.

That makes sense — you can influence parts of this, but not the whole outcome, and that ambiguity is exactly the kind of thing that can keep a mind spinning. Would setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to worry about the promotion piece help you park it for tonight, and what is the next worry on your mind?

Maybe, but “schedule your worrying” sounds a little too neat to actually work when my brain is already doing this on its own. I can try it, I guess, but I’m not convinced it’ll stop anything tonight. The next worry is that my manager is going to read my injury as me being unreliable.

That skepticism makes sense; when your mind is already racing, a neat-sounding tool can feel pretty flimsy. Looking at the manager worry, is there a concrete action you can take with it, or does it feel more like a conclusion about how they’ll see you that’s outside your control right now?

A bit of both again, which is frustrating. I can give my manager updates and try not to disappear, but I can’t control the conclusion they draw from it, and that’s the part my brain keeps latching onto. So yes, there’s an action, but it doesn’t really solve the main fear.

That frustration makes sense — you can do the part you control and still be left with the part your mind keeps grabbing onto. When you look at the manager worry, which piece feels more like a concrete next step you could take, and is there one more worry on your mind?

I mean, the concrete step is probably just sending a straightforward update and not overexplaining like I’m auditioning for sympathy. But that still doesn’t stop me from worrying they’ll read between the lines and decide I’m less dependable. The other worry is that if I keep working at half-speed, I’m going to start slipping in ways people notice before I can catch up.

That sounds like a really loaded worry, especially when you’re already trying to manage the injury and work pressure at the same time. Looking at the “slipping at half-speed” thought, is there anything in it you could actually act on, or does it mostly seem like a prediction about what others might notice before you can know?

Yeah, mostly it feels like a prediction, which is part of why it sticks so hard. I can try to pace myself and keep things on track, but I can’t really know what other people will notice or when. I guess the only action is to be as consistent as I can, even though that doesn’t fully calm the fear.

That makes sense; predictions about other people’s reactions can feel sticky because there’s no way to get certainty in the moment. So for this third one, it sounds like the part you can act on is pacing yourself and staying as consistent as you realistically can, while the rest stays in the “not knowable right now” bucket—now that each worry has a plan or container, what do you notice about how they feel compared to when they were all swirling together?

I mean, they feel a little less like one giant blob in my head, which is something. I’m not exactly relaxed, but breaking them apart does make it harder for them to all feel equally urgent at once. I still think the uncertainty part is the real problem, though.

That makes a lot of sense; the uncertainty is the part that keeps the mind hooked, even when the worries are separated out. When you say uncertainty is the real problem, what do you notice your mind tries to do in response to it—does it push for certainty, rehearse worst cases, or something else?

Mostly it pushes for certainty, but since it can’t get any, it goes straight into worst-case scenarios instead. It’s like my brain thinks if it can just think through every bad outcome enough, I’ll be prepared for it, even though all it really does is keep me awake. I can see that pattern a little more clearly now, which is annoying but maybe useful.

That’s a pretty sharp observation, even if it’s annoying to notice your brain doing it in real time. When it goes into worst-case mode, what do you notice happens to your sleep or your sense of control afterward?

It definitely makes the sleep worse — once it starts, I’m just more awake and more irritated that I’m awake, which doesn’t help. And the sense of control is weirdly the opposite of what my brain wants; it feels like I’m doing something useful, but afterward I usually just feel more stuck and less confident. So I guess it’s not actually preparing me much, even though it feels like it is in the moment.

That’s a really clear distinction: it feels useful in the moment, but the aftermath is more awake, more irritated, and less confident. If it isn’t actually preparing you, what do you think your mind is getting from the worst-case rehearsal that keeps it coming back to it?

I think it’s trying to create a feeling of control, even if it’s fake control. If I can imagine every bad outcome, then maybe I don’t have to sit with the uncertainty of not knowing how this injury will affect work. The problem is that it gives me the illusion of being on top of it, but it actually just keeps me stuck in the same fear.

That’s a very clear read on it, and it makes sense that “fake control” would be tempting when uncertainty feels so uncomfortable. When your mind offers that illusion of control, what does it seem to be protecting you from feeling in that moment?

I think it’s protecting me from feeling helpless, honestly. If I let myself just sit with the uncertainty, I start to feel this mix of fear and embarrassment, like I’m not in charge of my own life for a minute. The worst-case thinking lets me stay busy instead of feeling that, even though it clearly isn’t helping.

That makes a lot of sense; staying busy can feel safer than letting helplessness and embarrassment hit all at once. When you notice that mix of fear and embarrassment, what do you tend to tell yourself it means about you?

It usually turns into something like: “You’re not handling this well, and other people can probably tell.” Then it starts sounding bigger than the injury itself, like maybe I’m weak or less capable than I thought. I don’t fully believe that when I say it out loud, but that’s definitely the story my head reaches for when I’m tired and feeling behind.

That sounds like the tired-brain version of the story gets a lot harsher than the one you’d endorse in daylight. When you hear “weak or less capable,” what evidence is your mind using in that moment, and what evidence seems to get left out?

In the moment, my mind is mostly using the fact that I’m not functioning at my usual pace and that I’m having to ask for some flexibility, which it treats like proof that I’m slipping. It leaves out that I’m still showing up, still getting work done, and that the injury is a real thing, not some character flaw. I think it also ignores how temporary this might be and acts like one rough stretch says something permanent about me. When I’m tired, I guess I’m using the most dramatic interpretation and calling it “realism.”

That’s a pretty important shift to notice, especially given how convincing the dramatic version can feel when you’re tired. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed about how you’re seeing the injury and your work right now?

I think I’m starting to see that the injury isn’t automatically the same thing as me being unreliable or less capable, even though that’s where my mind goes when I’m stressed. It’s more like I’m in a temporary situation that’s affecting my pace, and my brain has been turning that into a permanent judgment about my whole career. I still worry about how people see it, but I can see there’s a difference between what’s actually happening right now and the story I’m telling myself about what it means.

It sounds like you’ve caught a really important distinction between what’s happening in this moment and the harsher meaning your mind tends to attach to it when the pressure is on. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I keep thinking that if our family get-togethers keep changing, we’re going to drift apart and lose the closeness we’ve always had. I should be able to handle this, but I can’t stop worrying that I’m not doing enough to keep everyone connected.

…Yeah, I can stay with it. It just feels like if I don’t keep it together, things will start slipping.
That makes a lot of sense, especially when it feels like the whole family connection is resting on your shoulders. Is someone else's opinion overly influencing my own?
…Maybe. I guess I’m really hearing my own fear more than anything else. I don’t know if it’s someone else’s opinion exactly.
That sounds like you’re noticing the fear itself may be doing a lot of the talking, which is an important step. When that fear says you’re “not doing enough,” is my thought overly critical?
…Yeah, probably. It does feel pretty harsh when I say it to myself.

…Yeah, probably habit. I think I’m reacting like this has to stay the same, even though things are different now.

…A lot of it, I think. The facts are mostly that things are changing, but the feeling makes it seem bigger and more urgent than it is.
That’s a really clear shift, and you’ve already started separating the facts from the alarm the feeling creates. In your own words, what feels different now about this worry?

It feels a little less like an immediate warning and more like something I’m reacting to because I’m scared of change. I still care a lot about keeping the family close, but I can see now that changing plans doesn’t automatically mean we’re drifting apart. That makes it feel a bit more manageable.

It sounds like you were able to notice that the alarm feeling has a lot to do with how much you care, and that seeing the change more clearly has made it feel a bit less overwhelming. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. Over the past two weeks, the client has been going to bed later than usual because of changes in her evening routine and has had trouble falling asleep on several nights before work. I keep telling myself: "My sleep is getting worse all the time, and if this keeps up I’ll never be able to function at work or get back to normal." and I've been feeling anxious, discouraged, frustrated.

That sounds really distressing, and it makes sense that those thoughts would leave you feeling anxious and frustrated. In CBT, we often look at how the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m curious, when those thoughts showed up, what did you notice yourself doing in response?

When those thoughts showed up, I started monitoring my sleep really closely, almost obsessively, and that seemed to make me more tense. I’d lie in bed trying to force myself to fall asleep, and then I’d get more frustrated when it didn’t happen right away. I also noticed I was checking the time a lot and dreading the next day at work, which made it harder to relax. A few nights I even considered getting up and doing something else, but I felt like if I left the bed, I was “failing” at sleep, so I just stayed there and kept worrying.

That sounds like a really exhausting cycle, and it makes sense that the more you monitored it, the more tense and stuck you felt. I’m wondering, if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what might be another way they could interpret what was happening with your sleep?

I think someone else might say that what’s happening is a temporary reaction to a change in routine, not proof that my sleep is permanently getting worse. They might see a few rough nights as pretty normal, especially when I’m already anxious and paying so much attention to it. Maybe they’d say I’m putting a lot of pressure on myself, and that pressure is actually making it harder to fall asleep. If I looked at it that way, it feels a little less scary and less like I’m “failing,” even though I still feel frustrated by it.

That’s a really thoughtful alternative, and it makes sense that seeing it as temporary and pressure-driven would soften some of the fear around it. If you actually believed that interpretation instead, how do you think you would feel—what emotion comes up most strongly?

If I really believed that, I think I’d feel more relieved than anything, because it would take away some of the sense that something is seriously wrong with me. I’d probably still feel a little frustrated, but it would be less panicky and more like, “Okay, this is hard right now, but it’s not permanent.” I also think I’d feel more hopeful and calmer, because I wouldn’t be bracing myself so much for the next night. That said, I can tell there’s still a part of me that doesn’t fully trust that yet, so the relief feels possible, but not completely natural to me right now.

That makes a lot of sense—there’s a real difference between feeling panicky and feeling more relieved and calm, even if the calmer view doesn’t feel fully believable yet. With that steadier feeling in mind, how do you imagine your behavior might have been different in that moment?

If I felt more steady and less panicked, I think I would have stopped checking the time so much and maybe not paid as much attention to every little sign of whether I was “sleeping right.” I might have been more willing to get out of bed for a bit instead of lying there forcing it, because it wouldn’t feel like such a big failure. I also think I would have approached the night with less dread, which might have made it easier to just let sleep happen instead of trying so hard to control it. Even saying that, I can notice how much my behavior is tied to fear, so it feels helpful to think about it this way.

It sounds like you’re noticing a meaningful shift from “something is seriously wrong” toward “my fear and pressure may be making this harder,” and that’s a really important distinction. When you put that new perspective into your own words, how would you summarize what’s changed for you about the way you see these nights?

I think what’s changed is that I’m seeing these nights less as evidence that my sleep is permanently broken and more as a temporary pattern that’s being fueled by my anxiety and how much pressure I’m putting on myself. Before, I felt like every bad night was proof that things were getting worse, but now I can at least see that my fear is probably making the problem feel bigger and harder to manage. That doesn’t make it disappear, but it does make it feel less hopeless. I’m still frustrated, but I feel a little more understanding toward myself and a little less like I’m failing.

It sounds like there’s been a meaningful shift from seeing each difficult night as evidence that you’re failing to recognizing how much anxiety and pressure can magnify what’s happening, and that new understanding seems to be softening the hopelessness a bit. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed about yourself in this moment?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that moving to a new place will make me less focused at work and I’ll start missing deadlines. Then there's I keep thinking my manager will notice I’m distracted by the move and decide I’m not reliable enough for bigger responsibilities. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried that if I’m slower to respond while settling into the new place, my performance review will suffer and it could hurt my career growth.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind keeps looping when the stakes feel this high. In CBT, some worries are productive because they point to something actionable, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical, uncontrollable, or about things that may never happen, and we handle those differently. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

I mean, I get the distinction, but it feels a little academic when I’m the one lying there awake with my brain on fire. If I had to pick one, it’s probably the deadline issue—because that’s the most concrete one and the easiest to imagine snowballing.

Yeah, when you’re exhausted in the moment, the theory can feel pretty abstract, and it makes sense that the concrete deadline worry grabs you first. Looking at that one closely, is it something you can take a concrete action on right now, or is it more a hypothetical chain of events that’s partly outside your control?

I mean, some of it is concrete and some of it isn’t, which is kind of the problem. I can make a plan for my workload, sure, but I can’t control whether the move derails me more than I expect or whether people interpret that as me dropping the ball.

That makes sense — part of this is something you can influence, and part of it is the uncomfortable unknown of how it will land with other people. What would be one small, concrete next step on the workload side, and exactly when tomorrow would you do it?

I guess I can make a list of the three deadlines that are actually at risk and block out 20 minutes tomorrow morning to sort them, but I’m not convinced that’s going to magically calm my brain. It feels like one of those “take action” suggestions that sounds neat on paper and still leaves me awake at 2 a.m. anyway.

That’s a fair pushback; I’m not hearing you expect a list to erase the 2 a.m. noise, and it makes sense to be skeptical of anything that sounds too tidy. Putting the deadline piece aside for a moment, when you notice the worry that your manager will see you as unreliable, is that something you can take direct action on, or is it mostly outside your control?

Mostly outside my control, which is part of why it’s annoying. I can do my job and communicate, but I can’t exactly manage my manager’s interpretation if they decide “moving apartments” means “not dependable.”

That’s frustrating, and it makes sense that the part you can’t control feels especially irritating. If the manager’s interpretation is mostly outside your control, would it help to set that worry aside for a specific time later rather than letting it keep interrupting you now, and is there one more worry you want to look at?

Maybe? I’m not sold on “set it aside” as if my brain is going to politely reschedule itself. But I get the point that I can’t control my manager’s interpretation, so I can at least try not to feed it at 2 a.m. The third worry is the review one, because that’s the one that feels like it could quietly poison everything.

That makes sense — it’s the kind of worry that feels less dramatic than a single missed deadline but more corrosive because it can color how everything else gets interpreted. When you look at the review worry closely, is it something you can take a concrete action on now, or is it mainly a hypothetical outcome that you can’t really know or control yet?

I mean, it’s mostly hypothetical right now, which is annoying because my brain acts like it’s already happening. I can control whether I keep up communication and do solid work, but I can’t really know how a future review will be framed until I get there. So, yeah, I guess this one is less of a thing I can solve tonight and more of a thing I’m pre-panicking about.

That “pre-panicking” description fits really well here, and it sounds frustrating to watch your mind treat a future review like it’s already underway. Since this one is mostly hypothetical, what would it look like to give it a container later rather than letting it run tonight, and when tomorrow would you choose to revisit it?

I guess “giving it a container” would mean writing it down somewhere and telling myself I’m not solving my performance review at midnight, which sounds a lot more realistic than pretending I can just shut it off. Tomorrow afternoon might be the least bad time to revisit it, maybe after work when I can actually think. I’m still skeptical that this will do much, but I can see how it’s at least better than letting it spiral all night.

That skepticism makes sense, and it also sounds like you’re noticing a difference between “solving” the worry and just not letting it run your night. If you write it down and revisit it tomorrow afternoon, what do you think you’d be testing about the worry itself versus your ability to handle it?

I guess I’d be testing whether the worry is actually as urgent as it feels at 2 a.m., or whether it gets smaller once I’m not exhausted. And I’d be testing whether I can let it sit without immediately trying to wrestle it into submission. I’m not saying that proves anything huge, but maybe it would at least tell me I’m not as helpless as my brain is making it sound.

That’s a pretty grounded read on it, and I hear you not overselling it while still noticing there may be something useful there. If you were to test that tonight, what would count as evidence that the worry was more about exhaustion than about an actual emergency?

If I can write it down and then not immediately feel the need to keep mentally reheating it for the next hour, that would probably be one sign it’s more exhaustion than emergency. Also, if I wake up tomorrow and the same worries feel less urgent or more manageable once I’m not half-brained and staring at the ceiling, that would tell me a lot. I’m not saying that means the problem disappears, just that my brain might be inflating it because it’s tired.

That’s a careful, skeptical way to test it, and I hear you staying honest about not claiming too much from it. If the “reheating” is the thing you’re watching for, what do you notice happens in the first minute when you try to let the thought sit instead of chasing it?

In the first minute, I usually feel this immediate urge to jump back in and keep analyzing it, like if I stop, something important will slip through the cracks. Then there’s this spike of discomfort—almost like my brain interprets not thinking about it as being careless. But if I stay with it a little longer, I can see that the thought isn’t actually changing much; I’m just keeping it alive by poking at it.

That’s a really clear observation, and it sounds like the discomfort is less about the thought itself and more about the meaning your mind gives to stepping back from it. When you notice that “if I stop, something important will slip through the cracks” feeling, what does your mind seem to be predicting would happen if you didn’t keep poking at it?

I think my mind is predicting that if I let go for even a little bit, I’ll miss some crucial detail and then I’ll be scrambling later because I was too relaxed to catch it. It’s like it equates constant vigilance with responsibility, so not worrying starts to feel almost reckless. But when I say that out loud, it does sound a bit extreme — like I’m treating a move in residence as if it’s some kind of professional disaster in disguise.

That’s a pretty sharp catch, and I hear you noticing the gap between vigilance and actual responsibility. Given everything you just said, how would you summarize the new perspective you’re starting to see in your own words?

I’m starting to see that my brain is treating this move like a bigger threat than it actually is, and that constant worrying isn’t the same thing as being responsible. A lot of what’s keeping me up is not something I can solve at midnight anyway — it’s more the feeling that if I stop analyzing, I’m being careless. I guess the new perspective is that I can handle the concrete parts tomorrow and let the hypothetical career stuff wait instead of acting like it needs to be figured out right now.

It sounds like you just noticed how much of the pressure has been coming from treating uncertainty like an emergency, and that “staying on it” hasn’t actually been the same thing as taking good care of yourself. What might you want to carry forward from that distinction the next time your mind starts insisting everything has to be solved tonight?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. Probably when I start reopening the same apps over and over and realizing I’m not actually looking for anything new. I think the spike happened when I got a message from my family talking about the new addition and all the changes that are coming. Even though it was meant to be happy news, my mind immediately went to, “Everything is going to change and I’m not ready for it.” I felt this wave of dread in my stomach, like I was suddenly expected to handle something huge without knowing how. It also brought up a fear that I’m going to lose my sense of stability and not be able to keep up emotionally.

That sounds like a really sharp moment—the message seemed to land not just as news, but as a signal that something big and uncertain was already happening inside you. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment, and what was the automatic thought—the thing you told yourself right then, even if it was just a flash?

The automatic thought was basically, “I’m not going to handle this well, and I’m going to fall apart if I’m expected to just be okay with it.” There was also a quieter thought underneath that, like, “I should be happy about this, so why am I reacting like this?” That made me feel guilty and even more anxious, because then it felt like I was failing at having the right emotional response. In that moment, it honestly felt like the change was bigger than me, and I was already behind.

That sounds like a painful mix of fear and guilt, and it makes sense that the thought of “falling apart” would feel so overwhelming in the moment. When that feeling hit, what did you do right away, and what did you start avoiding afterward?

Right away, I kind of froze and then tried to distract myself by scrolling on my phone and doing anything that would keep me from sitting with the message. I also noticed I started avoiding replying to my family because I didn’t know how to sound normal or happy when I felt so unsettled inside. After that, I began avoiding thinking too much about the new addition or imagining what the changes would actually look like, because every time I did, my chest would tighten again. I think I was trying to protect myself from the feeling, but it also made everything feel more real and more frightening.

That makes a lot of sense—you were trying to protect yourself from a feeling that already felt too big, and the short-term relief from scrolling and avoiding probably came with a cost. What did that choice seem to do for you right away, and what has it seemed to do over time to your anxiety, your sense of control, or your connection with your family?

Right away, it gave me a little relief because I didn’t have to sit in that panicky feeling, but it was very temporary. Over time, it seems like the avoidance has actually made my anxiety louder, because the more I put it off, the more this whole situation starts to feel huge and unmanageable in my head. I also feel like I’m losing a sense of control, because I’m not really facing it—I’m just trying to outrun it, and that leaves me feeling stuck. With my family, it’s made me feel more distant and guilty, because I want to be supportive, but I also feel like I’m hiding how hard this is for me.

That’s a really clear noticing—you’ve already put words to how the avoidance brings brief relief but then seems to enlarge the anxiety, distance, and guilt over time. As you sit with that, how would you summarize the new perspective you’re beginning to see about what’s been happening for you?

I’m starting to see that my anxiety isn’t just coming from the new family change itself, but from how quickly I’ve been trying to avoid the feelings it brings up. The avoidance helps me for a moment, but then it seems to make the whole situation feel even more overwhelming and out of my control. I also notice that I’ve been judging myself for not reacting the “right” way, which adds guilt on top of the fear. So the new perspective is that I may not be failing at this—I may just be getting stuck in a cycle of fear, avoidance, and self-criticism that’s making everything feel heavier.

It sounds like you’ve just noticed a really important pattern: the fear has been getting bigger not because you’re doing this “wrong,” but because the effort to push the feelings away and judge yourself has been weighing on you too. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of frustration lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really uncomfortable, and it makes sense you’d want some way to make sense of it. If we slow it down together, what would you call the feeling as specifically as you can right now, and how intense does it feel from 0 to 100?

I think the feeling is mostly irritation, but there’s also a kind of anxious restlessness underneath it. It feels pretty strong right now, maybe around a 70 out of 100, because I keep feeling on edge and unable to settle. I notice it gets worse at night when I’m trying to sleep, which is frustrating because I used to have a much easier rhythm. There’s also a little sadness in it, like I’m not quite adjusting to this new stage of retirement the way I thought I would.

That sounds like a lot to carry at once, and it makes sense that the frustration feels so strong when it’s tangled with restlessness and sadness, especially at night. When you think of one specific moment that stands out most recently, what was happening right then, or what thought seemed to set it off?

One moment that stands out was last night when I got into bed and realized I wasn’t sleepy at all, even though I’d been tired earlier. I remember thinking, “Why can’t I just fall asleep like I used to?” and then I started getting irritated with myself for being so wound up. After that, I began worrying that this is just how things are now in retirement, like my body and routine aren’t going to settle the way they used to. Once that thought started, I felt even more restless and a little discouraged.

That moment sounds really discouraging, especially when your body didn’t seem to match how tired you felt earlier. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment — what was the automatic thought, the thing you told yourself right then, even if it was just a flash?

The automatic thought was something like, “Something’s wrong with me, and I should be able to handle this better.” It felt very immediate, almost like I was judging myself for not being able to switch off and fall asleep. There was also a quieter thought underneath it, like, “If this keeps happening, I’m going to lose control of my nights and maybe even my sense of balance in retirement.” Saying it out loud, I can see how quickly I went from being a little restless to feeling like the whole situation meant more than just one bad night.

That’s a really clear insight, and it makes sense that one restless moment could quickly start to feel like it meant something bigger about you and this new stage of life. When that thought came up, what did you do right away, and was there anything you started avoiding afterward?

Right away, I think I started trying to force it, which probably made it worse. I kept checking the clock, shifting positions, and mentally arguing with myself about why I wasn’t asleep yet. After a while I began avoiding just lying there in the dark, because it felt like it turned into a kind of trap where I’d only get more frustrated. I also avoided thinking too much about the next day, because once I started worrying about being tired tomorrow, I could feel myself getting even more keyed up.

That sounds like a pretty understandable attempt to regain control, even if it ended up feeling trapping and frustrating. What were the consequences of that pattern right away in the moment, and over time how did it seem to affect your sleep, your mood, or your confidence about nights in retirement?

Right away, it made me more tense and less sleepy, which was almost the opposite of what I wanted. I’d end up feeling irritated with myself, and then the night started to feel like something I had to get through instead of a time to rest. Over time, I think it’s made me a little less confident about nighttime in general, like I’m waiting for the same struggle to happen again. It’s also affected my mood the next day, because I’m more tired and discouraged, and then I start carrying that into the evening too.

That’s a really clear picture of how the cycle is starting to feed itself, and it makes sense that your confidence at night would shift when the pattern keeps repeating. When you notice yourself waiting for the struggle to happen again, what do you find yourself expecting in that moment?

I think I’m expecting that I’ll lie there awake again, get frustrated, and then start spiraling into the same self-criticism. There’s also this expectation that once the night goes badly, the next day will feel off too, like I’ll be dragging and less patient with myself. In a way, I’m bracing for disappointment before it even happens. I can see that I’m almost preparing for the worst instead of giving myself a chance to just be in the moment.

That’s a thoughtful shift, and it sounds like you’re noticing how much of the distress comes from bracing for the pattern before it even unfolds. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you’re understanding these nights?

I think what’s changed is that I’m seeing these nights less as proof that something is wrong with me and more as a pattern that gets set off by my own worry and anticipation. Instead of just thinking, “I can’t sleep,” I’m starting to notice how quickly I go into self-criticism and start expecting the worst, which seems to make everything feel more intense. That doesn’t make the frustration disappear, but it does make the whole thing feel a little less mysterious and a little more workable. I also realize I may be putting a lot of pressure on myself to adjust perfectly to retirement, when maybe this is just part of the transition I’m still learning to live with.

It sounds like you’re noticing this experience with a lot more curiosity and less of that immediate sense that it defines you, and there’s something meaningful in seeing how the self-criticism and pressure to “get retirement right” can amplify the whole cycle. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?
