conversations.content: At the next family get-together, I worry I’ll say something awkward about my retirement or the family changes and everyone will go quiet or exchange looks. I imagine they’ll think I’m boring or out of touch, and I’ll end up feeling embarrassed and left out for the rest of the evening.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense your mind is trying to protect you by scanning for signs of rejection. When we worry, our minds can start treating what could happen as if it will happen, even though those are very different; what are some concrete, observable clues you can think of that suggest this worst-case outcome may not actually come true?

A concrete clue is that my family usually doesn’t respond that dramatically—they may tease a little, but they tend to move on quickly and keep the conversation going. I also can think of times when I’ve said something a bit clumsy and people just laughed it off or changed the subject kindly, rather than making it into a big deal. My sister in particular usually tries to include everyone, so I don’t think she’d let me sit there feeling isolated if she noticed I was uncomfortable. When I look at it that way, the image of everyone silently judging me feels more like my fear filling in the blanks than something I actually know will happen.

Those are real pieces of evidence, not wishful thinking, and you’re noticing patterns from actual past experiences rather than just hoping for the best. If those clues are accurate and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you imagine is the realistic, most likely outcome at the gathering?

I think the most likely outcome is probably much more ordinary than my fear makes it seem. I may say something a little awkward or ramble a bit about retirement, and people might smile, tease me lightly, or just move the conversation along. I can imagine feeling a little self-conscious for a moment, but not being rejected or shut out—more like a normal family interaction with a few awkward edges. Honestly, the realistic picture seems to be that I’ll probably be okay, even if I don’t feel perfectly smooth or confident the whole time.

That sounds like a really balanced, realistic picture, and I can hear you softening the grip of the fear a bit. If we imagine, just for a moment, that the worst did happen and you felt awkward or left out, what do you think you would actually do step by step in that moment, and how might you eventually find your way back to okay?

If I felt awkward or left out, I think my first step would be to go quiet for a moment and probably tell myself not to panic, even if I felt embarrassed. I might excuse myself to get a drink, use the bathroom, or help in the kitchen just to reset and give myself a little space. After that, I’d probably try to rejoin the conversation by asking someone a question or sitting near the person who feels easiest to connect with, like my sister. And even if I still felt rattled, I think I’d eventually settle back down by reminding myself that one awkward moment doesn’t define the whole evening or how my family sees me.

You just mapped out a path through the very situation you were afraid of, which is important because it shows there would still be options if you felt awkward. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what seems different about it?

It feels less overwhelming now than it did at the beginning. I can still feel the worry there, but it seems more like a possibility I could handle rather than a disaster waiting to happen. What’s different is that I can see there are actual steps I could take if I started feeling awkward, instead of just imagining myself getting stuck and humiliated. Thinking it through makes the whole situation feel more manageable and less like it has all this power over me.

That sounds like a meaningful shift, and it makes sense that having a few concrete options changed how powerful the worry feels. If you put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say you now believe about the upcoming family get-together?

I’d say I now believe the family get-together is probably going to be a normal, somewhat imperfect evening rather than some big disaster. I may feel awkward at moments, but that doesn’t mean I’ll be rejected or judged the whole time. I also believe I have ways to handle it if I start feeling uncomfortable, so I’m not as powerless as I first felt. Overall, it seems more likely that I’ll be okay than that the night will go badly.

It sounds like you’ve moved from seeing the evening as something all-powerful and threatening to holding a much more balanced view of it, one that leaves room for both discomfort and your own ability to cope. As you leave today, what feels like the most important part of that shift for you to carry into the next family get-together?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that all these family get-togethers changing is making me so tense that I’ll start getting headaches or stomach issues. Then there's I keep thinking that if I’m stressed about family plans, I’ll sleep badly and feel exhausted at work tomorrow. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried that the stress from these changes means I’m not taking care of myself enough, and I might get run-down or sick.

That sounds really exhausting, especially when the thoughts keep circling at night. Sometimes it can help to sort worries into ones that are productive—about something you could actually do something about—and ones that are unproductive, meaning more hypothetical or outside your control; what is the first worry that is keeping you up?
Um… the first one is probably the family get-togethers changing. I keep thinking about what that means and it’s making me tense.

That sounds tense, and it makes sense your mind keeps going to it when the changes feel unsettled. When you look at this worry about the family get-togethers changing, is there a concrete action you can take, or does it feel more hypothetical and outside your control?
…It feels more outside my control, I think. I can’t really make the family plans go back to how they were.

That makes sense, and it sounds frustrating to have something matter this much and still not be able to change it. Would setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to think about it help you put it down for tonight, and what is the next worry on your mind?
…Maybe. I could try that for tomorrow. The next worry is that if I keep stressing about the family plans, I’ll sleep badly and be exhausted at work.

That sounds really understandable, especially when your mind is already tired and starts forecasting tomorrow. When you look at this worry about sleeping badly and feeling exhausted at work, does it feel like something you can take a concrete action on, or more like it’s outside your control?
…It feels kind of outside my control. I can try to sleep, but I can’t really force it.

That makes a lot of sense, and it’s hard when sleep feels partly out of your hands. If it feels outside your control, what would it be like to set that worry aside for tonight and check it tomorrow during a planned worry time, and is there one more worry on your mind?
…Yeah, I could try setting it aside for tonight. The last worry is that all this stress means I’m not taking care of myself enough and I might get run-down or sick.

I think they all feel a little less huge when I say them out loud like this. They still worry me, but they seem more like anxious thoughts than actual things happening right now. I also feel a bit calmer knowing I can put them off until tomorrow instead of trying to solve everything tonight.

It makes sense that saying them out loud helped the worries feel a little less overwhelming, and I’m noticing how you were able to see the difference between anxious thoughts and what’s actually happening right now. As you leave today, what stands out most to you about that shift?

metadata.stressor: Change in health of family member

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. My adult child had a medical appointment and told me the test results are still being looked at. I keep telling myself: "This is just how things go now. Something always ends up being wrong with my family’s health, and I’m never going to get good news." and I've been feeling anxious, discouraged, helpless.

That sounds really heavy, and I can see why your mind would go straight to the worst-case story when you care about your family. In CBT terms, the appointment itself is just the situation, and the thoughts you had about it are what seem to be driving the anxiety and helplessness—when that thought showed up, what did you actually end up doing?

Honestly, I don’t know that I “did” anything special—mostly I just sat there worrying and checking my phone too much, which feels like a pretty normal reaction, not some big CBT pattern. I guess I also kept replaying the appointment in my head and trying to imagine every possible bad outcome, though I’m not convinced that tells us much.

That does sound pretty normal, and I get the skepticism—this isn’t about labeling you, it’s more about noticing a very human mind-move where one uncertain health situation starts to stand in for “this always happens” or “it’ll never be okay.” If someone else looked at the exact same appointment and the “results are still being looked at” piece, what is another way they might interpret it?

I suppose someone more optimistic would say it just means the doctor is still reviewing things, not that there’s automatically bad news. But honestly, I’m not sure that’s much comfort when you’ve seen enough health scares to know things can go sideways fast.

That makes sense, and it’s reasonable that past health scares make the “wait and see” part feel loaded rather than reassuring. If you actually believed the idea that the doctor is still reviewing things and that it doesn’t automatically mean bad news, how do you think you would feel—would it be relief, less fear, cautious hope, or something else?

I mean, maybe I’d feel a little less on edge, but “believed it” feels like a stretch. I’m not sure I can just talk myself into being calm when the whole situation is still unresolved and I’ve got enough experience to know that sometimes the worry turns out to be justified.

That sounds fair—if the situation is still unresolved and you’ve seen real scares before, “just think positive” would probably feel pretty unhelpful. If you’d had that slightly less on-edge feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

Maybe I would’ve checked my phone less, or at least not every five minutes, which I guess counts for something. But I’m not sure my behavior would’ve changed much—when you’re waiting on medical results, it’s hard to act like everything is fine just because you’ve reframed it a bit.

That’s a very reasonable pushback, and I’m not hearing “everything is fine” in what you’re describing—just a small shift in how you’d experience the same uncertain situation. When the appointment and the test results stayed exactly the same, but the level of checking and tension could change depending on the thought, what does that suggest to you about the link between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I guess it suggests my thoughts do have some effect, sure, but that doesn’t mean they’re the whole story or that I can just think my way out of a real uncertainty. To me it mostly says I’m reacting to something stressful in a pretty ordinary way, not that the thought itself is the main problem.

That’s a very grounded way to put it, and I hear you not wanting therapy to overclaim what it can do in real uncertainty. If the thought isn’t the whole problem, what part of the reaction do you think your mind is adding on top of the uncertainty that makes it feel more intense?

I suppose the mind is adding a kind of catastrophe on top of the uncertainty—like treating “we’re still waiting” as if it already means something bad is confirmed. And once that starts, I think I also add this feeling that I should be able to know more or do more, which just makes me more tense. I’m still not sure that’s the main issue, but I can see it probably makes the whole thing feel bigger than the facts themselves.

That sounds like a pretty clear read on it, even if you’re not ready to call it the main issue, and I appreciate how carefully you’re separating the uncertainty itself from the extra layer your mind adds. When you notice that “I should be able to know more or do more” feeling, what do you think it’s asking of you that can’t actually be done in that moment?

I think it’s asking me to somehow get certainty right now, which obviously I can’t do. Or maybe it’s asking me to fix something that isn’t fixable until the doctor actually has the results, so I end up just spinning my wheels. I can see that part a little more clearly now, even if I don’t exactly like it.

That makes a lot of sense, and I can hear how frustrating it is to be pushed toward certainty when the situation simply doesn’t offer it yet. If your mind is demanding certainty or a fix that isn’t available, what does that help you avoid feeling for a moment, and what does it cost you?

I guess it helps me avoid sitting with the raw uncertainty and fear for a minute, which is probably why my brain jumps there so fast. But it costs me sleep, focus, and honestly a lot of unnecessary tension, because I end up acting like I can solve something that isn’t solvable yet. I don’t love admitting that, but it does seem to be part of what’s going on.

That’s a pretty honest observation, and it sounds like you’re already seeing the tradeoff your mind is making. If the push for certainty is mainly a way to avoid raw fear, what does that tell you about why it keeps showing up even when it doesn’t actually help?

I suppose it keeps showing up because it works in the short term, even if it doesn’t solve anything. If I’m honest, my brain probably thinks worrying is a kind of preparation, or at least a way to stay on top of things, even though it mostly just keeps me tense. So yes, maybe it’s less about logic and more about fear trying to protect me in a clumsy way.

That’s a very thoughtful way to frame it, and it sounds like you’re catching the difference between protection and effectiveness. If worrying feels like “staying on top of things,” what does it seem to promise you in the moment that actually keeps you hooked?

It seems to promise me that if I keep thinking hard enough, I won’t be blindsided—that I’ll somehow be ready if the news is bad. There’s also this false sense that worrying is the same as caring, so if I stop, it feels like I’m being careless or naive. When I look at it that way, I can see why it’s hard to let go, even though it doesn’t actually give me any more control.

That’s a really clear shift, and I can hear you separating “worrying” from actually having control or being a caring person. If you had to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you’re seeing the worry now?

I think I’m seeing that the worry isn’t really giving me information or control, even though it feels that way. It’s more like my mind is trying to prepare me for bad news and calling that “being responsible,” when really it just keeps me stuck and more on edge. I still care a lot and I still don’t like the uncertainty, but I can see a little more clearly that the anxious looping is adding something on top of the actual situation.

It sounds like you’re noticing a real difference between caring deeply and getting pulled into the anxious loop that tries to look like responsibility. As you leave today, what feels like the most useful thing to carry forward from what you just noticed?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m going to fall behind at work because the divorce is distracting me and people will think I’m not reliable. Then there's If my performance dips even a little, I could lose my job and put my family’s finances at risk. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried I won’t have the energy or focus to keep up with meetings and deadlines, and my career could stall.

That sounds exhausting, and I can see why your mind keeps spinning when the stakes feel so high. One way to sort this is to separate worries that point to something actionable from worries that are more hypothetical or outside your control, because they get handled differently. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

I mean, maybe, but that sounds a little too neat when I’m the one lying awake at 2 a.m. It’s not like my brain is politely separating “actionable” from “hypothetical” — it’s just dumping all of it on me at once. If I had to pick one, it’s probably the work thing, because that feels most immediate.

Yeah, that makes sense — at 2 a.m. it probably feels like a pileup, not a tidy list, and I get why the “neat” framing lands a bit off. If we stay with the work worry for a moment, what parts of it could you actually take a concrete action on, and what parts are more hypothetical or outside your control?

I get the idea, but honestly it still feels a bit like you’re asking me to sort chaos into labeled boxes when the problem is the chaos. The only concrete thing I can think of is trying to keep up with deadlines and not look scattered, which is easier said than done when I’m running on no sleep. The rest — whether people think I’m unreliable or whether this snowballs into me losing my job — that’s mostly out of my hands, which is exactly what makes it hard to shut off.

That does sound real, not neat, and I can see why the “boxes” idea feels frustrating when the bigger pieces aren’t really under your control. Given that, would setting aside a specific 10 minutes tomorrow at a set time to think about this make it any easier to park for tonight, and what is the next worry on your mind?

Maybe for some people, but I’m not convinced a “worry appointment” is going to convince my brain to stop at night. It sounds a little too engineered for something that feels more like a fire alarm going off. The next worry is my energy and focus — I keep thinking I’m going to drag through meetings and miss something important.

That “fire alarm” description makes a lot of sense, and I can hear why the worry-appointment idea feels a bit too engineered for what you’re dealing with. With the energy and focus worry, what part of it is something you can actually take action on, and what part is outside your control?

Honestly, I’m not sure splitting it up helps much when the main issue is that I’m exhausted and my brain feels fried. I can maybe do the basics — get to bed earlier, not pile on extra work if I can avoid it — but I can’t exactly control whether I’m going to feel sharp in a meeting or not. And if I’m being blunt, that uncertainty is what keeps me stuck.

That sounds really draining, and it makes sense that the uncertainty itself feels like the part that traps you, especially when you’re already running on fumes. When you look at the “get to bed earlier” and “don’t pile on extra work” pieces, which one feels like the most realistic concrete step to test first, and is there one more worry on your mind?

I mean, I guess getting to bed earlier is the obvious one, but it’s not exactly a thrilling breakthrough and I’m not convinced it’ll fix much if my head’s still spinning when I get there. “Don’t pile on extra work” is probably more realistic in theory than in practice, because work doesn’t always care what I can handle. The other worry is probably that this is all going to bleed into home life too — I’m already feeling less present with my family.

That sounds painful, and I can see why “thrilling breakthrough” doesn’t fit when the worry is already following you home. When you think about being less present with your family, is that worry pointing you toward something you can influence, or is it mostly another loop that drains you without helping?

Yeah, probably both, which is annoying. Part of it is a loop — I can tell when I’m just replaying the same worst-case stuff and not actually solving anything. But part of it is real too, because I have noticed I’m more distracted and short with my family than I want to be, so I guess there is something I can try to influence there.

That’s a pretty clear distinction — some of it is the same loop repeating, and some of it is showing up in how you’re acting at home, which sounds frustrating but also gives us something to work with. For that family piece, what seems like the most realistic way to influence it without pretending you can control every feeling or thought?

I guess the most realistic thing is probably just catching myself before I get too short with them and not bringing the work spiral to the dinner table. I can also try to be more deliberate about actually listening for a few minutes instead of half-hearing everyone while I’m stuck in my head. I’m not saying that fixes much, but it does feel more doable than trying to “control” how I feel.

That sounds grounded and pretty honest, especially given how little you trust the “fix it” language. When you imagine doing even a small version of that tonight, what do you notice might get in the way first?

Probably the first thing that gets in the way is just my own head — I’ll sit down with them and still be half elsewhere, replaying work stuff instead of actually being present. And if I’m tired enough, I can get impatient faster than I want to, which doesn’t exactly help. I guess the other part is that I’m not used to being intentional about this, so it feels a little forced, even if I can see why it might matter.

That makes a lot of sense — when your mind is already pulled toward work, “being present” can feel less like a choice and more like another thing to fail at, and the forced feeling fits with that. When you notice yourself getting half-elsewhere or impatient, what seems to happen right before that shift, and what would you want to be different in that moment?

Usually it’s when I sit down and there’s even a tiny lull — that’s when my brain jumps right back to work and starts running the same worst-case script. Then I notice I’m answering people half a beat too fast or getting annoyed over something small. What I’d want instead is just to stay in the conversation long enough to actually hear them, even if my head is still noisy in the background.

That’s a very clear pattern: the lull shows up, the worst-case script kicks in, and then your tone shifts before you even fully notice it. When you catch that half-beat-too-fast moment, what do you think it’s telling you about what your mind is trying to do for you right then?

I guess it’s trying to keep me ahead of things, like if I stay on top of every possible bad outcome maybe I won’t get blindsided by one. Which sounds protective on paper, but in practice it just keeps me tense and on edge all the time. So when I’m snapping or answering too fast, I think that’s my brain trying to prevent trouble, not just being random. I’m starting to see that the problem isn’t that it cares too little — it’s that it’s working overtime in a way that’s not actually helping.

That’s a pretty sharp read on it — it sounds like your mind is trying to protect you by staying on high alert, even if the cost is that you end up tense and snappier than you want to be. When it’s “working overtime” like that, what do you notice it’s predicting will happen if it lets up even a little?

If it lets up, I think it’s predicting I’ll miss something important and then get hit with the consequences later — at work, at home, all of it. It’s like my brain treats any drop in vigilance as the start of a chain reaction I won’t be able to stop. I can see that’s probably why it feels safer to keep me on edge, even though it’s making me less effective. Maybe the real fear is not just the divorce itself, but that I won’t be able to keep everything else from slipping too.

That sounds like you’ve really gotten to the core of it: the alarm isn’t just about the divorce, it’s about what your mind fears will unravel if it eases up. When that chain-reaction picture shows up, what evidence does your mind use to treat it as certain rather than as a possibility?

I think it latches onto the fact that I’m already not sleeping well and then treats that as proof that things are starting to slip. If I’m a little distracted in a meeting or shorter with my family, my mind goes, “See, this is how it starts,” and it acts like that’s the same as a real downward spiral. I can see now that it’s taking a few rough moments and turning them into evidence of a bigger collapse. That doesn’t make the fear go away, but it does make it feel a little less like a fact and more like my brain jumping ahead.

That’s a thoughtful shift, and I hear you separating the rough moments from the story your mind builds around them. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you?

I think what’s changed is I’m seeing that the stress isn’t automatically proof that everything is falling apart — it’s more that my brain is treating every slip as if it means a collapse is already underway. I still feel the pressure, but I’m less convinced that every bad night or distracted moment means I’m actually losing control. It makes the whole thing feel a bit less like a verdict and more like a reaction my mind is having. That doesn’t solve it, but it does make it seem a little more manageable.

It sounds like you’ve started to separate the feeling of pressure from the idea that it automatically means disaster, and that shift is giving you a little more room to breathe without pretending the stress isn’t real. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that after retiring, I won’t know how to describe my career clearly when people ask, and I’ll sound irrelevant or forget what I accomplished. Then there's I keep thinking I should have done more with my career, and now it feels like I missed my chance to be recognized for it. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried that if I ever need to consult, volunteer, or take on part-time work, I won’t be able to keep up with new expectations or technology.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind is grabbing onto those concerns at night. Sometimes it helps to sort worries into ones that are productive—something you could actually act on—and ones that are unproductive, meaning hypothetical or not really under your control; with that in mind, which of those three worries is the first one that’s keeping you up?

I’m not sure I buy the whole “productive versus unproductive” thing—it sounds tidy, but my brain doesn’t really work that way at 2 a.m. If I had to pick one, it’s probably the fear of sounding irrelevant when people ask what I did, because that’s the one that keeps looping back first.

That makes sense—at 2 a.m., a neat label can feel pretty artificial, and I’m glad you named the one that keeps coming back first. When you think about sounding irrelevant, is that something you can take a concrete action on, or is it more hypothetical and outside your control?

I mean, some of it is concrete and some of it isn’t, which is part of why I find these categories a bit annoying. I could probably work on a short way to describe my career, but the bigger issue is the feeling behind it—that’s not exactly something I can just “control” on command.

That’s a fair pushback—the feeling part doesn’t respond to command, and it makes sense that the categories feel a bit tidy. Since you can see a concrete piece here, what small next step could you take to draft a short way of describing your career, and exactly when tomorrow would you do that?

I suppose I could jot down a rough 2-3 sentence version after breakfast tomorrow, but I’m not pretending that will magically fix the whole issue. It still feels like we’re polishing a problem that’s really more about how I see myself now than about the wording.

That makes a lot of sense—you’re noticing the wording piece is only part of it, and the deeper issue is how you’re seeing yourself now. When you turn to that second worry about feeling like you missed your chance to be recognized, is there anything you can actually take action on there, or does it sit more outside your control?

Honestly, that one mostly sits outside my control, which is exactly why it’s frustrating to keep chewing on it. I can’t go back and change who noticed what, and I’m not sure “take action” is the right phrase for something that’s really about regret and disappointment.

That sounds frustrating, and I can see why “take action” doesn’t fit something that’s really regret and disappointment. If that one sits outside your control, what happens when you set it aside even briefly, and is there one more worry left on your mind?

I’m not sure I really “set it aside” so much as it comes back the minute I stop distracting myself, so that’s not exactly reassuring. And yes, there’s the third worry about not being able to keep up if I ever need to consult or volunteer, which feels more practical than the regret stuff, even if I’m not thrilled about it.

That sounds pretty familiar and not very comforting, especially when distraction only works until your mind catches up again. With the consulting or volunteering worry, what parts of it seem like something you could realistically prepare for, and what parts feel more like “what if” thinking?

I guess I could realistically brush up on whatever tools or platforms are common in my field, if I ever actually needed to do something like that. The “what if” part is the bigger monster—what if I’m too slow, what if everyone expects me to already know everything, what if I embarrass myself. And I can see that some of that is me filling in the blanks with worst-case scenarios, even if I’m not ready to call it irrational.

That’s a pretty sharp observation, and I hear you—you’re not buying the “irrational” label, but you can see the worst-case blanks getting filled in. For this third worry, if there’s a part you could realistically prepare for, what would a low-stakes first step look like, and what would you call the rest if it’s mainly “what if” thinking?

I suppose a low-stakes first step would be just making a short list of the tools or skills I’d actually need to brush up on, instead of spiraling about every possible scenario. The rest is probably just anxious forecasting—my brain acting like it has to solve a problem that may never even happen. I’m still not thrilled about it, but I can see that distinction a little more clearly than I did at the start.

That’s a meaningful shift, especially given you’re still not thrilled but can see the difference a bit more clearly. When your mind starts that anxious forecasting, what does it seem to be trying to protect you from, and how does that help or cost you in the moment?

I think it’s trying to protect me from feeling unprepared or foolish, like if I worry enough I won’t be caught off guard. In the moment, I guess it gives me the illusion of control, but the cost is that it keeps me wired and awake instead of letting me actually rest. So it helps a little in theory, but mostly it just keeps the whole thing alive longer than it needs to be.

That’s a pretty clear way of putting it—you’ve noticed the worry is trying to protect you, but it’s also keeping you awake and stuck. If you were to sum up the shift in your own words, what feels different now about this whole loop?

I think what feels different is that I can see the worry a little more as a habit of trying to protect me than as a true warning I need to obey. It still bothers me, but it doesn’t seem quite as mysterious or all-powerful when I notice it’s really just my mind running ahead and filling in gaps. I can also see there are a few concrete things I could do, instead of treating the whole mess like one huge impossible problem. That doesn’t make it feel good, exactly, but it does make it feel a bit less hopeless.

It sounds like you’ve moved from feeling at the mercy of that worry to seeing it more as something your mind does in an effort to look after you, and that shift has made the whole thing feel a little less like an unsolvable knot. As you leave today, what feels like the most useful thing to remember about that perspective the next time the worry shows up?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of shame lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.
That sounds really heavy, and I’m glad you said it out loud. Could we slow it down together and name the feeling as specifically as you can right now, then give it a 0–100 intensity?

It feels like shame mixed with embarrassment and a kind of sinking dread in my stomach. If I had to put a number on it right now, I’d say it’s around an 85 out of 100. It feels really intense because it’s tied to the holiday and being around people, like I’m already bracing myself for being judged or not measuring up. I can feel myself wanting to hide from it, but I also know it’s sitting right there in the background of everything.

That sounds very intense, and it makes sense that your body would want to pull back when shame and dread are that strong. When you think about the holiday and that sense of being judged, what was the specific moment or thought that first set this off?

I think it started when I realized how much this holiday brings up comparisons for me. There wasn’t one single moment, but I remember looking at messages and seeing people making plans, and I immediately felt like I was already behind or somehow failing at doing the holiday “right.” Then I started thinking about family and how I’ll probably be asked questions I don’t want to answer, and it hit me that I’m scared of looking like I’m not doing well enough in my life. Once that thought showed up, the shame kind of spread fast, like it attached itself to everything.

That makes a lot of sense—seeing other people’s plans and then anticipating family questions sounds like it hit a very vulnerable comparison point for you. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment, and what was the automatic thought—the thing you told yourself right then, even if it was just a flash?

The automatic thought was something like, “I’m behind, and everyone can tell.” It felt like I was instantly comparing my life to some invisible standard and coming up short, like I was failing at being an adult in a way that would be obvious the second someone looked at me. There was also a more painful thought underneath it: “If people ask me questions, I won’t have good answers, and then they’ll see that I’m not doing as well as I should be.” Even as I’m saying it now, it feels embarrassing, but that was the flash of it.

That’s a really painful thought to carry, and it makes sense that saying it out loud feels embarrassing. When that thought landed, what did you do right away, and what started to feel easier to avoid?

Right away, I think I started mentally pulling back and trying not to think too far ahead. I got this urge to avoid messages, avoid making plans, and basically keep myself as invisible as possible so no one could ask me anything. It felt easier to avoid the whole holiday, and also easier to avoid looking at my own life too closely because that’s where the shame gets louder. Even though I know isolating makes it worse, in the moment it felt like the safest option.

That makes a lot of sense; pulling back and making yourself invisible sounds like it gave you a little immediate protection from the shame. What were the consequences of that choice right away, and then over time?

Right away, it gave me a tiny sense of relief, like I didn’t have to face the panic for a few minutes. But almost immediately, I also felt lonelier and more trapped, because avoiding things made the holiday feel even bigger and more threatening. Over time, it tends to reinforce the idea that I can’t handle it, and then the shame gets stronger because I start interpreting my avoidance as proof that something is wrong with me. So it becomes this loop where I hide to feel safe, but then I end up feeling more disconnected and worse about myself.

That’s a really clear and painful loop to notice, and it sounds like you’ve already identified how the short-term relief turns into more shame later. As you sit with that, how would you put the shift in your own words about what hiding is doing for you now?

Hiding feels like it’s protecting me from immediate exposure, but it’s also shrinking my world and making the shame feel more believable. In the moment it tells me I’m avoiding judgment, but really it’s giving the shame more room to grow in the background. I think it keeps me from having to face the holiday anxiety directly, but it also keeps me from getting any evidence that I can survive it or that people might not be judging me as harshly as I fear. So right now, hiding feels less like rest and more like a way of disappearing into the problem.

It sounds like you just saw how what once felt like protection has been quietly feeding the very shame and fear it was meant to manage, and that’s a really important shift. As you leave today, what feels like the most meaningful thing you’re taking from that awareness?

conversations.content: I’m scared my marriage is falling apart, and if I can’t fix this, I’m going to lose my family and the life I’ve worked so hard to build. I keep wondering if I’m failing as a husband and whether everything at home is about to come crashing down.

That sounds incredibly heavy, and I really appreciate how honestly you’re putting it into words. Let’s slow this down together—not to dismiss how frightening it feels, but to look closely at the thought and see how it holds up when we examine it carefully; could you stay with that with me?

Yeah, I can stay with that. When I really look at it, the thought that I’m “failing” as a husband feels true in the moment, but I can also see it’s probably more like I’m scared and overwhelmed than that I’ve already failed. I’m putting a lot of pressure on myself to hold everything together, and when things feel unstable at home, my mind jumps straight to worst-case scenarios. I think part of me is afraid that if I don’t fix this quickly, I’ll lose not just the marriage, but also the sense of security I’ve built for my family.

That makes a lot of sense, especially the way fear and pressure can pull your mind toward the worst-case story even when another part of you sees it more clearly. As you sit with both sides, is my thought based more on habit or a past experience than what's true now?

Yeah, I think it’s probably more habit and past experience than what’s actually true right now. I’ve always been someone who feels responsible for keeping things stable, so when something in my marriage feels off, my mind goes straight to, “This is my fault, and I need to fix it before it gets worse.” I also think I carry some old fear from earlier times when things felt uncertain, so I react like I’m in danger even if the current situation is more complicated than that. What’s true right now is that we’re struggling, but that doesn’t automatically mean everything is doomed.

That’s a really thoughtful distinction, and it sounds like you’re seeing how responsibility and old fear can make the alarm feel louder than the evidence. When you look at what’s happening right now, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

I think it’s more of a possibility than a likely scenario, even though it can feel very likely when I’m anxious. Right now, the reality is that we’re going through a hard patch and there’s real tension, but that’s not the same thing as the marriage ending. My mind tends to treat uncertainty like proof of disaster, and I can see that’s not actually fair to what’s happening. There are still signs that this could be worked through if we can stay engaged and honest with each other.
That’s a really grounded insight, and I’m hearing you separate the real tension from the catastrophic meaning your mind wants to add on top of it. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what’s true?

Yes, I think it is an exaggeration of what’s true. The truth is that things are strained and I’m scared, but my mind turns that into “everything is falling apart” or “I’m about to lose my family,” which is bigger than what’s actually happening right now. When I slow down, I can see there’s conflict and uncertainty, but there’s also still connection, history, and reasons to keep trying. It feels important to admit that my fear is making the situation look more extreme than it really is.

That sounds like a meaningful shift, and I can hear how carefully you’re separating fear from the fuller reality of what’s happening. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you?

What’s changed is that I’m starting to see my fear as a reaction, not a verdict on my marriage. I still feel scared and unsettled, but I don’t feel as convinced anymore that this means I’m failing or that everything is about to collapse. I can see more clearly that we’re in a difficult season, not necessarily at the end of the road. That gives me a little more room to breathe and think about what’s actually happening instead of just panicking about what might happen.

It sounds like you’re noticing a little more space between the fear and the meaning it was automatically taking on, and that shift is giving you room to stay with what’s real instead of getting pulled entirely into the worst-case story. As you leave today, what feels most important to carry forward from what you noticed in yourself just now?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of panic lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really overwhelming, and I can see why you’d want something concrete rather than just “talking about it.” If we map it out together, what would you call the main emotion right now as specifically as you can, and how intense is it from 0 to 100?

I mean, panic is probably the main thing, but it feels mixed with dread and anger too. If you want a number, it’s like an 85 most of the time, though I’m not sure these scales really help when the mortgage stuff is still hanging over everything.

That makes sense; when something as real as the mortgage is hanging over you, a number can feel pretty flimsy. What was one specific moment recently when the panic spiked—what was happening, or what thought went through your mind right then?

Honestly, it’s usually when I’m looking at the mailbox or my phone, expecting another notice from the bank or the lender. Then my brain just jumps straight to “we’re going to lose the house,” which probably sounds dramatic, but that’s where it goes.

That sounds like a really sharp trigger, and it makes sense your mind would go straight to the worst-case place when the mailbox or phone becomes a warning signal. When that happened in that moment, what went through your mind right then—what was the automatic thought, even if it only flashed by?

Yeah, the automatic thought is basically, “This is it, we’re screwed.” I know that sounds extreme, but when I see the mail or a bank number pop up, it feels less like a thought and more like a fact for a second.

That doesn’t sound extreme to me—it sounds like your mind is treating a threat as immediate, which can make it feel like fact in the moment. What did you do right away when that hit, and what started getting avoided after that?

Usually I just shut down and start pacing or checking my phone over and over, which doesn’t exactly help. And I guess I avoid opening more mail or calling the lender back, because I’m half convinced it’s just going to make things worse anyway.

That sounds like a pretty understandable loop: the panic hits, then pacing and checking give a little relief, while mail and calls get avoided because they feel like they could make it worse. What were the consequences of that pattern right away, and then over time, and when you look at the whole chain, is there any link where even a small shift might interrupt it?

Right away it mostly just means I lose an hour pacing around and feeling sick, and then I’m even more behind because I still haven’t dealt with whatever the notice was. Over time, yeah, I guess avoiding it makes it pile up, but I’m not convinced “small shifts” are going to do much when the bank is the one with the power here.

You’re not wrong that the bank has the power here, and it makes sense that “small shifts” can sound almost insulting when the situation is this serious. When you notice that hour of pacing and feeling sick, what do you think it does to your ability to deal with the notice afterward, even a little?

I guess it makes it harder, because by the time I finally look at it I’m already worn down and pissed off, so I’m not thinking clearly. It probably does make me less able to deal with it, even if I don’t like admitting that. I still don’t think pacing is the main problem, though—it’s more like the whole thing has me cornered.

That makes a lot of sense—you’re not saying pacing is the root problem, just that it leaves you more drained before you have to face something already huge. When you say the whole thing has you cornered, what feels like the tightest corner right now: the fear of bad news, the uncertainty, or something else?

I think it’s mostly the uncertainty, honestly. If I knew for sure what was coming, even if it was bad, I’d probably handle it better than this constant waiting and guessing. The fear of bad news is there too, but it’s the not knowing that keeps me on edge all day.

That makes a lot of sense; uncertainty can keep the nervous system stuck on alert in a way even bad news sometimes doesn’t. When you’re in that waiting-and-guessing state, what do you notice you start telling yourself about what the uncertainty means?

Mostly I tell myself it means something bad is already happening and I just don’t know the full version yet. Like if they haven’t contacted us, it’s not because things are fine—it’s because the bad news is on the way. I know that’s probably not the most rational way to look at it, but that’s where my head goes.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind is trying to fill in the blanks with the worst-case version when the stakes feel this high. When that thought shows up—“bad news is on the way”—what evidence does your mind grab onto first, and what evidence, if any, gets left out?

It grabs onto every missed call, every letter-looking envelope, and the fact that I’ve already had a few bad conversations with the lender. What gets left out is that not every silence means disaster, and sometimes there’s just a delay or a generic notice. I can see that part a little, even if my first reaction still goes straight to the worst-case.

That’s a real shift, even if it’s partial—you’re noticing both the threat cues your mind locks onto and the fact that silence doesn’t automatically mean disaster. If you were to sum up this new perspective in your own words, what would you say it is?

I guess the new perspective is that my brain is treating every delay or unknown as proof that everything is falling apart, when that isn’t actually the same thing as knowing it is. I’m still scared, but I can see that the waiting itself is making the panic worse, not just the mortgage situation. It doesn’t mean things are fine, just that I may be jumping straight to disaster before I actually have the facts. That’s hard to admit, but it does seem true enough to matter.

It sounds like you noticed the panic has been using the waiting and the unknown as if they were proof, even when they’re not the same thing, and that’s a pretty significant shift to be able to name. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

The client visited a new school to help with a family member's enrollment and noticed crowded hallways, unfamiliar procedures, and several forms that needed to be completed. That sounds really overwhelming, and it makes sense that crowded halls and unfamiliar steps would bring up anxiety and frustration. In CBT, we often look at how the same situation can lead to very different feelings depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m curious what you noticed yourself doing after those thoughts and feelings showed up?

After those thoughts hit me, I noticed I started rushing and scanning everything for what might go wrong, almost like I was bracing for more problems before they even happened. I also got quieter and less patient, and I could feel myself wanting to just get through it as fast as possible instead of slowing down to ask questions. At the same time, I kept replaying the whole visit in my head afterward, which only made me feel more tense and frustrated. I think I was acting like the situation was already a failure, even though maybe it was just unfamiliar and messy.

That’s a very insightful observation, and it sounds painful to notice how quickly your mind narrowed in on the problems and then kept replaying them afterward. Sometimes that kind of mental filter shows up when something feels unfamiliar, and I’m wondering if someone else looking at the exact same school visit might interpret it in a different way—what else might they notice?

Someone else might notice that the school was simply busy, not necessarily disorganized or doomed to be difficult. They might see that the staff were probably handling a lot of people at once and that the unfamiliar procedures were just part of adjusting to a new place. I think they might also notice that I was already stressed going in, so I was more likely to read everything as a problem. If I were calmer, I might have seen it as a normal first-day kind of experience rather than a sign that things would go badly.

That feels like a very balanced reframe, and it makes sense that a busy, unfamiliar setting could be interpreted as adjustment rather than failure. If you really believed that interpretation in the moment, what emotion do you think you would feel most strongly?

If I really believed that in the moment, I think I’d feel calmer first of all, maybe more grounded. I’d probably still feel a little uneasy because it was unfamiliar, but the main emotion would shift from anxiety and frustration to something more like patience or even curiosity. I think I’d be less likely to take everything personally or assume the day was going badly. It would probably help me feel more capable of handling it instead of feeling like I was already behind.

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re noticing that a calmer, more grounded meaning could have changed the whole emotional tone from being on edge to feeling more capable. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

If I had felt calmer and more grounded, I think I would have slowed down instead of rushing through everything. I probably would have asked more questions, paid attention to the instructions, and given myself a little more time to understand the process. I also think I would have been less tense and less likely to assume something was going wrong just because it was unfamiliar. Overall, I imagine I would have handled the whole visit with more patience and confidence instead of feeling like I had to brace for the worst.

It sounds like you’re seeing how much of the distress came from the meaning you gave the situation, not just the situation itself. If you were to sum up this new perspective in your own words, what would you say has shifted for you?

I think what has shifted is that I’m seeing this school visit less as proof that something is wrong and more as a stressful, unfamiliar situation that I reacted to very quickly. I can see now that my thoughts were making it feel bigger and more threatening than it necessarily was. That doesn’t mean the visit was easy, but it does mean I may have been adding a lot of extra anxiety on top of it. I feel a little more understanding toward myself, and also a little more hopeful that I can handle things differently next time.

It sounds like you’re noticing the difference between the situation itself and the extra meaning your mind was layering onto it, and there’s a real shift there toward understanding yourself with more steadiness. The next time this shows up, what is the first question you might ask yourself?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I'm worried that if I can't work normally for a few weeks, I won't be able to keep up with the mortgage and household bills. Then there's I'm afraid the injury will create hidden costs like prescriptions, follow-up appointments, and extra transportation that I won't have planned for. And I also keep thinking about: I keep thinking that if I can't do my normal chores or errands, everything at home will fall apart and I'll let my family down.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense your mind is staying on alert when there are so many practical pressures. Sometimes it can help to sort worries into those that are productive—something actionable you can actually do something about—and those that are unproductive, meaning more hypothetical, uncontrollable, or about things that may never happen, and the approach is different for each. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

The first one that hits me is the mortgage and bills. That feels the most urgent because it’s not just a vague fear—it’s something concrete and immediate, and I keep imagining falling behind. I know I probably need to look at the actual numbers instead of just spinning my wheels, but at night it turns into this worst-case loop where I feel like one setback could throw everything off.

That sounds very concrete, and I can hear how quickly it turns into a worst-case loop at night. When you look at the mortgage and bills worry, is there a specific action you could take with the actual numbers, or does it feel more like a hypothetical fear that’s outside your control right now?

I think there is a specific action I could take, even though I’ve been avoiding it because I don’t want to see bad news. I could sit down with the mortgage statement, bills, and our bank account and actually figure out how much cushion we have and how long we could manage if my income dipped for a bit. Part of me knows that would probably make this feel more manageable, but another part of me is scared it will confirm what I’m afraid of. So right now it feels like a mix of both: it’s a real, solvable thing in one sense, but emotionally it’s still getting blown up into a bigger disaster in my head.

It makes sense that you’re avoiding it a bit if you’re worried the numbers might be painful to see, and at the same time you can already see that getting real information could make this feel less like a disaster in your head. What would be one small first step you could take to look at the mortgage, bills, and bank account, and exactly when tomorrow could you do that?

I think the smallest first step would be to just gather everything in one place tonight or first thing in the morning—mortgage statement, utility bills, and log into the bank account—without trying to solve it all at once. Tomorrow morning after breakfast seems like the best time, maybe for 20 minutes before I get pulled into the rest of the day. I’m nervous about it, but I also think having the actual numbers in front of me would probably calm the panic down a bit. It feels better to approach it as information-gathering rather than as a final judgment on whether we’re okay.

That sounds like a thoughtful, manageable way to approach it, and I can hear both the nervousness and the sense that information might help steady things. Looking at the second worry about hidden costs, does that feel like something you can take action on by gathering information, or does it feel more outside your control right now?

I think the hidden costs are also something I can take action on, at least partly. I don’t know the exact amounts yet, but I could make a rough list of what might come up—prescriptions, follow-up visits, maybe gas or rides—and try to estimate them instead of just letting them stay as this vague cloud. At the same time, I can feel how my mind wants to turn those unknowns into something much bigger than they probably are, so getting even a loose estimate might help me put some boundaries around it.

That sounds like a real shift from “a vague cloud” to something you can at least estimate and bound, and I can hear you noticing how much your mind has been amplifying the unknowns. If you put that new perspective into your own words, what feels different about this worry now?

It feels less like this huge, undefined threat and more like a set of possible expenses I can actually look at and plan for. I’m still worried, but it’s not as paralyzing when I think of it as something I can estimate instead of something that’s just hanging over me. I also notice that my mind was treating “unknown” like “unmanageable,” and that’s not necessarily true. Even if the numbers aren’t ideal, having a rough picture would probably make me feel more in control.

That shift from “hanging over me” to something you can estimate and look at feels important, and I’m hearing you recognize how your mind had been linking “unknown” with “unmanageable” in a way that made everything feel heavier. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed about the difference between uncertainty and impossibility?

conversations.content: If I end up imprisoned, I’m terrified I’ll do irreversible damage to my relationship with my partner. I keep imagining that the separation, the shame, and the uncertainty will make them feel abandoned or betrayed, and that by the time I’m free, they’ll have emotionally moved on and there will be no way to repair what I broke.

That sounds intensely painful, and it makes sense your mind is trying to protect the relationship by running to the worst-case image. When we worry, our mind can start treating what could happen as though it will happen, even though those are very different things—what are some concrete, observable clues you’ve noticed that suggest this worst-case outcome may not actually come true?

One clue is that my partner hasn’t responded to my fear with distance or disgust; if anything, they’ve been consistent and present when I bring it up. They’ve also said things that sound like commitment, like that they want to face hard things with me rather than disappear when it gets messy. I think another concrete clue is that our connection has survived other periods of stress before, which makes me think we’re not as fragile as my mind insists we are. So while the fear feels huge, there is actual evidence that their love is steadier than the story I’m telling myself.

Those are real, observable pieces of evidence, not just wishful thinking, and it sounds like you’re noticing that your partner’s behavior has been more steady than the fear story. If those clues are right and the worst case does not happen, what do you think would most realistically happen instead?

If the worst case doesn’t happen, I think what would most realistically happen is that this becomes a painful, complicated season rather than the end of us. There would probably still be fear, grief, and a lot of logistical and emotional strain, but not necessarily abandonment. I can imagine my partner being hurt and scared at times, but still trying to stay connected and figure it out with me. That feels more believable than the idea that everything would collapse permanently.

That sounds like a more grounded picture, and I can hear how it softens the all-or-nothing feeling a bit. If you imagined the harder possibility anyway, what would you actually do step by step, and as you picture that path, how do you think you might eventually be okay?

If I had to face that harder possibility, I think the first step would be to stay as honest and calm as I could with my partner, rather than disappearing into panic or trying to control everything. Then I’d focus on the practical pieces one at a time—legal support, communication, routines for staying connected, and making sure we both have some structure to hold onto. I think I’d eventually be okay because even if the situation was painful, I wouldn’t be alone in it, and I’d still have some agency in how I showed up. What helps me feel a little less overwhelmed is realizing that “okay” might not mean untouched or unhurt—it might mean surviving it with dignity, connection, and the possibility of repair.

What you just described shows there is a path through even the hardest version of this, and it makes sense that naming that would bring some relief. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what feels different about it?

It feels less like a total catastrophe now and more like something painful that I could actually move through, which is a noticeable shift. The fear is still there, but it feels less absolute and less convincing than it did at the beginning. What feels different is that I can see more than one possible outcome now, instead of just the worst one, and I can picture myself taking concrete steps if things got hard. I also feel a little more grounded because I’m remembering that my partner’s behavior has given me real reasons to believe we could face this together.

That’s a meaningful shift, and it makes sense that seeing more than one outcome would feel grounding. If you put it into your own words, what new perspective have you reached about this fear and your relationship?

I think my new perspective is that this fear is real, but it isn’t necessarily a prediction. I’m seeing that my mind has been treating imprisonment like an automatic ending for my relationship, when there’s actually evidence that my partner is more steady, loving, and committed than that story allows for. I also realize that even if something painful happened, it wouldn’t automatically mean complete abandonment or irreparable damage; it could be something we struggle through together. That makes me feel a little more hopeful and a little less trapped by the worst-case image.

There’s something important in the way you’re holding both the reality of the fear and the possibility that it hasn’t been telling the full truth about what it means for your relationship. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that my separation will damage my relationship with my children and they’ll feel like I chose this over them. Then there's I keep imagining that my family is judging me and that I’m becoming the reason everyone is disappointed or divided. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried my separation will make holidays, visits, and family plans impossible because no one will know how to include both sides without conflict.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind keeps grabbing onto the parts that feel most high-stakes. Sometimes it helps to sort worries into ones that are productive—something you could actually respond to—and ones that are unproductive, meaning hypothetical or outside your control; which of the three worries is the first one keeping you up?

I mean, maybe, but that feels a little too neat when my brain is just going in circles at 2 a.m. The kids one is probably the first thing, because it feels the most real and the hardest to ignore—like I can’t just label it “unproductive” and make it go away.

That makes sense, and I’m glad you pushed back on it because at 2 a.m. “labeling” a worry can feel pretty flimsy. When you focus on the kids concern, is there a concrete action you could take about it right now, or does it mostly stay in the realm of what you fear might happen and what you can’t fully control?

Honestly, it’s mostly fear about what might happen, which is exactly why it keeps looping. I guess a concrete thing I can do is think through how I’ll talk to my kids and be consistent with them, but that still doesn’t solve the part where I can’t control how they’ll feel or what this does to them.

That makes sense—the part you can’t control is exactly what keeps the worry sticky, even though you can see there’s at least one concrete piece in how you talk with them. What’s one small next step you could take on that conversation, and when exactly would you do it?

I get that you want a next step, but I’m not sure planning it down to a time is the thing that’s actually stopping my brain from spiraling. Maybe I could think through what I’d say to them this weekend, but I’m wary of pretending that having a script means I’m suddenly okay with any of this.

That sounds fair—you’re not buying the idea that a script magically fixes the pain, and I’m not hearing that as resistance so much as realism. Looking at the family-judgment worry, is there anything concrete you can do about it, or is it mostly outside your control and based on what you fear others might think?

Mostly outside my control, obviously. I can choose how I show up and maybe who I tell what, but I can’t really stop people from having opinions or assuming the worst. It’s frustrating because the part I can “do something about” feels tiny compared to the part that actually hurts.

That sounds frustrating, and it makes sense that the controllable part feels small compared with how much it hurts. If the opinions themselves are outside your control, what would it be like to set aside a brief worry time later and, in the meantime, ask yourself whether there’s one more worry in the same category that keeps pulling you back?

I guess I can try the worry-time thing, but it still feels a bit like scheduling panic instead of actually dealing with it. And yeah, there’s another one: the holidays and family plans worry, because that seems like one of those things where everyone will expect me to make it work and I already know it’s going to be awkward no matter what I do.

That does sound like a lot to carry, and I hear why “worry time” sounds more like containing panic than fixing anything. With the holidays and family plans, is there something you could realistically influence, or does it mostly sit in the category of other people’s reactions and expectations?

Mostly it’s other people’s reactions and expectations, which is annoying because that’s the part that makes it feel so loaded. I can influence how clear I am and maybe set some boundaries, but I can’t make everyone comfortable with it. I guess that’s part of why it keeps looping in my head — it feels like there isn’t a clean fix.

That makes sense, and it sounds like you’re seeing clearly that the loaded part is other people’s reactions, not something you can fully control. If you can influence clarity and boundaries but not everyone’s comfort, what would you want to do with that worry during your scheduled worry time so it has a place to go without running the whole night?

I guess I’d use the worry time to write down the specific holiday scenarios that are freaking me out, instead of letting them blur together all night. Maybe I could separate what I actually need to decide from what’s just me imagining everyone being upset with me. I’m still not thrilled about the whole idea, but that does seem a little more useful than just lying there replaying it.

That sounds like a pretty grounded way to make the worry feel less like one giant cloud, even if you’re not exactly sold on the process. When you separate the holiday pieces, what do you notice about which parts are actual decisions you need to make versus the parts that are really predictions about other people’s reactions?

I guess the actual decisions are things like where I’ll be, how much time I’ll spend with each side, and what I’ll tell people ahead of time. The rest is mostly me imagining people being hurt, awkward, or disappointed, which I know isn’t the same as knowing it will happen. That’s kind of annoying to admit, but I can see the difference a little more when I lay it out like that.

That’s a meaningful shift, even if it’s annoying to notice it, because you’re seeing the difference between decisions you can make and predictions your mind is generating. How would you put this new perspective into your own words, especially the part about what’s actually yours to decide versus what’s still just fear about other people’s reactions?

I guess I’m realizing that not everything my mind is throwing at me is a problem I can solve right now. Some of it is actual stuff I need to decide, like the practical holiday plans and what boundaries I want to set, but a lot of it is me filling in the blanks with worst-case reactions from everyone else. That doesn’t make it feel less painful, but it does make it a little clearer that I’m not actually dealing with one giant impossible mess. It’s more like a few real decisions buried under a lot of fear.

It sounds like you’re noticing a real distinction between what needs a decision and what’s fear trying to complete the story, and that clarity seems to be making the situation feel a little more workable even if it still hurts. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. After a long workday, the client noticed they had skipped lunch again and then saw a colleague casually eating takeout in a meeting, which brought up frustration about their own irregular eating habits and the pressure of trying to keep up at work. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It makes sense that this feels frustrating, and it also takes courage to look closely at it rather than just judging yourself for it. We can map this together with an anger diary by tracing the trigger, the early warning signs, your response, and the outcome; before the anger fully hit, what were the first signs in your body or behavior—like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

I think the first signs were mostly physical at first—I noticed my jaw getting tight and this kind of buzzing restlessness in my chest. I also realized I was getting more irritable and impatient, like even small things at work were starting to feel overwhelming. I had that urge to just snap or shut down, and I remember feeling strangely hollow too, probably because I was already running on empty from not eating. Looking back, I think the anger was building before I even fully noticed it.

That’s really helpful to notice, because those physical shifts sound like the earliest window where change is still possible, before the anger fully takes over. On a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was it when it peaked, and what did you actually do?

I’d say it peaked around a 7 or 8 out of 10. I didn’t fully explode, but I did get sharp with people and ended up shutting down more than I meant to—I remember giving short answers and kind of withdrawing so I wouldn’t say something worse. Afterward, I felt embarrassed and a little sad, because it felt like I was reacting to more than just that moment. I think the skipped meal made me much more vulnerable, and once I noticed that, it was hard not to feel frustrated with myself for letting it get that far.

Thank you for being so honest about that; it sounds like you were trying to protect yourself from saying something worse, even though it left you feeling embarrassed afterward. What happened externally in the room with the other person, and then what happened inside you afterward right away and over the next few hours or days?

Externally, I didn’t say much beyond giving short, clipped responses, and I could tell I came across as cold or checked out. I stayed physically there in the meeting, but I was pretty withdrawn and was trying hard not to make things worse. Right afterward, I felt embarrassed and kind of shaky, like I’d lost control of my mood even though I hadn’t fully blown up. Over the next few hours, it turned into a mix of guilt and self-criticism, and I kept replaying it in my head, especially because I knew I was already tired and hungry and could have handled it better if I’d taken care of myself earlier.

You’ve mapped the cycle really clearly: the trigger was skipping lunch and seeing the takeout, the warning signs showed up in your body and mood, the response was becoming clipped and withdrawing, and the outcome was embarrassment, guilt, and replaying it afterward. Looking at those warning signs you described, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment, before the response, that might change the outcome?

I think the biggest thing I could do is stop and actually treat the hunger like a real warning sign instead of pushing past it. Even something simple like stepping out for five minutes, getting water, or eating a snack before I re-enter the meeting might interrupt that spiral. I also think naming it to myself—like, “I’m not just irritated, I’m depleted”—could help me respond with a little more compassion instead of instantly getting defensive. It feels small, but I can see how catching it there could keep me from shutting down so hard.

That feels like an important shift—you’re seeing the hunger not as a personal failing, but as a real cue that your system is getting depleted. In your own words, what new perspective are you taking from this about the connection between eating, irritation, and the way you react at work?

I’m starting to see that the irritation isn’t coming out of nowhere or meaning I’m bad at handling stress—it’s often my body telling me I’ve pushed myself too far without enough fuel. When I skip meals, I think I become much more reactive and less able to stay patient, so even normal work stuff feels bigger and more personal. That makes me realize the anger is partly a signal that I need to take care of something basic, not just something to suppress. It’s a little relieving to think of it that way, because it gives me something concrete to notice and respond to instead of just blaming myself after the fact.

It sounds like you’ve started to see the irritation in a much more compassionate and accurate way, as information rather than a verdict about you, and that shift seems to be bringing some relief and clarity. The next time that feeling shows up, what might you want to notice first so you can understand what it may be asking of you?
