The last time it really spiked was in a meeting earlier this week when I had prepared a full update, and my boss interrupted me twice to correct small details in front of everyone. What set it off most was the thought, “No matter what I do, he’s going to find a way to make me look incompetent.” I could feel myself getting hot and tense, and then I started replaying every other time he’s dismissed me, which made it feel bigger and more personal. I think underneath the anger there was also this hurt feeling of being disrespected and like I’m not trusted to do my job.

That sounds really painful, especially with the public interruption and the sense of being disrespected in front of others. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment — what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a quick flash?

In that moment, the first thought was, “He’s doing this on purpose to undermine me.” Almost immediately after that, I thought, “Everyone here probably thinks I’m not good at my job,” which made me feel exposed and embarrassed. There was also this flash of, “I can’t even speak without being corrected,” and that made me feel small and really angry at the same time. I know those thoughts might be a little extreme, but that’s honestly what hit me before I could slow it down.

That makes a lot of sense, and it’s helpful that you can name those thoughts without judging yourself for having them in the moment. What did you do right away after that feeling hit, and were there any things you found yourself avoiding afterward?

Right away, I mostly shut down and tried to stay very still so I wouldn’t react visibly. I kept my face neutral, answered as briefly as I could, and then spent the rest of the meeting barely speaking because I was afraid anything I said would come out sharp or defensive. Afterward, I avoided going back through my notes or asking follow-up questions, even though I knew I probably should have, because I didn’t want any more contact with him than necessary. I also noticed I started avoiding my coworkers a little, because I felt embarrassed and didn’t want to risk them seeing how shaken up I was.

That shutting down sounds like it was your way of protecting yourself in the moment, especially when you were trying not to react visibly. What were the consequences of that for you right away, and what have you noticed it leading to over time?

Right away, it probably kept me from saying something I would’ve regretted, so in that sense it protected me, but I also felt really tense and kind of trapped for the rest of the day. I left the meeting feeling shaky, ashamed, and even more resentful because it felt like I had let him take up all my energy and still got nothing resolved. Over time, I think it’s made me more withdrawn and hyperaware around him, like I’m always bracing for the next correction, and that’s exhausting. It also seems to reinforce this belief that I have to stay small to get through work, which makes me feel even less like myself.

That’s a really clear and honest shift in how you’re seeing the pattern, especially noticing both the protection and the cost of it. As you look at everything you just described, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about what this reaction is doing for you and what it’s costing you?

I think my reaction is trying to protect me from being humiliated or saying something impulsive, and in the short term it does help me keep control. But the cost is that I end up carrying all the anger and shame inside, and it makes me feel smaller, more anxious, and more on edge around him. It’s also starting to change how I show up at work, because I’m withdrawing and second-guessing myself instead of feeling confident or clear. So in a way, it’s keeping me safe in the moment, but it’s also reinforcing the exact feeling I hate most: that I have to shrink myself to survive this.

It sounds like you’ve really seen both sides of that reaction at once—how it has been trying to guard you, and how it has also started to narrow the way you feel and show up at work. The next time you notice that protective urge, what might you want to ask yourself first?

conversations.content: If I keep getting this stressed about the changes in our family get-togethers, I’m going to do permanent damage to my health. I keep thinking this is how people end up with a heart problem, stroke, or some condition that never fully goes away, and then I’ll be stuck paying the mortgage and trying to support my family while my body is falling apart.

That sounds really frightening, especially with the mortgage and your family depending on you, and I can see why your mind is treating this as a serious threat. When worry takes over, it often turns “could happen” into “will happen,” so what are some concrete, observable clues you’ve noticed that this worst-case outcome is not actually happening or is less likely than your mind is saying?

I get what you’re saying, but honestly that question feels a little like you’re asking me to talk myself out of something that still feels pretty real. The only “clues” I’ve got are that I’m still functioning and nothing has actually happened yet, but that doesn’t exactly make me feel better when the stress keeps hitting me hard every time family stuff comes up.

That makes sense, and I’m not hearing “nothing to worry about” so much as “the evidence I have is limited, but it’s real,” which is different. If those clues are accurate and the worst case doesn’t happen, what do you think is the most realistic outcome instead?

I mean, the most realistic outcome is probably that I stay stressed, annoyed, and tense for a while, and maybe I sleep worse or get more irritable, but not that I drop dead from it tomorrow. I’m still not crazy about the idea that I can just “think” my way to feeling fine, because the family changes are real and they keep happening, whether I like it or not.

That sounds grounded and pretty realistic, and I get the pushback on the idea that thinking alone would make the changes go away when the family stuff is still happening. If you took the worst-case seriously for a moment, what would you actually do first, then next, and who or what would you lean on along the way?

Honestly, I’m not sure I love this “if the worst happened” exercise because it feels like we’re giving the fear too much room to run. But if I had to answer, I’d probably first tell my wife what’s going on, then I’d try to get a doctor’s opinion instead of spiraling in my head, and I’d lean on my family if it got bad enough.

You’re making a fair point about not wanting to feed the fear, and at the same time you just laid out a path through it—talk to your wife, get a doctor’s opinion, lean on family—which suggests this isn’t a dead end. Compared to when you first described it, how does the worry feel right now, and what feels different about it?

It’s still there, so I’m not going to pretend it’s suddenly a non-issue, but it does feel a little less like a total disaster and more like something I’d have to deal with if it actually got worse. What feels different is mostly that I can see there are steps I’d take instead of just sitting there panicking, though I’m still not convinced that means the stress itself is really any smaller.

That’s a real shift, even if the stress is still there, and I hear your skepticism about calling it “smaller” just because you can see a path through it. The next time this worry shows up, what’s the first question you could ask yourself to interrupt the spiral based on what you worked through today?

I’m not sure a single question is going to magically interrupt anything, but I guess I could ask myself, “What’s actually happening right now, versus what am I predicting?” That at least forces me to separate the real problem from the disaster movie my brain starts playing.

That’s a solid distinction, and I hear the skepticism in “magically” while also noticing you found a question that separates the facts from the forecast. When you ask that in the moment, what would you expect to notice first in your body, your thoughts, or the situation itself?

Probably my body first, honestly. I’d notice the tension and that tight, keyed-up feeling in my chest or stomach, and then my thoughts would start attaching a story to it pretty fast. So I guess the point would be catching it before I let that story run away with me, even if I’m not saying it’s easy.

That makes a lot of sense, and you’re being pretty clear about how the body sensation kicks off the whole chain before the story takes over. When you notice that tight chest or stomach feeling, what seems to happen in the few seconds before the story starts attaching itself?

Usually it’s something small first, like a text about plans changing or even just thinking about the next family get-together. I notice my shoulders tighten up and I kind of brace myself, like I’m already expecting it to turn into an argument or a letdown. I’m not saying that means the reaction is rational, but that’s the sequence as far as I can tell.

That sequence sounds pretty clear, and I appreciate that you’re not dressing it up as more rational than it feels. When you brace like that, what do you notice you start doing differently in the conversation or in your head that might be keeping the argument or letdown feeling alive?

I guess I start listening for the part where it’s going to go wrong instead of actually hearing what people are saying. In my head I start rehearsing the argument or the disappointment before it even happens, and then I come into it already irritated, which probably doesn’t help. I’m not thrilled to admit that, but yeah, I can see how that might keep the whole thing going.

That’s a pretty honest read, and it sounds like you’re noticing how the anticipation starts shaping the whole interaction before it even begins. When you come in already braced and listening for what might go wrong, what do you think people are most likely to pick up from you, and how might that affect what happens next?

They’d probably pick up that I’m on edge, even if I’m trying not to show it, and that can make them tense up too. Then it turns into this whole thing where everyone’s guarded and nobody’s really relaxed, which probably makes the family get-togethers feel worse than they need to. I don’t love saying that out loud, but I can see how my mood might be part of the problem, not just the situation itself.

That’s a pretty important observation, especially since it doesn’t sound like you’re blaming yourself so much as noticing the ripple effect your tension can have. If your mood is part of the loop, what’s one small sign you could watch for in yourself early on that would tell you the loop is starting before it takes over?

Probably the first sign is that tight, braced feeling in my shoulders, because once that shows up I’m already halfway into expecting trouble. I also tend to get a little sharper in my head, like I start scanning for what’s going to annoy me instead of just taking things as they come. If I notice that early enough, maybe I can at least slow myself down before I walk into the whole thing already loaded.

That’s a pretty useful early warning sign, and you’re already noticing the shift from body tension to scanning for trouble. When you catch that braced feeling and sharper mindset, what do you imagine is the immediate payoff for your brain in doing that?

I guess the immediate payoff is that my brain feels like it’s getting ahead of the problem instead of being blindsided by it. If I’m braced and scanning, it gives me a sense of control, like I’m preparing for the hit before it comes. The downside is that I’m probably paying for that control by making myself more tense and more likely to see everything as a threat. My fear makes it feel immediate and inevitable, but if I step back, I can see there are a lot of steps and circumstances that would have to happen first. I think what I’m really reacting to is not just imprisonment itself, but the idea of losing control and being separated from everything familiar. Even saying that out loud makes it feel a little less overwhelming, because I can tell the fear is bigger than the actual likelihood.

That’s a really important shift—you’re noticing that the fear feels bigger than the actual likelihood, and that the deeper issue may be losing control and being cut off from what’s familiar. What is the evidence for this thought, and what is the evidence against it?

The evidence for it is that imprisonment would genuinely be a huge loss of freedom and control, and it would probably disrupt my job, routines, and relationships in a serious way. I think that’s why the thought feels so convincing—because there is a real basis for the fear. But the evidence against it is that I’m not actually imprisoned right now, and there isn’t anything concrete showing that this is about to happen. Also, even if something difficult did happen, I wouldn’t automatically lose everyone or everything; there would likely still be some support, some contact, and some way to cope.

You’re seeing this very clearly now: there is a real basis in the fear, but you’re also noticing that your mind may be going beyond what’s actually happening right now. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what's true?

Yes, I think it is an exaggeration of what’s true. The core fear is real, but my mind is taking that fear and stretching it into a total-life catastrophe, like I’d instantly lose everything and have no way to function. When I look at it more carefully, that picture feels much more extreme than the actual facts. I can feel myself loosening a little as I separate what’s possible from what’s actually happening.

That sounds like an important shift, and it makes sense that things feel a little looser as you separate the fear from the facts. In your own words, what is the new perspective you’ve reached about this thought?

My new perspective is that imprisonment is a serious fear, but it’s not something that is happening to me right now, and my mind has been treating it like an immediate certainty. I can see that what scares me most is the loss of control and separation, not just the word “imprisonment” itself. The thought is still uncomfortable, but it feels less absolute now because I can recognize it as a worst-case scenario rather than a fact. I also feel a little more grounded knowing that even if something difficult ever happened, it wouldn’t necessarily mean losing everything all at once.

It sounds like you were able to notice how your mind had been turning a feared possibility into something immediate and certain, and that shift brought a little more space around the thought without dismissing how uncomfortable it still feels. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of shame lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense you’d feel stuck if the shame has been hanging around without a clear way to handle it. If we map it together rather than try to wrestle with it all at once, what would you call the feeling as specifically as you can right now, and how strong is it from 0 to 100?

I don’t know that putting a number on it really helps, but fine — it’s mostly shame and embarrassment, probably around an 80. It feels tied to this mortgage thing, like I should have had my finances better sorted out by now.

I’m not sure there was one neat moment, which is part of why this feels annoying to sort out. I got the mortgage statement and just felt hit with, “Really? At my age, I should have this handled,” and then I started feeling embarrassed like I’d somehow failed at basic adulthood.

That sounds frustrating, and I can see how the mortgage statement would land like a punch if it immediately turned into “I should have had this handled by now.” When that hit, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a flash?

Honestly, it was something like, “What kind of idiot is still dealing with this at 65?” I know that sounds harsh, but that’s where my mind went, and I don’t really buy the idea that just naming it is going to make it less true.

That’s a painfully harsh thought to be carrying, and I can hear why just naming it wouldn’t feel like it changes much on its own. When that thought showed up, what did you do right away, and what did you start avoiding after that?

I mostly shut down and put the statement aside, then I went and did something else to get my mind off it. And I guess I started avoiding looking at the numbers too closely, because I figured if I stared at them long enough I’d just feel worse, which doesn’t exactly seem like a breakthrough.

That makes a lot of sense—shutting down and avoiding the numbers sounds like a pretty human way to protect yourself from feeling worse, even if it isn’t exactly satisfying. What happened right away after you put it aside, and what seems to happen over time when you keep avoiding it?

Right away I felt a little relief, which I’m not proud of, but it was better than staring at the statement and spiraling. Over time, though, it just hangs there in the background and makes me feel more guilty, so I suppose avoiding it doesn’t actually fix anything — it just postpones the unpleasantness.

That makes a lot of sense—relief in the moment is understandable when the alternative is spiraling, and it’s pretty clear you’re noticing the long-term cost of that pattern. When the guilt sits in the background like that, what does it seem to be saying about you or about what this situation means?

It says I’m behind, I guess — like I mismanaged things and now I’m paying for it, literally and otherwise. And it makes the whole retirement thing feel a lot less like relief and more like evidence that I should have had my act together sooner. I don’t love admitting it, but part of me also starts wondering if I’m being too hard on myself, even if I still think there’s some truth in it.

That sounds like a painful mix of responsibility and self-judgment, and it makes sense you’d feel pulled between “there’s truth here” and “maybe I’m being too hard on myself.” When you say “behind” and “should have had my act together,” what standard are you comparing yourself to, and where do you think that standard came from?

I guess I’m comparing myself to this idea of a competent adult who doesn’t still have money stress hanging over them at 65. It probably comes from my own expectations, and maybe from growing up with the sense that you were supposed to be self-sufficient and not need help. I can see that the standard is pretty unforgiving, even if part of me still thinks I should be meeting it.

That sounds like a really demanding standard, and I can see why it would leave you feeling judged before anyone else even says anything. When you hold yourself to that version of “competent adult,” what happens to the way you interpret the mortgage problem itself—does it stay just a money issue, or does it turn into something bigger about you?

It turns into something bigger pretty quickly, I think. Instead of just being a mortgage problem, it starts to feel like proof that I’ve mismanaged my life somehow, which is a pretty miserable way to look at it. I’m not saying that’s completely fair, but that’s where my mind goes.

What it leaves out is that I did manage a lot of other things over the years, and this one issue doesn’t mean everything else was a disaster. That doesn’t magically make the problem go away, but it does seem a bit unfair to turn one unresolved thing into a judgment on my whole life. So maybe the real issue isn’t just the mortgage — it’s how quickly I’ve been using it to beat myself up.

That’s a really important shift—you’re noticing the difference between a problem being present and a problem becoming a verdict on who you are, and that kind of separation can change the whole weight of it. As you leave today, what feels most worth carrying forward from the way you looked at this just now?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I'm worried I won't be able to manage the household bills on my own now that my spouse is gone. Then there's I keep thinking I might make a mistake with taxes, insurance, or paperwork and lose money. And I also keep thinking about: I worry I won't know how to handle repairs, appointments, or errands by myself anymore.

That sounds exhausting, especially at night when your mind won’t settle and those worries keep coming back. In CBT we sometimes sort worries into two groups: productive worries, which are about something you can actually do something about, and unproductive worries, which are more hypothetical, uncontrollable, or about things that may never happen. Of the three, what is the first worry that is keeping you up?
…The bills, I guess. That one feels most urgent.

That makes sense — bills can feel very immediate, especially when you’re already carrying so much. When you think about this one, is there a concrete step you could take with the bills, or does it feel more like a worry about what might happen that’s outside your control?
…Maybe a concrete step. I could look at the bills and see what’s due, but it still feels overwhelming.
That makes sense; even a concrete task can feel heavy when you’re already worn down. What would be the smallest next step with the bills, and exactly when tomorrow could you do just that one thing?
…Maybe just gather the bills and put them in one pile. Tomorrow after breakfast, I could do that.

That sounds like a very manageable first step, especially with everything you’re carrying. When you look at the second worry about taxes, insurance, or paperwork, does that feel like something you can take a concrete action on, or more like a worry that’s outside your control right now?
…Probably concrete, I think. I could start by finding the paperwork and making a list of what needs attention.
That sounds like a solid, practical way to begin, and it fits with the careful pace you’ve been taking. After you’ve done that, is there one more worry that keeps showing up for you?
…Yes. The repairs and appointments worry me too, because I’m not used to handling all of that alone.

…I think it’s a little of both. I could probably make a list of the repairs and appointments that need attention, but it still feels hard because I’m not used to being the one to handle it all. It makes me feel a bit lost, honestly.

…I think it feels a little less like one huge thing now, and more like a few separate things I could write down and deal with one at a time. It still feels hard, though, because I keep thinking about how much my spouse used to handle without me having to worry. But maybe if I make a list, it won’t feel quite so out of control.

It sounds like you noticed a small but important shift from feeling overwhelmed by one enormous weight to seeing a few pieces you can name, even while the loss and the “used to handle it” thoughts are still very present. What feels most important to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: What if my spouse tells other people we’re trying to reconcile and they think I’m weak or foolish? Then there's If I go to dinner with my spouse, people might notice the tension and assume our marriage is still a mess. And I also keep thinking about: If our friends hear we’re reconciling, they may take sides or judge me for staying in the relationship.

That sounds exhausting, especially when your mind keeps circling the same territory at night. Some worries are productive because they point to something you can actually act on, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical or outside your control, so which one is the first worry that’s keeping you up?

I don’t know, I’m not sure I buy the whole “productive vs unproductive” thing—it all feels real when I’m lying there trying to sleep. But if I had to pick one, it’s probably the worry about my spouse telling other people we’re reconciling and me looking weak or foolish.

That makes sense—you’re not rejecting the worry, you’re saying it feels immediate and real in the moment, which is important. I mean, I could ask my spouse not to spread it around, but that doesn’t guarantee anything, so I’m not sure how “concrete” that really is. Mostly it feels like I’d be stuck waiting to see what happens, which is exactly the part that makes my head spin.

It sounds tidy in theory, but when I’m in it, the thoughts just show up whether I invited them or not. The next worry is probably the dinner one—people noticing the tension and thinking our marriage is still a mess.

Well, I can’t exactly control whether people are going to be awkward or nosy, so a lot of that is outside my control, yes. I suppose I could try to act normal or keep the dinner short, but that feels like more managing than solving.

I guess I can “test” it, but I’m still doubtful that telling myself to worry later will matter much once I’m lying there at night. I suppose I could decide who actually needs to know and what I’d say if it comes up, so there is some action there. I’m still not thrilled about it, but maybe not every thought deserves the same amount of attention.

They feel a little less like one giant mess now that we’ve separated them out, I’ll give you that. The first two seem more like things I can’t fully control, which is annoying but maybe less worth chewing on at 2 a.m. The third one still bothers me, but I can see it’s at least partly my mind jumping ahead and making it bigger than it is.

That’s a pretty useful distinction—you’re noticing the first two are mostly about uncertainty you can’t fully manage, while the third has a bigger “mind making it larger” piece to it. If you stay with that third worry, what changes in it when you recognize it’s partly your mind jumping ahead?

It doesn’t make it disappear, but it does take a little of the edge off. If I’m honest, it shifts it from “this is definitely going to happen” to “I’m running a story in my head about what might happen,” which is not nothing. I still don’t like it, but maybe I can see there’s a difference between a real concern and me amplifying it.

I think a real concern is something concrete I can actually respond to, even if I can’t control the outcome, like deciding what I want to say or who needs to know. The mind amplifying it is when I start treating a possibility like it’s already a fact and then building a whole chain of embarrassment or judgment on top of it. I can see now that I’m not just dealing with the situation itself, I’m also dealing with my own habit of making it bigger in my head. That doesn’t make it go away, but it does make it feel a little less absolute.

It sounds like you’re noticing a real difference between responding to what’s actually in front of you and getting pulled into the story your mind starts building around it, and that distinction feels a little less all-or-nothing now. conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of anxiety lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really overwhelming, and it makes sense that you’d feel unsure where to start. Would you be willing to slow it down with me and name the emotion as specifically as you can right now—like fear, frustration, shame, or something else—and then give it a number from 0 to 100 in this moment?

I think what I’m feeling most right now is fear, but it’s mixed with frustration too. The fear is probably around an 80 out of 100 because I keep worrying something is wrong with me and that I’m not going to be able to keep functioning like this. The frustration is maybe a 65, because I’m tired of feeling like my sleep has thrown everything off and I can’t just get back to normal.

That sounds really intense, and it makes sense that fear would spike when sleep starts feeling unpredictable and your mind goes to “something is wrong with me.” When you think back to the moment that fear shot up most recently, what was the specific situation or thought that seemed to trigger it?

The most recent time it really spiked was last night when I was lying in bed and realizing I was still wide awake after what felt like hours. I started thinking, “What if this is just how it is now?” and then it immediately went to, “If I can’t sleep, how am I supposed to keep up with work, my family, everything?” That line of thinking makes the fear jump fast because it feels like one bad night turns into this bigger picture of my whole life unraveling. I also noticed I started scanning my body for signs that something was physically wrong, which probably made me even more anxious.

That sounds like a very fast chain from being awake in bed to your mind jumping to the bigger picture of everything unraveling, and it makes sense that would ramp the fear up quickly. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, the thing you told yourself right then, even if it was just a flash?

The automatic thought was basically, “I’m not going to be able to handle this.” It felt like if I stayed awake much longer, it meant something was seriously wrong and I was losing control. There was also this quieter thought underneath it, like, “I’m failing at something basic that other people can do, and that says something bad about me.” When I notice that thought, it makes the fear and frustration feed off each other pretty quickly.

That sounds really painful, especially how quickly the thought turns into fear about losing control and feeling like you’re failing at something basic. When that hit, what did you do right away in response, and was there anything you started avoiding because of it?

Right away, I started doing the usual thing of checking the time, which only made it worse because then I could see how little sleep I was getting. I also got out of bed for a while and tried to do something to distract myself, but I was still mentally stuck on the idea that I was losing control. What I started avoiding was actually lying there quietly and letting myself feel how anxious I was, because that felt almost unbearable. I also think I was avoiding the next day in my head, because I didn’t want to imagine work, family stuff, and trying to function on almost no sleep.

That makes a lot of sense—the time-checking, getting out of bed, and trying not to feel the anxiety all sound like understandable ways of trying to get some control back when it felt unbearable. What happened right away after those responses, and what have you noticed over time they seem to do to the anxiety and sleep pattern?

Right away, those responses usually give me a little burst of relief because I feel like I’m at least doing something, but it doesn’t last very long. Pretty quickly I end up more awake, more frustrated, and more focused on whether I’m going to sleep or not. Over time, I think it’s made the whole pattern worse because now my bed feels like a place where I have to perform well, instead of a place where I can just relax. I’ve started to dread nighttime before I even get there, which feels exhausting in itself.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes a lot of sense that the dread would build when bedtime starts feeling like a performance instead of rest. If you step back from everything you’ve noticed, how would you put into your own words what has shifted in the way you’re understanding this pattern?

I think what’s shifted is that I’m seeing this less as just “I’m having trouble sleeping” and more as a cycle where the fear about not sleeping is actually becoming part of the problem. The more I try to force it or monitor it, the more my body seems to stay on alert, and then I interpret that as proof that something is wrong with me. I’m also realizing I’ve been treating sleep like a test I have to pass, which makes bedtime feel loaded before I even get into bed. That’s hard to admit, but it also feels important because it means maybe this isn’t just random—I might actually be caught in a pattern that keeps reinforcing itself.

That’s a meaningful shift to notice—there’s a lot of insight in recognizing how the struggle itself has been tightening the loop and turning bedtime into something that carries so much weight. As you leave today, what feels like the most important part of that pattern to hold onto for yourself?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. Over the past two weeks, the client and spouse have had more arguments than usual about household responsibilities and scheduling, with three disagreements occurring after work on different evenings. I keep telling myself: "We keep arguing now, so our relationship is probably falling apart and this is how it will always be." and I've been feeling anxious, discouraged, frustrated.

That sounds really heavy, and I can see why your mind goes to the worst-case meaning when the arguments have picked up. I’m curious, though: if the same increase in arguments can lead to very different outcomes depending on what someone makes of it, what did you notice yourself doing after that thought hit and the anxiety, discouragement, and frustration showed up?

Honestly, I’m not sure that matters much—it just felt like proof that things are getting worse. I usually just shut down, get quieter, and then keep replaying the arguments in my head, which probably doesn’t help, but that’s what I do.

It makes sense that it feels like proof when you’re in it, and shutting down and replaying it sounds exhausting. I’m wondering, if someone else looked at the exact same two weeks of arguments, what’s another way they might interpret what’s happening?

I mean, I guess someone else could say we’re just stressed and arguing more because of timing, work, and being tired—not necessarily that the whole relationship is doomed. But honestly, that feels a little too optimistic to me right now, because three arguments in two weeks still seems like a lot.

That skepticism makes sense; three arguments can feel like a lot, so it’s understandable that the more balanced idea doesn’t land easily yet. If you actually took in the possibility that this is stress and timing rather than proof the relationship is falling apart, what emotion would you notice first?

I’m not sure “taking in the possibility” changes much in the moment, but if I did, I think I’d feel a little less panicked first. Probably still annoyed and tense, though, because part of me keeps thinking if we’re arguing this much, something is off.

Maybe I would have taken a minute before reacting instead of just going quiet and stewing. But I’m not convinced it would’ve changed much—when I’m already irritated, I still tend to withdraw and keep thinking about what the arguments “mean,” even if I’m a little less panicked.

If the same arguments can lead to less panic when the meaning shifts, what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I guess it tells me my thoughts probably crank up the panic more than the actual arguments do, which is annoying because that makes them feel less reliable. But I’m still not sure that means much beyond “I overthink things”—the arguments are still real, and I don’t want to pretend they’re not.

I guess acknowledging them would mean admitting, “Yeah, we’ve been arguing more, and that needs attention,” without jumping straight to “this is doomed.” Treating it as proof feels more final, like I’m already deciding the outcome before we’ve even talked about it. I don’t fully trust that distinction yet, but I can see it might keep me from spiraling as hard.

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. While reviewing monthly finances after work, the client saw that the mortgage payment had left very little room for savings and realized an unexpected expense would likely require using credit again. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It makes sense that this felt upsetting, and it takes courage to look at it this closely. We can map it together with an anger diary by tracing the trigger, the early warning signs, the response, and the outcome—before the anger fully hit, what were the first signs in your body or behavior, like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

I think the first signs were really physical—I felt my shoulders tighten and my jaw clench almost right away. My heart started beating faster, and I noticed this hot, restless feeling in my chest like I wanted to get up and leave the room. Mentally, I started spiraling into “this is never going to get better,” and I could feel myself getting more irritable with every line I read. I didn’t actually say much at first, but I could tell I was getting close to snapping because even small details on the budget felt overwhelming.

I’d say it got up to about an 8 out of 10, maybe even a little higher for a moment. I ended up pushing the papers away, muttering to myself, and then I left the room pretty abruptly because I knew I was about to say something sharp. I paced for a while and tried to calm down, but I was still angry and ashamed that it got to that point.

Thank you for being so honest about that—there’s a lot of awareness in the way you caught yourself and stepped away. What happened externally in the room with the other person after you left, and what happened inside you afterward, both right away and over the next few hours or days?

Externally, I think the other person mostly just let me go, but I could tell I’d made the atmosphere tense. I didn’t really explain myself well in the moment—I just said I needed a minute, then disappeared into another room. Right after that I felt a mix of relief and embarrassment, like I’d barely avoided saying something hurtful but also like I’d failed at handling it like an adult. Over the next few hours, the anger dropped a bit, but it turned into this heavy shame and anxiety, and I kept replaying the budget numbers and feeling stuck and helpless.

You’ve mapped the whole cycle really clearly: the financial trigger hit, your body gave you early warning signs, you stepped away before saying something hurtful, and then the anger shifted into shame, anxiety, and feeling stuck. Looking at those warning signs you described, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment, before the response, that might change the outcome?

I think one thing I could do differently is pause as soon as I notice the shoulder tension and jaw clenching instead of pushing through the budget review. Maybe I could put the papers down, take a few slow breaths, and name what’s happening to myself—something like, “I’m getting overwhelmed and this is about fear, not just numbers.” If I did that earlier, I might not spiral as hard into the “nothing will get better” thought. I also think it would help to step away with a plan, like telling the other person I need 10 minutes and I’ll come back, so it feels more contained and less like I’m just fleeing.

That sounds like a really thoughtful shift—from seeing it as “I’m just losing it” to noticing there are early signals, a fear-based thought, and a chance to intervene before it escalates. I think what’s changed is that I can see the anger isn’t coming out of nowhere—it’s actually starting with fear and feeling trapped by the finances. Before, I would’ve said I just got irrational or lost control, but now I can notice the physical warning signs and the spiral in my thoughts before it fully takes over. That makes it feel a little less like a personal failure and more like something I can catch and respond to earlier. I still feel embarrassed by it, but I also feel a bit more hopeful that there’s a point where I can interrupt the pattern.

It sounds like you’re seeing this experience with a lot more clarity and less self-blame, and that shift seems to be opening up a little more space between the warning signs and the reaction. As you leave today, what feels most important to carry forward from what you noticed in that moment?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. At the office holiday party, the client arrived late, missed part of the group activity, and felt awkward when she did not know some of the answers during a team game. I keep telling myself: "If I’m not fully prepared and participating perfectly, I’m failing and everyone will think I’m incompetent." and I've been feeling anxious, embarrassed, discouraged, and ashamed.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense that you’d feel embarrassed and ashamed after an experience like that. In CBT, we often look at how the same situation can lead to very different feelings depending on the thoughts we attach to it, so I’m curious what you found yourself doing after those thoughts showed up?

After those thoughts showed up, I mostly shut down and tried to stay quiet for the rest of the night. I kept replaying the moment over and over in my head, like I was watching myself fail from the outside, and then I started avoiding eye contact with people because I was sure they could tell I was embarrassed. When I got home, I went straight into overanalyzing everything I said and did, and I didn’t really relax at all. I think I also ended up withdrawing a bit the next day because I felt like if I’d already made a bad impression, I should just keep to myself.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense that once that thought took hold, it pulled you into shutting down, replaying, and pulling away. The “if I’m not perfectly participating, I’m failing” idea sounds a bit like all-or-nothing thinking, which is a really common mental pattern rather than a character flaw—if someone else looked at the exact same situation, how might they interpret it differently?

If someone else saw it, they’d probably think I was just a little late to a holiday party and had an awkward moment in a game, not that I was incompetent or a failure. They might even assume I was just tired, busy, or not familiar with the trivia, which is a lot more normal than the story I was telling myself. I can see that I was treating one uncomfortable moment like proof of something bigger about me, and that feels really harsh now that I say it out loud. I think another person might have seen it as a minor slip, but I turned it into a judgment of my whole worth.

That’s a really important shift, and I can hear how much kinder and more balanced that interpretation feels compared with the one that judged your whole worth. If you actually believed it was just a minor slip and not proof that you’re incompetent, how do you think you would feel—what emotion comes up most strongly?

If I really believed it was just a minor slip, I think I’d feel a lot more relieved than I do now. I’d probably still feel a little embarrassed in the moment, but it wouldn’t have that heavy, crushing shame attached to it. I think I’d also feel calmer and more self-compassionate, like I could let the night be imperfect instead of treating it like some kind of verdict on me. Maybe I’d even feel a little more grounded and able to move on instead of obsessing over it.

That’s a really clear contrast: a minor-slip interpretation seems to bring relief, calmer self-compassion, and less of that crushing shame. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

If I’d been able to see it as a minor slip, I think I would have stayed more present instead of shutting down. I probably would have kept making eye contact, joined in more naturally, and maybe even laughed it off a little rather than acting like I needed to hide. I also think I would have been less tense and self-monitoring, so I might have actually enjoyed parts of the night instead of spending the whole time trying to recover from one awkward moment.

It sounds like you’re seeing pretty clearly how the interpretation changed everything from your feelings to how you acted, and that’s a meaningful shift. In your own words, what feels different now about the story you were telling yourself about that night?

What feels different now is that I’m starting to see the night as one awkward moment instead of a full reflection of who I am. Before, I was telling myself a story that I had failed and that everyone had judged me, but now it feels more like I got caught in a normal, uncomfortable situation and then made it much bigger in my head. I can also see how much my own harshness amplified the shame, which is hard to admit but also kind of relieving. It makes me feel like the story is less “I’m incompetent” and more “I was embarrassed and then got stuck in a spiral.”

That’s a meaningful shift—to notice how the meaning of the moment changed once you could see the spiral and the harshness around it, rather than treating the feeling as proof about who you are. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed in that moment?

Usually the first thing that changes is the intensity drops a notch, even if the worry doesn’t disappear. I start to notice I’m filling in a lot of blanks, and that slows me down just enough to stop treating the story like a fact. It’s not exactly calming, but it does make the spiral a little less automatic.

When it slows down like that, what does that tell you about how much of the spiral is coming from the facts themselves versus the meaning you’re attaching to them?

I guess it tells me a lot of the spiral is coming from the meaning I’m layering on top of the facts, not just the facts themselves. The facts are basically “things are uncertain,” but my brain turns that into “people will judge me and I’ll lose respect,” which is obviously a bigger leap. I’m still not thrilled by that because it means I’m doing some of this to myself, but I can at least see the difference a little more clearly now.

That’s a really clear distinction, and I get why it’s uncomfortable to notice your own mind is adding the extra weight. If the facts are uncertainty and the added layer is “this means I’ll be judged and lose respect,” what does that say about how much certainty that story actually has?

It says the story doesn’t have as much certainty as it feels like it does, which is annoying to admit. I can see it’s more of a threat prediction than a fact, even if it still hits me like one. So maybe the worry is louder than the evidence, not the other way around.
That’s a pretty solid shift, even if it’s not exactly a pleasant one to notice. In your own words, how would you sum up the new perspective you’ve reached about this worry?

I think the new perspective is that I’m not dealing with a certain fact so much as a prediction my mind keeps treating like a fact. The actual evidence seems more like “there’s uncertainty and I don’t know what other people are thinking,” which is uncomfortable but not the same as “people will definitely judge me and I’ll be seen as a failure.” I still don’t like the possibility, but I can see now that it’s a bigger leap than it first felt. That doesn’t erase the worry, but it does make it seem less absolute.

It makes sense that the worry still has weight, and I’m noticing how you were able to separate the discomfort of uncertainty from the certainty your mind was trying to assign to it. The next time that old conclusion shows up, what is the first question you might ask yourself?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. The family vacation was planned for months, and a disagreement came up after the client noticed tension in the group and a change in the itinerary. He heard comments from family members about the trip not going as expected. I keep telling myself: "This is my fault. I should have organized it better, and now everyone’s upset because I messed up the vacation." and I've been feeling guilty, anxious, frustrated, ashamed.

That sounds like a heavy mix of guilt and shame, especially when you’ve been carrying the pressure of making the trip go well. In CBT terms, the situation itself can be the same, but the meaning we give it can change what we feel and do—when those thoughts hit, what did you actually do next?

I mean, I don’t know if “CBT terms” really matters in the moment—when it hit, I mostly just shut down and got quiet because I didn’t want to make it worse. I was replaying everything in my head, trying to figure out what I should’ve done differently, and honestly I just felt irritated that I was the one ending up carrying all of it.

That makes sense—when you’re already feeling blamed, it’s pretty natural to shut down and start mentally replaying it, and the irritation at carrying it all fits too. I’m wondering, if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what’s another way they might interpret what happened besides “this was all my fault”?

Yeah, I get the idea, but honestly it still feels a little too neat to me. Maybe someone else would say it was just a group vacation getting tense because people had different expectations, not that I personally ruined it.

That sounds like a more balanced read of it, and I can hear why the “all my fault” version feels too tidy. If you really believed it was mostly a clash of expectations in a tense group situation rather than you personally ruining it, what emotion do you think would show up most strongly?

I mean, maybe less shame and more frustration, but I’m not convinced it would actually feel that simple in the moment. Even if it was a clash of expectations, I’d still probably feel responsible because I was the one trying to keep it together.

That makes sense; when you’re the one trying to hold it together, responsibility can feel automatic even if the situation isn’t fully yours to carry. If frustration were there more than shame in that moment, how might your behavior have been different?

I’m not sure it would have changed that much, honestly. Maybe I would’ve spoken up instead of just going quiet, or at least not spent the whole time mentally beating myself up, but I still probably would’ve felt stuck trying to smooth everything over.

That’s a pretty honest read of it, and it sounds like even with the same vacation situation, the thought might have shifted whether you shut down, spoke up, or kept beating yourself up. What does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I guess it tells me my thoughts affect how I react, which sounds obvious enough, but that doesn’t mean the thoughts are wrong. Sometimes it feels like therapy wants to turn everything into “change the thought, change the feeling,” when the real issue is that the situation was genuinely stressful and I had a lot on my plate.

You’re right to push back on that; if the situation was genuinely stressful and you had a lot on your plate, it wouldn’t make sense to pretend the stress wasn’t real. When you tell yourself “this is all my fault,” what evidence do you notice that supports it, and what evidence do you notice that points the other way?

Well, the evidence for it is that I was the one planning most of it, so when things went sideways it’s easy to think I should’ve prevented it. And I did notice people sounding disappointed, which made it feel like I’d failed them. But the other side is that it wasn’t just me—there were different expectations, people changed what they wanted, and some of the tension was already there before I said or did anything.

That’s a pretty nuanced view—you can see why it landed on you, and you can also see it wasn’t only on you. Given both sides of that, what seems most accurate to call your role in it: full responsibility, some responsibility, or something else?

Probably some responsibility, but not full responsibility. I was involved in planning it, so I can’t say I had nothing to do with it, but it feels more accurate to say I was one part of a bigger mess. I’m still not thrilled about that answer, but it does seem closer to reality than “I ruined the whole trip.”

That feels like a more reality-based way to put it, even if it’s not exactly a comfortable one. When you say “one part of a bigger mess,” what does that suggest about how much power you actually had over the whole outcome?

Probably less than I keep acting like I had. I could influence parts of it, but I didn’t control everyone’s expectations or how they reacted once things got tense. Saying that out loud is a little uncomfortable, but it also makes it feel less like I personally caused all of it.

That’s an important shift, and I can hear both the discomfort and the relief in it. If you had to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed about how you see your role in the vacation now?

I think I’m starting to see that I wasn’t the sole reason the trip got tense, even though I kept acting like I was. I did have a role in planning it, but that’s different from saying I caused everyone’s disappointment or ruined the whole vacation. It’s still frustrating, because I wanted it to go well and I hate when things feel out of control, but I’m noticing I may have been taking on more blame than I actually owed.

It sounds like you’re beginning to separate having some influence from carrying the whole weight of everyone’s disappointment, and that’s a meaningful shift in how you’re seeing yourself in this. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I'm worried that the tension with my spouse is making me less focused at work, and I might start missing important details on projects. Then there's I'm worried my recent stress is making me seem less capable to my manager, and I could be passed over for future opportunities. And I also keep thinking about: I'm worried that if I keep feeling overwhelmed, I won't perform well in my upcoming presentation and it could hurt my career progress.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind keeps looping when all of those concerns feel important. Sometimes it helps to sort worries into ones that are productive, meaning there’s something actionable you could actually do, versus unproductive ones that are hypothetical or outside your control, and we handle those differently. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

The first one that keeps grabbing me is the worry about tension with my spouse affecting my focus at work. It feels the most immediate because when we’ve argued, I notice I’m distracted the next day and then I start second-guessing myself on even small tasks. Part of me knows I can’t fully control how I feel after a fight, but I do think there are things I could do to protect my focus. I’m just not sure yet what’s actually productive versus me spiraling about it.

It makes a lot of sense that this feels immediate, especially when you can see the link between a tough argument and the next day’s distraction. When you look at this worry closely, does it seem like something you can take a concrete action on, or does it feel more hypothetical and outside your control?

I think it’s a mix of both, but there are some concrete actions in it. I can’t control whether my spouse and I argue, and I can’t instantly shut off the emotional aftereffects, but I can probably do more to protect my focus afterward. What feels productive is figuring out a way to decompress after conflict and maybe give myself a little buffer before jumping into demanding work. What starts to feel hypothetical is the fear that one rough night means I’m suddenly becoming unreliable at my job.

That’s a really clear distinction, and it sounds like you can already see where the part within your control begins and ends. What would be one small, concrete step you could take after the next conflict to help you decompress, and exactly when would you do it?

One small step I could take is to give myself a 15-minute reset before I try to go back to anything work-related. I could do that right after the argument ends, or if it happens late at night, then first thing the next morning before checking email or starting the day. During that time, I’d probably take a short walk, sit somewhere quiet, and just let myself calm down instead of immediately replaying everything in my head. That feels doable to me because it’s not about solving the conflict right away, just creating a little space so I’m not carrying it straight into work.

That sounds like a thoughtful, realistic way to create some space between the conflict and your work, and I can hear how much more manageable it feels when you frame it that way. Looking at the second worry now, does it seem like something you can take a concrete action on, or does it feel more hypothetical and outside your control?

I think the second worry is more mixed, but it leans a little more toward hypothetical and outside my direct control. I can’t fully control how my manager interprets me on a stressful week, and that uncertainty is what makes it feel so heavy. At the same time, there are some concrete things I can do, like being more intentional about communicating, staying organized, and not assuming that one rough stretch defines how capable I am. So I’d say the action part is in how I show up, but the fear part is mostly about the story I start telling myself about what my manager must be thinking.

That’s a really insightful distinction, and it sounds like you’re separating what you can influence from the story your mind builds around uncertainty. If you put that new perspective into your own words, what seems to have shifted for you about this worry?

What’s shifted is that I’m seeing this worry less as a sign that something is actually going wrong at work and more as my mind trying to fill in the blanks with worst-case assumptions. I still care a lot about how I’m showing up, but I’m noticing that the fear of what my manager might think is bigger than the evidence I actually have. That makes it feel a little less overwhelming, because I can focus on the parts I do control instead of treating every stressful week like proof that I’m falling behind. It doesn’t erase the anxiety, but it does make it feel more manageable and less like an emergency.

It sounds like you were able to step back from the alarm the worry was sounding and see the space between the fear and the facts, which feels like an important shift. The next time that anxious story starts to get loud, what might you want to remind yourself of first?

Yeah, I’m willing to stay with it. When I really sit with it, the fear is less about just the numbers and more about feeling like I’d lose control and not be able to protect my family. I know part of me is jumping to the worst-case scenario, but it feels so immediate that it’s hard not to. At the same time, I can see there’s a difference between “we’d have to adjust” and “everything would collapse,” even though emotionally those feel almost the same to me right now.

That makes a lot of sense, especially the way the fear hooks into wanting to protect your family and makes the worst-case feeling so immediate. If you slow it down, is my thought based more on habit or a past experience than what’s true now?

I think it’s a mix of both, but probably more habit than a specific past event. I grew up with a lot of financial uncertainty, so I learned to treat any shift in income like a warning sign that things could fall apart fast. Even now, when my situation is more stable than it used to be, my mind still reacts as if I have to stay on constant alert. So I can see that the fear is real, but it may be coming from an old pattern of expecting instability rather than from what’s actually happening in this moment.

That’s a really insightful distinction, and it sounds like you’re noticing how an old warning system can make the present feel more dangerous than it is. If you look at the situation as specifically as you can, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

I think it’s more of a possibility than a likely scenario, even though my body reacts like it’s almost certain. If I look at it realistically, a change in my spouse’s work would probably be stressful and would require us to adjust, but it wouldn’t automatically mean we’d lose everything. What makes it feel likely is how fast my mind jumps to the worst outcome, not the actual evidence in front of me. You’ve done a thoughtful job separating the feeling of danger from the actual likelihood, and it sounds like you’re noticing how quickly your mind turns possibility into certainty. When you look at this fear, is someone else’s opinion overly influencing my own?

It’s almost like I’m carrying an internal audience that would see any financial wobble as failure, and that makes the fear feel bigger and more personal. When I step back, I can see that my own values are more about stability and care than perfection, but those old voices still have a lot of power over me.

That’s a very clear and compassionate observation, and I can hear how much you’re noticing the difference between old voices and your own values. As you look at everything you’ve said so far, how would you put the new perspective into your own words?

I think the new perspective is that a change in my spouse’s work would be a real stressor, but it wouldn’t automatically mean disaster or that I’d fail my family. A lot of the panic comes from old beliefs about needing to be constantly on guard and from internal pressure to be the perfect provider, not just from what’s actually happening right now. I can see more clearly that my values are really about caring for my family and adapting together, even if things get uncomfortable. That doesn’t erase the fear, but it makes it feel less like a fact and more like a pattern I can challenge.

It sounds like you’re noticing that the fear can be real without having to define the whole situation, and that there’s a steadier place in you that’s rooted in caring for your family rather than in having to be on constant alert. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed about the difference between a stressor and a disaster?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. After retiring, the client reviewed their monthly budget and saw that their savings balance was lower than expected because of recent expenses and reduced income. That sounds really unsettling, and it makes sense that seeing the numbers change would stir up worry and frustration. In CBT, the situation itself and the meaning we give it can lead to very different feelings and actions, so I’m curious: when those thoughts showed up, what did you actually do next?

Honestly, I mostly just sat there and kept rechecking the budget, which probably wasn’t helpful. I’m not sure what that has to do with anything, though — it seems pretty obvious that if the numbers are down, that’s a problem. It makes sense that rechecking felt like the only way to get a handle on it, and I hear your point that the numbers being down does mean something real. I mean, they might say I’m overreacting, sure, but that doesn’t magically make the money problem go away. Maybe they’d say it’s a temporary dip or I need to adjust spending, but to me it still feels like a warning sign, not just “one snapshot.”

That makes sense — you’re not denying the problem, you’re just noticing there may be more than one way to read it. If you actually believed it was a temporary dip or a spending adjustment rather than a sign that retirement is going to unravel, what emotion do you think would show up most strongly?

I guess maybe less panic and more just annoyance, if I’m being honest. But I’m not sure that’s the real question here — the part that bothers me is that it could still be a warning sign, and “temporary dip” doesn’t exactly pay the bills.

You’re right that a temporary dip doesn’t pay the bills, and I hear the distinction you’re making between a real warning sign and the bigger panic it triggered. If the feeling had been annoyance rather than panic in that moment, how might your behavior have been different?

Maybe I would’ve looked at the budget once, made a note, and moved on instead of obsessing over it for half the afternoon. But I’m not convinced that changing the feeling changes much in real life — if the numbers are bad, they’re bad.

That’s a fair pushback, and you’re right that the numbers themselves didn’t change in that moment. You’re making a very reasonable point, and I’m not hearing you say the problem is imaginary — just that the thoughts may be amplifying it. I suppose the difference is that one version would make me more likely to sit down and actually figure out what needs changing instead of spiraling. The “unravel everything” thought just makes me tense and stuck, which probably isn’t helping the situation. I’m still not thrilled by the idea that this is mostly about my thoughts, but I can see that the way I talk to myself probably affects what I do next.

Usually my first reaction is physical — I feel tense, my stomach tightens, and I start to get this restless feeling like I need to do something right away. Behavior-wise, I end up going back to the numbers over and over, which just keeps me focused on the worst-case scenario. I can see how that might be part of what keeps me stuck, even if I’m still not sure it’s the whole story.

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that now I’m retired, I won’t know how to fill my days and I’ll end up feeling useless or stuck. Then there's I’m worried that my social circle will keep shrinking, and in a few months I’ll have no one to see or talk to. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried that if my routine keeps changing, I’ll never figure out what my life is supposed to look like now.

That sounds exhausting, especially when your mind keeps circling the same themes at night. Some worries are productive, meaning there’s something real and actionable in them, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical or not really controllable, and they need to be handled differently. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

I’m not sure splitting them into “productive” and “unproductive” really changes much when I’m the one lying awake with all of it at once. If I had to pick one, I guess it’s the social circle shrinking—that feels pretty real, not hypothetical.

That makes sense; when you’re the one awake with all of it, the label can feel pretty academic, and the social circle worry does sound concrete to you. If you look closely at that one, is there a specific action you could take that might affect it, or does it mostly sit in the “I can’t really control this” category?

I mean, sure, there are things I could do on paper—call people, join something, whatever—but that sounds a lot easier than it feels. A lot of my friends are busy with their own lives now, and I’m not convinced forcing myself into activities is going to stop the feeling of being left behind.

That makes sense; “on paper” and “in real life” can feel miles apart, especially when it already feels like people are moving on without you. Would you be willing to set aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to let yourself think about this worry on purpose, so we can see whether that makes it a little easier to leave alone for the rest of the night? What is the next worry on your mind?

I’m not sure “worrying on purpose” is going to teach my brain much, but I suppose it’s better than lying there stewing about it. The next one is the routine changing—I keep feeling like without a set structure, the days are just going to blur together and I’ll end up wasting them.

That sounds like a real concern, and I can hear the skepticism about whether these exercises actually change much. When you look at the routine changing worry, does it seem like something you can take any action on, or does it feel more like one of those things that’s outside your control?

It’s probably somewhere in between, which is annoying—there are parts I can control, like making a schedule, but I’m not convinced that fixes the bigger feeling of my days being empty. I can try something practical, I guess, but I don’t want to pretend that having a calendar suddenly gives retirement a purpose.

That’s a fair pushback; a calendar doesn’t magically create purpose, and it makes sense that you’d be wary of pretending otherwise. If you look at the part you can control, what would a small, concrete experiment with your schedule be that could test whether structure changes the emptiness at all, and is there one more worry we should put on the list?

I guess I could try blocking out two or three things each day for a week and see if that changes anything, but I’m not expecting miracles. It still feels like a pretty thin test when the bigger issue is that retirement itself has thrown everything off. And yes, the other worry is still there: I keep wondering what I’m supposed to do with all this time now that work isn’t organizing my life.

That sounds like a big shift, and it makes sense that retirement having taken away the structure of work would leave you wondering what to do with the time. When you look at that worry closely, does it seem like there’s something you can actually influence, or does it feel more like a question that doesn’t have a clear answer right now?

It feels like both, honestly. I can influence some of the time I fill, but I can’t just manufacture a clear answer about what retirement is “supposed” to be, and that’s the part that bothers me. I guess I’m starting to see that maybe I don’t need the whole thing figured out at once, but I’m still not exactly comfortable with that.

That makes sense; not having a neat answer about what retirement is “supposed” to be can feel unsettling, even if you can see that some parts are still influenceable. Since we’ve now given each worry either a place to act on it or a time to hold it, what do you notice about how they feel compared to when they were all swirling together?

I guess they feel a little less like one giant knot when you break them up, but I’m not ready to say they’ve gotten smaller. The social circle and routine stuff still feel very real, though maybe less impossible than they did a few minutes ago. I’m still skeptical that this will do much once I’m alone at night, but I can admit it’s a bit easier to look at them one at a time.

That’s a pretty honest read: the knot is still there, but it’s not quite as tangled, and I get why you’d stay skeptical about nighttime being the real test. When you imagine being alone at night and one of those worries shows up, what seems to change first now that you can look at them one at a time?

I think the first thing that changes is I can at least tell myself, “Okay, this is the social circle worry” or “this is the retirement-purpose worry,” instead of treating it like one disaster. That doesn’t make it go away, but it does make it feel a little less like I’m drowning in everything at once. I’m not saying that’s enough, but it might keep me from spiraling quite as fast.

That sounds like a meaningful shift, even if it’s not a cure, and I hear you staying realistic about what it does and doesn’t do. When you catch the worry in that more specific way, what seems to happen to the sense of “drowning” right after that?

It eases off a little, I think—not gone, just less all-consuming. When I can name it, the feeling goes from “everything is collapsing” to more like “this is one painful thought I’m having right now.” I’m still not thrilled about any of it, but that does seem to slow the spiral down some.

That makes a lot of sense, and it’s useful that you can see the shift from “everything is collapsing” to “one painful thought,” even if you’re not pleased about it. When that change happens, what do you notice about your body or your urge to keep arguing with the thought?

My body loosens a little, I think—my chest isn’t quite as tight, and I’m not as wound up in my shoulders. I still get the urge to argue with it, but it’s a bit less urgent when I can name what’s happening instead of treating it like a verdict on my whole life. It’s almost like the thought loses some power once I stop wrestling it as hard. I’m not comfortable with that yet, but I can see that the fight itself may be part of what keeps me so keyed up.

That’s a pretty important observation, especially noticing that the fight itself may be feeding the keyed-up feeling. If wrestling the thought gives it more power, what do you notice happens when you let it be there without arguing with it for a moment?

If I don’t jump in and argue with it right away, it doesn’t seem to get as loud as fast. It’s still uncomfortable, but there’s a little more space around it, like the thought is there without taking over the whole room. I’m not sure I like admitting that, because it sounds almost too simple, but maybe the constant fighting is what keeps me stuck. That doesn’t solve the bigger retirement stuff, but it does seem to take the edge off in the moment.

That sounds like a pretty honest experiment with your own experience, and I can hear the hesitation about it being “too simple.” When the thought takes over less of the room, what do you notice that you’re doing differently in that moment, and what might that suggest about the fighting being part of the problem?

I’m probably doing less of the automatic “prove it wrong” thing, and more just noticing, “there it is again,” without immediately grabbing onto it. In that moment I can usually breathe a little slower and stop tightening everything up, which I guess means I’m not feeding it as much. That does suggest the fighting may be part of what makes it stick around so hard, even if I still don’t like the idea of just letting the thought sit there. It’s uncomfortable to admit, but maybe the struggle is doing more damage than the thought itself.

That’s a pretty significant observation, and it makes sense that it feels uncomfortable to say out loud. When you notice the struggle doing more damage than the thought, what does that suggest about how you might respond the next time the thought shows up?

I suppose it suggests I might try not to go straight into battle with it every time. If I can catch myself and just name it, maybe I can let it pass without turning it into a whole argument about my life. I’m not saying that sounds easy, but it does seem like a better response than getting hooked and spending half the night wrestling with something I can’t fully solve at 2 a.m.

That sounds like a thoughtful shift, especially given how late-night wrestling has been wearing you down. When you picture catching it, naming it, and not going straight into battle, what would be the first sign that you’re doing that differently?

I think the first sign would be that I pause instead of immediately trying to fix or disprove the thought. Maybe I’d notice my shoulders dropping a little, or I’d stop pacing around in my head quite so fast and just say, “Right, this is that retirement worry again.” It doesn’t feel like much, but that pause would probably be the difference between letting it run the whole night and giving myself even a small chance to calm down.

That pause sounds small, but you’re noticing it changes the whole sequence before the worry takes over, which seems important. If that pause is the first sign, what do you think it might be protecting you from in those late-night moments?

I think it’s protecting me from getting swept into that spiral where one thought turns into a whole story about my life falling apart. If I can pause, maybe I don’t end up pacing, arguing with myself, and making the anxiety worse just because it showed up. It’s a small thing, but it might keep me from feeling completely hijacked by it. I guess in a strange way, the pause gives me a little room to remember this is a worry, not a fact.

That’s a really clear insight: the pause seems to interrupt the jump from a worry to a whole catastrophe story, and I can see why that would matter at night. When you remember “this is a worry, not a fact,” what seems to change in your body or in the way the rest of the thought unfolds?

I think my body loosens a bit again, like I’m not bracing for impact quite as much. The thought still shows up, but it doesn’t automatically turn into proof that everything is falling apart, so it has a little less momentum. I can see now that when I treat it as a worry instead of a fact, the rest of the thought doesn’t spiral as fast. That’s not the same as being okay, but it does feel like a real difference.

That sounds like a real shift, even if it’s not “okay” yet, and I hear how carefully you’re naming the difference without overselling it. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed about how you relate to the worry?

I think I’m starting to relate to it less like it’s announcing some final truth about my life and more like it’s just my mind getting alarmed. I still don’t like the worry, but I’m noticing I don’t have to meet it with the same amount of force every time, and that changes how much it takes over. It feels a little less personal and a little more like something I can observe instead of immediately obey. That’s not a huge victory, but it is a different way of standing with it.

What stands out is the way you’re beginning to see the worry as an alarm rather than a verdict, and that shift seems to give you a little more room to choose how you stand with it. As you leave today, what feels most worth carrying forward from that different way of relating to it?
