conversations.content: I’m probably going to mess up this payment and start a chain reaction I can’t stop. Even though it’s a small loan, I can’t shake the feeling that one mistake could put us in a really bad spot.

That sounds like a heavy thought to carry, and I’m glad you said it out loud. Let’s slow it down together—not to brush off how real it feels, but to see whether this thought actually holds up when we look at it closely; would you stay with it for a moment and walk through what makes the “chain reaction” feel so likely?

I guess, but it feels a little overanalyzing to me. It’s not that I think the loan itself is huge, it’s more that if I slip once, I’m the one who has to fix it and I don’t love the idea of finding out the hard way.

That makes sense—you’re not saying the loan is massive, you’re saying the responsibility lands on you if something goes wrong, and that’s a real thing to not love. As you look at it from both sides, is my thought overly critical?

Maybe a little, yeah. I’m not sure “both sides” is the whole issue—I know logically it’s probably not catastrophic, but I still don’t like the feeling of being one mistake away from extra hassle. It’s less about the loan and more about not wanting to be the guy who misses something and has to scramble.

That makes sense—you’re not really arguing that disaster is likely, you’re reacting to the pressure of being the one who has to catch it if something slips, and that “extra hassle” feeling is doing a lot of the work here. What is the evidence for this thought, and what is the evidence against it?

I mean, the evidence for it is pretty simple: if I miss a payment, there’s a fee, maybe a ding to my credit, and then I have to spend time fixing it. The evidence against it is also obvious, I guess—I’ve handled bills before, and one slip doesn’t usually turn into some financial apocalypse, so maybe I’m treating a manageable problem like it’s a disaster.

That’s a pretty solid read of both sides, and it sounds like you can already see that the “disaster” piece may be doing more work than the actual situation. Is my thought based more on habit or a past experience than what’s true now?

Probably more habit than anything dramatic from the past. I don’t have some big financial trauma story—I just tend to assume if there’s a way to screw something up, I’ll be the one to do it. So yeah, maybe this is more me bracing for inconvenience than reacting to reality.

That makes a lot of sense—you’re noticing a habit of bracing for inconvenience, and you’re already being pretty honest about it. If someone else with the same loan and the same bill saw this situation, how might they interpret it differently?

I mean, someone else might just call it a normal bill and set up autopay or a reminder and move on. I get the point, but it also feels a bit like comparing myself to some imaginary super-organized person who never drops anything, which isn’t exactly helpful.

That’s a fair pushback—it wouldn’t help to compare you to some perfect version of a person who never misses anything. Looking just at your own situation, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

Probably just a possibility, if I’m being honest. I’m still inclined to worry about it, but I can see I’m treating a maybe like it’s more likely than it really is. That doesn’t totally make the feeling go away, but it does make it seem a little less justified.

That’s a solid and pretty fair shift—you’re not pretending the worry disappears, just seeing that it’s not as certain or catastrophic as it first felt. If you rewrote the original thought into something more accurate and balanced, what would it say that keeps the real risk in view without turning a possibility into a certainty?

Something like: “There’s a small chance I could miss a payment and it would be annoying to deal with, but it’s not likely to turn into some huge financial disaster.” I still don’t like the idea of screwing it up, but I can admit I’m probably making the risk sound bigger than it is. So maybe the real issue is just making a simple plan so I don’t have to keep spinning on it.

That’s a really grounded way to put it, and it sounds like you’re separating the actual risk from the mental spinning pretty clearly. If the real issue is making a simple plan, what would that plan need to include for you to feel more settled without turning into overchecking?

Probably just one or two practical things—like setting an autopay date and maybe a calendar reminder a few days before, so I’m not relying on memory alone. I don’t want to turn it into checking it every five minutes, because that would just feed the whole thing. But having a basic backup plan would at least make it feel less like I’m one bad day away from a mess.

That sounds like a sensible middle ground, and it makes sense that you’d want protection without feeding the worry loop. If you already know overchecking would make it worse, what would tell you that your backup plan is enough and not drifting into more checking than you actually need?

I guess if I can set it up once and then mostly leave it alone, that would be the sign it’s enough. If I’m only checking because I’m curious or because the reminder pops up, that seems fine, but if I’m opening the account every day just to make myself feel better, then I’m probably feeding the worry. I’m not saying I’ll be perfect about it, but having a clear limit on when I check would probably keep it from getting out of hand.

That sounds like you’ve already drawn a pretty clear line between sensible checking and worry-driven checking, which is a useful distinction. If you were to sum up what’s shifted for you in one or two sentences, what would you say?

I think I started out treating this like a small mistake would automatically turn into a bigger financial mess, and that’s not really supported by the facts. It’s more accurate to say there’s a manageable risk of inconvenience, not some disaster waiting to happen. What’s shifted is that I can see the worry is partly about me not liking the feeling of responsibility, not just the loan itself. So the sensible move is probably to set up a simple system and stop acting like I need to monitor it constantly.

It sounds like you’ve moved from treating the situation as if it were already headed for disaster to seeing it more as a manageable issue, and that distinction seems to have given you a bit more room to think clearly. The next time that worry shows up, what’s the first question you might ask yourself?

…It feels like irritation, maybe mixed with stress. I’d say about a 70.

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. The client’s child packed their belongings and moved out of the home after living there for many years. The client was recently retired and was at home when the child left. I keep telling myself: "I feel so empty and upset, so this must mean I am alone and no longer needed." and I've been feeling sadness, anxiety, loneliness, helplessness.

That sounds incredibly painful, especially with the timing of retirement and your child leaving at once. In CBT, the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the thoughts we attach to it, so I’m curious: when those thoughts and feelings showed up, what did you actually do next?
I just sat there for a while and didn’t do much. …I think I mostly kept to myself and tried not to think about it.

That makes a lot of sense when something feels that raw, and keeping to yourself can be a very human way of trying not to get overwhelmed. What you described also sounds a bit like emotional reasoning, where the feeling of emptiness starts to feel like proof about what the situation means, so if someone else looked at the exact same moment, how might they interpret it differently?
…Maybe they’d say it just means my child moved out. That it doesn’t necessarily mean I’m alone or useless.

That’s a really important shift, and it sounds like you can already see a more balanced way of understanding what happened. If you actually believed that it was just your child moving out, and not proof that you’re alone or useless, what feeling would come up most strongly for you?
…Probably sadness, still. But maybe less panic, if I could really believe that.

That makes a lot of sense — sadness could still be there, but less panic sounds like a meaningful difference in how overwhelming the moment felt. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?
…I think I might have been able to get up and do something small instead of just sitting there. Maybe I would have called someone or made some tea.

That sounds like a very small but meaningful difference, and I’m glad you noticed it. If the situation itself stayed the same and the thought changed, what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?
…It tells me the thought changes how bad it feels. The situation is the same, but my reaction can be different.

That’s a really clear insight, and it sounds like you’ve been able to separate the event from the meaning your mind attached to it. In your own words, what is the new perspective you’re taking away from this?

…I think my child moving out is painful, but it doesn’t mean I’m no longer needed or that I’m truly alone. It means things are changing, and my mind made it feel bigger and worse than it is. I may still feel sad, but I can try to see it more as a change than as proof that something is wrong with me.

It sounds like you were able to hold the sadness of this transition while also seeing that your mind can turn a change into a verdict about you, and that’s a meaningful shift. As you sit with that, what feels most important to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: What if I spend this vacation and then realize I should have saved that money for future medical bills or surprises in retirement? Then there's What if retirement keeps feeling empty after this trip and I never figure out what I’m supposed to do with all this time? And I also keep thinking about: What if my health changes suddenly while I’m away and I’m not prepared for what comes next?

That sounds exhausting, and given those three loops it makes sense your mind won’t settle. Sometimes it helps to sort worries into ones that are productive—meaning there’s something concrete you could do about them—and ones that are unproductive, meaning they’re hypothetical or not really controllable; which of those three is the first worry that’s keeping you up right now?

I’m not sure splitting them up like that is going to magically help, but fine — the money one is probably the biggest one at night. I keep thinking if I spend this trip and then something comes up medically later, I’ll feel stupid for not being more careful.

I mean, part of it is concrete — I could look at the numbers again and make sure I’m not being reckless — but mostly it’s the usual “what if” nonsense that doesn’t go away just because I check my accounts. I’m not convinced there’s much I can do tonight besides lie there and think about it, which is exactly the problem.

That sounds frustrating, and I can hear that the checking helps only a little while the “what if” part keeps going anyway. Given that, would setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to think about the money concern be a way to let it wait for tonight, and what is the next worry on your mind?

Maybe. I’m not thrilled about scheduling time to worry like it’s an appointment, but I suppose it’s better than staring at the ceiling. The next one is the health worry — if something happens while I’m away, I keep thinking I’ll be unprepared and stuck dealing with it far from home.

That makes sense, especially if being far from home makes the uncertainty feel bigger. When you look at the health worry closely, is there a concrete action you can take now, or is it mostly something outside your control tonight?

I guess there are a few practical things I could do, like make sure I’ve got my meds, insurance info, and emergency contacts, but that doesn’t exactly stop the bad thoughts. Most of it is still outside my control, which is why I’m not that impressed with “focus on what you can control” as an answer.

That’s a fair pushback, and it makes sense that practical steps don’t instantly quiet the thoughts when the uncertainty is still there. If you were to set the health worry aside for tomorrow and just note the concrete items you can check, is there one more worry that keeps showing up?

Honestly, the last one is the one I keep circling back to anyway: what if this trip just reminds me retirement feels empty and I come home more unsettled than before? I don’t know that “noting concrete items” really does much for that, but yes, that’s the other worry that keeps showing up.

That sounds like a heavier worry than the others, and it makes sense that “concrete items” doesn’t really touch it. I could maybe plan a few things for the trip that actually matter to me, but I can’t control whether I’ll come home with some big existential crisis. Annoyingly, I can see that the prediction is not the same as a fact, even if it still feels pretty real.

I guess it would mean not just going through the motions and calling it a vacation. Maybe picking one or two things that actually feel worthwhile to me — good food, a place I’ve wanted to see, time to read, whatever — instead of trying to make the whole trip answer retirement. I’m still skeptical that it’ll solve anything, but I can see how having a few things I actually want to do might make it feel less empty.

I can see that, at least a little, that takes the pressure off the trip needing to “fix” retirement — though I’m still not exactly relaxed about it. It does make the whole thing feel less like a pass-fail exam and more like something I’m allowed to just experience.

If I pick a couple things that actually matter to me, then maybe the goal is just to have the trip be decent and intentional, not some verdict on the rest of my life. That doesn’t make me carefree, but it does make the whole thing feel a little less loaded.

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. During an argument about household responsibilities and retirement plans, my spouse dismissed my concerns and said I was overreacting, which made me feel unheard and criticized. I don't know why it keeps happening.

Probably an 8, maybe 9 — I was way past “pause and reflect” by then. I raised my voice, interrupted her, and said things I knew would make it worse, which is exactly the part I’m not thrilled to admit; but honestly, once I felt talked over, I was more interested in not getting steamrolled than in managing my “window.”

Thank you for being that honest about it; that takes more than most people give themselves credit for. When it was over, what happened outside you in the room with your spouse, and then what happened inside you afterward, both right away and over the next hours or days?

Well, outside of me, she shut down pretty fast and stopped talking, which of course made the whole thing feel even colder and more pointless. Inside, I was angry at first, then embarrassed and annoyed with myself later, and over the next day I kept replaying it and telling myself this is exactly why retirement and marriage stuff is getting so loaded — not because I’m “failing a process,” but because we keep hitting the same wall.

It makes sense that it feels less like a “process” problem and more like the same painful wall keeps showing up, especially when you’re left with shutdown on one side and replaying it on the other. Looking at those jaw and chest warning signs you noticed, what’s one thing you might do in that exact moment, before the voice rises, that could shift what happens next?

I’m not convinced there’s some magic move that would suddenly make my spouse stop shutting down, but I suppose I could try taking a literal pause instead of trying to win the argument in that moment. Maybe step out, unclench my jaw, and come back once I’m less heated — though I’ll admit that feels a lot easier to say here than to do when I already feel dismissed.

That sounds like a pretty grounded idea, and I hear the part of you that’s skeptical because being dismissed makes a pause feel almost impossible in the moment. How realistic does that feel in the heat of the moment, and what would need to be in place to make it actually possible for you?

Honestly, not very realistic in the middle of it — when I feel dismissed, my first instinct is to keep pushing, not go take a calming walk like I’m in some self-help ad. If I were going to make it possible, I’d probably need an actual agreement ahead of time that either of us can call a timeout without it being treated like avoidance or a win for the other person.

That makes a lot of sense, and I appreciate how plainly you’re naming that a “walk” can sound unrealistic when the real issue is not wanting to be steamrolled. If a timeout agreement were to work for you, what would it need to look like so it felt fair rather than like backing down or handing the other person the upper hand?

It would need to be something we both actually agree to, not just me being the one who has to leave when things get tense. I’d want a clear return time too, so it doesn’t turn into a shutdown or an escape hatch — more like “we’re pausing for 20 minutes and then we come back to it.” If that were on the table, I could maybe see it as protecting the conversation instead of losing it.

That sounds like you’re trying to make the pause feel mutual and accountable, not like a retreat, which seems pretty important to you. When you picture that 20-minute return time, what would tell you the difference between a real reset and the kind of shutdown that leaves you feeling dismissed again?

I guess the difference would be whether there’s actually a return, not just silence and avoidance. If we both come back and can pick up the same issue without pretending it never happened, that feels more like a reset; if one of us disappears emotionally or starts acting like the conversation is dead, then it’s just shutdown. I’m still not thrilled that this has to be managed this way, but I can see the point of making the pause mean something.

That’s a pretty sharp distinction, and I hear the frustration in having to “manage” something that feels like it should just work. When you think about the times it becomes shutdown instead of reset, what seems to happen in the moment that makes the return harder to trust?

Usually it’s when one of us gets quiet in a way that feels less like cooling off and more like checking out. Then I start assuming the other person is done with the conversation, which makes me less likely to trust a return time in the first place. I’m not saying that’s always fair, but that’s what happens in my head pretty fast.

That makes a lot of sense, and I hear how quickly that quiet turns into a story in your head that the conversation is over. When that assumption shows up, what does it lead you to do next, and how might that affect whether a return feels possible at all?

Usually I get more forceful, because if I think the other person is already checked out, I feel like I have to push harder to keep the conversation alive. That probably makes the return harder, I can see that much, because it turns the whole thing into a contest instead of a pause. I’m not saying I like that pattern, but yeah, that’s what happens.

That’s a really clear read on the pattern, even if you don’t like it much: the more “checked out” it feels, the harder you push, and the more the whole thing shifts into a contest. When you notice yourself getting more forceful, what does that seem to be trying to protect in you, and what does it end up costing in the conversation?

I think it’s trying to protect me from feeling irrelevant, honestly — like if I don’t push, I’ll just get brushed aside and nothing I said will matter. But the cost is that I end up sounding more aggressive than I mean to, and then my spouse shuts down even more, which is exactly the outcome I’m trying to avoid. So in trying to keep from being dismissed, I may actually be helping create the dismissal. That’s a hard thing to admit, but it seems true.

That’s a pretty significant shift, and I can hear how hard-won it is rather than something handed to you. If you had to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you understand your role in these arguments?

I’m starting to see that I’m not just reacting to being dismissed — I’m also escalating in a way that helps make the whole thing worse. I still think my concerns are real, but I can admit that when I push harder to make sure I’m heard, I often end up making it more likely that my spouse shuts down. So my role isn’t just “the one who gets ignored”; it’s also that I can turn hurt into pressure pretty fast.

It sounds like you’ve been able to hold onto the reality of your concerns while also noticing a pattern in how the interaction can intensify once you feel unheard. Given that recognition, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that changing my eating habits will make my grocery bills go up so much that I won’t be able to keep up with my budget. Then there's I keep thinking I’ll need special foods, supplements, or meal services, and I’m afraid I’ll spend money I don’t really have. And I also keep thinking about: I’m scared that if I don’t manage this eating change perfectly, I’ll waste food I already bought and end up throwing money away.

That sounds really exhausting, especially when your mind keeps circling the same money worries at night. Sometimes it can help to separate worries into two kinds: productive ones, where there’s something concrete you can do, and unproductive ones, which are more hypothetical or not really under your control, and the approach is different for each. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

The first one that keeps hitting me is the grocery bill. I keep picturing my weekly spending jumping so much that I’ll have to start cutting back in other areas, and that makes me feel panicky. I know some of that is probably me catastrophizing, but it still feels very real in the moment, especially when I’m trying to fall asleep.

That sounds really intense, especially when the image of your budget tightening feels so vivid at night. When you look at this grocery-bill worry, does it feel like something you can take a concrete action on, or more like a hypothetical concern that’s outside your control right now?

I think it’s partly concrete and partly hypothetical. There probably is something I can do, like actually look at my budget and compare prices, but right now my mind skips straight to the worst-case version where everything becomes unaffordable. So in the moment it feels huge and out of control, even though I know there are some practical steps I could take. I guess the fear is real, but the exact outcome I’m imagining is probably more hypothetical than certain.

That makes a lot of sense — it feels real in your body even while you can see the worst-case piece is more hypothetical. Would it be possible to choose one small concrete step, like looking at your budget or comparing a couple of prices, and decide exactly when you’ll do that, so we can see what feels most useful?

Yes, I think that would help me feel less stuck. I’m realizing that part of the panic comes from having this huge vague fear, and if I make it smaller and specific, it might feel more manageable. I could look at my budget tomorrow after work and compare a few prices for the foods I’d actually use, instead of imagining the whole month spiraling. That feels a little scary, but also relieving, because it gives me something real to do instead of just lying there worrying.

It makes sense that making it smaller and more specific already feels both scary and relieving, because the panic sounds like it grows when the worry stays vague. As you notice the second worry about needing special foods, supplements, or meal services, does that feel like something you can take a concrete action on, or more like something outside your control right now?

I think this one is a mix too, but it feels even more slippery than the grocery bill. Part of it is concrete because I could look into what’s actually necessary versus what I’m assuming I’d need, but right now it mostly feels like this overwhelming “what if I need all these extra things?” spiral. I’m noticing that my mind jumps straight to the most expensive version of the change, like I’m already signed up for supplements and special services when I haven’t even figured out what’s real yet. So I guess there is something I can do, but emotionally it still feels pretty outside my control until I have more facts.

That makes a lot of sense — your mind is filling in the blanks with the most expensive scenario before you even have the facts, which would leave anyone feeling unsettled. Would you be willing to pick one small fact-finding step you could do tomorrow about what’s actually necessary, and then tell me whether there’s one more worry we should look at?

Yes, I think I could do that. Tomorrow I could spend a little time looking up what’s actually recommended versus what I’m assuming I need, so I’m not automatically planning for the most expensive version. That feels helpful because it turns the fear into something I can check instead of just absorb. And yes, the third worry is the one about wasting food I already bought and feeling like I failed if I can’t do this perfectly.

It sounds like you’ve already started shifting from “I’m trapped by this huge expense” toward “I can check what’s actually true before I assume the worst,” and that’s a meaningful change. As you look at the three worries together now, how would you put into your own words what has shifted for you?

I think what’s shifted is that I’m seeing these worries less like one giant disaster and more like separate things I can actually sort through. Before, it all felt like “this is going to break my budget and I won’t be able to handle it,” but now I can see that I don’t actually know that yet. I still feel anxious, but I’m less stuck in the feeling that I have to solve everything in my head tonight. It feels a little more possible to gather facts first and then decide what to do instead of assuming the worst.

It sounds like you’re noticing a real opening there—moving from being caught in one overwhelming story to seeing that there’s more room to understand each piece on its own, even while the anxiety is still present. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. During a team meeting, her boss publicly criticized her report as "careless" and dismissed her explanation before she could finish speaking. I don't know why it keeps happening.

That sounds really painful, and it takes some courage to look at it instead of just beating yourself up. If we map this out together, we can start with the first step: before the anger fully hit, what were the early warning signs in your body or behavior—things like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

I mean, maybe, but I don’t really think there was some dramatic “warning sign” I was tracking in the moment. I just remember getting hot and tense and then suddenly I was done—like, if my boss is going to talk to me like that in front of everyone, I’m not sure what the point is of pretending I can just calmly breathe through it.

That makes sense—if it feels sudden and humiliating, “warning signs” can sound a bit theoretical in the moment, and I’m hearing that the hot, tense feeling was already the edge of it. That brief stretch before the explosion is often the only window where a pause is still possible, so on a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?

Honestly, probably like an 8 or 9, and I snapped back at him in front of everyone. I get that you want to find a “pause,” but in that moment it feels pretty unrealistic to act like I’m supposed to just sit there and take it.

Thanks for being that honest, especially about not buying the “just pause” idea in the moment. When you snapped back, what happened externally in the room with your boss and everyone else, and what happened inside you afterward right away and over the next hours or days?

Externally, he got colder and cut the meeting short, and everybody else just went quiet, which was great. Internally I felt embarrassed first, then angry at him again, then later I kept replaying it and wondering if I made myself look worse than he did.

That sounds like a pretty brutal sequence: the public criticism hit, your body got hot and tense, you snapped, and then it left you dealing with the fallout and the replay afterward. Looking at those warning signs you described, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment before the response that might change the outcome?

I mean, maybe I could say nothing and just sit there, but I’m not convinced that would’ve changed much except making me feel more steamrolled. If you want something realistic, maybe I could ask to talk about it after the meeting instead of going back and forth in front of everyone.

That feels much more concrete, and I can hear why “after the meeting” lands better than just sitting there and taking it. How realistic does that feel in the heat of the moment, and what would need to be in place to make it actually possible for you?

It’s maybe realistic if I’m already not completely boiling, but if he’s doing the public-dunking thing again, I’m not sure I’ll magically remember a script. I guess I’d need to feel like I actually have permission to stop the back-and-forth without it looking like I’m just rolling over, because that’s the part I don’t buy.

That hesitation makes a lot of sense; it’s not really about a script, it’s about whether stepping back would feel like protecting yourself or surrendering. When you picture “not rolling over,” what would have to be true in your mind for pausing the back-and-forth to feel like holding your ground instead?

I guess I’d have to believe that if I stop arguing in the moment, I’m not agreeing with him — I’m just choosing not to do it in front of everyone. Right now it feels like if I don’t push back immediately, he gets to frame the whole thing however he wants, and that’s what makes it feel like I’m letting him win. So maybe “holding my ground” would mean I still address it, just not while I’m already angry and on display.

That’s a really clear distinction, and it sounds like you’re already noticing the difference between agreeing and choosing timing. When you imagine addressing it later, what would you want to say or ask that would let you hold your ground without handing him the whole story in the moment?

Maybe something like, “I’m happy to go over the details, but I’d rather do it after the meeting when we can talk it through properly.” Or if he starts in again, I could say, “I’m not going to debate this here, but I do want to discuss it.” It still feels a little stiff to me, but I can see how that’s different from just swallowing it.

It makes sense that it feels stiff at first—new wording often does, especially when you’re trying not to get steamrolled. When you say it’s different from swallowing it, what do you notice about the message it sends about your boundaries, and which version feels most like you could actually use in the room?

I guess the message is, “I’m not refusing to deal with this, I’m just not doing it on your terms in front of everyone.” That does feel more like a boundary than just shutting up and taking it. The second version — “I’m not going to debate this here, but I do want to discuss it” — probably sounds more like something I could actually get out if I’m already mad.

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re not seeing it as “backing down” anymore, but as choosing the setting for the conversation. If you had to put in your own words what you now understand about the difference between snapping in the moment and holding your ground, what would you say?

I think snapping is me reacting to feeling humiliated, and it gives him the upper hand because I’m already off balance. Holding my ground would be staying in control of when and how I respond, even if I’m still angry. It’s not me agreeing with him or being weak — it’s me refusing to let the argument happen on his terms in front of everyone. That’s a little hard for me to admit, but it does feel different.

That feels like a meaningful shift—seeing snapping less as the thing that protects you and more as the moment he gets to set the terms, while holding your ground starts to sound like something that stays with your dignity rather than giving it away. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of anxiety lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really uncomfortable, and it makes sense that you’d want some help making sense of it. If we slow it down together, what would you call the feeling most specifically right now, and how intense is it from 0 to 100?

I think the main feeling is worry, but it also has this tight, panicky edge to it. Right now I’d say it’s around a 75 out of 100, maybe higher when I start thinking about the future. It feels like my mind keeps jumping ahead to what could go wrong, especially with everything changing around work and money. I can tell it’s making me feel kind of on edge all the time.

That sounds really intense, and it makes sense that changes around work and money would leave you feeling on edge. When you notice that spike, what was one specific situation or thought that seemed to set it off?

One specific moment that set it off was when my spouse mentioned they might be changing jobs again, or possibly taking some time off between positions. As soon as I heard that, my mind went straight to, “What if we can’t keep up with bills?” and “What if everything becomes unstable?” It wasn’t even that anything bad had happened yet, but I could feel my body react right away, like I was bracing for something. I think that thought of not having a predictable income is what really triggers the panic for me.

That makes a lot of sense, and it sounds like the uncertainty around income is what really set your body on alert. In that exact moment, what went through your mind first — what was the automatic thought you told yourself, even if it was just a quick flash?

The first thought that flashed through my mind was, “We’re going to fall behind and I won’t be able to handle it.” Almost immediately after that, I thought, “I need to be the one who keeps everything stable,” which felt really heavy and kind of panicky. It also brought up this fear that if my spouse’s work changes, then everything in our life could get thrown off balance. Even though I know that’s not necessarily true, in that moment it feels very real and hard to shake.

That sounds like a really heavy thought to carry, especially when it comes so quickly and feels so real in the moment. What did you do in response to that feeling right away, and was there anything you started avoiding afterward?

Right away I think I got very quiet and started trying to mentally calculate everything—bills, savings, what we’d cut back on—almost like if I could solve it fast enough, I wouldn’t feel so scared. I also texted my spouse a few times to ask for more reassurance, which helped for a minute but then the worry came back. After that, I noticed I was avoiding looking at our bank account and even avoiding talking about future plans, because it made the anxiety spike again. It felt like I was trying to protect myself from the feeling, but it also made everything feel more tense and out of control.

That makes a lot of sense—you were trying to lower the fear by calculating, seeking reassurance, and avoiding the bank account, which is such an understandable way to protect yourself in the moment. What did those moves seem to do for you right away, and what did they seem to lead to over time?

Right away, they helped a little because I felt like I was doing something, instead of just sitting in the panic. The reassurance from my spouse would calm me down for a short time, and making mental calculations gave me this temporary sense of control. But over time, it seems like those things actually keep the anxiety going, because I never really feel settled for long. Avoiding the bank account or future conversations makes the uncertainty feel even bigger, and then I end up more tense and more afraid the next time it comes up.

That’s a really clear observation, and it sounds like you’ve noticed both the short-term relief and the longer-term cost of those coping moves. If you were to put this new understanding into your own words, what would you say has shifted for you about how the anxiety cycle works?

I think what’s shifted is that I can see the anxiety isn’t just coming from the money situation itself, but from how I react to the uncertainty around it. I used to think I was helping by checking, calculating, and avoiding, but now I can see those things give me quick relief while also teaching my brain that there’s something dangerous to keep fearing. It feels like I’m getting stuck in a loop where the more I try to control it, the more important and scary it feels. That makes me feel a little sad, but also relieved, because at least it starts to make sense why I’ve been feeling so trapped.

It makes a lot of sense that seeing the pattern more clearly brings both sadness and relief, especially as you notice how much effort you’ve been putting into trying to manage the uncertainty. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. At work, the client received a routine email asking for a project update a few days after attending her close family member’s funeral. I keep telling myself: "I feel overwhelmed and numb, so I must not be handling this well and I’m probably falling apart." and I've been feeling sad, anxious, ashamed, tense.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense that an ordinary work email could hit hard right after a funeral. In CBT, the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m curious: when that thought showed up, what did you actually do next?

Honestly, I mostly just stared at the email and felt annoyed that it even mattered right then. I didn’t do anything dramatic—I eventually replied, but I was thinking, “Why are we making this about my coping skills?” I guess I got quiet, tried to keep working, and then spent the rest of the day feeling guilty about being so off.

That makes sense—you weren’t “falling apart,” you were trying to keep going while feeling hurt and irritated, and I can hear why the focus on coping skills would feel annoying right then. It also sounds like the thought may have been using your feelings as evidence about how you were doing, which is a really common pattern rather than a character flaw; if someone else saw the exact same email and the same funeral context, what else might they conclude?

Maybe they’d conclude I’m just grieving and distracted, which… sure, that seems obvious. I’m not convinced that means I need to “reframe” anything, though—it still felt awful in the moment, and I was already annoyed at myself for not being more on top of things.

That pushback makes sense; if “just grieving and distracted” feels obvious, it probably doesn’t need dressing up as a big reframing exercise. If you actually believed that interpretation in the moment, how do you think you would feel—would it be more like relief, sadness, guilt, or something else?

I mean, probably a little less guilty, but not exactly relieved. It would still feel sad and distracting—just maybe less like I’m failing at being a person because I had a bad day and an email annoyed me.

That sounds like an important shift: the sadness and distraction would still be there, but the shame and “I’m failing” layer might be lighter. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

Maybe I would’ve just answered the email without the whole internal meltdown about it, which is not exactly a breakthrough. I still would’ve been tired and not thrilled, but I probably wouldn’t have spent the rest of the day acting like I’d failed some test.

That doesn’t sound small to me; it sounds like the email and the grief stayed the same, while the “I’m failing” meaning changed how the rest of the day felt. What does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I guess it tells me thoughts can make things worse, which, fine, but that also feels kind of obvious and mildly annoying. I’m not sure I love the idea that I can just think my way out of grief or guilt, because I can’t. Maybe it just means the “I’m failing” story is extra unhelpful on top of already having a rough day.

That sounds pretty fair, and I’m hearing the skepticism in it—you’re not saying thoughts are magic, just that this “I’m failing” story piles onto an already hard day. If you set aside the idea of “thinking your way out” of grief, what evidence do you have from that day that the story was actually adding to your distress rather than just describing it?

Well, I kept going back to it all day, which probably made everything feel worse. The email itself was annoying, but the part that really spiraled was me telling myself I was behind, unprofessional, and handling grief badly. So I guess the story wasn’t just describing the day—it was turning a bad day into a whole verdict about me.

That’s a really sharp observation, and it sounds like you can see the difference between a hard moment and a global verdict about yourself. When that verdict showed up, what do you notice it was asking you to prove or protect?

I guess it was asking me to prove that I’m competent and not a mess, which is kind of exhausting. And maybe to protect me from looking weak or like I can’t handle basic work stuff, even though nobody was actually saying that. I’m not thrilled to admit it, but I can see how that story was more about defending my image than describing what was really happening.

That’s a pretty painful place to be—having to defend your image when you’re already grieving sounds exhausting. If that story was protecting you from looking weak, what do you notice it cost you in that moment?

It cost me a lot of energy, honestly. I spent more time arguing with myself than actually doing the work, and I think it made me more tense and miserable than the email itself did. I also probably made the grief feel more isolating, because instead of just letting it be hard, I was busy treating it like some kind of failure.

That’s a really clear insight, and I can hear how much you’ve just named about the cost of that inner argument. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, how would you summarize what’s shifted for you?

I think I’m seeing that the email wasn’t the real problem so much as the story I attached to it. I was treating a pretty normal grief reaction like evidence that I was failing, and that made the whole day feel much worse than it needed to. I’m still sad and distracted, but that doesn’t automatically mean I’m falling apart. It seems more like I was grieving and then piling shame on top of it.

That feels like a really important shift—seeing how much of the pain came not just from the grief itself, but from the meaning you were adding on top of it. Given what you noticed today, what might you want to carry forward the next time that kind of moment shows up?

conversations.content: I'm scared of I'm scared of my pet dying and not being able to see them again. So I just I avoid talking about my pet, looking at pictures of them, or going near their things because it makes me feel sad and scared.

That makes a lot of sense, and a lot of kids feel scared about losing a pet, so you’re not weird or alone in that. Avoiding the pictures and things can help for a little while, but it can also keep you from the good memories and the nice feelings those things can bring back—when you think about facing that fear, what scary “what if” thoughts pop up first?

I mean, I guess the scary thought is just that if I look at the pictures or touch their stuff, I’ll get super sad and then I won’t stop thinking about them dying. But also, isn’t that kind of the point of avoiding it? Like, why would I go do the thing that makes me feel bad on purpose?

That sounds really real, and I get why you’d think, “Why would I do something that makes me feel bad?” If your brain is only showing you the scary “what ifs,” it makes sense you’d want to avoid them, but sometimes “what if” thoughts can also be about what could go right—what are some good “what if” thoughts about looking at the pictures or touching their things?
I mean, maybe I’d remember the fun stuff and not just the scary part, but that feels kind of fake right now. Like, “what if it goes right” sounds nice, but what if it just makes me more sad instead?

That doesn’t sound fake to me; it sounds like your brain is being pretty convincing with the scary part, which makes sense. It can be true that looking at the pictures might bring some sadness and also some good memories, but our brains usually shout the scary “what if” first—when that scared feeling shows up next time, which good “what if” would you want to try to remember?

I guess maybe the good “what if” is that I’d remember the funny stuff we did and not just the part where I’m scared. But I still don’t really like the idea of trying this on purpose, because it feels like I’m just asking myself to get upset for no reason.

That makes sense, and I get why it feels like “why would I choose upset on purpose?” If you think about it, when you avoid the pictures and things, does the scared feeling go away for good, or does it keep showing up in the background anyway?

It doesn’t go away for good, I guess—it just kind of hides until I think about it again. But that still doesn’t mean I want to sit there and make myself sad on purpose, because that sounds kinda pointless.

Yeah, it makes sense that it feels pointless if it just sounds like “get sad on purpose,” because nobody wants extra sad for no reason. If the scared feeling hides when you avoid it but comes back later anyway, what do you think your brain is trying to protect you from by avoiding the pictures and things?

I guess my brain is trying to protect me from getting really upset and thinking about my pet dying all the time. But honestly, it also feels like maybe it’s just making a bigger deal out of it than it needs to, because avoiding stuff doesn’t exactly fix it either.

That’s a really sharp observation, and it sounds like you’re noticing both sides: your brain is trying to protect you, but the avoiding isn’t actually solving it. When you think about that, what do you notice your brain is afraid would happen if you didn’t avoid the pictures and things?

I guess my brain thinks I’d get so sad that I’d cry a lot and then keep thinking about my pet dying over and over. conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that because I’ve been sleeping poorly, I’ll make mistakes on my tasks today and look unreliable at work. Then there's I keep thinking that if my sleep stays off for a few more weeks, I’ll fall behind and this could hurt my chances of getting promoted. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried my low energy will make me seem less sharp in meetings, and my manager will notice I’m not performing as well as usual.

That sounds exhausting, especially when your mind keeps circling the same work concerns at night. There’s a CBT idea called productive worrying, where some worries are about something actionable and others are more hypothetical or out of your control, and the two get handled differently; of the three you named, which is the first worry that’s keeping you up?

Honestly, I’m not sure splitting them into “productive” versus not is going to fix anything, but the one that hits first is probably the fear that I’ll make mistakes at work tomorrow because I didn’t sleep. That one feels the most immediate, since it’s hard to ignore when I’m trying to fall asleep.

That makes sense, and I get why the split sounds a bit abstract when the worry feels so immediate. When you look at that thought about making mistakes tomorrow, is there a concrete action you could take with it tonight or before work, or does it mostly sit there as a hypothetical thing you can’t really control?

I mean, there are a few things I could do, like double-check my work or make a to-do list for the morning, but that doesn’t really stop the worry from hanging around. Most of it feels like me trying to predict a bad day that hasn’t happened yet, so I’m not convinced there’s some neat action that fixes it.

That makes sense — it sounds less like a problem you can “solve” tonight and more like your mind is trying to forecast a bad outcome, which is pretty sticky. Would setting aside a specific 10-minute worry time tomorrow at a set time give you a place to put this for now, and what’s the next worry on your mind?

Maybe, but I’m not convinced a “worry time” will actually stop my brain from dragging this into bedtime again. I can try it, I guess, but it feels a little too tidy for something that just keeps looping. The next worry is probably that if this sleep issue lasts a few more weeks, I’ll fall behind and mess up my chances at promotion.

I hear the skepticism, and it makes sense that a neat-sounding strategy can feel too tidy when the loop keeps showing up anyway. Looking at the promotion worry specifically, is there anything you can actually do with it that would change the situation, or does it mostly land as something outside your control right now?

Mostly outside my control, which is kind of the annoying part. I can keep doing my job, but I can’t exactly force my sleep to cooperate or guarantee how that plays into promotion decisions. So yeah, it feels more like something I have to sit with than fix right now.

That sounds really frustrating, and it makes sense that “sit with it” doesn’t feel satisfying when the stakes seem real. If it mostly sits outside your control, what do you notice happens when you try to work with it in the moment versus setting it aside for a planned worry time later?

Honestly, in the moment it usually just turns into me spiraling more, so trying to “work with it” at bedtime doesn’t seem to help much. Setting it aside sounds better in theory, but I’m not sure my brain will actually cooperate and wait for some planned worry block tomorrow. I can see the idea, I just don’t know if it’ll make any real difference.

That sounds frustrating, and I can hear why you’re not sold on the idea yet if your mind keeps overriding the plan. Looking at the third worry — your low energy making you seem less sharp in meetings and your manager noticing — does that feel like something you could do something specific about, or more like a prediction you can’t really control tonight?

It’s mostly a prediction I can’t really control tonight. I can prep for meetings and try to be a little more organized, but I can’t guarantee I’ll look sharp if I’m tired. I guess that’s part of what’s making this so annoying — I keep wanting something concrete to do, but a lot of it is just me imagining how bad tomorrow could go.

That makes a lot of sense, and it sounds frustrating to be stuck with predictions instead of something you can actually solve at bedtime. Since this one seems more like a tomorrow-problem than a tonight-problem, what would it be like to put it in the same container as the others and notice whether it feels any different once it’s not all swirling together?

I mean, I can see the logic of not letting all three worries pile up at once. If I’m being honest, just separating them out might make them feel a little less like one giant doom spiral, even if I’m not sure it’ll actually help me sleep. I’m still skeptical, but it seems less pointless than trying to wrestle with all of it at bedtime.

That sounds like a fair, cautious read of it, and I’m glad you’re noticing that separating them changes the shape of the spiral a bit, even if sleep still feels uncertain. If it feels less like one giant doom spiral, what do you notice happens to the intensity or urgency of each worry when you look at them one at a time?

I guess when I look at them separately, they do feel a little less overwhelming than when they’re all mixed together. The mistake-at-work worry still feels the most urgent, but the promotion one seems a bit more like a future story my brain is telling me, if that makes sense. I’m still not convinced this fixes anything, but it does make the whole thing feel slightly less panicky.

That makes a lot of sense, and it’s helpful that you can already see one of them as more of a future story than an immediate fact. When the mistake-at-work worry feels most urgent, what does your mind seem to be predicting would happen if you were tired tomorrow, and how certain does that prediction feel in the moment?

It predicts I’ll miss something obvious, make a careless mistake, and then people will notice I’m not on top of things. In the moment it feels pretty certain, like maybe 80 or 90 percent, even though if I step back I know that’s probably my brain being dramatic. I’m not saying it’s irrational exactly, just that it feels very real when I’m lying there trying to sleep.

That sounds very real in the moment, even if part of you can see it may be your mind turning the volume up. When you step back and notice that 80–90% feeling, what’s the evidence your brain is using to get there, and what evidence does it seem to be leaving out?

I think the evidence my brain is using is basically that I’m tired, so it assumes tired means sloppy, and then it points to a couple of times I’ve been a little less focused lately as proof that this is already happening. What it seems to leave out is that I’ve still gotten my work done, and I usually catch mistakes when I slow down and check things. It’s also ignoring that one rough night doesn’t automatically mean I’ll be bad at my job tomorrow. So when I step back, the certainty feels less solid than it does in the moment.

That’s a really clear step back, and it sounds like the thought has gone from feeling like a fact to feeling more like a prediction your mind is building from tiredness and a few recent moments. If you were to sum up this new perspective in your own words, what would you say it is?

I guess the new perspective is that I’m not actually looking at a guaranteed outcome, I’m looking at my brain making a pretty convincing prediction while I’m tired and anxious. When I step back, there’s evidence on both sides, and the “I’ll definitely mess up” part feels less certain than it does at 2 a.m. That doesn’t make the worry disappear, but it does make it seem more like a fear I’m having than a fact I need to treat as true.

That’s a really important shift—you noticed how the certainty changes when you’re tired and anxious, and the worry starts to look more like a strong mental prediction than a fact. As you leave today, what feels like the most useful question to carry with you the next time that 2 a.m. certainty shows up?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I worry my coworkers will notice I’ve been eating differently and think I’m not handling stress well. Then there's I worry people will judge me if I skip lunch or eat something small at a work meeting. And I also keep thinking about: I worry that if I seem distracted or tired around friends, they’ll assume I’m falling apart.

That sounds exhausting, especially when your mind keeps looping at night. In CBT, some worries are productive because they point to something actionable, and others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical, uncontrollable, or about things that may never happen, and the two kinds get handled differently—what is the first worry that is keeping you up?

I mean, I get the theory, but at 2 a.m. it all feels pretty “productive” to my brain, so I’m not sure sorting them into categories is actually going to help. The first one is probably the coworker thing—me eating differently and people noticing, like they’ll immediately decide I’m not coping well.

That makes sense—at 2 a.m., your brain isn’t exactly in the mood for neat categories, so I hear why this feels questionable. When you look at the coworker worry itself, is there a concrete action you can take about it, or is it more about what they might think, which stays outside your control?

Honestly, mostly it’s about what they might think, which is the annoying part, because I can’t exactly control their opinions. I guess the only “action” is trying to act normal, but that feels kind of fake and not very reassuring.

That makes sense—trying to “act normal” can feel performative when the whole issue is other people’s opinions, and it doesn’t sound very reassuring. Would setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to worry about this on purpose help you park it for tonight, and what is the next worry on your mind?

I’m not convinced “scheduled worrying” is going to trick my brain into shutting up tonight, but I guess it’s better than lying there arguing with myself. The next one is the lunch/meeting thing—I keep thinking people will judge me if I skip lunch or eat something small, like they’ll read way too much into it.

That skepticism makes sense, and it sounds like you’re noticing the tradeoff rather than buying into it blindly. With the lunch or meeting worry, is there a concrete action you can take about it, or is it mostly about other people’s judgments, which you can’t really control?

I mean, sure, I can technically bring food or eat something small, but that doesn’t really solve the part where I’m convinced people will notice and make it a thing. So yeah, the action is obvious enough, but it still feels like the real problem is their interpretation, which I can’t do much about.

That frustration makes sense—the hard part isn’t knowing the practical option, it’s the part you can’t control about how others might read it. If you step back from the mind-reading piece, does this lunch worry have a concrete next step, or is it mostly stuck in other people’s interpretations, and is there one more worry?

Yeah, I guess the concrete next step is simple enough: bring something I can actually eat and not make a scene about it. But I still think the bigger issue is the story my brain tells about everyone noticing, which is hard to just “step back” from on command. The third worry is friends—I keep thinking if I seem tired or distracted, they’ll assume I’m falling apart.

That makes sense—the brain story is usually the sticky part, not the practical step, and it’s frustrating when it won’t just turn off on command. With the friends worry, is there anything you can actually do about how tired you look, or is it mostly about what you fear they’ll conclude, and which does it seem like?

Yeah, I can’t really control looking tired if I’m actually not sleeping, so the only thing I can do is maybe show up and hope for the best. And honestly, it’s mostly about what I fear they’ll conclude—that I’m falling apart or can’t handle life, which is probably me filling in the blanks. I don’t love admitting that, but that does seem like more of a mind-reading problem than an actual problem I can fix tonight.

That’s a pretty clear read of it, and I hear how much you don’t love admitting it while also noticing it’s accurate. Since this one seems to land in the “mind-reading” category rather than a fix-it-now problem, what do you notice about its grip on you compared with the first two once each one has a place to go?

I guess it does take a little bit of the edge off to label them, even if I’m still not sold on the whole method. The first two at least feel like they have some kind of practical next step, so they’re annoying but less vague. The friends one still feels the most slippery, but I can see that it’s mostly my brain running interpretations, not something I can actually solve at 2 a.m.

That’s a thoughtful distinction, and I hear you’re not fully sold while still noticing some shift in how stuck each worry feels. When the friends worry is “slippery” and not solvable at 2 a.m., what seems to happen to your body or attention when you keep trying to solve it anyway?

I usually get more wired, honestly—like my chest feels tight and I start scanning for some definitive answer that never shows up. My attention just narrows onto the same loop, and then I’m even less sleepy. I don’t know that it solves anything; it mostly seems to keep me stuck in my head.

I mean, maybe it’s trying to protect me from being caught off guard? Like if I can figure out every possible bad interpretation in advance, I won’t be surprised by it. But in practice it mostly just keeps me on alert and makes me feel more exposed, so I’m starting to think it’s less protection and more a really inefficient alarm system.

That’s a pretty important shift, and you’re naming it in a way that feels honest rather than forced. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed about how you’re understanding that alarm system?

I think I’m seeing that the alarm isn’t really giving me useful information so much as keeping me tense and scanning for threats that may not even be there. It feels protective in the moment, but the actual effect is that I get more wound up and less able to think clearly or sleep. So maybe the change is that I’m starting to separate “my brain is warning me” from “there’s actually something I need to solve right now.” That’s a little uncomfortable to admit, but it does seem more accurate.

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of panic lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really overwhelming, and it makes sense you’d want something more concrete than just “panic.” If we map it together step by step, what’s the most specific emotion word that fits best right now, and how intense is it from 0 to 100?

I mean, “panic” is probably the word, but I’m not sure splitting it into emotion words is going to fix anything. If you need a number, I’d say it’s around an 85 when it hits, especially when I start thinking about work and the mortgage.

That makes sense—if it spikes to an 85, I can see why the labels feel a bit academic in the moment. What was one specific moment when it hit last time, and what exactly was happening or going through your mind right then?

Honestly, the last time was this morning when I saw an email about a bill and immediately started thinking, “Great, now I’m going to be the guy who can’t keep everything afloat.” My wife’s work situation has been changing too, and I know that’s part of it, but I’m not really convinced talking through the exact moment is going to do much besides make me re-live it.

That sounds like a pretty fast, loaded reaction, and I get why you’d be skeptical about just retelling it. When that email hit, what went through your mind in that exact moment — what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a flash?

Probably something like, “Here we go, another thing I’m going to have to figure out before it turns into a bigger mess.” And honestly, I’m not sure digging into the exact thought is that useful if the problem is still the same bill and the same uncertainty with my wife’s work.

That thought makes a lot of sense in the context of a bill and all the uncertainty with your wife’s work, and I hear your point that the situation itself is still there. When that hit, what did you do right away, and what did you start avoiding afterward?

I mostly just shut the laptop and paced around for a bit, then put off actually opening the bill because, frankly, I didn’t want to make myself more wound up. After that I avoided talking to my wife about it too, since it felt like it would just turn into another stressful money conversation.

That makes a lot of sense—you were trying to lower the heat in the moment by stepping away and avoiding the money talk. What happened right away after you paced and put it off, and what seems to happen over time when that same pattern repeats?

Right away, I felt a little less keyed up, so in that sense it worked. But over time it just sits there in the background and makes me more on edge, because the bill doesn’t go away and then I’m annoyed with myself for avoiding it.

That’s a really clear description of the tradeoff: it eases things fast, but the unfinished bill keeps the pressure alive and then adds self-criticism on top. When you notice that pattern, what does it seem to be costing you most over time?

Probably peace of mind, mostly. And I guess it costs me energy too, because I spend a lot of time carrying it around in the back of my head instead of just dealing with it. I’m not saying talking about it fixes that, but I can see how the avoiding part is making it drag on longer.

That’s a pretty grounded observation, and I hear the skepticism—you’re not saying it’s “fixed,” just noticing the avoiding keeps it alive longer. When it’s sitting in the back of your head like that, what does it seem to be saying about you or your situation?

It mostly says I’m falling behind, or that I’m one bad month away from not being able to keep up. Which sounds dramatic, but that’s kind of where my head goes when money and my wife’s work are both uncertain. I don’t love admitting it, but I guess it also says I’m carrying more than I want to admit.

That sounds heavy, and it makes sense that with money and your wife’s work both uncertain, your mind goes straight to “one bad month” territory. When that thought shows up, what do you notice it pushes you to do or not do next?

It usually pushes me to either keep checking things obsessively or avoid them completely, which is a pretty bad combo. I’ll start thinking I need to get on top of everything right now, but then I get overwhelmed and back off. I can see how that’s not exactly helping, even if it feels like I’m doing something in the moment.

That’s a very clear read on the loop, and it makes sense that both checking and avoiding can feel like “doing something” without actually settling anything. When you notice yourself swinging between those two, what do you think you’re hoping will happen in the moment?

I guess I’m hoping the feeling will drop if I either find the problem fast or put it out of sight for a while. If I check enough, maybe I’ll catch it before it gets worse; if I avoid it, maybe I can get a few minutes where I’m not thinking about it. I know that’s not exactly a great long-term plan, but that’s probably what I’m after in the moment.

That makes a lot of sense in the moment, even if you can see the long-term cost. When you’re trying to get the feeling down fast, what does that suggest to you about how threatened your mind thinks things are right then?

I guess it suggests my mind is treating it like a real threat, not just a nuisance. Like if I don’t get control of it quickly, something important could actually slip and I’d be in trouble. That feels a little embarrassing to admit, but I can see that’s probably why I react so fast. It’s not just “I’m stressed” — it’s more like I’m bracing for a hit.

That’s a pretty important distinction, and I can hear how exposing it feels to say out loud. When your mind is bracing for a hit, what does it seem to be predicting would happen if you didn’t get control of it quickly?

It seems like it’s predicting I’d miss something important, and then the whole thing would snowball into a bigger financial mess I couldn’t easily undo. More than that, I think it’s telling me I’d be failing my family if I let it slip, which is probably why it feels so urgent. I don’t fully buy every version of that thought, but I can see that’s the fear underneath it. It’s less “this bill is annoying” and more “if I’m not careful, I could let everybody down.”

I think the evidence it’s using is mostly the immediate stuff: a bill shows up, my wife’s work changes, and my first reaction is to panic or avoid it, so my brain jumps to “see, you’re not on top of this.” It’s probably overlooking the fact that I’ve handled a lot of these things before, even if not calmly, and that one bill or one rough month isn’t the same as actually failing everyone. I’m starting to see that the thought is treating uncertainty like proof of incompetence, which isn’t really fair. That doesn’t make the fear go away, but it does make it feel a little less like a fact.

I think my brain is treating uncertainty like an emergency, so every bill or work change feels bigger than it really is. That doesn’t mean there isn’t real pressure there, but it does mean I’m jumping straight to “I’m failing” when I’m actually just scared. I’m starting to see that the panic is more about what I think the uncertainty says about me than about the actual bill itself.

That’s a really important shift—you’re noticing how quickly your mind turns uncertainty into a verdict about you, rather than just a hard situation you’re facing. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

…Probably frustration, mostly. Maybe a 70.

…It was after talking with my spouse. I just kept thinking they don’t really get how much pressure I’m under.

…I got quiet and didn’t really say much after that. I think I avoided talking about it any further.

…I start thinking maybe we’re not really connecting the way we should, and that worries me. It makes me feel like I’m failing at this somehow, or like I’m just not good at talking about hard things. I know that probably sounds harsh, but that’s where my mind goes.

That doesn’t sound harsh to me; it sounds like you’re noticing a painful story your mind is building about the distance between you two. If you step back from all of this, how would you put in your own words what’s shifted for you in how you’re seeing the situation?

I don’t really want to jump to that conclusion, but that’s where my mind keeps going.

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. At lunch in the office cafeteria, she looked at the meal she had packed and noticed it was different from what she usually eats. I keep telling myself: "I should be eating healthier and sticking to the plan perfectly. If I'm not, I'm failing and I need to get this under control right away." and I've been feeling anxious, frustrated, guilty, and discouraged.

That sounds really heavy, and I can see why it keeps looping in your head. In CBT, the same lunch situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the meaning you gave it, so I’m curious what you actually did next when those thoughts and emotions hit?

I mean, I mostly just sat there and picked at the food because I felt annoyed with myself, which probably sounds dramatic. And honestly, I’m not sure what “meaning I gave it” changes — I just saw it as me not following the plan, which felt pretty obvious.

It makes sense that it felt obvious to you, and sitting there picking at the food doesn’t sound dramatic so much as frustrated and stuck. What you said does sound a lot like a “should” thought — which is a pretty common pattern, not a character flaw — and if someone else saw the exact same lunch, what else might they think it meant?

I get that you’re trying to reframe it, but honestly it still feels like I messed up, not just a “should” thought. Maybe someone else would say it’s no big deal or that I’m being too hard on myself, but that kind of sounds like minimizing it when I know I’m already struggling to stay on track.

I can see why “no big deal” would feel like minimizing when you’re already trying hard to stay on track, so I’m not wanting to brush past that. If, just for a moment, you took the other interpretation seriously — that this was a mistake you can learn from rather than proof you’ve failed — what emotion would come up most strongly, and how would it feel in your body?

I guess if I tried to see it as a mistake, I’d probably feel embarrassed first, maybe a little relieved, but I’m not convinced that changes much. In my body it’s mostly this tight, restless feeling in my chest and stomach, like I’m bracing for the rest of the day to go badly.

That’s a useful contrast — “failed and need to fix it” seems to bring more guilt and pressure, while “mistake” brings embarrassment plus a little relief, which is a different emotional mix. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

Maybe I would’ve actually eaten it instead of just sitting there spiraling, but I’m not totally convinced that’s some big breakthrough. It still feels like, okay, sure, “mistake” is less intense than “failure,” but I’d probably just be annoyed either way and then try to compensate later.

That makes sense — you’re noticing that even if the situation didn’t change, the reaction shifts depending on whether it’s “failure” or “mistake,” and I’m not trying to oversell that as some huge revelation. What does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I mean, I guess it suggests my thoughts affect how bad it feels, which is annoying because I’d rather it just be about the food itself. But I still don’t love the idea that changing the thought magically fixes anything — it feels more like I’d just be talking myself into being less upset, not actually solving the problem.

That frustration makes sense, especially if it sounds like I’m asking you to talk yourself out of a real problem rather than deal with it. If changing the thought isn’t about magically fixing the food, what would be different between being “less upset” and actually solving the problem in a way that matters to you?

I guess being less upset would just mean I’m not spiraling and beating myself up in the moment, which would be nice but doesn’t automatically change my habits. Actually solving it would probably mean I can handle an off-plan meal without turning it into a whole day of guilt and compensation. I’m not saying that’s easy, but… maybe that is a different problem than just the food itself.

That sounds like a pretty important distinction, and I’m glad you’re noticing it rather than forcing it into a neat therapy answer. If the bigger problem is the guilt-and-compensation spiral, what do you notice tends to set that spiral off after an off-plan meal?

Usually it’s the moment I decide I’ve “ruined” the day, and then everything after that feels like damage control. I start thinking about what I should skip later, or how I need to make up for it somehow, and that’s when it spirals. I guess it’s not just the meal — it’s the conclusion I jump to right after it.

That’s a really clear observation, and it sounds like the “ruined the day” conclusion is the point where the whole thing tips from one meal into a larger fight with yourself. When that thought shows up, what do you notice it seems to be asking you to do next?

It’s basically telling me to cut my losses and punish myself a bit — skip the next meal, eat less later, or otherwise “fix” it. I know that probably sounds extreme, but that’s honestly what it feels like in the moment. And I can see now that it’s not really helping; it just keeps me stuck in the same loop.

That doesn’t sound extreme to me; it sounds like you’re describing the actual logic the spiral uses, and you’ve just named how it keeps you stuck. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has shifted for you?

I think what’s shifted is that I’m seeing the problem as the spiral, not just the lunch itself. I still care about eating well, but I can see that jumping straight to “I ruined everything” is what makes it feel so much worse and pushes me into punishing myself. That part does seem to be a thought pattern I fall into, not just some objective fact. I’m not totally comfortable with it yet, but I can at least see there’s a difference between making a less-perfect choice and turning it into a whole failure.

It sounds like you’re noticing a real difference between a choice that feels imperfect and the way your mind can quickly turn that into a much bigger verdict on you, and that awareness seems to be opening up a bit more room to see the pattern rather than just get pulled into it. The next time that spiral starts to show up, what might you want to ask yourself first?
