conversations.content: I keep thinking that being dismissed means I’m no longer useful and that maybe I never really mattered at work. I’m worried I’m too old to start over and that I’ve lost my security for good.

That sounds really painful, and it took courage to say it out loud. Could we slow this down together and look at that thought carefully, not to dismiss how hard this feels, but to see how well it holds up when we examine it a bit more closely?
…Maybe. I’m not sure what there is to examine, but I can try.
That makes sense, and it’s okay not to see it clearly yet; trying is enough for now. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what's true?
…Maybe a bit. I know it feels bigger in my head than it probably is.
That’s a thoughtful observation, and it sounds like you can already see that the thought may be stretching beyond the facts a little. How might others interpret the same situation differently?
…They might say it was just a job ending, not a judgment on me. I suppose they’d see it as one part of my life, not the whole thing.

That’s a really important shift, and I can hear you beginning to separate the event from your worth. When you look at the thought that being dismissed means you’re no longer useful, what feels like the evidence for it, and what feels like the evidence against it?
…Well, for it, I was let go, so it does feel like they didn’t need me anymore. Against it… I did the job for years, and people did rely on me.

That’s a very balanced way of looking at it, and it sounds like you’re noticing both the hurt of being let go and the reality of the years you were relied on. When the thought says “they didn’t need me anymore,” whose voice does that sound most like, and how much should that voice get to decide how you see yourself?
…It sounds a bit like my own voice, but also like what happened at work talking. I don’t think it should decide everything about me, but it still gets in my head.

That sounds like a meaningful shift, even though it still feels intrusive at times. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed about how you’re seeing yourself now?

I’d say I’m starting to see that being dismissed doesn’t automatically mean I’m useless or that I never mattered. It still hurts, and I still hear that old voice sometimes, but I can also remember that I did contribute for a long time. That feels a little steadier, even if I’m not fully there yet.

That sounds like a steadier place to be in right now, with the hurt still there but also some room for the part of you that knows your years of contribution were real. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: If I can’t get my eating under control, I’m going to ruin my health and end up leaving my family with a mess I should have prevented. I hate that I can’t just fix this on my own like I’m supposed to.

That’s a heavy thought to carry, and it makes sense you’d feel a lot of pressure and shame around it. I’m glad you said it out loud, and I’d like to slow it down with you so we can look at whether it holds up under a closer look, not to brush off how serious this feels, but to see what’s actually there—can you stay with it for a moment and look at the thought together?

I guess, but I don’t really see how picking apart the thought changes the fact that my eating is still a problem. It feels a little like talking around it instead of dealing with what I’m actually doing. Still, fine—what exactly are you wanting me to look at?

That makes sense—you’re not wrong to want something practical, and it’s fair to push back if this feels like sidestepping the real problem. I’m wondering, when that thought shows up, am I basing this thought on feelings rather than facts?

Maybe, but honestly it feels like both. The facts are I’m eating badly more than I should, and the feelings are that I’m terrified it means I’m headed for a bigger disaster. So sure, maybe I’m adding fear on top of what’s real—but that doesn’t exactly make the problem go away.

You’re seeing it pretty clearly: there’s the real issue of eating more badly than you want, and then there’s the fear that it means a much bigger disaster is coming, which sounds exhausting to carry. If we separate those for a second, is my thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

I mean, it’s a possibility, sure, but it doesn’t feel like some random, tiny chance either. If I keep doing this long enough, it seems pretty likely things get worse—though I guess I don’t know that it’s this immediate catastrophe my brain is making it into.

That’s a really useful distinction—you’re not dismissing the problem, but you are noticing that your mind may be jumping from “this is a real issue” to “this is an immediate catastrophe,” which is an important difference. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what's true?

Yeah, probably, but I don’t love the word “exaggeration” because it sounds like you’re saying I’m overreacting for no reason. I’m not inventing the problem—I just think my brain goes straight to the worst-case version of it. So maybe it’s exaggerated, but it still feels grounded in something real.

I hear you—you’re not making this up, and it makes sense that “exaggeration” would land like I’m dismissing a real problem rather than the fear attached to it. If we stay with the thought as it comes up, what evidence do you notice that supports it, and what evidence do you notice that pushes against it?

Honestly, the evidence for it is that my eating has clearly gotten worse, and when I’m stressed I keep defaulting to the same bad choices, so it doesn’t feel like I’m imagining nothing. What pushes against it is that I’m still functioning—I’m working, taking care of my family, and I haven’t actually fallen apart, which my brain tends to ignore when it’s freaking out.

That sounds like a pretty fair and grounded look at it—you’re not denying the eating has gotten worse, and you’re also noticing that your mind is overlooking the parts that show you’re still holding things together. Given both of those, is my thought overly critical?

Yeah, I think it probably is overly critical. I’m treating one problem like it says everything about me, and that’s not really fair, even if the problem itself is real. I still don’t like how bad it’s gotten, but I can admit my brain is being harsher than the facts maybe justify.

That sounds like a solid, honest shift—you’re not pretending the eating problem isn’t there, you’re just seeing that the “this means everything is ruined” part goes beyond the evidence. If you were to rewrite the original thought so it’s fairer and more accurate, without turning it into forced positivity, what would it say?

Something like: “My eating habits are a real problem, and I need to take them seriously, but this does not automatically mean I’m ruining everything or that my family is doomed.” It’s still uncomfortable, and I’m not suddenly okay with it, but that feels more accurate than telling myself I’ve already failed at everything. I guess it leaves room for me to actually do something about it instead of just panicking.

That sounds more balanced and grounded, and it makes sense it still feels uncomfortable because it doesn’t let you off the hook while also not sentencing you to disaster. When you say it leaves room to actually do something, what do you notice changes in your reaction to the problem when you hold that version of the thought?

It makes me feel a little less panicked, honestly. Not calm or anything, but less like I need to mentally punish myself before I can even start fixing it. I can at least think about one actual step instead of spiraling into “I’ve ruined everything.”

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re noticing that the harsher self-talk doesn’t actually help you start; it seems to add punishment on top of the problem. If the goal is to stay out of the spiral and focus on one real step, what does that tell you about how useful the “I’ve ruined everything” thought actually is?

It tells me it’s not very useful, even if it feels convincing in the moment. All it really does is make me feel worse and less capable of doing anything about it. I’m still not thrilled about the situation, but I can see that thought is more of a brake than a motivator.

That’s a clear way of putting it, and I hear both the honesty and the shift in how you’re seeing the thought. If you were to sum up the new perspective you’ve reached in your own words, what would you say it is?

I’d say my eating is a real problem, but I’ve been turning it into proof that everything is already falling apart, and that’s not accurate. The more catastrophic thought just makes me feel ashamed and stuck, which doesn’t help me change anything. I can take this seriously without treating it like my whole life is ruined. That feels harder in some ways, but also more honest and more workable.

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re noticing how quickly the more catastrophic story pulls you into shame and paralysis, and also recognizing that a more honest view leaves room for change without making this feel like a verdict on everything else in your life. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that the stress from my marriage is making my headaches and fatigue worse, and I’m not taking care of my body enough. Then there's I keep thinking that if I don’t sleep well tonight, I’ll feel physically awful tomorrow and won’t be able to function at work. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried that I’ve been skipping meals or eating poorly because of stress, and it might be affecting my energy and health.

That sounds really exhausting, and it makes sense your mind keeps circling when your body already feels worn down. Sometimes it can help to sort worries into two kinds: productive worries, which point to something you can actually do something about, and unproductive worries, which are more hypothetical, uncontrollable, or about things that may never happen; what is the first worry that is keeping you up?
…The first one is my headaches and fatigue getting worse because of the marriage stress. I keep thinking I’m not taking care of myself enough.

That sounds heavy, especially when you’re already feeling worn down. When you look at this worry—about stress making your headaches and fatigue worse—does it point to a concrete step you can take, or does it feel more like something uncertain and outside your control?
…It feels like both, but mostly uncertain. I know I should take better care of myself, but it still feels hard to control.

That makes sense — it feels real, and when something seems only partly controllable, it can be hard to know where to put your energy. Would it help to set aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to think about this worry, so you can try to leave it for now, and what is the next worry on your mind?
…Maybe. I can try that. The next worry is that if I don’t sleep well tonight, I’ll feel awful tomorrow and won’t be able to function at work.
That sounds like a really scary thought to sit with at night. When you notice that worry about tomorrow, does it seem like something you can take action on, or does it feel more outside your control?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of panic lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really overwhelming, and it makes sense that you’d want some way to make sense of it. Could we slow it down together and see if we can name the emotion as specifically as possible right now—maybe panic, fear, shame, or something else—and what number from 0 to 100 would you give its intensity at this moment?

It feels like a mix of panic and shame, but panic is the strongest right now. I’d say it’s around an 80 out of 100, because my chest feels tight and my mind keeps jumping to worst-case scenarios. I keep thinking about the foreclosure and how I’m supposed to be handling my life better at this point, which makes the shame spike too. It’s like I’m scared, but I’m also angry at myself for being scared.

That sounds really intense, and it makes sense that the panic and shame would feed into each other like that. If we zoom in on one specific moment, what was the exact situation or thought that seemed to set this wave off?

It hit me hardest when I opened an email from the mortgage company this morning and saw the subject line before I even read it. My stomach dropped immediately, and my mind went straight to, “This is the beginning of losing everything,” even though I know I haven’t read the full details yet. Right after that, I started telling myself I should have been more organized, more disciplined, more successful by now, so the shame came in fast. It felt like one small email turned into this whole story about me failing at life.

That makes a lot of sense—the email itself seems to have become a trigger for a much bigger story very quickly. When that happened, what went through your mind in that exact moment; what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a flash?

The very first thought was, “I’m in trouble, and I’m about to lose everything.” It was so immediate that I almost felt it before I fully thought it, like my body reacted first and my mind caught up afterward. Then it quickly turned into, “I’ve failed, and this is proof I can’t manage my life the way I should.” Underneath all of that, I think there was also a scared thought of, “I’m going to end up trapped and powerless.”

That sounds like a really fast and painful chain, and it makes sense that your body would react before you even had time to sort it out. When that thought hit, what did you do right away, and what if anything did you start avoiding afterward?

Right away I froze for a few seconds, then I closed the email and started pacing around my apartment because I couldn’t sit still. I avoided opening anything else from the mortgage company, and I also put off checking my bank account because I was afraid it would confirm the worst. After that, I kind of avoided work for a while too, because I felt too overwhelmed and embarrassed to focus. It was like I was trying to outrun the whole situation, but really I think I was just trying not to feel how scared I was.

That sounds like a very understandable way of trying to protect yourself when the fear felt so intense, even if it left you feeling more stuck afterward. What were the consequences of that pacing and avoiding, both right away and over time, and now that you can see the whole chain, is there any link where even a small shift might interrupt the pattern?

Right away, the pacing made me feel a little less trapped in my body, but it also kept the panic going because I never actually dealt with the email, so the fear just hovered there. Over time, the avoiding seems to make everything worse—I feel more behind, more ashamed, and then even small tasks start to feel impossible because I’m already in that overwhelmed state. I can see now that the first link might be the moment I see the subject line and immediately assume the worst, because that’s when the spiral really starts. Maybe even pausing for a minute before opening the email, or grounding myself first, could interrupt it just enough to keep me from going straight into panic.

It sounds like you’ve started to see the sequence more clearly, and that can be a meaningful shift. If you were to put into your own words what’s changed in how you’re understanding this panic, what would you say?

I think what’s changed is that I’m seeing the panic less like this vague, all-consuming truth and more like a chain reaction that gets set off really fast. Before, it felt like the emotion was just proof that everything was falling apart, but now I can see there’s a trigger, then a thought, then my body spirals, and then I start avoiding things. That doesn’t make it feel small, but it does make it feel a little more understandable and maybe less like I’m completely broken. I also notice more clearly how much shame is making the panic worse, because I’m not just scared of the foreclosure—I’m scared of what it says about me.

What stands out is how you’re starting to see this as something that unfolds, rather than as a verdict on you, and there’s a lot of clarity in noticing how shame has been amplifying the fear. The next time that chain reaction starts to build, what might you want to remind yourself of first?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. After retiring, the client was assigned to help train a new part-time worker at the community center on a schedule that changed from mornings to late afternoons. The client was asked to adjust to the new hours and to follow a different way of organizing tasks. I keep telling myself: "I should be able to handle this without any trouble. At my age, I should already know how to adapt, and I shouldn't need to keep changing my routine just because someone else decided to change the schedule." and I've been feeling frustrated, anxious, resentful, discouraged.

That sounds really frustrating, especially when it feels like the change was imposed on you rather than chosen. In CBT, the idea is that the same situation can land very differently depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m curious what you noticed yourself doing after those thoughts and feelings showed up?

I guess I got tense and started avoiding the whole thing as much as I could. But I’m not sure what “the meaning I give it” has to do with the fact that my routine was just changed and I don’t like it.

That makes sense—you’re not denying the change itself, you’re saying the change is real and unwelcome. What stands out to me is the “should” in your thought, which is a very common kind of mental habit rather than a character flaw; if someone else were looking at the exact same situation, what’s another way they might interpret it?

I mean, maybe they’d say I’m being stubborn or overreacting, but that doesn’t make the schedule change any less annoying. It still feels like I’m being asked to give up a routine that was working for me, and I don’t see why I’m supposed to reframe that as something positive.

You’re right that calling it “positive” would miss how annoying and disruptive it feels, and it makes sense that you’d push back on that. If you actually believed the idea that you’re being asked to give up a routine that was working for you, how do you think you would feel—say, frustrated, disappointed, angry, or something else?

Probably all of the above, honestly—frustrated and angry, mostly. I’m not sure why we need to label the feelings so carefully when the problem is pretty straightforward: the schedule changed, and I don’t like it.

That sounds pretty straightforward, and I can see why the labeling feels unnecessary when the change itself is the main issue. Still, there’s a difference between feeling frustrated and angry versus feeling discouraged and anxious, so with that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

I’m not convinced it would’ve been that different, to be honest. Maybe I would’ve complained less or tried to just get through it, but I still would’ve been irritated and probably avoided some of it anyway. It feels like you’re making a big deal out of labels when the real issue is that my routine got disrupted.

You’re making a fair point—the disruption itself didn’t change, and the irritation was still there. Given that you noticed the same situation but a slightly different response in how much you complained or avoided it, what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

I suppose it tells me my thoughts can make things feel worse, but that still doesn’t change the fact that the situation itself is the problem. I’m not really sold on the idea that if I think about it differently, it suddenly becomes manageable—maybe just less irritating, if I’m being generous.

You’re being pretty clear that the change itself is still the problem, and I get why you’d be skeptical that “thinking differently” would fix that. If it may not make the situation disappear, what might be different for you if it were just less irritating rather than as overwhelming as it feels now?

I guess I’d be less on edge all the time, and maybe I wouldn’t dread going in quite so much. I’d probably still dislike the new schedule, but it might not take over the whole day in my head. I’m not saying that’s a huge breakthrough, but it does sound a little better than feeling constantly wound up.

That sounds like a pretty honest shift—you’re not pretending the schedule is fine, just noticing that it could take up less space in your mind. I guess the “should” thought just makes me dig in harder. It turns the whole thing into me failing at something I’m supposed to be able to do, instead of just dealing with an annoying change. I can see how that would ramp up the tension, even if I still think the change itself is what set it off.

That’s a really clear observation, and it makes sense that you’d still see the schedule change as the trigger while noticing the “should” turns it into a verdict about you. If that thought is turning an annoying change into “I’m failing,” what do you notice it does to your willingness to adjust in the moment?

It probably makes me less willing, honestly. If I’m already telling myself I’m failing, then I just want to resist or shut down instead of figuring out how to deal with it. I don’t love admitting that, but I can see how that thought would make me dig in and make the whole thing harder.
That’s a pretty important realization, and I appreciate how honestly you put it. If you were to sum up what’s shifted for you so far in your own words, what would you say?

I’d say I’m starting to see that the schedule change is one thing, but the way I talk to myself about it is making it feel a lot bigger and more personal. I still don’t like the change, and I still think it was disruptive, but I can see that my reaction is partly what’s keeping it so intense. That’s not exactly comforting, but it does make a little more sense now.

conversations.content: If my family member’s health gets worse, I’m not going to be able to keep it together at work or make the right decisions for them. I hate feeling this helpless, and it’s like everything could fall apart at once.

That sounds really heavy, and I appreciate you saying it out loud even though it feels scary. If it’s okay, I’d like to slow this down with you—not to brush off how intense it feels, but to see whether this thought holds up when we look at it carefully; can you stay with it for a moment?

I guess, but I’m not sure “looking at it carefully” changes much if the situation actually gets worse. It feels a little like you’re trying to talk me out of being worried instead of dealing with the fact that I might have to handle a lot at once.

I mean, some people would probably say I’m catastrophizing or that I’m assuming the worst, but that doesn’t magically make the risk go away. I guess someone else might say I’m more prepared than I feel, but honestly that sounds a little too neat when I’m the one who has to deal with it if things change.

Maybe, but it also feels like another way of saying “calm down” in a more polite form. I can think of reasons it’s not totally irrational—my family member’s health has changed, and I do have a lot on my plate—but I also know I’m jumping straight to the worst-case version because it feels more controllable than uncertainty.

I get the logic of the question, but it still feels a little like a worksheet when what I’m dealing with is pretty messy. The evidence for the thought is that the health issue is real and my workload is real; the evidence against it is mostly that I haven’t actually fallen apart yet, so maybe I’m treating a possibility like it’s already a fact.

Maybe, but I’m not sure it’s that clean. It could be a habit, or it could just be a pretty rational response to a genuinely uncertain situation—those aren’t mutually exclusive. conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. Externally, they mostly went quiet and the meeting got awkward, which honestly just made me more annoyed in the moment. That sounds practical, and it fits with what you’ve noticed about how fast it escalates once you’re already at an 8 or 9. If you were to treat the jaw clench or heat as the first cue, what would you want that cue to mean in the moment—before the anger starts running the meeting for you?

I guess I’d want it to mean, “stop talking and buy myself a few seconds,” instead of assuming I have to respond immediately. Maybe it’s basically a warning that I’m no longer being objective, so I should step back before I say something I’ll regret. I’m not thrilled to admit that, but it does seem better than just plowing ahead.

That’s a useful shift, and it sounds like you’re noticing the cue could be less about “fixing” the meeting and more about preventing a regretful reaction. When you say you’re “no longer being objective,” what would you notice in yourself that tells you that threshold has been crossed?

I think it’s when I stop actually listening and start mentally preparing my rebuttal before they’ve even finished talking. Everything feels more black-and-white, and I get this urge to prove I’m being treated unfairly instead of figuring out what’s actually being said. That’s probably the point where I’m not really objective anymore, even if I still feel completely justified in the moment.

That’s a very clear read on the shift, and I can see why it still feels justified in the moment even while you recognize it’s narrowing your view. When you notice that black-and-white, prove-it mode kicking in, what do you think you’re trying to protect in yourself?

I think I’m trying to protect my competence, mostly. If I let it slide in the moment, it feels like I’m accepting that they can just override me and I’m supposed to smile and take it. So the anger is probably covering up feeling disrespected, even if I hate admitting that.

That sounds like a pretty important shift: the anger may be showing up to defend competence and dignity when you feel overridden. If you put that new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you understand these blowups?

I think what’s changed is that I’m starting to see these blowups as less about me “just losing it” and more about me feeling cornered or dismissed, and then reacting like I have to defend myself immediately. The anger still feels real, but it’s probably covering up the fact that I feel disrespected and not taken seriously. That doesn’t excuse snapping, but it does make it clearer why I go from zero to defensive so fast. So I guess the issue isn’t only the meeting itself—it’s also what I decide it means about me in that moment.

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. The client was invited to a social gathering after work, but the usual group of friends had changed plans and several familiar activities were no longer part of the event. I keep telling myself: "I feel uncomfortable and out of place, so this must mean I don’t belong here anymore and everyone can tell I’m awkward." and I've been feeling anxious, embarrassed, rejected.

That sounds really painful, especially when something familiar suddenly feels different and your mind fills in the blanks with rejection. In the CBT model, the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the interpretation we attach to it, so I’m curious what you noticed yourself doing in response to those thoughts and feelings?

I kind of shut down and got really quiet. I stayed physically there, but I was mostly scanning the room, overthinking everything I said, and trying not to draw attention to myself. I also left earlier than I normally would have because I felt so tense and exposed, and then I spent the rest of the night replaying it in my head, wondering if people noticed I was uncomfortable. It felt like the more I tried to act normal, the more awkward I became.

That makes a lot of sense—when you’re feeling tense and exposed, it’s very natural to pull back and then replay everything afterward. I’m wondering if part of what’s happening is that the feeling of being awkward starts to feel like proof that you are awkward, which is a really common pattern rather than a character flaw; if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what’s another way they might interpret it?

I think someone else might see it as a normal adjustment to a change in the group, not as evidence that I don’t belong. They might think I was quiet because I was thrown off by the shift in the usual dynamic, not because I’m inherently awkward or unwelcome. Honestly, if I saw a friend in that situation, I’d probably assume they were just uncomfortable and self-conscious in the moment, not that everyone was judging them. It’s hard for me to believe that about myself, though, because once I feel out of place, it quickly turns into this story that I’m being rejected.

That alternate interpretation sounds much kinder and, importantly, more balanced, and it makes sense that it feels hard to hold onto when the rejection story gets so loud. If you actually believed that you were just thrown off by a change in the group rather than being rejected, how do you think you would feel—what emotion comes up most clearly?

If I really believed that, I think I’d feel a lot less ashamed and panicked. The strongest emotion would probably be relief, but also sadness, because I’d be realizing how quickly I turned a change into a judgment about myself. I’d still probably feel uneasy in the moment, but it would feel more manageable and less like I was being personally rejected. I think I’d also feel a little more grounded, like I could breathe and not have to defend myself so much.

That’s a really important shift—you can feel how much less trapped it would be to have relief and grounding instead of shame and panic. With that feeling in the moment, how might your behavior have been different?

If I felt more grounded, I think I would have relaxed enough to actually stay engaged instead of just monitoring myself the whole time. I might have talked to people more naturally, asked questions, or even joined in on whatever was happening without assuming I was being judged. I probably would have stayed longer too, because I wouldn’t have felt such a strong need to escape. It makes me realize how much of my behavior was driven by fear rather than what I actually wanted to do.

That’s a really clear insight, and it sounds like you’re noticing the difference between fear steering the moment and your actual preferences getting buried. What would you say is the new perspective you’ve reached about what happened and what it meant?

I think my new perspective is that the event itself wasn’t proof that I don’t belong, it was just a change that caught me off guard and activated a lot of old insecurity. I’m seeing more clearly that I took feeling uncomfortable and turned it into a story about rejection, even though there wasn’t really evidence for that. What happened meant I was anxious and self-protective, not that I was awkward or unwanted. That feels hard to admit, but also kind of relieving, because it means the experience says more about my fear in that moment than about my worth in the group.

That’s a meaningful shift—from treating the discomfort as a verdict about you to noticing how quickly old insecurity can shape the story you tell yourself in the moment. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that taking time off for the holiday will make me fall behind on my work and look less reliable to my team. Then there's I keep thinking that if I don’t perform perfectly at work right now, I could hurt my chances of advancing in my career. And I also keep thinking about: I’m concerned that the holiday slowdown will make me seem less committed compared with coworkers who are staying visible.

Some worries are productive because they point to something you can actually do something about, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical or outside your control, and we handle those differently; which is the first worry that’s keeping you up?

The first one is probably the fear that taking time off for the holiday will make me fall behind and look less reliable to my team. That feels the most immediate because I can picture work piling up while I’m away, and then I start imagining people noticing and judging me. I know some of that might be me catastrophizing, but it still feels very real when I’m lying there at night.

That makes a lot of sense—when you can picture the pile-up and the judging, it can feel very immediate and heavy. As you look at this worry more closely, is there a concrete action you can take that would actually address it, or does it seem more hypothetical and outside your control?

I think there is some concrete action I can take, at least partially. I can make sure my current priorities are wrapped up before I leave, and I can leave a clear handoff for the team so nothing important is just sitting there unclear. I could also set an out-of-office message and maybe let a couple of key people know what’s covered and when I’ll be back, which would probably calm me down a bit. But I also think part of this is outside my control, because I can’t completely prevent work from piling up or control how other people interpret my absence.

That’s a really clear and balanced way of seeing it—you’ve identified both what you can influence and what you can’t. What’s one small, concrete next step you’d like to take, and exactly when will you do it?

I think the next small step I want to take is to make a short handoff list for the team, with my top priorities, anything still pending, and who to contact if something comes up while I’m out. I can do that tomorrow afternoon after I finish my main work block, so it feels specific instead of just staying in my head. I think having it written down would help me feel more prepared and less like I’m leaving things to chance. It also seems like a realistic step that I can actually control, which is reassuring.

That sounds like a solid, practical step, and it makes sense that having it written down would feel reassuring. When you turn to the second worry about not performing perfectly and hurting your chances of advancing, does that feel like something you can take action on, or does it seem more outside your control?

I think it’s a mix, but it feels more outside my control than the first one. I can obviously keep doing solid work, staying organized, and being thoughtful about my responsibilities, but I can’t fully control whether “perfect” performance is even possible or how my advancement gets judged in the bigger picture. That’s part of what makes it stressful at night, because my mind wants to treat it like if I just worry hard enough, I can guarantee the outcome. But when I’m honest, I know I can influence my performance, not control the entire career result.

That sounds like an important shift—you’re seeing more clearly the difference between what you can influence and what you can’t, even though the worry still pulls hard at night. In your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about this second worry?

I think the new perspective is that I can show up consistently and do my job well, but I can’t make everything perfect or guarantee a specific career outcome just by worrying about it. My effort matters, but the bigger result depends on a lot of things I don’t fully control. That takes some pressure off, even though it doesn’t completely erase the anxiety. It feels a little more realistic to focus on doing my part well instead of trying to mentally secure the future.

It sounds like you’re noticing a more grounded way to hold both your responsibility and the limits of your control, and that shift is easing some of the pressure without asking you to pretend the anxiety is gone. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed about the difference between doing your part and trying to mentally secure the outcome?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. At dinner, his partner mentioned that he had left his running shoes by the door again and asked whether he was still planning to keep up with the new routine he had talked about. I keep telling myself: "She thinks I never follow through and that I’m failing at changing my habits." and I've been feeling embarrassed, defensive, discouraged.

That sounds pretty painful, especially when you were already trying to change and then heard it in that moment. In CBT terms, the same situation can land very differently depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m wondering what you did next when the thought “I’m failing” and those embarrassed, defensive feelings showed up?

Honestly, I probably got quieter and sort of shut down instead of saying anything useful. I know you’re probably going to say I should’ve challenged the thought or whatever, but in the moment it just felt like proof that she was right, so I went into defensive mode and started thinking, “Why bother trying if I’m just going to screw it up again?”

That makes a lot of sense, especially if it felt like evidence in the moment rather than just a thought, and I can hear how quickly it turned into “why bother,” which is a pretty human reaction. Sometimes that kind of thought is a jumping-to-conclusions move rather than a character flaw, so if someone else saw the exact same dinner scene, what else might they think it meant?

Maybe they’d think she was just pointing out the shoes because they were in the way, not delivering some big verdict on my character. I get the “jumping to conclusions” thing, but it still feels like there’s usually some truth under it, and I’m not convinced it’s just me overreacting.

That’s a fair pushback, and it makes sense that you’d want some truth in it rather than a neat therapy label. If you actually took the “she was just commenting on the shoes being in the way” interpretation as the more accurate one, what emotion do you think would show up most strongly—relief, irritation, embarrassment, something else?

Probably irritation, if I’m being honest. Even if it wasn’t some huge judgment, it still hits a nerve because it feels like I’m being reminded I’m not doing what I said I would. So yeah, maybe less “I’m a failure” and more “I hate being called out,” which is annoying but probably closer to the truth.

That’s a meaningful shift, because “I’m a failure” tends to pull people into shame and shutdown, while “I hate being called out” sounds more like irritation and defensiveness. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

Maybe I would’ve at least said something instead of going silent, though I’m not sure it would’ve been anything particularly helpful. Honestly, I still think the whole “what would you have done differently” thing can get a bit too neat, because in real life I’m usually just trying not to make it worse.

That’s a fair criticism; real life isn’t tidy, and often the goal is just not to make things worse. If the dinner scene stayed the same but the thought shifted from “I’m a failure” to “I hate being called out,” what does that tell you about the relationship between your thoughts and how you experience situations?

It tells me the thought changes the feeling, sure, but I’m not sure that means I can just think my way out of it. The situation still irritates me, and part of me thinks the “shift” is more about naming what I already felt than some big breakthrough.

That’s a pretty grounded way to look at it, and I hear your skepticism about turning this into some big therapy win when it may just be clearer language for what was already there. If naming it more accurately matters even a little, what difference do you notice between “I’m failing” and “I’m irritated and feeling called out” in how much power the moment has over you?

I mean, “I’m failing” makes it feel bigger and more personal, like the whole thing is about whether I’m competent or not. “I’m irritated and feeling called out” is still uncomfortable, but it feels less like a verdict and more like a reaction I’m having. I’m not saying that fixes anything, but I can see how the second one gives me a little more room before I spiral.

That’s a pretty important distinction, especially if the second version gives you a little more room before things snowball. If “I’m failing” turns it into a verdict and “I’m irritated and feeling called out” turns it into a reaction, what do you notice about which one is more likely to keep you stuck?

Yeah, “I’m failing” is definitely the one that keeps me stuck, because once I’m there I basically stop trying and start defending myself in my head. “I’m irritated and feeling called out” still isn’t fun, but at least it sounds like something I can work with instead of some final judgment. I’m not thrilled about admitting that, but I can see the difference.

That’s a pretty honest distinction, and I can hear you not exactly enjoying it, which makes sense. If “I’m failing” is the one that shuts you down and “I’m irritated and feeling called out” is the one you can actually work with, what do you make of the fact that the more accurate-sounding thought is also the less damaging one?

I guess it makes me think the problem isn’t just that I’m being too negative, it’s that I’m making it way more absolute than it needs to be. “I’m failing” sounds dramatic and probably not very useful, even if it feels true in the moment. I’m still not thrilled about all this, but I can see how the more accurate version gives me a little less reason to spiral.

That’s a solid observation, and I hear you not exactly celebrating it, which feels honest rather than forced. If you were to sum up the shift in your own words, what’s the new perspective you’re taking from this?

I think the shift is that I’m not actually reacting to some objective proof that I’m a failure—I’m reacting to feeling called out and embarrassed. When I turn it into “I’m failing,” it gets bigger and more hopeless than it really is, and that’s probably what sends me into shutdown mode. It doesn’t make the situation feel good, but it does make it feel more manageable and less like some final verdict on me.

That sounds like a really important distinction—you noticed how the sting of being called out can get translated into a much bigger, harsher story about you, and that translation is what seems to shut things down. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. I guess there was some tension, but I’m not sure why you want me to catalog every little body sensation like this is some puzzle. Probably like an 8, maybe higher in the moment—I wasn’t exactly measuring it. I snapped at my coworker, then I just shut my laptop and sat there trying not to say anything worse, which honestly didn’t feel very controlled.

Thanks for being that honest about it; that gives us something real to work with. What happened externally right after you snapped—what did your coworker do or say—and then what was happening inside you right after, and as the hours or days went on?

She just looked at me like I was being unreasonable, which was probably fair, and then she kind of backed off. Honestly, I don’t know that there’s some magic move that fixes it in the moment, but I guess I could step away before I say something stupid. Maybe just close the app, get water, and not keep staring at the numbers like they’re personally attacking me.

conversations.content: I’m terrified this pregnancy is going to blow up our whole life—what if something goes wrong and I’m the one who has to keep everything together for my family and the mortgage?

I guess the strongest part is that if something goes wrong, there isn’t really a backup plan—I can’t just “feel better” and make the bills or the family stress disappear. And honestly, I’m not sure picking apart the thought is the point when the reality is we’ve got a kid coming and a mortgage, so yeah, it feels pretty damn real.

You’re making a fair point—it does sound academic if it feels like the stakes are genuinely huge, and I’m hearing that you want something grounded, not a lecture about irrational anxiety. What is the evidence for this thought, and what is the evidence against it?

Evidence for it is pretty obvious: pregnancy is unpredictable, money is tight, and if something serious happens, I’m the one who’s supposed to hold it together. Evidence against it? I guess we’ve handled hard stuff before and haven’t collapsed yet, but that doesn’t exactly make me feel reassured right now.

Honestly, it feels like more than a random possibility, but I can’t say it’s likely either—I’m stuck in that ugly middle where my brain keeps treating “could happen” like “probably will.” So yeah, maybe it’s just a possibility, but it’s a possibility with enough weight that it’s hard not to plan around it.

That “ugly middle” makes a lot of sense, and I can hear how your mind is treating uncertainty like a forecast rather than a maybe. When you notice it getting pulled from “could happen” toward “probably will,” what evidence does it use to make that jump, and what happens if you test whether it may be exaggerating what’s actually true?

I mean, the “evidence” is mostly just my brain going straight to worst-case because that’s what’s easiest to imagine, not because I’ve got a spreadsheet proving disaster. If I test whether it’s exaggerating, maybe it calms down a notch, but I’m not convinced that changes the fact that the risk is still real and I still have to deal with it.

That makes sense—you’re not denying the risk, just noticing your mind may be filling in the blanks with the worst-case because it’s vivid and easy to imagine. How might others interpret the same situation differently?

I guess other people might see it as “yeah, this is stressful, but lots of people get through pregnancy and the money part without everything falling apart.” My wife would probably say I’m jumping way ahead of what’s actually happening and acting like we’re already in the worst-case scenario. I can see that perspective, even if part of me still thinks it’s easy to say when you’re not the one lying awake doing the math.

You’ve pulled together a pretty honest picture: there’s real uncertainty and pressure here, but also evidence that your mind may be jumping ahead of what’s actually known. If you were to rewrite the original thought so it’s fairer and not fake-positive, what would it sound like?

Maybe something like: “This pregnancy is a real stress test, and there are things I can’t control, but I’m not actually in disaster mode yet.” It’s still scary, and I do need to plan for problems, but it’s not the same as saying everything is going to blow up. I guess that feels a little more accurate, even if I’m not exactly relaxed about it.

That sounds more balanced and a lot more grounded than “everything is going to blow up,” even if it hasn’t made the fear vanish. When you say it that way, what changes in how you see the situation, even just a little?

I guess it takes it down a notch from “we’re doomed” to “we’re under serious pressure and need a plan.” That doesn’t make me feel good, exactly, but it does make it feel a little more manageable and less like I’m already standing in the wreckage. I’m still tense about it, though.

That’s a meaningful shift, even if the tension is still there, and it makes sense that “more manageable” isn’t the same as feeling okay. If it’s less like standing in the wreckage and more like being under pressure, what do you notice changes about what you’re actually responsible for right now?

I guess it means I’m responsible for dealing with what’s in front of me instead of acting like I have to solve every possible disaster before it happens. Right now that probably looks more like making a realistic plan, staying involved, and not spiraling every time my brain jumps ahead. I’m not saying that makes it easy, but it does feel a bit different than “I have to carry the whole future on my back.”

That’s a pretty important shift, and you’ve put it in your own language in a way that feels more solid than the original thought. If you had to sum up the new perspective in one or two sentences, what would you say it is?

I think the new perspective is that this is a serious stressor, but not proof that everything is about to fall apart. I don’t need to solve every possible outcome right now—I need to stay grounded in what’s actually happening and make a practical plan for the parts I can control. The fear is still there, but it’s less convincing when I stop treating it like a prediction.

That’s a meaningful shift—from treating the fear like a forecast to recognizing it as a signal you can notice without handing it the final word. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of shame lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense that you’d feel stuck if the shame is just sitting there without a clear handle on it. If we map it together step by step, what’s the most specific word for what you’re feeling right now, and how intense is it from 0 to 100 in this moment?

I mean, “shame” is already the word, so I’m not sure what squeezing it into a more specific label is supposed to do. It’s probably around an 85 right now—maybe higher when I start thinking about work and how much I feel like I should have achieved by now.

Yeah, that makes sense—you’re already naming it clearly, and the 85 tells me this isn’t mild or theoretical, it’s hitting hard. When you think of the most recent moment it spiked, what was the specific situation or exact thought that set it off?

Probably when I saw a colleague get praised for a project and my first thought was, “Great, everyone else is moving ahead and I’m just… here.” I know that sounds dramatic, but that’s the kind of thing that sets it off. I’m not convinced digging into the exact moment changes much, though.

That makes sense—you’re noticing the trigger pretty clearly, and I hear the skepticism about whether zooming in helps. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment, what was the automatic thought you told yourself right then, even if it was just a flash?

Honestly, the automatic thought was something like, “I’m behind, and everyone can tell.” It’s not exactly a groundbreaking insight, which is why I’m not sure naming it is doing much, but that’s what flashed through.
That’s a very clear snapshot of the thought, and I get why it feels obvious rather than revelatory. When that hit, what did you do right away, and what did you start avoiding afterward?

I mostly just shut down and kept scrolling through email like that would fix anything. Afterward I avoided looking at the team updates and definitely avoided thinking too hard about my own goals, because apparently that’s what I do instead of being a functional adult.

That sounds like a pretty understandable shutdown response, especially when the shame is that high and it feels safer to numb out than to face more comparison. What were the consequences of scrolling and avoiding the updates right away, and what do you notice it does over time to your mood or to how you see yourself?

Right away, the consequence was basically that I got nothing done and felt even more useless, so it was a great little productivity spiral. Over time it just reinforces the idea that I’m the kind of person who can’t handle seeing other people succeed, which is fun, I guess. I’m still not totally convinced that pointing out the pattern is doing anything except making it sound neater than it feels.

Yeah, I hear that—the pattern can feel annoyingly tidy when the experience itself feels messy and humiliating. If we stay with just this one loop for a moment, what do you make of the fact that the avoidance gives short-term relief but also seems to hand the shame more evidence afterward?

Yeah, I mean, I can see that in principle. It does give me a few minutes of not feeling like I’m being judged, but then I end up with less done and more evidence for the whole “I’m falling behind” story, which is kind of the problem. I’m not saying that’s some huge revelation, but I guess it’s not helping in the long run.

That’s a pretty sharp read of the loop, even if it doesn’t feel like a breakthrough, and I hear the frustration in how predictable it is. When you say it gives you a few minutes of not feeling judged, what do you notice that you’re protecting yourself from in those moments?

Probably from the feeling that if I actually look at it, I’ll confirm that I’m not measuring up. There’s also this weird sense that if I stay busy enough, I can avoid having to admit how embarrassed I am about where I am compared to other people. So I guess the protection is against feeling exposed, or maybe just having to sit there with the idea that I’m not as far along as I should be.

That makes a lot of sense—you’re not just avoiding the feeling, you’re protecting yourself from what you think that feeling would mean about you. If you imagine not staying busy for a moment, what do you think that exposure would say about you that feels so hard to sit with?

I think it would say that I’m not exceptional, which is apparently a bigger deal to me than I want to admit. More bluntly, it feels like it would confirm I’m ordinary in a way that’s somehow unacceptable, especially at this point in my career. I can see that’s probably what’s underneath the shame, even if I don’t love saying it out loud.

That’s a really honest and painful thing to name, and it makes sense that saying it out loud doesn’t feel great. When you tell yourself “ordinary is unacceptable,” what do you imagine that would mean about your worth or your place with other people?

I think it would mean I’m less valuable than the people around me, or at least less worth paying attention to. Which sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but that’s kind of the internal logic. I guess I’m starting to see that the shame isn’t just about work—it’s tied to this much bigger fear of being forgettable or easily replaceable.

That doesn’t sound dramatic to me; it sounds like you’re putting words to a pretty painful rule you’ve been living with. When you notice that “less valuable” idea, what do you tell yourself would happen if other people really saw you that way?

I think I tell myself they’d lose interest pretty quickly, or at least stop taking me seriously. Like I’d still be around, but I’d be background noise instead of someone who matters. Saying it makes it sound kind of childish, but that’s the fear: not just being judged, but being quietly dismissed.

That doesn’t sound childish to me; it sounds like a really sharp fear of disappearing in other people’s eyes. When that “background noise” idea shows up, what does it make you assume about what you’d need to be in order to matter?

I guess it makes me assume I’d need to be exceptional in a pretty visible way—like, not just competent, but clearly ahead of the pack. If I’m not doing something impressive enough to get noticed, my brain seems to decide I don’t really count. Saying that out loud, it feels a little embarrassing, because it’s such a harsh standard to live by.

That does sound harsh, and I can hear why saying it out loud feels embarrassing rather than clarifying. If that “only exceptional counts” rule were a standard you had to keep living by, what would it be costing you day to day?

It’s probably costing me a lot more than I want to admit. Day to day, it means I’m never really allowed to feel okay unless I’ve done something impressive, so even normal days feel like failures. I think it also makes me tense and kind of guarded around other people, because I’m always checking whether I’m measuring up instead of just being present. And honestly, it probably keeps me from enjoying anything I do, because the second something stops being outstanding, my brain treats it like it doesn’t count.

That sounds exhausting, like the bar keeps moving just enough that you never get to land anywhere and feel settled. When you notice that “if it’s not outstanding, it doesn’t count” rule operating, what does it seem to be trying to protect you from?

I think it’s trying to protect me from the possibility of being average and then having to admit that average might still be enough for most people, just not for me. More than that, it seems to protect me from feeling the disappointment of wanting a bigger life and not having evidence that I’m already living one. If I keep demanding exceptional, then I don’t have to sit with the quieter fear that maybe I’m not failing at greatness so much as I’m just a person with limits. That’s a hard thing to say, but it feels closer to the actual fear than the work stuff does.

That’s a really important shift, and I hear how it moves from “work isn’t enough” to something much more personal about limits, disappointment, and what you’ve been demanding of yourself. If you had to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you understand the shame?

I think I’m starting to see that the shame isn’t really just about not achieving enough at work; it’s about this rule I’ve been carrying that says I have to be exceptional to be worthwhile. And when I’m not, I don’t just feel disappointed — I start treating myself like I’m basically not enough as a person. That makes the shame feel less random and more like a defense against admitting I have limits and that ordinary might be part of my life too. I don’t like that, but it feels more true than the simpler “I’m behind” story.

It sounds like you’ve put your finger on something deeper than the work pressure itself, and even if it’s uncomfortable, there’s a kind of honesty in seeing how quickly that “not enough” story turns into a judgment about your worth as a person. Given that, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. My manager told me that my work hours would be changed at the last minute, with no real explanation, and I was expected to adjust my schedule immediately to cover the new conditions. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It takes courage to look at this so honestly, especially when you’re already feeling ashamed about how it went. We can map it together in four steps — trigger, warning signs, response, and outcomes — and I’d like to start with the moment before the anger fully hit: what were the early warning signs in your body or behavior, like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

Yeah, I definitely noticed it in my body before I actually said anything. My chest got tight, my jaw clenched, and I could feel my heart start beating faster, like I was bracing for a fight. I also got really hot and restless, and I had this strong urge to interrupt her and just say, “That’s not fair.” Looking back, I think I was already so tense from the unpredictability that the moment she said it, I went straight into feeling cornered.

That’s a really important observation, because those body signals are often the earliest moment when change is still possible, before the anger fully takes over. When it peaked, how intense was the anger on a scale of 0 to 10, and what did you actually do?

It was probably a 9 out of 10, honestly. I felt like I was right on the edge of either yelling or crying, and I hated how powerless I felt in that moment. I did interrupt her and said something like, “You can’t just change this on me with no warning,” and my voice was sharper than I intended. After that I was still angry, but mostly I felt embarrassed and shaky, like I’d already crossed a line I couldn’t take back.

Thank you for being that honest about how intense it got and what it felt like afterward. I’m wondering, when you look at the outcome in the room, what happened externally with your manager right after you spoke, and then what happened inside you afterward, both in the moment and over the next hours or days?

Externally, she kind of froze at first and got very quiet, and then she said she’d “look into it,” but her tone felt more guarded after that. I didn’t get the sense that the conversation was resolved at all, just that it got awkward and ended quickly. Inside, I felt a mix of relief and immediate regret, like I’d finally said what I was feeling but also made things worse. Over the next few hours I kept replaying it in my head, feeling embarrassed and angry at myself, and by the end of the day I was mostly drained and anxious about how she’d see me after that.

You’re describing the whole chain very clearly: the last-minute change hit as the trigger, your body gave you early warning signs, then the sharp response led to awkwardness, regret, and a lot of replaying afterward. Looking at those warning signs you described, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment, before the response, that might change the outcome?

I think one thing I could do is pause and ask for a minute before responding, even if I’m still upset. If I noticed the tight chest and clenched jaw, I could step away, take a few slow breaths, and maybe say, “I want to respond thoughtfully, but I need a moment to process this.” That would probably give me a chance to calm down enough to speak more clearly instead of reacting from feeling cornered. I also think it might help me feel less powerless, because I’d be choosing my response instead of just getting swept up in it.

That sounds like a meaningful shift — from feeling cornered and swept along to seeing a small pause as a way to protect your voice and regain some choice. If you put that new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you?

I think what’s changed is that I’m starting to see the pause not as me giving in or being weak, but as me actually taking back some control. Before, I felt like once I got that activated, I had no options except to react, and that made me feel even more trapped. Now it feels a little more possible to notice the signs earlier and choose how I want to respond, even if I’m still angry. That feels important to me because I don’t want my only choices to be either exploding or staying silent.

It sounds like you’re beginning to experience that pause as a form of agency rather than a loss of strength, and that shift seems to open up a little more space between what you feel and how you respond. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of frustration lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really hard, and it makes sense that you’d want some way to make sense of it rather than just sit with it. If you’re willing, what’s the most specific word for what you’re feeling right now, and how strong is it from 0 to 100?

I don’t know, “frustrated” still feels like the closest word, even if that sounds vague. Maybe a 60? I’m not totally convinced putting a number on it changes much, but I guess it’s a little more useful than just saying “bad.”

That makes sense, and I hear the skepticism about numbers while also noticing you found it a bit more useful than just “bad.” What was one specific moment or thought that kicked off that 60 for you, just a single concrete instance you can picture?

Honestly, it’s kind of hard to pin down one moment because it’s been building up. Maybe it started when the school-year stuff ramped up and everyone at work suddenly acts like the whole office has to revolve around it, which is annoying more than anything else. I guess that was one of those moments where I thought, “great, now my day is going to get hijacked by other people’s chaos.”

That sounds really irritating, especially when it feels like other people’s school-year chaos starts taking over your workday. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a quick flash?

Probably something like, “of course this is happening now,” and then “why does everyone else get to treat their schedule like it’s my problem?” I know that sounds dramatic, but it was basically instant annoyance, not some deep insight.

That doesn’t sound dramatic to me; it sounds like a pretty immediate reaction to feeling put on the spot by other people’s schedules. What did you do next in response to that annoyance, both right away and anything you started avoiding afterward?

I mostly just kept my head down and got through the meeting, because what else am I supposed to do, make a scene about it? Afterward I avoided checking my email for a bit and put off a couple things I knew were going to turn into more school-related nonsense, which probably wasn’t ideal, but it felt easier in the moment.

That makes a lot of sense: you kept things contained in the meeting, and then avoiding email and those tasks probably gave you some immediate relief even if it came with a cost later. What were the consequences of that, both right away and over time, and now that you can see the full chain, is there any link where even a small shift might interrupt the whole pattern?

Right away, the consequence was mostly that I felt less irritated because I didn’t have to deal with it immediately, but then it just sat there and made me more annoyed later when I had to catch up. Over time it probably turns into me feeling behind and cranky for no dramatic reason, which is annoying to admit, and I guess the only “small shift” would be not avoiding the email for an hour or so—but that’s easier said than done.

That makes a lot of sense: avoiding the email gave you short-term relief, and then the delayed pile-up cost you more later. When you picture that one-hour delay, what do you imagine would happen in the first few minutes that makes it feel harder than it sounds?

Honestly, in the first few minutes I’d probably just feel myself getting irritated all over again, like I can already picture the subject lines and know I’m going to hate it. Then I’d start telling myself it’s going to turn into a whole thing, which is probably part of why I avoid it in the first place. I guess the annoying part is that the delay feels like buying peace, but only for a little while.

That “buying peace for a little while” sounds like it captures the tradeoff pretty well, even if it’s frustrating to notice. When you tell yourself it’s going to turn into a whole thing, what do you think you’re predicting will happen if you open the email and stay with it for those first few minutes?

I’m probably predicting that it’ll snowball into a bunch of extra work or back-and-forth, and then I’ll get stuck dealing with other people’s timing again. It’s not like I think the email itself is catastrophic, just that it tends to open the door to more annoying stuff, which is why I hesitate. I can see that I’m kind of assuming the worst before I even look, which is… annoying to admit.

That’s a pretty clear read on the pattern, even if it’s annoying to notice yourself doing it. When you say you’re “assuming the worst before you even look,” what evidence do you have that the email usually does snowball, and what evidence do you have that it sometimes doesn’t?

Yeah, I mean, there are definitely times where one email turns into three more replies and then I’m stuck coordinating around everyone else’s timing, so it’s not like I made that up. But I also know there are plenty of emails that are just annoying for a minute and then basically done, and I usually don’t give those enough credit. So I guess part of me is reacting to the pattern, and part of me is probably treating every message like it’s going to be a whole ordeal.

That sounds like a pretty balanced read of it: you’re not imagining the annoying pattern, and you’re also noticing that not every email deserves the same level of dread. If you were to put that shift into your own words, what would you say is the new perspective you’ve reached?

I guess the new perspective is that I’m not just being irrationally annoyed for no reason, but I also might be overgeneralizing based on the emails that do turn into a hassle. So instead of treating every school-related message like it’s automatically going to ruin my day, I can at least admit some of them are just brief annoyances. That doesn’t make them fun, but it does make it seem less like I’m trapped in this inevitable pattern.

It sounds like you were able to hold onto both parts at once: that the annoyance is real, and that it doesn’t have to mean every school email is destined to take over your day. What might you want to carry forward from that distinction the next time one of those messages lands in your inbox?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I'm worried I won't perform well enough during this business readjustment and could end up looking incompetent to my manager. Then there's I keep thinking this restructuring means my role is probably next to be cut, and I can't stop imagining being out of work. And I also keep thinking about: I'm worried that if I don't adapt fast enough to the new direction, I'll lose momentum in my career and get stuck in a dead-end position.

That sounds exhausting, especially with your sleep getting hit by all three at once. I’m wondering, if we separate them a bit, which of those worries feels like it’s the first one keeping you up right now?

Honestly, I’m not sure splitting them up helps much—they all feed into each other. If I had to pick one, I’d say the job-cut thing is probably the biggest one because it makes everything else feel pointless if I’m going to be out anyway.

That makes sense—if the job-cut worry feels like the one that makes everything else collapse, it would be hard to separate them neatly. When you look at that thought, is there a concrete action you can take with it right now, or is it more of a hypothetical outcome that’s outside your control?

Mostly hypothetical, honestly. I mean, I can do my job and stay visible, but I can’t exactly control whether management decides to cut roles. So asking me to “act” on it feels a little pointless unless you mean just keep my head down and hope for the best.

That makes sense; if the outcome is outside your control, “just act on it” can sound pretty empty. Would it be worth setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to think through the job-cut worry, so for tonight it doesn’t have to keep running the show, and what is the next worry on your mind?

I get what you’re aiming for, but “schedule worry time” sounds a bit artificial to me—I’m not convinced my brain will care what time I assign it. That said, the second worry is probably the performance one; I keep imagining I’m going to look like I don’t have it together in front of my manager.

I get why that sounds artificial; if your mind is already revved up, a scheduled slot can seem like a gimmick. On the performance worry, when you picture looking like you don’t have it together in front of your manager, is there something specific you could influence there, or does it still feel mostly outside your control?

A bit of both, I guess. I can prepare and try to be clear in meetings, but I can’t control how I’m perceived if people are already looking for signs I’m not up to it. So yeah, there are things I can do, but it still feels like a lot of this is just me trying not to get judged.

That sounds frustrating—especially when it feels like you can do the preparation and still not control the judgment part. If the useful piece here is the part you can influence, what would “preparing and being clear” look like in one concrete meeting this week, and is there one more worry still sitting in the background?

I mean, sure, I can prep more than usual and keep my points tighter in the next meeting, but I’m not pretending that guarantees anything. At some point it turns into overpreparing just to feel less anxious, which isn’t exactly the same as solving the problem. And yeah, the last worry is the career one—this whole thing could stall me out if I don’t adapt fast enough.

That makes a lot of sense—you’re noticing the line between useful preparation and anxiety-driven overpreparing, which is a pretty important distinction. With the career-stall worry, when you look at it closely, what would count as productive concern there, and what would start tipping into unproductive rumination?

Productive concern would be something like, “What skills do I actually need to pick up for this new direction, and what’s a realistic plan to do that?” Unproductive rumination is me replaying worst-case scenarios about becoming irrelevant and then losing half the night to it. I’ll admit there’s probably a difference there, even if my brain doesn’t always cooperate.

That’s a sharp distinction, and it sounds like you can tell the difference between a useful question and the kind that just drags you into the weeds. Since this third worry has a more concrete angle, what feels like the smallest realistic first step for figuring out the skills or plan you’d actually need for the new direction?

I guess the smallest first step would be to look at the actual expectations for the new direction instead of just guessing at them. Maybe I could skim the internal notes or role requirements and see what gaps are real versus what I’m inventing at 1 a.m. I’m not saying that fixes the anxiety, but it would at least give me something more concrete to work with.

That sounds like a pretty practical shift from spinning in the dark to checking what’s actually there, even if it doesn’t magically erase the anxiety. If you did look at those notes or role requirements, what would you be hoping to learn that would tell you the worry is based on real gaps rather than the 1 a.m. version of the story?

I’d be looking for something concrete, like whether the new direction actually requires a different skill set than what I already have, or if it’s mostly the same job with different wording. If there are specific gaps, I’d want to know whether they’re big ones or just things I can catch up on pretty quickly. I’m still skeptical that this will calm my brain much, but it would at least tell me whether I’m reacting to real information or just filling in blanks with worst-case stuff.

That skepticism makes sense; it sounds like you’re not expecting calm so much as a reality check, which is a pretty different goal. If you did get that concrete information and found the gaps were either small or manageable, what would that change about the story your mind is telling at 1 a.m.?

I suppose it would take some of the “I’m doomed” edge off it. If the gaps are small or manageable, then the story at 1 a.m. shifts from “this is the beginning of the end” to “this is a stressful adjustment, but not necessarily a career death sentence.” I’m not saying my brain will instantly buy that, but it would give me something more grounded to push back with when the worst-case version starts running the show.

That sounds like a more grounded way to frame it, and it makes sense that your brain wouldn’t instantly buy it just because it’s more reasonable. When the “career death sentence” version shows up at 1 a.m., what would you notice in yourself that tells you it’s the worst-case story rather than the grounded one?

I think I’d notice how absolute it sounds. The worst-case version has that all-or-nothing feel to it—like one rough restructuring automatically means I’m done, when that’s probably not actually what’s happening. I also tend to feel it in my body first: I get tense, my mind starts jumping ahead, and I stop asking whether the thought is true and just assume it is. So maybe the clue is that it feels urgent and final, not just concerned.

That’s a clear observation—you’re noticing both the all-or-nothing language and the body alarm that pulls you into assuming the worst. Putting it together, how would you sum up the new perspective you’ve reached on this worry in your own words?

I think the new perspective is that I’m not dealing with three separate disasters so much as one stressful situation that my mind keeps turning into a worst-case story. The story feels urgent and convincing at night, but that doesn’t mean it’s accurate or that it’s already decided. I do have some control over the parts I can check—like understanding the new expectations and preparing for the next meeting—even if I can’t control management’s decisions. So maybe this is less “my career is ending” and more “I’m in an uncomfortable transition and need to get more concrete before my brain fills in the blanks.”

It sounds like you’ve moved from being pulled around by the night-time story to seeing it as a story your mind is generating, while also recognizing there are concrete pieces you can get clarity on without pretending you can control everything. As you leave today, what’s the first question you’d want to ask yourself the next time that worst-case version starts to feel so convincing?
