conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that this stress about the mortgage is going to make my blood pressure worse and I’ll end up harming my health. Then there's I keep thinking that if I feel tired lately, it means something serious is wrong with my body. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried that I’m not taking good enough care of myself and I’ll end up getting run down from not sleeping or exercising enough.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind is scanning for danger when sleep is already hard to come by. In CBT we sometimes sort worries into productive ones, which point to something actionable, and unproductive ones, which are more hypothetical or outside your control, because they’re handled differently; what is the first worry that is keeping you up?

The first one that keeps grabbing me is the mortgage stress turning into something bigger, like it’s going to affect my blood pressure and then spiral into a health problem. It feels almost automatic at night, like my brain goes, “You’re stressed, that’s bad for your heart,” and then I can’t shut it off. I know on some level it’s not helpful to keep replaying it, but it still feels very real when I’m lying there awake.

That sounds really intense, especially when it shows up automatically at night and feels so convincing in the moment. When you look at this worry closely, is there a concrete action you can take about it right now, or does it feel more hypothetical and outside your control?

I think it’s mostly hypothetical at that point, at least in the middle of the night. I can’t really do anything about the mortgage or my blood pressure at 2 a.m., so it turns into this mental loop that feels urgent but isn’t actually solvable right then. The only concrete thing I could do is maybe check in with my doctor or make a plan for the mortgage during the day, but the worry itself is definitely bigger than what I can act on in that moment. That’s part of what makes it so frustrating, because it feels important, but it’s not something I can fix by thinking harder about it.

That makes a lot of sense—when a worry feels urgent but can’t be solved at 2 a.m., it can keep your mind stuck in a loop. Would setting aside a specific 10-minute worry time tomorrow at a set time help you park it for now, and what is the next worry on your mind?

Yeah, I think that could help. Having a set time tomorrow would make it feel less like I’m ignoring it and more like I’m containing it until I can actually do something useful with it. The next worry is the one about feeling tired lately and then assuming it means something serious is wrong with my body. When I’m already anxious and sleep-deprived, I start reading every little symptom as a sign that something bad is happening, and that makes it hard to tell what’s real and what’s just worry.

That sounds really understandable—when you’re tired and already on edge, it can be hard to tell whether you’re noticing a real body signal or your mind amplifying it. Looking at this worry closely, do you see anything concrete you can act on right now, or does it feel more like an unproductive worry that’s outside your control in the moment?

It feels mostly like an unproductive worry in the moment, because once I start scanning my body, I just get more anxious and less clear. I don’t think there’s anything immediate I can do at 2 a.m. besides keep myself stuck in that loop, which usually makes the tiredness feel even worse. The concrete thing would be to notice the pattern and maybe bring it up with my doctor if it keeps happening, but the actual fear in the moment is more about catastrophizing than solving anything. So I think this is one of those worries where I need to step back rather than keep checking and interpreting every sensation.

That’s a thoughtful shift—you’re noticing how body-scanning pulls you into more anxiety rather than giving you clearer information. In your own words, what feels different now about how you’re understanding this worry?

What feels different is that I’m seeing the tiredness less as proof that something is medically wrong and more as something that gets amplified by anxiety and lack of sleep. Before, it felt like every sensation had to mean something serious, but now I can see that the checking and interpreting are actually making me feel worse. I’m starting to understand that the worry is not the same thing as evidence. That makes it a little easier to step back and treat it like anxiety rather than a real-time emergency.

It sounds like you’re noticing a real shift from treating every sensation as an urgent verdict to seeing how the worry itself can intensify what you feel, and there’s something steadying in being able to step back from that cycle. What feels most important to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I lost my temper again and I'm not proud of it. During a conversation about the pregnancy, his partner brought up another round of prenatal appointments and expenses, and he felt blindsided by how much was still left to plan. I don't know why it keeps happening.

It takes a lot of courage to look at this honestly, especially when you’re already feeling ashamed about it. If we map one of these moments together, we can look at the trigger, the early warning signs, your response, and what happened after—before the anger fully hit, what were the first signs in your body or behavior, like muscle tension, a racing heart, or wanting to snap?

Honestly, I’m not sure why we need to break it down like that—I already know I lost my temper. But if you want the early signs, I guess I got tight in my chest and started feeling trapped the second the money and appointments came up, like we were already behind and I couldn’t see a way out.

That makes sense—you already know the blow-up happened, and the tight chest and trapped feeling sound like the first real warning signs, which is often the moment change is still possible before it tips over. On a scale of 0 to 10, how intense was the anger when it peaked, and what did you actually do?
Probably an 8, maybe 9. I raised my voice, cut her off, and said something like we’re never going to get ahead if every week there’s another surprise—so yeah, not my finest moment.

Thanks for being that direct about it; that level of honesty is useful, even if it doesn’t feel good to say out loud. What happened next in the room with your partner, and then what happened inside you afterward—right away and over the next few hours or days?

She shut down pretty fast, which honestly just made me feel more irritated in the moment because it felt like now I was the bad guy and the whole conversation was over. Afterward I felt guilty, but mostly I was still spun up and replaying the bills in my head for hours, like I had to figure it all out immediately or something else would blow up.

It makes sense that her shutting down would crank up the irritation, and it also sounds like the guilt and the hours of replaying left you carrying it long after the argument ended. Looking at that tight chest and trapped feeling as the warning signs, what is one thing you could do differently at that exact moment, before the response, that might change the outcome?

I mean, in the moment it doesn’t feel like I’ve got some neat little pause button, but I guess I could say I need to stop talking before I make it worse. Maybe take a minute, walk into the other room, and not keep pushing when I feel that trapped feeling—though honestly that’s easier said than done.

That sounds pretty grounded, and I get the skepticism—when you’re at an 8 or 9, “just pause” can sound almost insulting. How realistic does that feel in the heat of the moment, and what would need to be in place to make it actually possible for you?

Honestly, at an 8 or 9 it’s not very realistic unless I catch it early, because once I’m there I’m already halfway into reacting. If it’s going to work, I’d need something concrete—like agreeing ahead of time that I can call a timeout without it turning into a bigger fight, and maybe having a specific place to go so I’m not just storming off.

That sounds practical, and it also shows you’re thinking in terms of what would actually hold up under pressure rather than some perfect theory. If you did have that timeout set up ahead of time, what would you want your partner to hear or understand in that moment so it feels like a reset rather than you abandoning the conversation?

I’d want her to hear that I’m not walking away from the issue, I’m trying not to say something worse. If I can say, “I need ten minutes and I will come back,” then maybe it feels less like I’m ditching her and more like I’m trying to keep it from blowing up. I guess I’d also want her to understand that when I get that trapped feeling, I’m not trying to be controlling—I’m usually just panicking about not being able to fix it fast enough.

That’s a really important distinction—you’re not trying to disappear, you’re trying to stop the panic from driving the conversation. When you say “I’m panicking about not being able to fix it fast enough,” what does that panic seem to be saying about you or the situation in that moment?

It’s basically saying I’m already failing, or at least falling behind, and if I don’t get ahead of it right now then we’re going to be buried. It makes everything feel urgent, like there’s no room to just talk things through, which is probably why I come off so sharp. I don’t love admitting that, but that’s what it feels like.

That sounds painful to carry around, and it makes sense that urgency would make your voice sharper if the message in your head is “we’re already behind.” When that thought shows up, what evidence is it using, and what evidence might it be ignoring?

I guess the evidence it grabs onto is the stack of bills, the appointments, and the fact that there’s always another thing we haven’t fully sorted yet. What it ignores is that we’re not actually in some disaster right now—we’re still paying things, still planning, still moving forward, even if it feels messy. I’m not saying the thought is totally wrong, but I can see it may be blowing the whole thing up into something bigger than it is.

That’s a pretty important shift—you’re seeing that the bills and unfinished planning are real, but the “we’re already failing” part may be the piece that’s amplifying the panic. If you had to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you’re seeing the situation?

I think what’s changed is I’m starting to see that the problem isn’t just the money or the appointments themselves—it’s the story I tell myself that if it’s not handled immediately, then everything is going off the rails. That probably makes me come in hot before we’ve even had a chance to talk it through. It doesn’t mean the situation isn’t stressful, but I can see now that I’m turning stress into panic pretty fast.

I’m hearing a real shift in how you’re making sense of that spike from stress into panic, and there’s something important in noticing that the alarm is getting louder because of the meaning your mind is attaching to it. As you leave today, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed about that first story your mind tells?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. A new family member was added to the household, and the client noticed that family routines, schedules, and attention from relatives changed during the adjustment period. I keep telling myself: "This is happening because I’m not doing enough. I should be able to keep everything stable, and if things feel harder now, it means I’m failing my family." and I've been feeling anxious, guilty, overwhelmed, discouraged.

That sounds really ծանր and painful, and it makes sense that those thoughts would leave you feeling anxious and guilty. In the CBT model, the same situation can lead to very different feelings depending on how it’s interpreted, so I’m curious what you noticed yourself doing when those thoughts and feelings showed up?

When those thoughts hit, I notice I start overcompensating. I try to take on more, check on everyone constantly, and make sure everything looks okay on the outside, even when I’m falling apart internally. I also pull back from people a little because I feel ashamed that I’m not handling this better, and then I end up replaying everything in my head, looking for what I did wrong. It’s like I’m stuck between trying to fix everything and feeling too overwhelmed to actually rest.

That sounds like a really exhausting push-pull, and it also shows how hard you’re trying to protect everyone while carrying a lot on your own. I’m noticing the thought seems to place a very large share of responsibility on you, which can be a form of personalization, and I wonder if someone else looking at the exact same situation might interpret what’s happening in a different way?

Yeah, I think someone else might see it as a normal family adjustment rather than proof that I’m failing. They might say that when a new family member enters the household, routines shifting and people’s attention changing is just part of the transition, not something one person can control completely. I can also imagine they’d see that I’m actually trying very hard and that my overcompensating is coming from care, not incompetence. But emotionally, it’s still hard for me to believe that when I’m in the middle of it, because it feels so personal.

That alternate interpretation sounds thoughtful and compassionate, especially the part about your overcompensating coming from care rather than incompetence. If you actually believed that version in the moment, what emotion do you think you would feel most strongly?

If I really believed that in the moment, I think the strongest emotion would be relief. It would feel like I could breathe a little more and stop treating every change as evidence that I’m failing. I think underneath that, there’d also be sadness, because I’d probably realize how much pressure I’ve been putting on myself. And maybe some hope too, because it would mean this situation is hard, but not hopeless or proof that I’m not enough.

That makes a lot of sense—relief, sadness, and hope sound very different from anxiety, guilt, and overwhelm, and it’s important that you can see that shift. With that feeling in the moment instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different?

If I felt relief instead of guilt and overwhelm, I think I would probably slow down and stop trying to monitor everything so intensely. I might be more willing to let some routines be messy for a while and trust that everyone is adjusting, not just me failing to hold things together. I also think I’d be less likely to withdraw, because I wouldn’t feel as ashamed, so I might actually reach out for support or be more honest about needing a break. Overall, I think I’d act with more patience toward myself and the family instead of constantly trying to fix what I’m afraid is wrong.

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re already describing a version of this situation that feels calmer, more compassionate, and less all-or-nothing. If you were to put that new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed?

What’s changed is that I can see this situation more as a shared family adjustment than as a personal failure on my part. I’m starting to recognize that the discomfort and disruption don’t automatically mean I’m not doing enough—they may just mean everyone is adapting to something new. I think I’m also seeing that my urge to control everything comes from care and fear, not from being incapable. Even though it still feels hard, this perspective makes it feel more possible to be kind to myself and let things be imperfect for a while.

It sounds like you’ve been able to meet this with a much less harsh lens, and that there’s real strength in noticing how care and fear have been driving some of the control rather than a lack of ability. As you leave today, what feels most important to carry forward from what you noticed about yourself?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of frustration lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds pretty frustrating, especially if it’s been building and you’re not sure where to put it. If we map it out together, what would you call the emotion as specifically as you can right now, and how intense is it from 0 to 100?

I mean, “frustrated” is probably the closest word, but honestly it feels more like being wound up and irritated by everything. If I had to put a number on it, maybe 80-ish, but I don’t know how much that matters.

That makes sense—“wound up and irritated by everything” sounds pretty intense, and an 80 tells us it’s not just a passing annoyance. Rather than the whole pattern, can you think of one specific moment when it spiked, like the exact situation or thought that set it off?

I guess, but I’m not sure one “specific moment” really explains it—it’s been kind of constant. The last spike was probably around the holiday stuff and all the pressure that comes with it, plus people asking me to be cheerful when I’m already tapped out.

Yeah, that makes sense—if it’s been constant, a single moment may not explain all of it, and holiday pressure plus having to “perform” cheerfulness sounds draining. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, the thing you told yourself right then, even if it was just a flash?

Honestly, I’m not sure there was some neat “automatic thought” like in a worksheet. It was more like, “Here we go again, I have to deal with this crap and keep it together,” and maybe, “No one actually gets how much is on me.”

That doesn’t sound neat at all—it sounds like a very real “I have to hold it together while carrying too much” moment, and I can see why that would hit hard. What did you do next in response to that feeling, both right away and anything you started avoiding?

I mostly just shut down and got through it, because what else am I supposed to do—make a scene at a holiday thing? After that I avoided talking to people much and put off a couple things I should’ve dealt with, which probably wasn’t great but it felt easier than dealing with everyone’s expectations.

That makes a lot of sense—you shut down to avoid making a scene, then pulled back from people and delayed a few things because it felt like the easier way to get through the pressure. What happened right away after you did that, and what did it seem to cost you over the next day or two?

Right away it felt like I could breathe a little, which is probably why I did it. But over the next day or two I just felt more behind, more annoyed, and honestly kind of guilty for letting it pile up. I’m not sure this is some deep insight, it just seems like the obvious fallout from trying to get through the holiday without losing my temper.

Yeah, that sounds pretty obvious in one sense, and also pretty important that the relief was immediate while the annoyance and guilt showed up later. When you look at that pattern, what does it suggest to you about what the shutdown is doing for you in the short term versus what it’s costing you afterward?

I guess in the short term it’s basically giving me a break — like I’m not having to deal with people or say the wrong thing. But afterward it just leaves me carrying the same stuff, plus I’m more behind and more annoyed with myself. So yeah, it helps me get through the moment, but it doesn’t really solve anything.

That’s a pretty clear read of it: the shutdown is buying you temporary relief, but it also seems to leave you with more weight and self-criticism afterward. If that’s the trade-off, what do you notice it’s protecting you from in the moment that feels so hard to face?

Mostly it’s protecting me from snapping at people or having to explain myself when I’m already maxed out. If I stay shut down, I don’t have to deal with the look on everyone’s face or the whole conversation about why I’m “off.” I guess it also keeps me from admitting how overwhelmed I actually am, which is annoying to even say out loud.

That sounds really important—and I get why admitting you’re overwhelmed feels annoying if you’ve been trying to keep it together. When you notice that shutting down keeps you from snapping or explaining yourself, what do you think it says about how much pressure you feel you’re under in those moments?

I guess it says I’m under more pressure than I want to admit, or than I think I should be under. It’s like if I don’t clamp down, I’m worried I’ll either say something I can’t take back or just fall apart in front of people. I don’t love saying it that way, but yeah, that’s probably what’s going on.

That sounds like a pretty honest read, even if it’s not one you like having to say out loud. When you picture “clamping down” to prevent saying something irreversible or falling apart, what does that tell you about what you believe would happen if you let even a little bit of it show?

It tells me I don’t really trust the margin much—like if I let even a little out, it could turn into more than I can control. I probably believe people would either overreact, get hurt, or think I’m not handling things well, which would make everything worse. Saying that out loud makes it sound a bit dramatic, but honestly that’s closer to what it feels like.

That doesn’t sound dramatic so much as like you’re trying to prevent a real chain reaction, and I can see why that would make you clamp down. When you picture people overreacting or seeing you as not handling it well, what do you imagine that would mean about you in their eyes?

I think it would mean I’m the guy who’s supposed to have it together but doesn’t, which is a hard thing to sit with. Maybe they’d see me as weaker or less reliable, and that’s embarrassing when you’ve got a family, a mortgage, all that stuff depending on you. I know that’s probably part of why I keep tightening up instead of saying how overwhelmed I am. I don’t like admitting it, but I think I’m afraid it would change how people look at me.

That makes a lot of sense—when reliability feels tied to being seen as “having it together,” even small cracks can feel risky. If you weren’t trying so hard to protect that image, what do you imagine people would actually notice about you?

They’d probably notice I’m worn out and carrying too much, not that I’m lazy or incapable. Maybe they’d see that I’m still showing up, just not with the same energy I wish I had. I think part of me assumes they’d judge me for that, but if I’m being honest, some of them might just see a guy who’s struggling and could use a little slack. That’s not easy to admit, but it feels closer to the truth than pretending I’m fine.

That sounds like a pretty real shift—from “if I’m not fine, people will judge me” to “some people may just see I’m worn out and carrying too much.” If you put that change into your own words, how would you summarize what’s different in the way you’re seeing this now?

I think I’ve been assuming that showing I’m overwhelmed would automatically make me look weak or unreliable, but that may not be the whole picture. More likely, I’m just worn down and trying to carry too much at once, and other people might see that if I let them. I’m still not comfortable with it, but I can see that clamping down all the time is probably making things harder, not better. So the difference now is I’m starting to think this isn’t about me failing—it’s about me being stretched thin and not really giving anyone a chance to know that.

It sounds like you’re beginning to see that what’s been happening may be less about a personal failing and more about the load you’ve been carrying and how tightly you’ve had to hold it together. As you leave here with that in mind, what might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I keep thinking that my divorce means I’ve failed, and everyone probably sees me as someone who couldn’t make it work. I’m worried I’ll never feel stable again, especially while I’m trying to keep up at work.

That sounds really painful, and I appreciate how openly you said it. Let’s slow this down together, not to dismiss what you’re feeling, but to see whether this thought holds up when we look at it carefully—would you be willing to stay with it for a moment?
…Yeah, I can stay with it for a minute. I’m not sure what I’ll say, but okay.
I hear that you’re willing to stay with it even though it feels a bit uncertain, and that makes sense given how heavy this is. Is someone else's opinion overly influencing my own?
…Yeah, maybe. I think I’m assuming people are judging me more than they actually are.

That’s an important observation, and it makes sense that your mind would fill in the blanks when you’re already under so much strain. What is the evidence for this thought, and what is the evidence against it?
…Evidence for it is that the divorce happened, and I do feel embarrassed. Evidence against it is that most people haven’t actually said anything negative to me.

That’s a very thoughtful way to look at it, and you’re noticing both the embarrassment and the fact that people haven’t actually been saying negative things. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what's true?
…Yeah, probably. It feels bigger in my head than it might actually be.

That sounds like a really important shift, and it takes honesty to notice when the thought feels harsher in your mind than in reality. When you look at it closely, in what ways does it seem overly critical toward you?
…It makes me feel like one mistake defines me, which seems pretty harsh. I guess I’m not sure it’s fair to myself.

That sounds like a really meaningful realization, and it makes sense that it feels harsh to see how much weight you’ve been giving this one event. In your own words, what new perspective are you starting to see here?

…I’m starting to see that the divorce is something that happened, but it doesn’t automatically mean I’m a failure as a person. I’m still embarrassed, but maybe I’ve been turning it into a bigger judgment about myself than it needs to be. It’s a little relieving to say that out loud.

That sounds like an important shift—there’s a little more space now between what happened and the story you’ve been carrying about what it means about you, and even saying it out loud seems to have eased something. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of helplessness and fear lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense that helplessness and fear would feel hard to sit with when so much is uncertain. If we map this together for a moment, what would you call the main emotion as specifically as you can—more like fear, helplessness, sadness, frustration, or something else—and how strong is it right now from 0 to 100?

I’m not sure putting a label on it is really the issue, but if you need one, it’s mostly fear mixed with helplessness. It’s probably around an 80 most of the time, maybe higher when I’m thinking about my family member.
That makes sense—if the feeling is hitting that hard, a label may matter less than what sets it off. What was one specific moment, situation, or thought when you noticed it spike most recently?

Honestly, I’m not sure picking apart one moment is going to solve much, but fine — it spiked yesterday when I got an update about my family member not doing well. The thought was basically, “This could get worse fast, and I can’t do anything about it,” which is probably why it hit so hard.

That makes sense, and I hear the skepticism too—when something already feels this overwhelming, it can seem like dissecting it won’t change the reality of it. When that update landed, what went through your mind right then, in that exact moment, even if it was just a flash of an automatic thought?

Honestly, the first thing that flashed through my mind was, “This is getting worse and I’m not going to be able to stop it.” And right behind that was, “I should be doing something, but I don’t know what, and that’s making me feel useless.”

That sounds like a brutal thought to have in the moment, and it makes sense that it would leave you feeling useless rather than calm. What did you do right away after that thought hit, and what, if anything, did you start avoiding?

I mostly just sat there and stared at my phone for a while, then I called one person to get more information, which didn’t really help much. After that I avoided thinking too hard about it and kept busy with small stuff, because honestly I don’t see how dwelling on it is supposed to be useful.

That sounds like a very understandable sequence: freezing, trying to get information, then shifting into avoiding and staying busy when it didn’t seem to help much. What were the consequences of that right away, and then over time—what happened to the fear, the helplessness, or the sense of being useless after you did that?

Right away it took the edge off a little because I was occupied, but not in a real way—it just pushed the fear to the background for a while. Over time it basically came back the same or worse, and the useless feeling stuck around, which is part of why I’m not convinced “staying busy” is much of a solution.

That’s a fair pushback, and it sounds like you’ve already noticed the tradeoff pretty clearly: it helps a little in the moment, but it doesn’t really change the fear and may leave you feeling more useless later. When you look at that pattern, what does it seem to say about what “staying busy” is doing for you—and what it isn’t doing?

I guess it’s doing the job of keeping me from spiraling completely in the moment, so I can function a little. But it’s not actually helping me face what’s happening or feel any more capable, and that’s the part that bothers me. If anything, it kind of lets me avoid the fear for a bit and then leaves me right back where I started.

That’s a pretty clear read on it, and I can hear why it bothers you if it only buys a little breathing room without changing the bigger fear. When you say it lets you avoid the fear for a bit, what do you notice that avoidance costs you afterward, even if it seems to help in the moment?

I think it costs me a sense of being present, first of all. I can get through the day, but I’m sort of half in it, and then later I feel guilty that I’ve been skirting around something important instead of dealing with it. I suppose it also keeps me from feeling like I have any real grip on the situation, which is exactly what I’m afraid of.

That sounds like a painful loop: it helps you function, but it also leaves you feeling less present, guilty, and even less in control. When you notice that guilt and the sense of not having any grip on things, what do you think you’re telling yourself about what it means to be “dealing with it”?

I think I’m telling myself that “dealing with it” means I should be able to do something concrete and effective, and if I can’t, then I’m failing somehow. Part of me knows that’s probably too hard on myself, but it’s still how it feels. I guess I’m also equating not worrying all the time with not caring enough, which is maybe not fair, but there it is.

That’s a really important observation, and it makes sense that the fear would hook into a “if I’m not fixing it, I’m failing” story. What would you say has shifted for you just now, in your own words, about what “dealing with it” or “caring enough” might actually mean?

I think I’m starting to see that dealing with it doesn’t necessarily mean solving it, because I may not actually have that power right now. Maybe caring enough looks more like staying informed, being available, and not disappearing into avoidance, even if I can’t fix the outcome. That’s a bit uncomfortable to admit, because it means accepting limits instead of fighting them. But it also feels a little more realistic than telling myself I should somehow stop this from happening.

I’m hearing a real shift in how you’re relating to this—there’s a steadier, more realistic way of staying connected to it now, even with the discomfort of not being able to control the outcome. What do you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that my recent sleep changes mean I’m not as sharp as I used to be, and I could have made mistakes that hurt my reputation at work before I retired. Then there's I keep thinking that if I had managed my career better, I’d be retiring with more accomplishments and fewer regrets. And I also keep thinking about: I’m afraid that poor sleep is making me less reliable, and if I ever need to consult, volunteer, or take on part-time work, I won’t be able to perform well enough.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind would keep circling when those worries feel so important. Sometimes it can help to sort worries into two kinds: ones that are productive because there’s something actionable to do, and ones that are unproductive because they’re hypothetical, uncontrollable, or about things that may never happen, and the two get handled differently. What is the first worry that is keeping you up?

The first one that really grabs me is the fear that my sleep changes mean I’m not as sharp as I used to be, and that I may have already made mistakes that affected my reputation at work before I retired. That worry feels very real to me because it connects to who I’ve always been — someone dependable and competent — so even a small lapse feels bigger than it maybe is. I keep replaying old decisions and conversations, wondering if there were things I missed or handled badly. It’s hard to let it go because part of me feels like I should be able to figure out whether this is a real problem or just anxiety talking.

That sounds really painful, especially because it touches your sense of competence and the image you’ve carried of yourself for so long. When you look at this worry closely, is there a concrete action you can take with it now, or does it seem more hypothetical and outside your control?

When I look at it honestly, I think it’s mostly hypothetical and outside my control now, at least in the sense that I can’t go back and inspect every decision I made. I could maybe ask someone I trust whether they ever noticed any real problems, but even that feels limited because I’m not sure it would settle the deeper fear. What I really want is certainty that I didn’t damage my reputation or miss something important, and I don’t think I can get that certainty now. So I’m left with the feeling that this worry keeps asking me to solve the unsolvable, which is part of why it keeps me up.

That makes a lot of sense, and I can hear how much you’re wanting certainty from something that can’t really offer it now. Would setting aside 10 minutes tomorrow at a specific time to think about this give your mind a place to put it for now, and what is the next worry on your mind?

Yes, I think setting aside a specific time tomorrow could help a little, because right now my mind just drags me into it at night when I’m most vulnerable to it. I’m willing to try giving it a container instead of letting it spill all over bedtime, though part of me worries I’ll still feel pulled back into it. The next worry that comes up is the one about retiring with fewer accomplishments and more regrets, like I didn’t manage my career as well as I should have. That one feels sadder than the first, because it’s not just fear of a mistake — it’s a kind of grief about what I can’t change now.

That sounds like a deeper kind of pain, and I can hear the grief in it because it’s tied to what you hoped your career would stand for. When you look at that regret now, does it seem like something you can still take any action on, or does it feel more like something outside your control?

It feels mostly outside my control now, in the sense that I can’t go back and rewrite the career I had or recover opportunities I may have missed. I can still think about how I want to use retirement, and maybe that matters, but it doesn’t change the fact that part of me is grieving what I wish had been different. When I sit with it honestly, it’s less about a specific action and more about accepting that I’m measuring my life against an ideal I can’t fully reach anymore. That’s hard to admit, because it brings up sadness and a little shame, but it also feels more truthful than pretending I can fix it.

conversations.content: What if my family member’s health keeps getting worse and I’m not ready for what comes next? I’m supposed to be enjoying retirement, but instead I feel like I’m waiting for bad news and there’s nothing I can do about it.

That sounds like a heavy place to be, and I appreciate how directly you said it. Let’s slow it down and look at it together, not to brush off how real this feels, but to see whether the thought holds up when we examine it carefully—what feels most true in that “nothing I can do” part?

I don’t know, it just feels like people always say “look at it differently” when they can’t actually fix anything. I can’t stop the illness, so “what I can do” sounds like a pretty thin consolation prize. Maybe I can help with appointments or be around, but that doesn’t change the part that scares me.

That makes sense; “look at it differently” can sound pretty empty when the illness itself can’t be fixed, and I hear that the fear is still very much there. How might others interpret the same situation differently?

I’m not sure that really matters much when the facts are still the facts. Maybe other people would call it “staying positive” or “focusing on what you can control,” but that can sound like a polite way of telling me not to feel what I’m feeling. I guess some people would see it as making the best of it, but that doesn’t exactly make the fear go away.

You’re making a fair point: when the facts feel grim, “stay positive” can sound like an instruction to ignore what’s real, and the fear doesn’t just switch off because someone says the right words. Given that, am I basing this thought on feelings rather than facts, and what specific facts point you in that direction?

Well, I mean, the fear is a feeling, obviously, but it’s not coming out of nowhere. The facts are that my family member is getting worse, and I don’t know what happens next—so it’s not exactly irrational to think the worst could happen. I guess what I’m saying is the feeling is based on real information, even if it may be louder than the facts deserve.

That sounds like a pretty grounded way to put it: the fear isn’t invented, and you’re noticing it may be louder than the situation itself. In all of this, is someone else’s opinion or reaction overly influencing your own?

Maybe, but I’m not sure whose opinion you mean. I’m mostly reacting to the actual situation, not borrowing anxiety from other people—though I suppose if everyone around me is acting worried, that doesn’t exactly help.

That sounds pretty reasonable—you’re not inventing anxiety out of nowhere, and it makes sense that other people’s worry could add to it even if you’re mainly reacting to the situation itself. When you ask whether your thought is overly critical, what part of it feels like a fair appraisal of the facts, and what part starts to sound harsher than it needs to be?

The fair part is that things really are uncertain and my family member really is getting worse—that’s not me being dramatic. The harsher part is probably when my mind jumps from “this is bad” to “it’s all going to fall apart and I won’t handle it,” but honestly, that jump feels pretty automatic, not like some neat little thought I can just swap out.

That automatic jump makes sense, especially when uncertainty has been hanging around for a while, and I’m glad you can separate the more factual part from the harsher one. Is my thought based more on habit or a past experience than what’s true now?

Yeah, probably some of both. I think my mind has gotten used to going straight to the worst-case scenario because that’s what it does when I feel helpless, and I’ve seen enough bad outcomes before to know it’s not completely irrational. But I can also admit that what’s true right now is uncertainty, not certainty that everything will collapse.

You’ve done a careful job separating what’s actually happening from where your mind tends to rush, and that’s not the same as pretending things are fine. If you were to rewrite that original thought so it stays honest about the uncertainty and the fear without tipping into the worst-case story, what would a fairer version sound like?

A fairer version might be: “My family member’s health is changing, and that’s scary because I don’t know what comes next.” It’s not that I’m fine or that this isn’t serious — it’s that I don’t actually know the outcome yet, even if my mind keeps acting like I do. I still hate the uncertainty, but that seems a little more honest than assuming the worst is already decided.

That sounds honest and carefully measured, especially the part about not pretending you’re fine while also not treating the worst as already settled. When your mind starts acting like the outcome is decided, what seems to happen to the fear in that moment?

It gets a lot bigger, pretty fast. Once my mind decides it already knows how this ends, I start feeling tense all the time, like I’m bracing for impact instead of just dealing with what’s actually in front of me. I suppose that’s part of the problem — the fear stops being about the situation and turns into this constant background alarm.

That constant background alarm sounds exhausting, and it makes sense that once your mind writes the ending, your body starts living as if it’s already happening. When you notice that shift from “this is uncertain” to “it’s already decided,” what do you see that alarm costing you in the moment?

It costs me sleep, mostly, and probably patience too. I get snappier with people and I stop enjoying anything that’s happening right in front of me because I’m half somewhere else already. I can see that’s not helping, even if I’m still not thrilled about being told to “manage” something that feels pretty unmanageable.

That sounds frustrating, and I hear the pushback about “manage” when it already feels unmanageable. If you look at the sleep, the snappiness, and missing the present, what does that pattern suggest about what the alarm is doing for you versus what it’s costing you?

I guess it suggests the alarm is trying to prepare me for the worst, but it’s doing it so early and so constantly that it’s wearing me down before anything has even happened. It may feel protective in the moment, but it’s costing me sleep, peace, and probably making me harder to be around. So maybe it isn’t actually helping me face this any better — it’s just keeping me stuck in it.

That’s a really clear shift, and you’ve put words to something important without me having to push it. If you were to sum up the new perspective you’ve reached in one or two sentences, how would you say it?

I think the new perspective is that this is genuinely scary and uncertain, but my mind keeps turning uncertainty into a finished catastrophe before I actually know that’s where this is headed. That alarm may be trying to protect me, but it’s also stealing sleep, patience, and whatever good moments are still available right now. So the problem isn’t that I’m being unrealistic about the seriousness of it; it’s that I’m treating the worst-case as if it’s already confirmed. I may not be able to control the illness, but I can at least try not to live as though the ending has already been written.

That’s a really grounded shift—you’re seeing both the seriousness of what’s happening and the way your mind has been leaping ahead as if uncertainty were already proof. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

I keep coming back to three things: I'm worried that after retirement and this divorce, I won't know what to do with my career skills anymore, and I'll feel like I wasted years of work. Then there's I'm worried that if I look for part-time work or consulting, I won't perform well enough and people will think I'm not capable anymore. ...The first one is about my career skills. I keep thinking I’ve spent all these years working, and now I don’t know what that means anymore.

...Yes, I can try that. And the last worry is that with the divorce, I won’t have the energy or confidence to keep up with people or new opportunities.

…It feels more hypothetical right now, too. I know I’m drained, but I can’t tell yet what I’ll actually be able to handle. I guess the divorce makes everything feel bigger and more uncertain than it used to.

That sounds like a really honest shift in how you’re seeing it now, especially with how much the divorce is amplifying everything. What would you say, in your own words, is the new perspective you’re noticing about these worries?

I think the new perspective is that these worries feel bigger because I’m already worn down from the divorce, not necessarily because they’re all true or permanent. I’m realizing I may not be able to judge my future career or energy level very clearly right now. It’s a little unsettling, but also somewhat relieving to think the uncertainty is part of the current stress.

conversations.content: I've been feeling a lot of loneliness lately and I'm not sure what to do with it.

That sounds really heavy, and I can see why you’d feel stuck with it. If we map this out together for just a moment, what would you call the feeling as specifically as you can right now, and where would you put its intensity from 0 to 100?
I mean, “lonely” seems obvious enough, doesn’t it? If you need a number, I’d say it’s around an 80, maybe higher some days, but I’m not sure putting a label on it really changes anything.

It makes sense that the label feels obvious, and I hear your point that naming it doesn’t magically fix anything. Could you think of one specific moment when that 80 showed up most strongly, and what was happening right then?

I guess it was last night when I got home and the apartment was just quiet, which is apparently supposed to be some deep therapeutic clue. My son’s room being empty still hits me hard, and then I just sit there thinking about how ridiculous it is that I’m expected to “process” that on command.

That empty apartment and your son’s room being gone sound like the sharpest part of this, and it makes sense that “processing” it on demand feels frustrating. When that happened, what went through your mind in that moment—what was the automatic thought, even if it was just a flash?

Honestly, my first thought was something like, “Well, this is my life now,” which sounds dramatic but that’s where my brain goes. And then immediately, “Great, now I’m supposed to sit here and dissect it for a worksheet or something,” because I’m not convinced naming the thought is actually useful.

That doesn’t sound dramatic to me; it sounds like a pretty immediate, painful reaction to what’s changed, and I get why the “worksheet” part feels irritating. When that thought hit, what did you do right away, and was there anything you started avoiding after that?

I mostly just sat there for a while and then turned on the TV so I wouldn’t have to hear how quiet it was, if that counts as a strategy. And I guess I’ve been avoiding my son’s room a bit, because apparently staring at an empty room is not especially uplifting, despite whatever insight that’s supposed to produce.

It sounds like turning on the TV and avoiding his room gave you a quick way to not hear the quiet, and I can understand why that would feel more manageable in the moment. What happened right away after you did that, and then what has it seemed to do over time to the loneliness or the way you’re relating to your son’s room?

Right away it mostly just kept me distracted, which I guess was the point, but it didn’t exactly make me feel better. Over time it’s probably made the room feel even more off-limits, which is annoying because now I’m aware I’m “avoiding” it like that’s some useful insight instead of just me not wanting to feel miserable.

It makes sense that you’d be annoyed if the “insight” just sounds like a fancy label for not wanting to feel worse, and I’m not trying to dress that up. When the room starts feeling off-limits, what do you notice you’re telling yourself it would mean about you if you did go in?

I guess part of me thinks going in there would mean I’m just sitting around being pathetic about it, like I should be handling this better by now. And maybe it would mean I’m admitting, more fully than I want to, that he’s really gone from the house day to day. I know that sounds a bit dramatic, but I can see that’s probably what I’m avoiding.

That doesn’t sound dramatic; it sounds like you’re noticing two pretty painful meanings there, and I can see why both would make the room hard to face. If you stayed with that thought that going in would mean you’re “pathetic” or that he’s really gone day to day, which part lands hardest for you, and what does it say about what you believe you’re supposed to be handling?

I think the harder part is the second one, honestly — that he’s really gone from the house in this day-to-day way, not just “away” in some temporary sense. And I suppose I believe I’m supposed to be handling it without making a big emotional spectacle out of it, which is probably why I keep acting like the room is some problem to avoid instead of something I’m actually sad about. I don’t love saying that, but… yeah, that seems closer to the truth.

That feels like a pretty honest and painful connection, and it makes sense you wouldn’t love saying it out loud. When you tell yourself you’re supposed to handle it quietly, what does that rule seem to be protecting you from, and what does it cost you?

I suppose it protects me from looking like I’m falling apart over something everyone expects me to deal with, which is probably not a very flattering way to put it. And it also keeps me from having to sit in the full force of it, because if I stay “busy” or numb enough, I don’t have to feel how empty the house is. But the cost is that I end up more isolated, and it probably makes the sadness last longer than it needs to.

That sounds like a pretty important shift—you’re seeing both the protection and the cost of staying busy or numb, without me needing to dress it up any further. How would you put this new perspective into your own words, from where you started to where you are now?

I started out thinking this was just me being lonely and annoyed at being told to “process” it, but I can see there’s more going on. I’ve been keeping busy and avoiding my son’s room because it lets me dodge how final his absence feels in the day-to-day, even though it also keeps me more isolated. So I guess the new perspective is that the loneliness isn’t just random—it’s tied to me not really letting myself face the change. That’s uncomfortable to admit, but it does seem more accurate than my original way of putting it.

It sounds like you moved from seeing this as just an irritating loneliness to noticing how the way you’ve been managing the change has been shaping how alone it feels, even if that realization is uncomfortable. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: My mind keeps racing and I can't sleep. I keep coming back to three things: If my spouse starts working again, I’m worried our routines will change so much that I won’t know how to balance my job, home responsibilities, and time together. Then there's If my spouse stops working, I keep imagining that our financial future will become unstable and I won’t know how we’ll manage long-term plans. And I also keep thinking about: I’m worried that whatever happens with my spouse’s work, I’ll end up feeling stuck in uncertainty about where our life is headed.

That sounds exhausting, and it makes sense your mind is looping when each possibility seems to carry a different kind of pressure. Some worries are productive, in that they point to something actionable you could actually work with, while others are unproductive because they’re hypothetical, uncontrollable, or may never happen, and the approach is different for each. Which is the first worry that’s keeping you up?

The first one is the one that keeps grabbing me most at night: if my spouse starts working again, I worry our routines will change so much that I won’t know how to balance everything. It feels very real and immediate because I can picture the schedule shifts, the added logistics, and me trying to keep up with both work and home. I think part of why it sticks is that I’m already stretched thin, so the idea of losing the current rhythm feels overwhelming. At the same time, I know some of this is me imagining worst-case versions before anything has actually happened.

That makes a lot of sense—when you’re already stretched thin, even imagining a routine shift can feel heavy and immediate. As you look at this worry, does it feel like something you can take a concrete action on, or does it seem more hypothetical and outside your control?

I think it’s a mix of both, but mostly it feels like something I can take concrete action on. Even though the exact schedule change hasn’t happened, I can already see areas where I’d need more structure, like talking with my spouse about responsibilities, figuring out what parts of the routine are non-negotiable, and planning for how we’d handle busy mornings or evenings. What makes it feel less hypothetical is that the stress isn’t really about whether change could happen—it’s about me feeling underprepared if it does. So I think the worry is pointing to something real that I can start thinking through, even if I can’t control the final outcome.

That sounds thoughtful and grounded—you’re noticing both the real pressure and the parts you can actually work with. What would be one small, concrete next step you could take, and exactly when would you do it?

One small next step I could take is to sit down with my spouse and sketch out what a “working again” routine might actually look like, instead of just carrying the vague fear around in my head. I’d want to do that this weekend, probably Sunday afternoon when things are quieter and we’re less rushed. I think it would help me feel less powerless to name the non-negotiables, like sleep, meals, and some protected time together, even if the details are still uncertain. Just having a conversation and putting a few possible plans on paper feels like a manageable first step.

That sounds like a very grounded way to approach the uncertainty, and it makes sense that naming a few anchors could help you feel less stuck. Looking at the second worry now, does it feel like something you can take a concrete action on, or does it seem more hypothetical and outside your control?

The second worry feels a lot more hypothetical and outside my control, even though it still feels emotionally real. I can think about budgets, savings, and long-term planning, but I can’t actually control whether my spouse works or not, so my mind starts spinning around “what if” scenarios that I can’t fully solve right now. I think that’s part of why it feels heavier in a different way: it pulls me into future uncertainty instead of something I can take a clear step on today. I can see that there may still be some practical pieces to discuss, but the core anxiety feels more like me trying to prepare for an outcome I can’t predict.

That makes a lot of sense—you’re noticing that the emotional pull is real even when the situation itself isn’t something you can control right now. Given that, would it help to set aside a specific time to think through the practical pieces, and if so, when might that be, or is there one more worry you want to look at first?

Yes, I think setting aside a specific time would help, because otherwise I just keep letting it spill into the night and it becomes endless. Maybe I could do it later this week, like Thursday evening, when I’m not already worn out, and just spend a limited amount of time looking at the budget and any likely scenarios. I also think it would help to talk about it with my spouse rather than trying to carry it alone, because part of the anxiety is that I’m imagining all the responsibility by myself. I’m okay looking at the third worry too, but I do think having a plan for this second one might make the bigger uncertainty feel a little less overwhelming.

That’s a meaningful shift—you’re noticing the worry feels less endless when it has a time boundary and when you don’t have to hold it all alone. As you look at what you’ve said so far, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about this second worry?

I think my new perspective is that this worry is still real, but it doesn’t need to take over my whole night to be taken seriously. I can’t control whether my spouse works or not, but I can choose to set aside a specific time to look at the practical side of it instead of letting my mind spiral constantly. It also feels important that I don’t have to carry the uncertainty alone—I can treat this as something for both of us to think through together. That makes it feel more manageable, even if I still don’t know the outcome.

It sounds like you found a way to hold the uncertainty with more steadiness—still respecting how real it is, while noticing you don’t have to let it run the whole evening or face it by yourself. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. The client and their spouse had a disagreement about household responsibilities after work, and the conversation ended with both of them going quiet. I keep telling myself: "I'm a terrible spouse and I always ruin things." and I've been feeling Shame, sadness, anxiety, and hopelessness.

That sounds really painful, and it makes sense that the silence afterward would intensify those feelings. In CBT, we often look at how the same situation can lead to very different feelings and actions depending on the meaning we give it, so I’m curious what you noticed yourself doing after the thought “I’m a terrible spouse and I always ruin things” showed up?

I shut down pretty quickly and started replaying the whole argument in my head, almost like I was trying to find the exact moment I ruined everything. I avoided going back to my spouse because I was scared I’d make it worse, but that also made me feel more distant and guilty. I also noticed I got really tense and distracted, like I couldn’t focus on anything else after that thought took hold. Part of me wanted to apologize immediately, but another part felt so ashamed that I just froze.

It makes a lot of sense that shame would pull you into replaying every detail and make it hard to move toward your spouse. The thought “I’m a terrible spouse” sounds like it may be doing some labeling of the whole you from one painful moment, so if someone else looked at the exact same situation, what might be another way they could interpret it?

I think someone else might say it was a hard conversation between two stressed people, not proof that I’m a bad spouse. They might see it as a disagreement about chores and timing, with both of us getting overwhelmed and going quiet because we didn’t know how to keep talking productively. If I were being kinder to myself, I’d probably say I had a rough moment, not that I ruined everything. Even saying that, I can feel how much I still want to turn it into something much bigger about my worth.

That’s a really thoughtful alternative, and it sounds like you can already see how much gentler and more balanced it is than “I ruined everything.” If you actually believed that this was a hard moment between two stressed people rather than a statement about your worth, what emotion do you think would show up most strongly?

I think the strongest emotion would probably be sadness, but it would feel less crushing than shame. I’d still feel upset that we had that disconnect, but it would seem more like something we need to work through together instead of evidence that I’m fundamentally failing. There might also be a little relief, because I wouldn’t be carrying the whole thing as proof that I’m broken. And honestly, I think under that sadness there might be some hope that this is repairable.

That feels like an important shift — sadness with some relief and hope sounds much less crushing than shame carrying the meaning that you’re broken. With that feeling instead of the original one, how might your behavior have been different in that moment?

If I had felt mostly sadness with some relief and hope, I think I would have been less likely to shut down completely. I might have been able to take a breath, stay present, and say something like, “I don’t want us to end like this, can we talk about it again?” instead of disappearing into my head. I also think I would have been more willing to apologize without it feeling like I was admitting I’m a bad person. It feels like that different emotion would have made room for repair instead of just self-punishment.

That’s a really clear shift, and you’ve described how the emotion changes what becomes possible for you in the moment. In your own words, what feels different now about the situation and about what it means for you?

What feels different now is that I can see the argument as a difficult moment instead of a verdict on who I am. It still hurts, but it doesn’t feel quite as final or catastrophic, and that gives me a little more room to breathe. What it means to me is shifting from “I’m a bad spouse” to “we had a hard interaction and I felt overwhelmed,” which feels much more accurate. I also feel more hopeful that this is something we can repair rather than something that defines my relationship.

conversations.content: I’m worried this little mortgage payment is going to turn into a bigger problem than I can handle now that I’m retired. If I slip up even once, I’m afraid it could snowball and I’ll end up losing my peace of mind.

That sounds like a very real worry, and I appreciate how clearly you’re naming it. Let’s slow it down together—not to brush past how it feels, but to look at whether this thought holds up when we examine it carefully; would you be willing to stay with it for a moment?

I guess we can look at it, but I’m not convinced “examining it” changes much if the payment still has to be made. I’m not trying to be difficult—I just don’t see how talking it through makes the bill any smaller. Still, if there’s a practical point to it, I’m willing to hear it.
That makes sense—you’re not looking for a pep talk, you’re looking for something that actually helps, and I can respect the skepticism. What is the evidence for this thought? Against it?

Well, the evidence for it is pretty simple: I’m on a fixed income now, and if one unexpected expense hits at the same time as this payment, things get tight fast. Against it, I guess I haven’t actually missed a payment yet, and I do have some savings, so it’s not like I’m already in trouble—but I still don’t see that as proof it’s safe, just proof I’m managing so far.

That’s a fair distinction—you’re saying “not in trouble yet” isn’t the same as “nothing to worry about,” and the fixed income piece makes the risk feel real. How might others interpret the same situation differently, maybe someone looking at the same numbers and pointing to specific signs you’re actually managing okay?

I suppose someone more optimistic would say the fact that I haven’t missed a payment and still have some savings means this is manageable, not a disaster waiting to happen. But honestly, that can sound like wishful thinking to me—people always say “you’re fine” right up until you’re not. I can see the point, though, if we’re talking about actual numbers instead of just reassurance.

That’s a useful distinction, and I hear why “you’re fine” would feel flimsy to you when the real concern is what could happen if things go sideways. Looking at the actual numbers, is this thought a likely scenario or just a possibility?

Honestly, I’d call it a possibility, but not a likely scenario based on what I know right now. I don’t love reducing it to “just worry less,” because the margin is still thinner than I’d like, but I also can’t honestly say the numbers show I’m on the brink of disaster.

That sounds like a pretty grounded read: you’re not dismissing the risk, but you’re also not inflating it into a disaster, and I can see why “just worry less” wouldn’t sit well with you. When you notice the worry getting louder, whose voice does it sound most like, and how much weight do you think that voice deserves?

Honestly, it sounds like my own voice, just the more cautious, irritated version of it—not some dramatic outside influence. As for how much weight it deserves, probably some, since it’s not making things up out of thin air, but I don’t think it deserves to be treated like a financial expert either.
That sounds like a pretty fair, skeptical read of it—you’re giving the worry some credibility without handing it the whole microphone. Could my thought be an exaggeration of what’s true?

Yeah, I think it could be. The risk is real, but when I’m tired or already annoyed, I probably turn it into “this is going to unravel everything,” which is more dramatic than the facts support. I’m not ready to call it harmless, but I can admit it may be bigger in my head than it is on paper.

That feels like a solid, fairer read of it—you’re not pretending there’s no risk, just noticing the leap from “tight” to “everything unravels” may be bigger than the facts warrant. If you were to rewrite the original thought so it fits the evidence on both sides without turning into forced positivity, what would it say?

Maybe something like: “This payment is a real responsibility, and it could get tight if an unexpected expense comes up, but I’m not currently in danger of missing it.” I still don’t love how much headroom I have, but that version sounds more accurate than assuming the whole thing is about to fall apart.

That sounds more accurate and less catastrophic, even if it still leaves you uncomfortable about the margin. What happens to your anxiety level when you say it that way, and what does that tell you about the difference between “tight” and “danger”?

It comes down a bit when I say it that way—not gone, but less sharp. “Tight” feels like something I can plan around, while “danger” feels like everything is already slipping, and that’s probably where I’ve been overreaching. I still don’t like the margin, but I can see those two things aren’t the same.

That’s a clear distinction, and I hear you noticing the shift without pretending the worry vanished. If you put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed in how you’re understanding the mortgage situation?

I think what’s changed is that I’m seeing the payment as a manageable strain rather than an immediate threat. It’s still a real concern, especially with retirement income being fixed, but I’m less convinced now that one tight month means the whole thing is going to spiral. I can admit I’ve been treating “possible” like “probable” in my head. That doesn’t make the worry disappear, but it does make it feel more like something to plan for than something to panic about.

You’ve moved from treating this as an automatic disaster to seeing it more as a real but workable strain, and that shift seems to have brought some space between the worry and the conclusion. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: I’m worried this change at work means I’m not going to keep up, and if I start struggling, it could put my job and my family’s stability at risk. I keep thinking I should be able to handle this better, but right now it feels like too much.

That sounds like a heavy thought to carry, and I can hear how much you’re trying to protect your family in this. It takes courage to say it out loud, and I’d like to slow it down with you—not to dismiss how real it feels, but to look at it carefully and see how much it holds up when we examine it together; would you be willing to stay with that thought for a moment?

Yeah, I can stay with it. When I really slow it down, I notice the fear is less about this one change and more about what it would mean if I couldn’t provide or keep things steady for my family. I also think I’m making it bigger in my mind because I feel like I’m supposed to already have it under control, so struggling feels like failure. At the same time, I can see there’s a difference between feeling overwhelmed right now and actually being unable to handle it, and I’m willing to look at that more closely.

That’s a really thoughtful step back, and it sounds like you’re already noticing both the fear underneath this and the way the “I should have it handled” rule is adding pressure. As you look at it from both sides, am I basing this thought on feelings rather than facts?

Yes, I think a lot of it is feelings right now. The fear is very real, but when I look at the facts, I don’t actually have evidence yet that I can’t handle the change or that I’m going to lose my job. What I do have is a lot of anxiety, a high standard for myself, and the tendency to jump to worst-case scenarios because my family matters so much to me. So I’d say the thought is partly based on facts, but it’s being driven much more by fear than by what’s actually happening right now.

That’s a very clear observation, and it sounds like you can already see the difference between what’s happening and what fear is predicting. Given that, could your thought be an exaggeration of what’s true, and what specific examples make you say that?

Yes, I think it probably is an exaggeration of what’s true. The biggest example is that I’m treating “feeling overwhelmed” like it automatically means “I’m failing,” when those aren’t the same thing at all. Another example is that I’m assuming this change will definitely go badly, even though I haven’t actually seen that happen yet and I’ve handled difficult stretches before. When I step back, I can see the fear is making the situation look more dangerous and final than it really is.

That’s a strong insight, and you’re noticing how fear can turn uncertainty into something that feels final. When you look at that thought closely, is it based more on habit or a past experience than what’s true now?

Yes, I think it’s mostly a habit, and probably tied to past experiences where I learned to equate struggling with falling behind. I’ve spent a long time being the person who keeps things together, so when something shakes that, my mind goes straight to, “This is a problem and I need to fix it immediately.” I can also see that I’ve had periods before where I felt overwhelmed at first, but once I settled in and got support or time to adjust, I was able to manage. So what’s true now is that I’m under pressure, but the intensity of the fear seems to be coming from an old pattern more than the actual situation in front of me.

That’s a really clear and grounded shift, and it sounds like you’re seeing both the old pattern and the present situation more separately now. In your own words, how would you summarize the new perspective you’ve reached about this work change and what it means for you?

I think my new perspective is that this work change is stressful and I may need time to adjust, but that doesn’t mean I’m failing or that I’m going to lose control of everything. I’m seeing that a lot of the intensity comes from an old habit of equating struggle with weakness, rather than from clear evidence that I can’t handle this. It feels more accurate to say I’m under pressure right now, not that I’m incapable. That shift makes me feel a little less trapped, because it reminds me this is something I can work through rather than proof that I’m not up to it.

It makes sense that noticing the difference between being under pressure and being incapable would bring some relief, especially given how much responsibility you’re carrying. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

I keep coming back to three things: I’m worried that since I stopped my usual activities, my body will get weaker and I’ll lose my strength and balance. …It feels more like it’s outside my control right now. I don’t really know what I can do about it.

…Yeah, I think I can put it there for tomorrow. And… yes, the last one is worrying my joints will get stiff and I’ll have more pain.

conversations.content: If I lose control, everything will spiral and I won’t be able to function at work or at home. I’m afraid I’ll completely fall apart, miss deadlines, forget basic things, and end up unable to make any decisions on my own.

That sounds really frightening, and it makes sense your mind is trying to protect you by scanning for danger. When worry gets loud, it can start treating what could happen as though it will happen; what are some concrete, observable clues you’ve noticed that suggest this worst-case outcome may not actually come true?

I guess one clue is that even when I’ve felt really overwhelmed before, I’ve still gotten through the day and handled the essentials. I may not feel great, but I haven’t actually stopped functioning or totally lost my judgment. Another thing is that I’ve had moments where I thought I was about to break down, and then I was able to slow myself down and get one task done at a time. So the feeling is intense, but the evidence so far doesn’t really show that I completely fall apart.

Those sound like real pieces of evidence, not wishful thinking, and it seems important that your experience has repeatedly shown some steadiness even when the feeling was intense. If those clues are accurate and the worst-case spiral doesn’t happen, what do you imagine is the most realistic outcome instead?

I think the most realistic outcome is that I’d still be struggling, but I wouldn’t completely collapse. I’d probably be more emotional, slower, and less efficient for a while, but I could still get through the basics and keep showing up. I might need to lower my expectations and ask for more support, which is hard for me, but not the same as losing all control. So instead of everything spiraling, it’s more like I’d be functioning imperfectly while grieving, which feels a lot more believable.

That sounds like a very grounded and believable shift in perspective, especially the way you’re distinguishing struggling from collapsing. If we stay with the harder possibility for a moment, what would you actually do step by step if you did start to feel yourself losing control, and what tells you whether you’d eventually be okay?

If I started to feel like I was losing control, I think the first thing I’d do is stop trying to push through everything at once and focus on the absolute basics: sit down, breathe, drink water, and figure out the next one or two things that actually need attention. Then I’d probably tell someone I trust that I’m overwhelmed, because I know I tend to isolate when I’m scared, and that usually makes it worse. What would tell me I’d eventually be okay is if I could see myself coming back to the present, even slowly, and still being able to do small tasks or make one decision at a time. I think “okay” wouldn’t mean feeling fine right away, but more that I’m still able to recover some stability instead of staying stuck in panic.

You just mapped out a path through the worst case, which suggests there is a way to move with the fear rather than be completely overtaken by it. How does the worry feel right now compared to when you first described it, and what feels different about it?

It feels a little less overwhelming now. When I first talked about it, the worry felt like this huge, all-consuming thing that meant disaster was basically inevitable, but now it feels more like something I can notice and respond to instead of just drown in. I think what’s different is that I can see there are actual steps I’d take if it got bad, and that makes it feel less mysterious and less powerful. I’m still scared, but it feels more manageable than it did before.

It makes sense that it still feels scary, and it also sounds like something important has shifted in how you’re viewing the worry. If you were to put this new perspective into your own words, what would you say has changed for you?

I think what’s changed is that I’m no longer treating the fear like it’s a prediction I have to believe completely. It still feels real and intense, but now I can see it more as a warning signal from my mind rather than proof that I’m going to fall apart. I also feel more confident that if things did get hard, I wouldn’t be helpless—I’d have some steps I could take and people I could reach out to. So the worry is still there, but it has less control over how I think about myself and what I’m capable of.

It sounds like you’ve been able to hold onto the fear without letting it define what it means about you, and there’s something really important in recognizing that intensity isn’t the same as truth. What might you want to carry forward from what you noticed today?

conversations.content: Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. The client received a letter saying he missed one mortgage payment and there is a late fee. He has a family and is worried about the loan. I keep telling myself: "I always mess up money matters. This is going to turn into a big problem, and I am probably going to keep failing at providing for my family." and I've been feeling anxious, ashamed, overwhelmed, discouraged.

That sounds really heavy, and it makes sense that a missed-payment letter would stir up shame and worry. In CBT, the situation itself is one part, but the thoughts we attach to it can shape how we feel and what we do next; when those thoughts showed up, what did you find yourself doing?
I… just kind of shut down and kept replaying it in my head. I didn’t do much, just sat there and worried.

That shutting down and replaying it sounds exhausting, and it makes sense you’d feel stuck after a letter like that. …Maybe they’d say it’s just one missed payment and not the whole picture. I don’t know, it still feels like I messed up.

That makes sense, and it sounds like part of you can see the difference between one missed payment and your whole situation, even if the “I messed up” feeling is still strong. If you actually believed it was just one missed payment and not the whole picture, how do you think you would feel—would it be less ashamed, less panicked, something else?
…Probably less panicked. Still embarrassed, but maybe not as hopeless.

…I probably would have called the mortgage company instead of just sitting there. Maybe I would’ve been able to think a little clearer.
